Worked purity example: 1.42 g of an impure sample of Na₂CO₃ is made up to 250.0 cm³; 25.0 cm³ aliquots need a mean titre of 24.80 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ HCl. Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂. Moles HCl = 0.100 × 24.80/1000 = 2.48 × 10⁻³; moles Na₂CO₃ in 25.0 cm³ = 1.24 × 10⁻³; in 250 cm³ = 1.24 × 10⁻² mol; mass Na₂CO₃ = 1.24 × 10⁻² × 106 = 1.31 g; purity = 1.31/1.42 × 100 = 92.6%. Method marks: balanced equation, ratio 2:1, scaling by 10, purity formula. Back titrations reverse the logic: react the excess with a standard solution and subtract — moles of analyte = moles added − moles of excess found by titration. The same mole-math underpins water of crystallisation and percentage-yield questions, so master the four-step chain once and reuse it. Redox titrations use a redox reaction instead of neutralisation. The classic: manganate(VII) titrations — acidified KMnO₄ in the burette oxidising Fe²⁺: MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5Fe²⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O + 5Fe³⁺ . MnO₄⁻ is self-indicating : purple in the burette, colourless while reacting, permanent pale pink at the endpoint (first excess drop). No separate indicator needed. The acid must be dilute H₂SO₄ — HCl would be oxidised by MnO₄⁻ (giving Cl₂ and a too-large titre), and HNO₃ is itself an oxidising agent (oxidising Fe²⁺ before the titration, giving a too-small titre). This 'why not HCl/HNO₃' question is standard. Worked example: 25.0 cm³ of Fe²⁺ solution needs 21.60 cm³ of 0.0200 mol dm⁻³ KMnO₄. Moles MnO₄⁻ = 0.0200 × 21.60/1000 = 4.32 × 10⁻⁴. Ratio 1:5 → moles Fe²⁺ = 2.16 × 10⁻³. [Fe²⁺] = 2.16 × 10⁻³ × 1000/25.0 = 0.0864 mol dm⁻³. Other redox titrations: iodine/thiosulfate (I₂ + 2S₂O₃²⁻ → 2I⁻ + S₄O₆²⁻) used to find oxidising agents by adding excess KI and titrating the liberated I₂ (starch indicator, blue-black → colourless near the endpoint); dichromate(VI) titrations of Fe²⁺ (Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6Fe²⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O + 6Fe³⁺, ratio 1:6, diphenylamine indicator). Determining formulae: the Fe²⁺ percentage in an iron tablet, or x in FeSO₄·xH₂O, follows from the titre plus mass data. Percentage uncertainty handling is identical to acid-base titrations; the MnO₄⁻ titre reading can be against the meniscus top (dark colour obscures the bottom) as long as you are consistent. A pH titration curve plots pH against volume of titrant. The equivalence point is the near-vertical section — the volume at which the reaction is exactly complete. Curve shapes: strong acid-strong base starts at pH ~1 and ends ~13 with a huge vertical section; weak acid-strong base starts higher (partial dissociation) and the vertical section sits above 7 (equivalence pH > 7 because the salt hydrolyses — CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O ⇌ CH₃COOH + OH⁻); strong acid-weak base has its vertical section below 7; weak-weak curves are shallow with no vertical section. Half-equivalence: at half the equivalence volume [HA] = [A⁻], so pH = pKa — used to find Ka experimentally. Indicator choice (from the equivalence-point rule): the indicator's colour-change range must lie entirely within the vertical section. Phenolphthalein (8.3-10.0) for weak acid-strong base; methyl orange (3.1-4.4) for strong acid-weak base; either for strong-strong. Buffer regions of the curve: before the equivalence point the weak acid/conjugate base pair formed in the flask acts as a buffer, so pH changes slowly — the flat section around half-equivalence. Buffers in analysis: a buffer solution maintains approximately constant pH when small quantities of acid or base are added — made from a weak acid plus its conjugate base (or weak base plus conjugate acid). Buffer action: added H⁺ reacts with A⁻ (A⁻ + H⁺ → HA, equilibrium shifts left); added OH⁻ reacts with HA (HA + OH⁻ → A⁻ + H₂O, shifts right). Buffer pH: [H⁺] = Ka × ([HA]/[A⁻]) , or pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]) . Blood buffering (H₂CO₃/HCO₃⁻) is the standard application question. Half-equivalence gives pKa directly, so a titration curve is an experimental route to Ka — a common 6-marker combining curves, indicators and Ka. Recrystallisation (required practical: purifying an organic solid): (1) dissolve the crude solid in the minimum volume of hot solvent (hot so it dissolves; minimum so it crystallises on cooling); (2) filter hot to remove insoluble impurities; (3) cool slowly to crystallise the product (pure crystals form first — impurities stay in solution); (4) filter under reduced pressure (Buchner funnel) and wash with cold solvent; (5) dry. The solvent choice: product dissolves hot, not cold; impurities dissolve cold. Yields: percentage yield = actual/theoretical × 100; losses occur at every transfer and filtration step. Thin layer chromatography (TLC) : a spot of sample on a silica (polar stationary phase) plate is placed in solvent (mobile phase); components separate as they travel different distances — less polar substances travel further (weaker adsorption to the stationary phase). Rf = distance moved by substance / distance moved by solvent front (always ≤ 1). Compare Rf values with known data or run pure standards alongside; a single spot indicates purity. UV light or iodine vapour locates colourless spots. Two spots = impurity or two components. Melting point purity test : pure substances melt sharply at a characteristic temperature; impurities lower and broaden the melting point range. A mixed melting point — mixing the prepared solid with a pure standard — confirms identity: unchanged sharp melting point means identical; depressed/broadened means different. Gas chromatography (GC) separates volatile mixtures; retention time identifies components and peak area gives relative amounts — used with MS (GC-MS) for definitive identification. Distillation separates liquids by boiling point (simple/fractional); washing and drying with anhydrous agents (CaCl₂) removes residual water from organic liquids. These techniques together answer the standard 'how would you check the purity of your product' question: melting point sharpness + TLC single spot + comparison of Rf/melting data with pure samples.
