topics.subject: physics
topics.searchText: physics Physics Mechanics: Motion, Forces and Energy Use the SUVAT equations for constant acceleration and derive them from the definitions of velocity and acceleration (AO1/AO2) - AQA 7408 3.4.1.3, OCR A H556 3.1, Edexcel 9PH0 Topic 2 Analyse projectile motion by resolving into independent horizontal and vertical components and derive the range formula (AO2/AO3) - AQA 7408 3.4.1.4 Apply Newton's three laws, calculate momentum and impulse, and use conservation of momentum in collisions and explosions (AO2) - AQA 7408 3.4.1.5-3.4.1.6, OCR A H556 3.5 Calculate work, energy and power, use conservation of energy, and solve moments and equilibrium problems for rigid bodies (AO2) - AQA 7408 3.4.1.2, OCR A H556 3.3 Determine g by free fall and evaluate measurement uncertainty in mechanics practicals (AO3) - AQA required practical 3, OCR PAG1, Edexcel CP1 SUVAT: v = u + at, s = ut + ½at^2, v^2 = u^2 + 2as, s = ½(u + v)t - only for constant a. Newton's 1st: equilibrium → net force zero; 2nd: F = ma = Δ(mv)/Δt; 3rd: action-reaction pairs equal, opposite, same type. Momentum p = mv; impulse J = FΔt = Δp; conservation: Σp_before = Σp_after for an isolated system. Work W = Fs cos θ; KE = ½mv^2; GPE = mgh; elastic PE = ½kx^2; power = W/t = Fv. Projectiles: horizontal velocity constant, vertical a = -g; range = u^2 sin 2θ/g, max height = u^2 sin^2 θ/(2g). Moments: M = F × d (perpendicular distance); equilibrium: ΣF = 0 and ΣM = 0; couple = two equal, opposite forces. Displacement (s) Distance in a stated direction from a fixed origin; a vector, measured in m. Acceleration Rate of change of velocity, a = Δv/Δt; a vector, measured in m/s^2. SUVAT equations The five constant-acceleration formulae v = u + at, s = ut + ½at^2, s = ½(u + v)t, v^2 = u^2 + 2as, s = vt - ½at^2; valid only when a is constant. Projectile A body moving under gravity alone: constant horizontal velocity, vertical acceleration -g, with the two motions independent. Momentum (p) p = mv; a vector in kg m/s. The conservation law: in an isolated system the total momentum is unchanged. Impulse (J) Impulse = force × time = FΔt = Δp (change in momentum); equals the area under a force-time graph. Work (W) W = Fs cos θ, the energy transferred when a force moves its point of application; measured in joules. Power (P) Rate of energy transfer, P = W/t = Fv; measured in watts (1 W = 1 J/s). Moment of a force Moment = force × perpendicular distance from the line of action to the pivot (M = Fd); measured in N m. Principle of moments For a body in equilibrium, the sum of clockwise moments about any point equals the sum of anticlockwise moments. Kinematics is the description of motion: displacement s, velocity v and acceleration a. On a displacement-time graph the gradient is velocity; on a velocity-time graph the gradient is acceleration and the area under the graph is displacement (AQA 7408 3.4.1.3; OCR A H556 3.1; Edexcel 9PH0 Topic 2; WJEC/Eduqas and CCEA AS mechanics). The five SUVAT equations connect s, u, v, a and t when acceleration is constant - and you should be able to derive them, not just quote them. Derivation 1: v = u + at. Acceleration is defined as a = (v - u)/t for uniform acceleration. Multiply both sides by t: at = v - u, so v = u + at . Derivation 2: s = ut + ½at^2. Displacement is the area under the v-t graph: a rectangle of height u and width t (area ut) plus a triangle of base t and height at (area ½ × t × at). So s = ut + ½at^2 . The same result follows by integrating: s = ∫v dt = ∫(u + at) dt = ut + ½at^2 with s(0) = 0. Derivation 3: s = ½(u + v)t. For a straight-line v-t graph the area is the mean velocity times time: s = ((u + v)/2)t. Derivation 4: v^2 = u^2 + 2as. Rearrange derivation 1 for t = (v - u)/a and substitute into derivation 2: s = u(v - u)/a + ½a(v - u)^2/a^2. Expand: s = (uv - u^2)/a + (v^2 - 2uv + u^2)/2a. Put over a common denominator: 2as = 2uv - 2u^2 + v^2 - 2uv + u^2 = v^2 - u^2, so v^2 = u^2 + 2as . Selection routine: list knowns, list the unknown, use the equation that omits the quantity you do not need. Choose a positive direction and keep signs consistent; convert km/h to m/s by dividing by 3.6. Free fall is the standard application: with u = 0 downward, s = ½gt^2. Required practical: g by free fall (AQA RP3, OCR PAG1, Edexcel CP1) Drop a ball bearing through a measured height s past a light gate (or use two gates, or a video with a metre rule in shot). Timing starts when the ball is released (u = 0) and stops when it breaks the gate, so human reaction time - roughly 0.2 s, a large systematic error in stopwatch methods - is eliminated. Rearrange s = ½gt^2 to g = 2s/t^2, or better, plot s against t^2: a straight line through the origin with gradient g/2 , so g = 2 × gradient. Using many heights and a best-fit line averages random error. Uncertainty in the gradient comes from the scatter and the resolution of the rule (±1 mm on a metre rule read to 1 mm gives about 0.1% per metre). Percentage difference from the accepted value 9.81 m/s^2 concludes the evaluation. A projectile moves under gravity alone, so the two components are independent (AQA 7408 3.4.1.4): horizontal velocity stays constant at u cos θ (no horizontal force), and vertical velocity starts at u sin θ with acceleration -g. Resolve first, then apply SUVAT to each component separately; the link between them is time. Derivation: range on level ground. At maximum height the vertical velocity is zero, so from v = u + at: 0 = u sin θ - gt_half, giving t_half = u sin θ/g. By symmetry the total flight time is T = 2u sin θ/g. The range is the constant horizontal velocity times the flight time: R = u cos θ × 2u sin θ/g. Since 2 sin θ cos θ = sin 2θ, R = u^2 sin 2θ/g . Maximum range on level ground occurs at θ = 45 degrees because sin 2θ peaks at 1 when 2θ = 90 degrees - a favourite one-mark question. Maximum height: using v^2 = u^2 + 2as vertically with v = 0: 0 = u^2 sin^2 θ - 2gh, so h = u^2 sin^2 θ/(2g). Trajectory shape: eliminating t between x = u cos θ × t and y = u sin θ × t - ½gt^2 gives y = x tan θ - gx^2/(2u^2 cos^2 θ) - a parabola (y is quadratic in x). The path is symmetric only when launch and landing are at the same height; with air resistance the path shortens and steepens after the peak. Worked example: components and range A ball is projected at 20 m/s at 30 degrees above the horizontal from level ground (g = 9.8 m/s^2). Line 1: u_x = 20 cos 30 = 17.3 m/s, u_y = 20 sin 30 = 10.0 m/s (M1: resolve into components). Line 2: Vertical, at max height v = 0: 0 = 10.0^2 - 2(9.8)h, so h = 100/19.6 = 5.10 m (M1 A1). Line 3: T = 2u_y/g = 2 × 10.0/9.8 = 2.04 s (A1: symmetry). Line 4: R = u_x T = 17.3 × 2.04 = 35.3 m (A1). Typical follow-ups: state the modelling assumptions (no air resistance so horizontal velocity constant; the ball is a particle; g uniform) and describe the effect of removing one - naming the assumption and its consequence earns the mark. Newton's first law: a body remains at rest or in uniform motion unless acted on by a resultant force - equilibrium means ΣF = 0. Second law: the resultant force equals the rate of change of momentum; for constant mass this reduces to F = ma. Third law: if A exerts a force on B, B exerts an equal and opposite force on A of the same type (AQA 7408 3.4.1.5; OCR A H556 3.5; Edexcel 9PH0 Topic 2). Derivation: F = ma from F = Δp/Δt. Momentum p = mv. If the mass is constant and velocity changes from u to v in time t: F = Δp/Δt = (mv - mu)/t = m(v - u)/t = ma. For changing mass (a rocket) or changing velocity you must use the full F = Δp/Δt form. Derivation: conservation of momentum from Newton's third law. Consider two bodies A and B interacting. By the third law, F_AB = -F_AB (action on B equals minus reaction on A), and they act for the same time Δt. Impulse on A: Δp_A = F_AB Δt; impulse on B: Δp_B = -F_AB Δt. Adding: Δp_A + Δp_B = 0, so the total momentum change is zero and Σp_before = Σp_after - momentum is conserved provided no external resultant force acts. Impulse: J = FΔt = Δp, measured in N s; it equals the area under a force-time graph. This is the physics of safety design: crumple zones and air bags increase the collision time Δt, so for a fixed Δp the force F = Δp/Δt is smaller. Collisions: momentum is always conserved, but kinetic energy only in elastic collisions. In an inelastic collision KE decreases (transferred to deformation, heat, sound); an explosion converts stored energy into KE so total KE increases while momentum stays zero overall. Worked example: coupling collision A 1200 kg car at 10 m/s hits a stationary 800 kg car and they couple together. Find the common speed and the KE lost. Line 1: 1200 × 10 + 800 × 0 = 2000v (M1: conservation of momentum). Line 2: v = 12000/2000 = 6.0 m/s (A1). Line 3: KE before = ½ × 1200 × 10^2 = 6.0 × 10^4 J; KE after = ½ × 2000 × 6^2 = 3.6 × 10^4 J (M1). Line 4: KE lost = 2.4 × 10^4 J to deformation and heat (A1: inelastic). Work is energy transferred by a force: W = Fs cos θ, where θ is the angle between force and displacement - only the component of force along the displacement does work (AQA 7408 3.4.1.1/3.4.1.1 energy; OCR A H556 3.3). Derivation: KE = ½mv^2. Work-energy theorem: the work done by the resultant force equals the gain in KE. From Newton's second law F = ma and the constant-acceleration equation v^2 = u^2 + 2as with u = 0: a = v^2/2s. So W = Fs = m(v^2/2s)s = ½mv^2. Starting from rest, the work done on the body is W = ½mv^2 , which is therefore the kinetic energy. Gravitational PE near Earth's surface is GPE = mgh (work done lifting mass m through height h against weight mg). Conservation of energy: in the absence of friction, ΣE is constant - falling converts GPE to KE: mgh = ½mv^2, giving v = √(2gh) independent of mass. With friction, the 'missing' mechanical energy equals work done against friction (heat). Power is the rate of energy transfer: P = W/t, and since W = Fs, P = Fv. A car at steady top speed has engine driving force equal to total resistance, and P = Fv sets the limit. Efficiency = useful output/total input (× 100%). Moments (AQA 7408 3.4.1.2): the moment of a force about a point is M = Fd, where d is the perpendicular distance from the line of action to the point. A couple is a pair of equal, opposite, parallel forces; its moment is one force × separation and it produces rotation only. Equilibrium of a rigid body requires both ΣF = 0 and ΣM = 0 about any point. The centre of mass is the point where the weight appears to act; for a uniform body it is at the geometric centre. Take moments about a support to eliminate its (unknown) reaction. Worked example: reactions on a beam A uniform 4.0 m beam of mass 20 kg rests on supports at 0.5 m and 3.0 m from its left end (g = 9.8 m/s^2). Line 1: Weight 196 N acts at the centre, 2.0 m from the left end (B1: uniform beam). Line 2: Moments about the left support (at 0.5 m): weight is 1.5 m to the right of it, right support is 2.5 m to the right of it: R_2 × 2.5 = 196 × 1.5 (M1: principle of moments). Line 3: R_2 = 294/2.5 = 117.6 N (A1). Line 4: Vertical equilibrium: R_1 + R_2 = 196, so R_1 = 78.4 N (M1 A1). Beyond the free-fall practical (AQA RP3, OCR PAG1, Edexcel CP1), mechanics practicals measure g with a simple pendulum (T = 2π√(L/g), so g = 4π^2L/T^2 from the gradient of T^2 against L - the pendulum belongs properly to oscillations but is a standard g method), terminal velocity with falling filters or ball bearings (weight equals drag at terminal velocity, so the graph of velocity against time plateaus), and force-extension work with springs (elastic PE = ½kx^2 = area under the F-x graph). Uncertainty rules (AQA 7408 3.1.2; Edexcel 9PH0 Topic 1; OCR Module 1): the uncertainty in a single reading is at least half the resolution (±0.5 mm on a mm rule); for repeated readings use half the range of the repeats. Combining: adding/subtracting quantities - add absolute uncertainties; multiplying/dividing - add percentage uncertainties; raising to a power n - multiply the percentage uncertainty by n. Percentage error against an accepted value: |experimental - accepted|/accepted × 100%. Worked example: uncertainty in g from s = ½gt^2 A ball falls s = 1.200 ± 0.002 m in t = 0.495 ± 0.005 s. Find g and its uncertainty. Line 1: g = 2s/t^2 = 2 × 1.200/0.495^2 = 9.80 m/s^2 (M1 A1). Line 2: Percentage uncertainty: s contributes 0.002/1.200 = 0.17%; t^2 contributes 2 × (0.005/0.495) = 2.0% (M1: power rule for t^2). Line 3: Total: 0.17% + 2.0% = 2.2%, so Δg = 0.022 × 9.80 = 0.22 m/s^2 (A1). Line 4: g = 9.8 ± 0.2 m/s^2 - the timing uncertainty dominates, so improving the timing (light gates, video analysis) is the evaluation point (A1: conclusion). Exam evaluation points for mechanics: reaction time (eliminate with light gates), parallax in length measurement (read at eye level, use a set square to mark heights), air resistance on falling objects (limits the accuracy of g), and repeating measurements to average random error. State which uncertainty is largest and how to reduce it - that comparison earns the top evaluation mark.

topics.name: Materials
topics.subject: physics
topics.searchText: physics Physics Materials Apply Hooke's law F = kx, combine springs in series and parallel, and calculate elastic strain energy E = ½kx^2 (AO1/AO2) - AQA 7408 3.4.2.1 Define and calculate stress, strain and the Young modulus, with correct units and prefixes (AO1/AO2) - AQA 7408 3.4.2.2, OCR A H556 3.4 Determine the Young modulus of a wire from a force-extension experiment and evaluate the uncertainty (AO3) - AQA required practical 4, OCR PAG2, Edexcel CP5 Interpret force-extension and stress-strain graphs: limit of proportionality, elastic limit, yield, ultimate tensile stress, breaking point (AO2) Compare material behaviour: brittle, ductile, tough, stiff, strong, and energy dissipated in plastic deformation (AO2) Hooke's law: F = kx up to the limit of proportionality; springs in series share 1/k_total = Σ1/k; parallel k_total = Σk. Elastic strain energy: E = ½kx^2 = ½Fx = area under the F-x graph (linear). Stress σ = F/A (Pa); strain ε = x/L; Young modulus E = σ/ε = FL/(Ax). Stress-strain graph: linear to the limit of proportionality, then elastic limit, yield point, UTS, breaking point. Brittle = breaks with no plastic deformation; ductile = deforms plastically before breaking (drawn into wires). Energy recovered on unloading = area under the unloading curve; the loop area between loading and unloading is energy dissipated (heat). Hooke's law The force needed to extend a spring is proportional to the extension, F = kx, up to the limit of proportionality. Spring constant (k) Force per unit extension, k = F/x, in N/m; the gradient of the linear part of a force-extension graph. Stress (σ) Force per unit cross-sectional area, σ = F/A, in Pa (N/m^2). Strain (ε) Fractional extension, ε = x/L, where L is the original length; dimensionless (often quoted as a percentage). Young modulus (E) The ratio of stress to strain, E = σ/ε = FL/(Ax), in Pa; a property of the material, not the sample's shape. Limit of proportionality The point beyond which force is no longer proportional to extension; Hooke's law stops applying. Elastic limit The maximum extension (or stress) from which the material still returns to its original length; beyond it deformation is plastic. Ultimate tensile stress (UTS) The maximum stress a material can withstand before it starts to neck and fail; the peak of the stress-strain graph. Brittle material A material that breaks with little or no plastic deformation - a straight stress-strain graph ending suddenly (glass, ceramics). Elastic strain energy Energy stored in a stretched material, E = ½kx^2 = ½Fx for a linear force-extension graph; equal to the area under the graph. Density is mass per unit volume, ρ = m/V in kg/m^3 (1 g/cm^3 = 1000 kg/m^3) - a property of the material, useful in identifying substances and in floating arguments (an object floats if its mean density is less than the fluid's). Hooke's law (AQA 7408 3.4.2.1; OCR A H556 3.4; Edexcel 9PH0 Topic 4): up to the limit of proportionality the extension x of a spring is proportional to the applied force, F = kx , where k is the spring constant in N/m. This is an empirical law - it describes a region of behaviour, not a universal truth, so always state 'up to the limit of proportionality'. Springs in parallel share the load, so k_total = k_1 + k_2; springs in series each carry the full force and their extensions add, so 1/k_total = 1/k_1 + 1/k_2 (the same structure as capacitors in series and resistors in parallel - remember by which quantity adds). Elastic strain energy is the energy stored in a stretched material. Derivation: the force starts at 0 and rises linearly to F while the extension grows to x, so the average force during stretching is F/2. Work done = average force × distance = (F/2)x, so E = ½Fx = ½kx^2 (substituting F = kx). Geometrically, it is the area under the force-extension graph. When the force is removed, this energy is recovered - provided the material is within its elastic limit. Worked example: springs in series and energy stored Two springs with k = 200 N/m and k = 300 N/m are connected in series and support a 10 N load. Line 1: Series: 1/k_total = 1/200 + 1/300 = 0.005 + 0.00333 = 0.00833 (M1). Line 2: k_total = 120 N/m (A1). Line 3: Total extension x = F/k_total = 10/120 = 0.083 m (A1). Line 4: Energy stored = ½Fx = ½ × 10 × 0.083 = 0.42 J (A1: ½Fx form used directly). Check: energy is also ½kx^2 per spring summed - ½ × 200 × 0.05^2 + ½ × 300 × 0.033^2 ≈ 0.25 + 0.17 = 0.42 J - the series extensions are x_1 = 10/200 = 0.05 m and x_2 = 10/300 = 0.033 m, agreeing. Force-extension data describes a particular sample; to compare materials , normalise it (AQA 7408 3.4.2.2; OCR A H556 3.4). Stress σ = F/A (force divided by cross-sectional area, in Pa or N/m^2) spreads out the effect of different thicknesses. Strain ε = x/L (extension divided by original length, dimensionless) spreads out the effect of different lengths. The Young modulus is the gradient of the linear (Hookean) region of the stress-strain graph: E = σ/ε = (F/A)/(x/L) = FL/(Ax) in pascals, typically GPa for metals (steel ≈ 200 GPa, copper ≈ 120 GPa, rubber ≈ 0.01-0.1 GPa). It is a property of the material only - a thin long wire and a thick short rod of the same steel have the same Young modulus but very different spring constants. Units discipline: convert diameters to radii carefully (A = πr^2 = πd^2/4), watch M (mega) vs m (milli) prefixes, and quote strain as a fraction unless told otherwise. Worked example: Young modulus of a wire A wire of length 2.50 m and diameter 0.40 mm extends 2.0 mm under a load of 50 N. Line 1: A = πd^2/4 = π × (0.40 × 10^-3)^2/4 = 1.26 × 10^-7 m^2 (M1: area from diameter). Line 2: Stress = F/A = 50/1.26 × 10^-7 = 4.0 × 10^8 Pa (A1). Line 3: Strain = x/L = 2.0 × 10^-3/2.50 = 8.0 × 10^-4 (A1). Line 4: E = stress/strain = 4.0 × 10^8/8.0 × 10^-4 = 5.0 × 10^11 Pa (A1). Note: this is higher than steel - realistic wires give about 2 × 10^11 Pa, so always check magnitudes. Why stress and strain rather than force and extension? Because the comparison of materials is the point - the Young modulus lets an engineer predict the extension of any sample of the material: x = FL/(AE). The stress-strain graph is the examinable picture (AQA 7408 3.4.2.2). Described in words: starting at the origin the graph is a straight line through it - Hooke's law region, where the gradient is the Young modulus and the material behaves elastically. The limit of proportionality is where the line begins to curve (hard to pin down precisely); the elastic limit follows - beyond this point the material no longer returns to its original length when unloaded. For a ductile metal the graph then rises through a yield point (strain increases with little extra stress - large plastic deformation), reaching a maximum at the ultimate tensile stress (UTS) , after which necking occurs: the sample thins at one point, the force (and engineering stress) falls, and the curve ends at the breaking point / fracture stress . Material adjectives - know the precise meanings: strong = high breaking stress; stiff = high Young modulus (steep gradient); brittle = breaks with little or no plastic deformation (straight graph ending abruptly - glass, concrete, ceramics); ductile = undergoes large plastic deformation before breaking, so can be drawn into wires (copper); malleable = deforms plastically under compression (hammered into sheets); hard = resists indentation/scratching; tough = absorbs a lot of energy before fracture (large area under the graph) - the opposite of brittle. Energy interpretation: the area under a stress-strain graph is energy per unit volume (units J/m^3); the area under a force-extension graph is energy (J). On unloading within the elastic limit, the unloading curve retraces the loading curve and all energy is recovered. Beyond the elastic limit the unloading line is parallel to the initial linear section but does not pass through the origin - it intercepts the x-axis at the permanent (plastic) extension. The area of the hysteresis loop between the loading and unloading curves is the energy dissipated as heat per cycle - this is why a repeatedly stretched rubber band warms up. Worked example: loading and unloading a wire A wire is stretched beyond its elastic limit to a force of 60 N (extension 4.0 mm), then unloaded. On reaching zero force the permanent extension is 1.0 mm. The initial linear gradient was 2.0 × 10^4 N/m. Line 1: The unloading line is parallel to the loading line, gradient 2.0 × 10^4 N/m (B1). Line 2: It passes through (4.0 mm, 60 N) and drops 60 N at gradient 2.0 × 10^4 N/m: extension change = 60/2.0 × 10^4 = 3.0 mm (M1). Line 3: Final extension = 4.0 - 3.0 = 1.0 mm - the permanent set (A1). Line 4: Energy dissipated = area of the loop = area under loading minus area under unloading: ½ × 60 × 4.0 × 10^-3 - ½ × 60 × 3.0 × 10^-3 = 0.12 - 0.09 = 0.03 J (A1). The set-up (AQA required practical 4; OCR PAG2 materials; Edexcel CP5): a long thin wire (typically ~2 m of steel or copper, diameter measured with a micrometer) is clamped at one end over a pulley (or clamped to a bench edge) and loaded with masses. A sticky-tape marker on the wire moves past a fixed millimetre rule as weights are added. Measure the original length L from the clamp point to the marker with a tape measure; the diameter with a micrometer screw gauge at several points and orientations (the wire may not be uniform or circular) and average; add masses in equal increments, recording the marker reading each time (load and unload to check for the elastic limit and zero error). Analysis: plot a graph of load against extension (or stress against strain); the Young modulus is the gradient of the linear region times the geometry factor - for a force-extension graph, E = gradient × L/A. Using the gradient rather than a single data pair averages random error. Plot force against extension and compute E from the gradient to avoid dividing small differences. Uncertainty and evaluation - the marks live here: the wire diameter is small (≈0.2-0.4 mm), so its uncertainty dominates. A micrometer resolution of 0.01 mm on a 0.30 mm diameter gives 3.3% uncertainty, and since E depends on A = πd^2/4, the diameter uncertainty doubles to about 7% in E (power rule). Reduce it by measuring the diameter at many points and averaging. Extensions are small (a few mm on a mm rule: ±0.5 mm resolution) - use a longer wire, larger loads (staying elastic), or a vernier scale/Searle's apparatus to improve resolution. Other error sources: kinks in the wire (straighten before measuring L), the marker slipping (use a fine wax pencil line), thermal expansion, and masses below the elastic limit assumption (verify by unloading to check the wire returns to its original length). Quote the final result as E ± ΔE and give the percentage difference from the accepted value for the material. Worked example: percentage uncertainty in E L = 2.00 ± 0.01 m (0.5%), d = 0.30 ± 0.01 mm (3.3%), extension at 50 N = 1.8 ± 0.5 mm (28%), F = 50 ± 0.5% (balance resolution). Line 1: E = FL/(Ax); A ∝ d^2, so percentage uncertainty = ΔF/F + ΔL/L + 2Δd/d + Δx/x (M1: power rule on d). Line 2: = 0.5 + 0.5 + 6.6 + 28 = 35.6% ≈ 36% (A1). Line 3: The extension term dominates: increase the load (staying elastic) or use a more sensitive extension measurement - a Searle's apparatus with a vernier - to cut it (A1: evaluation).

topics.name: Waves and Optics
topics.subject: physics
topics.searchText: physics Physics Waves and Optics Describe progressive waves: amplitude, wavelength, frequency, period, phase and phase difference; use v = fλ (AO1/AO2) - AQA 7408 3.3.1, OCR A H556 4.3.1 Explain superposition, coherence, path difference and interference, and derive the Young fringe spacing w = λD/s (AO2/AO3) - AQA 7408 3.3.3/3.3.5 Analyse stationary (standing) waves on strings and in tubes: nodes, antinodes and harmonics (AO2) - AQA 7408 3.3.4, OCR A H556 4.3.3 Explain diffraction and use the diffraction grating equation d sin θ = nλ (AO2) - AQA 7408 3.3.6 Apply Snell's law, derive the critical angle, and explain total internal reflection and optical fibres (AO2) - AQA 7408 3.3.7 Explain polarisation and Malus's law, and why only transverse waves polarise (AO2) - AQA 7408 3.3.2 Wave equation: v = fλ; phase difference Δφ = 2πΔx/λ. Superposition: resultant = vector sum; constructive when path difference = nλ, destructive when (n + ½)λ (coherent, in-phase sources). Standing waves: nodes (zero amplitude) and antinodes fixed in position; adjacent nodes λ/2 apart; harmonics on a string fixed at both ends: f_n = n f_1 with f_1 = v/2L. Double slit: fringe spacing w = λD/s; grating: d sin θ = nλ; single slit: first minimum at a sin θ = λ. Polarisation: only transverse waves; Malus's law I = I_0 cos^2 θ. Refraction: n = c/v; Snell: n_1 sin θ_1 = n_2 sin θ_2; TIR when n_1 > n_2 and θ > θ_c = arcsin(n_2/n_1). Amplitude The maximum displacement from equilibrium; sets the intensity (I ∝ amplitude^2). Phase difference The fraction of a cycle by which two points (or waves) are out of step: Δφ = 2πΔx/λ for points separated by Δx on a wave, in radians or degrees. Coherence Two sources with a constant phase difference and the same frequency/wavelength - the requirement for a stable observable interference pattern. Superposition When two waves meet, the resultant displacement is the vector sum of the individual displacements. Node and antinode Node: point of zero amplitude on a stationary wave (destructive superposition). Antinode: point of maximum amplitude. Adjacent nodes are λ/2 apart. Path difference The difference in distance travelled from two sources to a point: nλ gives constructive interference, (n + ½)λ gives destructive (in-phase sources). Refractive index n = c/v, the ratio of the speed of light in vacuum to its speed in the medium; also n = sin i/sin r across a boundary. Critical angle The angle of incidence inside a denser medium at which the refracted ray travels along the boundary; sin θ_c = n_2/n_1 for n_1 > n_2. Total internal reflection (TIR) Complete reflection at a boundary when light travels from a denser to a less dense medium at an incidence angle above the critical angle. Polarisation Confinement of wave oscillations to one plane; only transverse waves can be polarised (evidence that light is transverse). A progressive wave transfers energy without transferring matter (AQA 7408 3.3.1; OCR A H556 4.3.1; Edexcel 9PH0 Topic 5). Key quantities: amplitude A (maximum displacement - sets intensity, I ∝ A^2), wavelength λ, frequency f, period T = 1/f, and the wave speed v = fλ. Transverse waves oscillate perpendicular to the direction of travel (all EM waves, waves on strings); longitudinal waves oscillate parallel (sound: compressions and rarefactions). EM waves travel at c = 3.00 × 10^8 m/s in vacuum and slower v = c/n in media. Phase difference derivation: a point on a wave one full wavelength further along has completed exactly one extra cycle, i.e. a phase difference of 2π radians. Points separated by Δx have phase difference Δφ = 2πΔx/λ. So points λ/2 apart are in antiphase (Δφ = π), and points λ apart are in phase. In time, a point completes 2π radians in one period, so Δφ = 2πΔt/T for a time lag Δt. Displacement of a point: y = A sin(2πft) for a wave starting at zero displacement - be able to sketch and read displacement-time and displacement-position graphs and convert between them. Polarisation (AQA 7408 3.3.2): only transverse waves can be plane-polarised because their oscillations occur in a choice of perpendicular directions; longitudinal waves oscillate along one line only, so there is nothing to filter - the standard proof that light is transverse. Two polarising filters at 90 degrees give extinction (crossed polaroids); at angle θ, Malus's law I = I_0 cos^2 θ gives the transmitted intensity. Applications: polaroid sunglasses cut glare reflected off horizontal surfaces (partially polarised light), and stress analysis in plastics. Worked example: phase difference A wave of frequency 50 Hz travels at 25 m/s. Find the phase difference between two points 0.25 m apart. Line 1: λ = v/f = 25/50 = 0.50 m (M1 A1). Line 2: Δφ = 2πΔx/λ = 2π × 0.25/0.50 = π radians = 180 degrees (M1 A1) - the points are in antiphase. Principle of superposition: when two or more waves meet at a point, the resultant displacement is the (vector) sum of the individual displacements (AQA 7408 3.3.3). Constructive interference occurs when waves arrive in phase (path difference nλ); destructive when in antiphase (path difference (n + ½)λ) - for coherent sources. Coherence - constant phase difference and equal frequency - is the condition for a stable pattern; two separate lamps are not coherent, which is why Young used a single source split in two. Standing (stationary) waves (AQA 7408 3.3.4; OCR A H556 4.3.3): form when two identical progressive waves travelling in opposite directions superpose - typically a wave and its reflection. The pattern has fixed nodes (zero amplitude, destructive superposition) and antinodes (maximum amplitude) with adjacent nodes λ/2 apart; energy is not transferred along the wave, it is stored between nodes. On a string fixed at both ends, both ends must be nodes. Harmonics derivation (string length L): the first harmonic (fundamental) fits half a wavelength between the two end nodes: λ_1 = 2L, so f_1 = v/2L where v = √(T/μ) is the wave speed on the string under tension T with mass per unit length μ. The second harmonic has an extra node at the centre: λ_2 = L, f_2 = 2f_1; in general the nth harmonic has n antinodes (n - 1 internal nodes), λ_n = 2L/n and f_n = n f_1 - a whole-number (harmonic) series. Same logic for tubes: closed at one end, only odd harmonics fit (λ = 4L, 4L/3, 4L/5...); open at both ends, all harmonics (like the string). Required practical: stationary waves on a string (AQA RP1, OCR PAG4-style, Edexcel CP-style) A string is stretched over a pulley with masses (setting the tension) and driven by a vibration generator at the far end. Adjust the frequency until clear loops appear: the driver end and pulley are (near-)nodes. Measure the length L of n loops - each loop is half a wavelength, so λ = 2L/n. Plot f against 1/λ: gradient = v, the wave speed on the string. Then v = √(T/μ) lets you verify the effect of tension (doubling T multiplies v by √2) or of the string's mass per unit length. Errors: judging the exact frequencies of resonance (amplitude changes continuously - use the frequency giving maximum amplitude at fixed driving amplitude), the end near the driver is not a perfect node (antinode correction), and parallax in measuring L. Uncertainty in f comes from the signal generator display resolution. Two-source interference (AQA 7408 3.3.5; Edexcel 9PH0 Topic 5): Young's double slits split one laser (or a lamp with a colour filter and single slit) into two coherent sources. Where the path difference is nλ, waves arrive in phase - a bright fringe; where it is (n + ½)λ - a dark fringe. The result is equally spaced alternating fringes. Fringe spacing derivation (w = λD/s): for slits separated by s and a screen at distance D, the nth bright fringe occurs where the path difference equals nλ. For D much larger than s, the geometry gives path difference ≈ s sin θ ≈ s tan θ ≈ sx/D for small angles (the small-angle approximation sin θ ≈ tan θ ≈ θ is the key step). Setting the path difference to nλ: sx_n/D = nλ, so the nth bright fringe sits at x_n = nλD/s from the centre. Fringe spacing w = x_(n+1) - x_n = λD/s . Hence: longer wavelength (red fringes wider than blue), larger screen distance, and closer slits all widen the pattern - and measuring w across many fringes (say 10, then divide by 10) reduces percentage uncertainty. Measuring λ this way (AQA required practical 2; Edexcel CP8): measure s with a vernier/travelling microscope (the dominant uncertainty), D with a tape, w across as many fringes as possible. Percentage uncertainty in λ = Δw/w + Δs/s + ΔD/D. White light gives a white central fringe with coloured edges - each wavelength produces its own spacing, overlapping away from the centre. Worked example: fringe spacing Light of wavelength 500 nm passes through double slits 0.20 mm apart. Fringes are observed on a screen 2.5 m away. Line 1: w = λD/s (M1: equation, coherent symbols). Line 2: w = (500 × 10^-9 × 2.5)/(0.20 × 10^-3) = 6.25 × 10^-3 m = 6.25 mm (A1: unit conversion). Line 3: Across 10 fringes the spacing would be 62.5 mm, measurable to better than 1% with a mm rule - the practical evaluation point (A1). Diffraction is the spreading of waves through gaps or around obstacles - significant when the gap width is comparable to λ (AQA 7408 3.3.6). A single slit of width a gives a central bright maximum twice as wide as the side maxima, with the first minimum at a sin θ = λ (one full wavelength of path difference across the slit cancels in pairs - Huygens construction in words: every point across the slit acts as a source, and pairs of sources λ/2 apart cancel in the direction where their path difference is λ/2). Narrower slit → wider pattern; longer wavelength → wider pattern. Diffraction grating : many equally spaced slits (spacing d = 1/N for N lines per metre) give sharp, bright maxima because many beams reinforce only at exact angles. The condition for the nth order maximum: d sin θ = nλ . The number of visible orders is the largest n with sin θ = nλ/d ≤ 1 - integer division of d/λ, and the 90-degree case (sin θ = 1) is not observable. Gratings resolve spectra (monochromatic light: one line per order; white light: a spectrum in each order with red at larger angles because λ is larger). Applications and standard questions: atomic spectra analysis, CD/DVD surface structure, X-ray crystallography (Bragg condition). For the grating experiment measure the angle θ to each order with a spectrometer and plot sin θ against n - a straight line of gradient λ/d - to average random error and check for systematic zero error. Worked example: second-order maximum Light of wavelength 640 nm is incident normally on a grating with 500 lines per mm. Find the angle of the second-order maximum and the number of visible orders. Line 1: d = 1/500 mm = 2.0 × 10^-6 m (M1: slit spacing from lines per mm). Line 2: d sin θ = nλ, so sin θ = (2 × 640 × 10^-9)/2.0 × 10^-6 = 0.64 (M1 A1). Line 3: θ = arcsin(0.64) = 39.8 degrees (A1). Line 4: Maximum order: n ≤ d/λ = 2.0 × 10^-6/6.40 × 10^-7 = 3.1, so n = 3 (integer part) (A1). Refraction is the change of direction when a wave crosses a boundary between media at an angle, caused by the change of speed (AQA 7408 3.3.7; OCR A H556 4.3). The refractive index of a medium is n = c/v (speed in vacuum over speed in the medium; n ≥ 1, air ≈ 1.00, water ≈ 1.33, glass ≈ 1.5). Across a boundary, Snell's law: n_1 sin θ_1 = n_2 sin θ_2 , with angles measured from the normal. Derivation from wavefronts: wavefronts must be continuous across the boundary, so the frequency is unchanged and the wavelength changes (λ = v/f = c/(nf)) - the wavefront geometry (shared hypotenuse) gives sin θ_1/sin θ_2 = v_1/v_2 = n_2/n_1. Total internal reflection (TIR) requires two conditions: travel from a denser to a less dense medium (n_1 > n_2) and incidence above the critical angle . Derivation: at the critical angle the refracted ray travels along the boundary (θ_2 = 90 degrees). Snell's law: n_1 sin θ_c = n_2 sin 90 = n_2, so sin θ_c = n_2/n_1 . For glass-air (n = 1.5): θ_c = arcsin(1/1.5) = 41.8 degrees. Below θ_c, partial reflection plus refraction; above, complete reflection - TIR is how optical fibres and prisms (periscopes, binoculars) work. Optical fibres: a high-refractive-index core surrounded by lower-index cladding keeps light in the core by TIR. Signal degradation: modal dispersion (rays at different angles take different path lengths, spreading pulses - fixed by single-mode/monomode fibres) and material/spectral dispersion (different wavelengths travel at different speeds - fixed by monochromatic light). Absorption/scattering also attenuates. The cladding also prevents light leaking between adjacent fibres (cross-talk) and protects the core surface. Worked example: critical angle and fibre timing A glass-air interface has n_glass = 1.52. A fibre of length 100 m has core refractive index 1.50. Line 1: sin θ_c = 1.00/1.52 = 0.658, θ_c = 41.1 degrees (M1 A1). Line 2: Light along the fibre axis: v = c/n = 3.00 × 10^8/1.50 = 2.00 × 10^8 m/s (A1). Line 3: t = 100/2.00 × 10^8 = 5.0 × 10^-7 s (A1); rays at larger angles take longer - modal dispersion spreads the pulse (A1: physics of the effect).

topics.name: Electricity and Circuits
topics.subject: physics
topics.searchText: physics Physics Electricity and Circuits Define current, potential difference and resistance; use I = nqvA to explain conduction (AO1/AO2) - AQA 7408 3.5.1.1, OCR A H556 4.1 Interpret I-V characteristics of ohmic and non-ohmic conductors (filament lamp, diode) and explain temperature effects on resistance (AO2) - AQA 7408 3.5.1.2 Calculate resistivity and determine it experimentally (AO2/AO3) - AQA 7408 3.5.1.3, required practical 5, Edexcel CP2 Apply Kirchhoff's laws and series/parallel resistor rules with conservation derivations (AO2) - AQA 7408 3.5.1.4 Determine EMF and internal resistance from V = ε - Ir and evaluate the experiment (AO2/AO3) - AQA 7408 3.5.1.6, required practical 6, Edexcel CP3, OCR PAG7 Design and analyse potential divider circuits with LDRs and thermistors (AO2) - AQA 7408 3.5.1.5 I = ΔQ/Δt; V = W/Q; R = V/I; drift velocity I = nqvA (n = charge carriers per m^3). Ohm: V = IR (ohmic, straight I-V line) vs non-ohmic (filament curves down, diode conducts one way above ~0.7 V). Series: I same, V shares, R_total = ΣR. Parallel: V same, I shares, 1/R_total = Σ1/R (always less than the smallest R). Power: P = IV = I^2R = V^2/R; energy E = Pt = IVt. Kirchhoff: junction rule (charge conservation); loop rule (energy conservation). EMF ε = I(R + r); terminal PD V = ε - Ir; maximum power transfer when R = r. Potential divider: V_out = V_in × R_2/(R_1 + R_2); LDR (resistance falls with light) and thermistor (falls with temperature) for sensor circuits. Current (I) Rate of flow of charge, I = ΔQ/Δt, in amperes (1 A = 1 C/s); conventional current flows from + to - (opposite to electrons). Potential difference (V) Work done per unit charge moving between two points, V = W/Q, in volts (1 V = 1 J/C). Resistance (R) R = V/I, in ohms (Ω); a measure of opposition to current flow. Ohm's law For an ohmic conductor at constant temperature, current is proportional to pd: V = IR; a straight I-V line through the origin. Resistivity (ρ) A material property: R = ρL/A, in Ω m; resistance of a sample increases with length and decreases with cross-sectional area. EMF (ε) The electrical energy given to each coulomb by a source: ε = W/Q; for a cell with internal resistance r, ε = I(R + r). Internal resistance (r) The resistance inside a source, causing terminal pd V = ε - Ir to fall as load current rises. Kirchhoff's first law At a junction, ΣI_in = ΣI_out - conservation of charge. Kirchhoff's second law Around any closed loop, Σε = ΣIR - conservation of energy. Potential divider Two resistors in series sharing a supply: V_out = V_in × R_2/(R_1 + R_2) across R_2; the basis of sensor circuits. Current is the rate of flow of charge: I = ΔQ/Δt (AQA 7408 3.5.1.1; OCR A H556 4.1; Edexcel 9PH0 Topic 3), measured in amperes. Potential difference is work done per unit charge, V = W/Q, in volts - 1 V means each coulomb gains 1 J of energy passing through. Resistance R = V/I in ohms; Ohm's law states that for an ohmic conductor at constant temperature, I ∝ V (straight I-V line through the origin) - the constant temperature condition is part of the law, so quote it. Drift velocity derivation (I = nqvA): in a wire of cross-sectional area A with n charge carriers per cubic metre, each of charge q moving at drift velocity v, in time Δt all carriers within a length vΔt pass a point. The volume is AvΔt, containing nAvΔt carriers with total charge Q = nqAvΔt. Current I = Q/Δt = nqvA . Typical drift velocities are ~mm/s (slow!), because n is enormous (~10^28-10^29 per m^3 in metals) - lights turn on instantly because the electric field propagates near light speed, not the electrons. I-V characteristics: ohmic conductor - straight line, constant R; filament lamp - curve flattening at higher V, because current heats the filament, lattice ions vibrate more, electrons collide more often and R increases; diode - zero current in reverse and below the forward threshold (~0.7 V for silicon), then steep conduction. Resistivity : R = ρL/A, in Ω m - resistance rises with length, falls with area; ρ is a material property. Semiconductors (thermistors, LDRs) behave oppositely to metals: resistance falls as temperature rises because more charge carriers are released, outweighing increased lattice vibration. Worked example: drift velocity A copper wire carries 5.0 A with n = 8.5 × 10^28 carriers per m^3 and area 1.0 mm^2. Find the drift velocity. Line 1: I = nqvA, so v = I/(nqA) (M1: rearrangement). Line 2: v = 5.0/(8.5 × 10^28 × 1.60 × 10^-19 × 1.0 × 10^-6) (A1: unit conversion of area). Line 3: v = 5.0/1.36 × 10^4 = 3.7 × 10^-4 m/s ≈ 0.4 mm/s (A1) - millimetres per second, the standard contrast point. Kirchhoff's first law (junction): the total current into a junction equals the total current out - conservation of charge (charge cannot pile up at a point) (AQA 7408 3.5.1.4). Second law (loop): around any closed loop the sum of EMFs equals the sum of IR products - conservation of energy (a coulomb gains energy in the source and loses exactly that amount around the loop). Series rule derivation: the same current I flows through each resistor (junction rule: no charge leaves the path). Total pd = V_1 + V_2 + ... = IR_1 + IR_2 + ... = I(R_1 + R_2 + ...), so R_total = ΣR - resistances add, and pds share in proportion to resistance. Parallel rule derivation: each branch has the same pd V (both ends of each branch connect to the same two nodes). Currents add: I_total = V/R_1 + V/R_2 + ... = V(1/R_1 + 1/R_2 + ...), so 1/R_total = Σ1/R - and the total is always less than the smallest individual resistance (a standard check). Two equal resistors in parallel halve the resistance; adding branches always lowers total resistance and raises total current. Worked example: mixed circuit analysis A 12 V battery of negligible internal resistance drives 4.0 Ω in series with a parallel pair of 6.0 Ω and 3.0 Ω. Line 1: Parallel pair: 1/R_p = 1/6 + 1/3 = 0.5, R_p = 2.0 Ω (M1 A1). Line 2: Total: R = 4.0 + 2.0 = 6.0 Ω (A1). Line 3: Total current: I = 12/6.0 = 2.0 A (A1). Line 4: pd across parallel pair: V_p = 2.0 × 2.0 = 4.0 V (M1). Line 5: Branch currents: 4.0/6.0 = 0.67 A and 4.0/3.0 = 1.33 A - sum 2.0 A, checking the junction rule (A1: Kirchhoff check). A real cell has internal resistance r : the EMF ε drives current through both the external circuit (R) and the cell itself (r), so the energy per coulomb divides: ε = I(R + r) (AQA 7408 3.5.1.6; OCR PAG7; Edexcel CP3). The terminal pd - what the circuit actually sees - is V = IR = ε - Ir: it falls below ε whenever current flows, by the 'lost volts' Ir. High current (low R) → large lost volts → dim lamps and flattened batteries; with no current (open circuit) the terminal pd equals ε. Maximum power transfer: P = I^2R with I = ε/(R + r); differentiating shows power peaks when R = r - the matched-load condition (efficiency is then only 50%, half the energy lost inside the source). Measuring ε and r (required practical): vary the load resistance (or a variable resistor) and record V and I with a voltmeter (high resistance, across the cell) and ammeter (low resistance, in series). Rearrange V = ε - Ir as V = -rI + ε: plot V against I - a straight line with gradient -r and y-intercept ε . Using the gradient and intercept averages random error across all data. Errors: the voltmeter draws some current (high-resistance voltmeter minimises this), contact resistance, heating of the cell changing r during the experiment (take readings quickly, switch off between readings), and zero errors on meters (check before starting). Worked example: V-I analysis Varying the load gives: I = 0.10 A, V = 1.44 V; I = 0.50 A, V = 1.20 V. Line 1: V = ε - Ir (M1: equation quoted). Line 2: Two points determine the line: gradient = (1.20 - 1.44)/(0.50 - 0.10) = -0.60, so r = 0.60 Ω (M1 A1). Line 3: ε = V + Ir = 1.44 + 0.10 × 0.60 = 1.50 V (A1). Line 4: Check with the second point: 1.20 + 0.50 × 0.60 = 1.50 V - consistent (A1: verification). A potential divider is two resistors in series sharing a supply (AQA 7408 3.5.1.5): the same current flows through both, so V_out (across R_2) = IR_2 = V_in × R_2/(R_1 + R_2) - the output is the input scaled by the resistance fraction. Derivation: I = V_in/(R_1 + R_2) from the loop rule; multiply by R_2. Sensor circuits replace one resistor with a component whose resistance depends on the environment: an LDR (resistance falls as light intensity rises) or a thermistor (resistance falls as temperature rises). Putting the sensor as R_2 makes V_out rise when the sensed quantity rises (light/temperature up → R_2 down → wait: R_2 down means V_out falls - the share follows the resistance). Getting the direction right is the examinable logic: V_out across a component rises when that component's resistance rises relative to the other . So for a light-activated circuit that switches on when dark, put the LDR as R_1 (dark → LDR resistance rises → V_out across R_2 falls... trace it carefully for the required behaviour). The potentiometer (a continuously variable divider) can compare EMFs: sliding the contact until the galvanometer reads zero gives a balance point where the pd per unit length equals the unknown EMF - no current drawn, so no lost volts, hence more accurate than a voltmeter. Worked example: divider with load V_in = 12 V, R_1 = 2.0 kΩ, R_2 = 4.0 kΩ; a load of 4.0 kΩ is connected across R_2. Line 1: Unloaded: V_out = 12 × 4/6 = 8.0 V (M1 A1). Line 2: Loaded: R_2 ∥ load = (4.0 × 4.0)/(4.0 + 4.0) = 2.0 kΩ (M1: parallel combination). Line 3: V_out = 12 × 2.0/(2.0 + 2.0) = 6.0 V (A1). Line 4: Loading pulls the output down - high-resistance loads (or low-resistance divider legs) minimise the loading effect (A1: conclusion). Power : P = IV, and with V = IR the alternatives P = I^2R (best when current is common, e.g. series) and P = V^2/R (best when pd is common, e.g. parallel) follow by substitution (AQA 7408 3.5.1.1). Energy : E = Pt = IVt, in joules; domestic units are kWh (1 kWh = 3.6 × 10^6 J). Fuses and power ratings: a fuse melts when I^2R_heat exceeds its rating - choose a fuse just above the appliance's normal current: a 230 V, 900 W kettle draws I = P/V ≈ 3.9 A, so a 5 A fuse. Power dissipated in transmission lines: P_loss = I^2R_lines motivates high-voltage, low-current transmission. Required practicals in this topic: (1) Resistivity of a wire (AQA RP5, Edexcel CP2, OCR PAG6-style): measure diameter at many points with a micrometer (A ∝ d^2 doubles its percentage uncertainty), length with a rule, resistance with an ammeter-voltmeter or multimeter; plot R against L - gradient = ρ/A, so ρ = gradient × A. Length and diameter are the dominant uncertainties; check the wire stays near room temperature (heating changes ρ). (2) EMF and internal resistance (AQA RP6, Edexcel CP3, OCR PAG7): V against I analysis as in section 3. (3) I-V characteristics: vary the supply, record I and V for a lamp, diode and fixed resistor; plot I-V curves - reverse the diode to show one-way conduction; keep the lamp's temperature from changing too fast by taking readings promptly. Worked example: resistivity with uncertainty A nichrome wire: L = 1.000 ± 0.001 m, d = 0.31 ± 0.01 mm, R measured 5.4 ± 0.1 Ω. Line 1: A = πd^2/4 = π × (0.31 × 10^-3)^2/4 = 7.55 × 10^-8 m^2 (M1 A1). Line 2: ρ = RA = 5.4 × 7.55 × 10^-8 = 4.1 × 10^-7 Ω m (A1) - the accepted value for nichrome, ≈1.1 × 10^-6 Ω m, is a little higher; check against data books. Line 3: Percentage uncertainties: d: 0.01/0.31 = 3.2%, doubled (power rule) = 6.5%; L: 0.1%; R: 0.1/5.4 = 1.9% (M1). Line 4: Total ≈ 8.5%, so ρ = (4.1 ± 0.3) × 10^-7 Ω m - diameter dominates, measure at more points (A1: evaluation).

topics.name: Particles and Quantum Phenomena
topics.subject: physics
topics.searchText: physics Physics Particles and Quantum Phenomena Explain the photoelectric effect with Einstein's equation hf = φ + KE_max, threshold frequency and stopping potential (AO1/AO2) - AQA 7408 3.2.2.1, OCR A H556 4.4 Use the photon model E = hf = hc/λ and calculate photon energies and momenta (AO2) - AQA 7408 3.2.2.1 Describe atomic line spectra and discrete energy levels; calculate photon wavelength from transitions ΔE = hf (AO2) - AQA 7408 3.2.2.2 Explain wave-particle duality and use the de Broglie relation λ = h/p (AO1/AO2) - AQA 7408 3.2.2.2, OCR A H556 4.4.2 Describe the standard model: quarks, leptons, hadrons (baryons and mesons), and apply conservation laws (charge, baryon number, lepton number, strangeness) (AO1/AO2) - AQA 7408 3.2.1, Edexcel 9PH0 Topic 8 Describe particle interactions (strong, weak, electromagnetic) and beta decay at quark level (AO2) - AQA 7408 3.2.1 Photon: E = hf = hc/λ; 1 eV = 1.60 × 10^-19 J. Photoelectric: hf = φ + KE_max; threshold f_0 = φ/h; one photon interacts with one electron - no time lag, intensity only changes the rate. Stopping potential: eV_s = KE_max. Energy levels: E_n = -13.6/n^2 eV (hydrogen); transitions give ΔE = hf; emission (excited → lower) and absorption (lower → higher). de Broglie: λ = h/p = h/√(2mE_k) for non-relativistic particles; electron diffraction proves wave nature. Quarks (u, d, s, c, b, t) in baryons (3 quarks) and mesons (q q̄); leptons (e, μ, τ and neutrinos); interactions: strong, weak, EM, gravity (negligible). Conservation: charge, baryon number, lepton number always; strangeness in strong interactions only (weak can change it by ±1). Photon A quantum of electromagnetic energy: E = hf = hc/λ; photons transfer energy in discrete packets. Work function (φ) The minimum energy needed to remove an electron from a metal surface; φ = hf_0 where f_0 is the threshold frequency. Threshold frequency (f_0) The minimum frequency of light that ejects photoelectrons; below it, no electrons are emitted however intense the light. Stopping potential (V_s) The pd that just stops the fastest photoelectrons: eV_s = KE_max. Energy level A discrete allowed electron energy in an atom; electrons absorb or emit photons only when moving between levels, ΔE = hf. Ionisation Removal of an electron from an atom; the ionisation energy of hydrogen is 13.6 eV (from the ground level E = -13.6 eV to zero). de Broglie wavelength λ = h/p - every moving particle has an associated wavelength; electron diffraction demonstrates it. Hadron A particle made of quarks that feels the strong interaction: baryons (3 quarks, e.g. proton, neutron) and mesons (quark-antiquark pair, e.g. pion). Lepton A fundamental particle that does not feel the strong interaction: electron, muon, tau and their neutrinos. Strangeness A quantum number conserved in strong interactions but allowed to change by ±1 in weak interactions. Shine light on a metal and electrons can be ejected - the photoelectric effect (AQA 7408 3.2.2.1; OCR A H556 4.4.1; Edexcel 9PH0 Topic 5). Three observations killed the wave theory: (1) there is a threshold frequency f_0 below which no electrons are emitted, however intense the light (wave theory: any frequency should work given enough intensity); (2) emission is instantaneous even for dim light (wave theory: energy should take time to accumulate); (3) the maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons depends only on frequency, not intensity (wave theory: brighter light should mean faster electrons). Einstein's photon model: light arrives in discrete packets of energy E = hf. One photon is absorbed by one electron in a one-to-one interaction: the electron gains hf, spends the work function φ (minimum energy to escape the surface) and leaves with the remainder: hf = φ + KE_max . Instantaneous, because the energy arrives in one packet. Intensity changes the number of photons per second , so it changes the rate of emission, not the energy per electron. Threshold: KE_max = 0 gives f_0 = φ/h. Electrons deeper in the metal need more than φ, so they leave with less than KE_max - hence a range of energies up to the maximum. Stopping potential derivation: apply a reverse pd V_s that just stops the fastest electrons. The electrons do work eV_s against the field, losing all their KE: eV_s = KE_max = hf - φ. Plotting V_s against f gives a straight line of gradient h/e and intercept -φ/h - one experimental route to Planck's constant. The gold-leaf electroscope demonstration: a negatively charged zinc plate loses its charge instantly under UV light (electrons ejected) but not under visible light even at high intensity - below threshold for zinc (φ ≈ 4.3 eV, UV ≈ 5+ eV). Worked example: photoelectric equation Light of wavelength 420 nm is incident on a metal with work function 1.9 eV. Find the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons. (h = 6.63 × 10^-34 J s, c = 3.00 × 10^8 m/s) Line 1: Photon energy E = hc/λ = (6.63 × 10^-34 × 3.00 × 10^8)/(420 × 10^-9) = 4.74 × 10^-19 J (M1 A1). Line 2: φ = 1.9 × 1.60 × 10^-19 = 3.04 × 10^-19 J (M1: eV to J conversion). Line 3: KE_max = hf - φ = 4.74 × 10^-19 - 3.04 × 10^-19 = 1.7 × 10^-19 J (A1) ≈ 1.1 eV. Electrons in atoms occupy discrete energy levels - negative values because the electron is bound (zero is free, at infinity) (AQA 7408 3.2.2.2). An electron can move between levels only by absorbing or emitting exactly the energy gap as a photon: ΔE = hf = hc/λ . Emission spectra (bright lines on dark) come from excited electrons falling to lower levels; absorption spectra (dark lines on continuous) from cool gas absorbing exactly those photons out of white light passing through. Each element has a unique set of levels, hence unique spectral lines - the fingerprint used to identify elements in stars. Hydrogen: E_n = -13.6/n^2 eV (n = 1 ground: -13.6 eV; n = 2: -3.40 eV; n = 3: -1.51 eV; n = ∞: 0, ionisation). Series names: transitions ending on n = 1 (Lyman, UV), n = 2 (Balmer, visible), n = 3 (Paschen, IR). Fluorescence : absorb UV, electrons excited, then cascade down emitting visible photons of lower energy each - energy is conserved overall. Excitation by collision : electrons in a fluorescent tube collide with gas atoms, transferring exactly the excitation energies; the fluorescent coating converts UV to visible. Line spectra evidence: discrete lines prove discrete levels - a continuum of possible energies would give a continuous spectrum. Worked example: hydrogen transition A hydrogen electron falls from n = 3 (E_3 = -1.51 eV) to n = 2 (E_2 = -3.40 eV). Find the photon energy and wavelength. Line 1: ΔE = E_3 - E_2 = -1.51 - (-3.40) = 1.89 eV = 1.89 × 1.60 × 10^-19 = 3.02 × 10^-19 J (M1 A1: energy difference, sign handled). Line 2: λ = hc/ΔE = (6.63 × 10^-34 × 3.00 × 10^8)/3.02 × 10^-19 (M1). Line 3: λ = 6.6 × 10^-7 m = 660 nm - red light, a Balmer line (A1). Light behaves as a wave (interference, diffraction) and as particles (photoelectric effect, photon momentum) - the photon model with E = hf and p = h/λ (AQA 7408 3.2.2.2). de Broglie's hypothesis extends duality to matter: every moving particle has an associated wavelength λ = h/p. For a non-relativistic particle with kinetic energy E_k, p = √(2mE_k) (from E_k = p^2/2m), so λ = h/√(2mE_k) ; for an electron accelerated through pd V: E_k = eV, so λ = h/√(2meV). Evidence: electron diffraction. Accelerate electrons through a pd and fire them at a thin polycrystalline graphite film: the screen shows concentric diffraction rings - the spacing matches the predicted λ = h/p. Faster electrons (higher accelerating voltage) give smaller λ and closer rings - the quantitative test. Neutron diffraction similarly probes crystal structure. Why don't we see cricket-ball diffraction? λ = h/p with a macroscopic p is ~10^-34 m - unobservably small; duality only shows when λ is comparable to the spacing of the obstacles (atomic spacings ~10^-10 m for electrons through ~100 V). Electron microscopes exploit the small λ: resolving power improves as wavelength shrinks, so electrons at ~100 kV (λ ~ 4 pm) resolve far finer detail than visible light (λ ~ 500 nm). Worked example: de Broglie wavelength An electron (m = 9.11 × 10^-31 kg) is accelerated through 150 V. Find its de Broglie wavelength. Line 1: E_k = eV = 1.60 × 10^-19 × 150 = 2.4 × 10^-17 J (M1 A1). Line 2: p = √(2mE_k) = √(2 × 9.11 × 10^-31 × 2.4 × 10^-17) = 6.61 × 10^-24 kg m/s (M1 A1). Line 3: λ = h/p = 6.63 × 10^-34/6.61 × 10^-24 = 1.0 × 10^-10 m = 0.10 nm (A1) - comparable to atomic spacing, hence electron diffraction works. Quarks (u, d, s, c, b, t) and antiquarks build hadrons - particles feeling the strong interaction (AQA 7408 3.2.1; Edexcel 9PH0 Topic 8; OCR A H556 6.5). Baryons are three quarks (proton uud, neutron udd); mesons are quark-antiquark pairs (pions, kaons). Leptons are fundamental, non-strong: electron, muon, tau and their neutrinos (ν_e, ν_μ, ν_τ). Quark charges: u = +2/3e, d = -1/3e - add them for hadron charges (proton: 2/3 + 2/3 - 1/3 = +1e). Interactions: the strong force binds quarks (gluons) and holds nuclei together - very short range (~10^-15 m); the weak force mediates beta decay (W±, Z^0 bosons) and can change quark flavour; the electromagnetic force acts on charged particles (photons); gravity is negligible at particle scales. Conservation laws for deciding if a reaction happens: charge, baryon number B (baryon +1, antiquark -1/3 per quark... in practice: baryon +1, meson 0, lepton 0), lepton number L (electron family: electron +1, electron neutrino +1, their antiparticles -1), and strangeness - conserved in strong interactions, changed by ±1 in weak interactions (kaons are strange particles, created in pairs by the strong force). Beta-minus decay at quark level: n → p + e^- + ν̄_e. At quark level, one d quark changes to a u quark via the weak interaction , emitting a W^- boson which decays into an electron and an antineutrino: d → u + W^-, then W^- → e^- + ν̄_e (Feynman diagram in words: incoming d line bends to u, W^- zigzag leaves the vertex and splits into the electron-antineutrino pair). Check conservation: charge 0 → (+1) + (-1) + 0 ✓; baryon number 1 → 1 ✓; lepton number 0 → 0 + (+1) + (-1) ✓. Pair production (photon → particle-antiparticle pair, needs E ≥ 2mc^2) and annihilation (particle-antiparticle → two photons) are the standard energy-bookkeeping examples - PET scanners use positron-electron annihilation. Worked example: conservation check Is p + π^- → K^+ + K^0 possible in a strong interaction? (π^-, K^+ and K^0 contain strange/anti-strange quarks; K^0 has strangeness +1.) Line 1: Charge: +1 - 1 = 0; K^+ + K^0 = +1 + 0 = +1 - not conserved (M1). Line 2: Charge conservation fails, so the reaction is impossible however the other numbers work (A1). (Check the others for practice: B = 1 + 0 → 0 + 0 fails too.) The standard practical for quantum phenomena is estimating h from LEDs (OCR PAG5; Edexcel practical work on quantum; AQA covers it under 3.2.2). Each LED emits photons of a known colour/wavelength λ when the pd across it reaches the activation voltage V_0: the electrical energy per electron eV_0 equals the photon energy hf = hc/λ. So eV_0 = hc/λ , giving h = eV_0 λ/c. Method: connect an LED in series with a resistor and a variable supply; increase the pd slowly in the dark until the LED just begins to emit - record that activation voltage (take several readings, average). Repeat for LEDs of several wavelengths (red, yellow, green, blue). Plot V_0 against 1/λ: a straight line through the origin of gradient hc/e , so h = gradient × e/c. Using the gradient across all LEDs averages random error and tests the model (a straight line confirms eV_0 ∝ 1/λ). Evaluation points: judging the exact activation point is subjective (the LED glows dimly before it is obvious) - use a consistent, dim criterion in darkness; the pd measured is across the LED plus any voltmeter loading - use a high-resistance voltmeter; some energy is lost as heat in the LED (non-radiative recombination), so the measured h tends to be high; wavelength spreads (LEDs are not perfectly monochromatic) add uncertainty. Quote h with its uncertainty and compare with 6.63 × 10^-34 J s using the percentage difference. Worked example: h from an LED A blue LED (λ = 470 nm) just lights at V_0 = 2.62 V. Line 1: eV_0 = hc/λ, so h = eV_0 λ/c (M1: energy balance). Line 2: h = (1.60 × 10^-19 × 2.62 × 470 × 10^-9)/(3.00 × 10^8) (M1: substitution). Line 3: h = 1.969 × 10^-25/3.00 × 10^8 = 6.6 × 10^-34 J s (A1) - within a few percent of the accepted 6.63 × 10^-34 J s.

topics.name: Gravitation and Fields
topics.subject: physics
topics.searchText: physics Physics Gravitation and Fields Describe the field concept and apply Newton's law of gravitation F = GMm/r^2 as an inverse-square law (AO1/AO2) - AQA 7408 3.7.2.1, OCR A H556 5.4 Calculate gravitational field strength g = GM/r^2 and use g = F/m (AO2) - AQA 7408 3.7.2.2 Use gravitational potential V = -GM/r, potential energy mV, and the field-potential gradient relation (AO2) - AQA 7408 3.7.2.3 Derive orbital speed and period for circular orbits, explain Kepler's third law, geostationary satellites and total orbital energy (AO2/AO3) - AQA 7408 3.7.2.4 Derive escape velocity and analyse orbital data with uncertainty (AO3) Newton's law: F = GMm/r^2 - always attractive, inverse-square; G = 6.67 × 10^-11 N m^2 kg^-2. Field strength: g = F/m = GM/r^2 (N/kg); uniform near Earth's surface (9.81 N/kg). Potential: V = -GM/r (always negative, zero at infinity); ΔW = mΔV; field strength = potential gradient, g = -dV/dr. Circular orbits: GMm/r^2 = mv^2/r gives v = √(GM/r) and T^2 = 4π^2r^3/GM (Kepler: T^2 ∝ r^3). Orbital kinetic energy = GMm/2r; total energy = -GMm/2r (negative - bound). Escape velocity: v_esc = √(2GM/R); independent of the launched mass. Force field A region where a body experiences a non-contact force; a gravitational field acts on mass, an electric field on charge. Newton's law of gravitation F = GMm/r^2 - the attractive force between two point masses, an inverse-square law with G = 6.67 × 10^-11 N m^2 kg^-2. Gravitational field strength (g) Force per unit mass, g = F/m = GM/r^2, in N/kg; 9.81 N/kg at Earth's surface. Gravitational potential (V) Work done per unit mass bringing a mass from infinity to a point: V = -GM/r, always negative, zero at infinity. Equipotential surface A surface of constant potential; no work is done moving along one, and field lines cross them at right angles. Geostationary satellite A satellite with period 24 hours orbiting above the equator in the same direction as Earth's rotation, so it stays above a fixed point. Escape velocity The minimum launch speed for a body to just reach infinity with zero speed: v_esc = √(2GM/R). Inverse-square law A law where the quantity falls as 1/r^2; doubling the distance quarters the force (flux spreading over a sphere of area 4πr^2). A force field is a region in which a body experiences a non-contact force - a useful bookkeeping idea that lets us assign a value (field strength) to every point in space (AQA 7408 3.7.1). Gravity is always attractive and acts on mass (AQA 7408 3.7.2.1; OCR A H556 5.4; Edexcel 9PH0 Topic 12). Newton's law of gravitation: F = GMm/r^2 - the force between two point (or spherically symmetric) masses is proportional to each mass and to the inverse square of their separation. G = 6.67 × 10^-11 N m^2 kg^-2. Why inverse square? The field lines spread out radially, crossing spheres of area 4πr^2 - the same 'flux' crosses a sphere twice the radius, spread over four times the area, so the force per unit mass falls as 1/r^2. The same geometry underlies Coulomb's law and the intensity of light - a favourite comparison question. Derivation of field strength: field strength is force per unit mass, g = F/m. Substitute Newton's law: g = GMm/r^2 ÷ m = GM/r^2 - independent of the test mass m, which is why all objects fall with the same acceleration in a vacuum. At Earth's surface (M = 5.97 × 10^24 kg, R = 6.37 × 10^6 m): g = 6.67 × 10^-11 × 5.97 × 10^24/(6.37 × 10^6)^2 = 9.81 N/kg. Higher altitude: g falls as 1/r^2 from the centre - at height h, use r = R + h. Worked example: g at satellite height Find g at the altitude of the ISS, 400 km above Earth's surface (M = 5.97 × 10^24 kg, R = 6.37 × 10^6 m). Line 1: r = R + h = 6.37 × 10^6 + 4.0 × 10^5 = 6.77 × 10^6 m (M1: distance from the centre). Line 2: g = GM/r^2 = (6.67 × 10^-11 × 5.97 × 10^24)/(6.77 × 10^6)^2 (M1 A1). Line 3: g = 3.98 × 10^14/4.58 × 10^13 = 8.7 N/kg (A1) - only ~11% less than the surface value; astronauts float because they are in free fall, not because gravity is absent. Gravitational potential at a point is the work done per unit mass bringing a small mass from infinity to that point: V = -GM/r (AQA 7408 3.7.2.3). Negative because gravity attracts - you do negative work (the field does the work) moving a mass in from infinity; V = 0 at infinity, the zero of potential by convention. Gravitational potential energy of a mass m at that point: E_p = mV = -GMm/r. Derivation of V = -GM/r: the work done moving mass m from radius r_1 to r_2 against the force F = GMm/r^2 is W = ∫F dr = ∫GMm/r^2 dr from r_1 to r_2 = GMm(1/r_1 - 1/r_2). Bringing the mass from infinity (r_1 = ∞) to r (r_2 = r): W = -GMm/r - the potential energy. Per unit mass: V = -GM/r. Field strength is the potential gradient: g = -dV/dr - the field points down the potential 'slope' (from high to low potential, i.e. towards the mass where V is more negative). Graphically, V against r for a point mass is a curve rising from -GM/r at small r towards zero; the gradient at any r gives -g. Moving between two points: ΔW = mΔV - work done equals mass times the change in potential. Equipotential surfaces are spheres of constant V: moving along one does no work (ΔV = 0), and field lines meet them at right angles - the two facts tested in diagram questions. Worked example: work done lifting a satellite Find the work done moving a 1000 kg satellite from Earth's surface to a 400 km orbit (M = 5.97 × 10^24 kg, R = 6.37 × 10^6 m). Line 1: V_surface = -GM/R = -(6.67 × 10^-11 × 5.97 × 10^24)/6.37 × 10^6 = -6.25 × 10^7 J/kg (M1 A1). Line 2: V_orbit = -GM/(R + h) = -3.98 × 10^14/6.77 × 10^6 = -5.88 × 10^7 J/kg (A1). Line 3: ΔV = -5.88 × 10^7 - (-6.25 × 10^7) = +3.7 × 10^6 J/kg (M1: potential increases, less negative). Line 4: W = mΔV = 1000 × 3.7 × 10^6 = 3.7 × 10^9 J (A1) - the minimum energy input (no kinetic energy included). For a circular orbit, gravity supplies the centripetal force (AQA 7408 3.7.2.4; OCR A H556 5.2/5.4): Derivation of orbital speed: GMm/r^2 = mv^2/r. Cancel m and one r: v^2 = GM/r, so v = √(GM/r) - orbital speed falls with orbit radius (outer satellites move slower). Orbital angular speed: v = ωr gives ω = √(GM/r^3). Derivation of Kepler's third law: period T = 2πr/v = 2πr/√(GM/r) = 2π√(r^3/GM). Square: T^2 = 4π^2r^3/GM - T^2 ∝ r^3, so a log-log or T^2 against r^3 plot of planetary data gives a straight line - how Kepler's law is verified and G or the central mass found. The constant T^2/r^3 = 4π^2/GM is the same for all satellites of one central body. Orbital energy: KE = ½mv^2 = GMm/2r (substituting v^2 = GM/r); PE = -GMm/r. Total energy = KE + PE = -GMm/2r - negative, meaning the satellite is bound to the planet; lower orbits are more strongly bound (more negative total energy, but faster and higher KE). Geostationary satellites : period 24 hours, above the equator, same rotation direction - fixed above one point on the surface for communications. Derivation of the orbit radius: T^2 = 4π^2r^3/GM with T = 24 × 3600 = 86,400 s gives r = (GMT^2/4π^2)^(1/3) ≈ 4.23 × 10^7 m - about 36,000 km altitude (6.6 Earth radii). All geostationary satellites share this radius - a standard one-mark fact. Polar orbits (over the poles) scan the whole surface - used for weather and mapping. Worked example: geostationary radius Find the orbital radius of a geostationary satellite (M = 5.97 × 10^24 kg, T = 86,400 s). Line 1: r^3 = GMT^2/4π^2 (M1: from T^2 = 4π^2r^3/GM). Line 2: r^3 = (6.67 × 10^-11 × 5.97 × 10^24 × 86400^2)/(4π^2) = 7.54 × 10^22 m^3 (M1 A1). Line 3: r = 4.23 × 10^7 m (A1) - altitude 4.23 × 10^7 - 6.37 × 10^6 ≈ 3.6 × 10^7 m above the surface. Escape velocity is the minimum launch speed for a body to just reach infinity with zero speed (all KE spent against gravity). Derivation: energy conservation. Launch from a planet's surface (radius R) with speed v: KE + PE = ½mv^2 - GMm/R. At infinity: KE = 0 and PE = 0. So ½mv^2 - GMm/R = 0, giving v_esc = √(2GM/R) - independent of the launched mass. For Earth: v_esc = √(2 × 6.67 × 10^-11 × 5.97 × 10^24/6.37 × 10^6) = 11.2 km/s. Comparison: v_esc = √2 × v_orbit at the same radius (since v_orbit = √(GM/r)) - a favourite link. Note also that escape velocity is independent of launch direction in the idealised model (energy, not vector direction, decides) - though launching eastward from the equator borrows Earth's rotation (~465 m/s), a small practical gain rockets exploit. Energy changes in orbit: a satellite in a decaying orbit (drag from the thin upper atmosphere) loses total energy, so it moves to a lower orbit - where its speed is higher (v = √(GM/r)) even though it lost energy. The apparent paradox resolves through the PE: the drop in PE (-GMm/r becomes more negative) exceeds the gain in KE (GMm/2r), with the difference dissipated as heat by drag. A satellite boosted to a higher orbit by a rocket burn gains PE and loses speed - the standard explanation question. Analysing orbital data: planetary periods and radii: plot T^2 against r^3 - straight line through the origin with gradient 4π^2/GM, so the central mass M = 4π^2/(G × gradient). Satellite speed data against radius: v^2 against 1/r gives a straight line of gradient GM. This is how the mass of the Sun (from planetary data) or of a planet (from its moons) is found. Uncertainty practice: orbital radii and periods are large, well-measured quantities; the derived mass uncertainty is dominated by the scatter of the line fit and by G's precision; quote the percentage difference of the derived mass from the accepted value in the conclusion. Worked example: escape velocity and orbital link A planet has M = 6.4 × 10^23 kg and R = 3.4 × 10^6 m. Find v_esc and the orbital speed at the surface. Line 1: v_esc = √(2GM/R) = √(2 × 6.67 × 10^-11 × 6.4 × 10^23/3.4 × 10^6) (M1 A1). Line 2: v_esc = √(2.51 × 10^7) = 5.0 km/s (A1). Line 3: Orbital speed at the surface: v = √(GM/R) = √(1.25 × 10^7) = 3.5 km/s (M1 A1). Line 4: Check: v_esc = √2 × 3.5 = 5.0 km/s - consistent (A1). The gravitational and electric field topics are deliberately parallel - exam boards set six-mark synthesis questions on the comparison, so learn the pairs (AQA 7408 3.7.1-3.7.3; OCR A H556 5.4/6.2; Edexcel 9PH0 Topics 7/12): Quantity Gravitational Electric Source Mass (always positive) Charge (±) Force law F = GMm/r^2 F = q1q2/(4πε0r^2) Field strength g = GM/r^2 (N/kg) E = Q/(4πε0r^2) (V/m or N/C) Potential V = -GM/r (always negative) V = Q/(4πε0r) (either sign) Gradient relation g = -dV/dr E = -dV/dr Equipotentials Spheres; no work along them; field ⊥ to them Same geometry Attraction Always attractive Attract or repel Shielding Impossible Conductors shield electric fields Relative strength Weak between particles Vastly stronger between particles (~10^36 times for two protons) The pattern: every quantity maps one-to-one (source, force, field strength, potential, gradient, equipotentials), and the differences are exactly two - the sign of the source (making electric forces either attractive or repulsive, and electric potential either sign) and shielding. Both forces are inverse-square because field lines from a point source spread over spheres of area 4πr^2 - the same geometry argument serves both. Uniform versions also pair: a uniform gravitational field near Earth's surface (g constant) and a uniform electric field between parallel plates (E = V/d) - both give parabolic trajectories for projectiles and charged particles respectively, the deepest symmetry of the pair. Worked example: relative strength Compare the gravitational and electric forces between two protons 1.0 × 10^-10 m apart. Line 1: Electric: F = e^2/(4πε0r^2) = (1.60 × 10^-19)^2/(4π × 8.85 × 10^-12 × (1.0 × 10^-10)^2) = 2.3 × 10^-8 N (M1 A1). Line 2: Gravitational: F = Gm_p^2/r^2 = 6.67 × 10^-11 × (1.67 × 10^-27)^2/(1.0 × 10^-10)^2 = 1.9 × 10^-44 N (M1 A1). Line 3: Ratio ≈ 1.2 × 10^36 - the electric force is enormously stronger; gravity only dominates for astronomical bodies because they are electrically neutral in bulk (A1: interpretation).

topics.subject: physics
topics.searchText: physics Physics Electric Fields and Capacitance Apply Coulomb's law F = q1q2/(4πε0r^2) and compare with gravity (AO1/AO2) - AQA 7408 3.7.3.1, Edexcel 9PH0 Topic 7 Calculate electric field strength for point charges and uniform fields (E = V/d) (AO2) - AQA 7408 3.7.3.2 Use electric potential V = Q/(4πε0r), equipotentials and the field-potential gradient (AO2) - AQA 7408 3.7.3.3 Analyse the motion of charged particles in uniform electric fields (parabolic paths) (AO2) - AQA 7408 3.7.3.2, OCR A H556 6.2 Define capacitance, calculate energy stored, and combine capacitors (AO2) - AQA 7408 3.7.4.1 Describe and calculate exponential charge/discharge with the time constant RC (AO2/AO3) - AQA 7408 3.7.4.2-3.7.4.3, OCR PAG8, Edexcel CP9 Coulomb: F = q1q2/(4πε0r^2) - inverse square, like charges repel; compare with F = GMm/r^2. Point charge field: E = Q/(4πε0r^2); uniform field between plates: E = V/d. Potential: V = Q/(4πε0r); field = potential gradient, E = -dV/dr; ΔW = qΔV. Capacitance C = Q/V (farad); parallel plate C = Aε0εr/d; series: 1/C_total = Σ1/C; parallel: C_total = ΣC. Energy stored: W = ½QV = ½CV^2 = ½Q^2/C (area under the Q-V graph). Discharge: Q = Q0e^(-t/RC); time constant RC = time to fall to 37%; after n time constants, Q = Q0e^-n. Charging: Q = Q0(1 - e^(-t/RC)). Electric field strength (E) Force per unit positive charge, E = F/q, in N/C or V/m; a vector pointing from high to low potential (away from positive charges). Coulomb's law F = q1q2/(4πε0r^2) - the force between two point charges; like charges repel; ε0 = 8.85 × 10^-12 F/m. Electric potential (V) Work done per unit charge bringing a small positive charge from infinity: V = Q/(4πε0r); positive near positive charges, zero at infinity. Capacitance (C) Charge stored per unit pd: C = Q/V, in farads (1 F = 1 C/V); practical capacitors are μF or pF. Time constant (RC) The time for the charge (or current) on a discharging capacitor to fall to 1/e (≈37%) of its initial value; RC has units of seconds. Permittivity (ε) A measure of how an electric field is affected by a medium; ε = ε0εr with εr the relative permittivity (dielectric constant). Equipotential surface A surface of constant potential; no work is done moving a charge along one; field lines cross at right angles. Dielectric An insulating material between capacitor plates that increases capacitance: its molecules polarise, reducing the field for the same charge. Coulomb's law: F = q1q2/(4πε0r^2) - the force between two point charges is proportional to each charge and to the inverse square of their separation; like charges repel, unlike attract (AQA 7408 3.7.3.1; Edexcel 9PH0 Topic 7; OCR A H556 6.2). ε0 = 8.85 × 10^-12 F/m (permittivity of free space); in a medium, replace with ε = ε0εr. The inverse-square form matches gravity (F = GMm/r^2) - same geometry (field lines spreading over spheres of area 4πr^2) - but charge has two signs, so electric forces attract or repel while gravity only attracts, and the electric force between subatomic particles is vastly stronger than gravity. Electric field strength is force per unit positive charge: E = F/q, in N/C (= V/m). For a point charge, substitute Coulomb's law: E = Q/(4πε0r^2) - radially outward from a positive charge, inward for negative. Field lines point in the direction of the force on a positive test charge; denser lines mean stronger field. Between two parallel plates the field is uniform : E = V/d (derivation: work done moving charge q between plates = qV; also W = Eqd; equate: Eqd = qV, so E = V/d) - field lines parallel, evenly spaced, from the positive to the negative plate. Worked example: field between plates Two parallel plates 5.0 mm apart are connected to a 200 V supply. Find E, and the force and acceleration on an electron between them (m = 9.11 × 10^-31 kg). Line 1: E = V/d = 200/5.0 × 10^-3 = 4.0 × 10^4 V/m (M1 A1: uniform field). Line 2: F = eE = 1.60 × 10^-19 × 4.0 × 10^4 = 6.4 × 10^-15 N (M1 A1), towards the positive plate. Line 3: a = F/m = 6.4 × 10^-15/9.11 × 10^-31 = 7.0 × 10^15 m/s^2 (A1) - enormous compared with g. Electric potential at a point is the work done per unit charge bringing a small positive test charge from infinity: for a point charge Q, V = Q/(4πε0r) (AQA 7408 3.7.3.3). Positive near positive charges (repulsive - you do positive work pushing in), negative near negative charges, zero at infinity. Potential energy of charge q: E_p = qV = q1q2/(4πε0r). Moving a charge between two points: ΔW = qΔV - work done equals charge times potential difference; the pd is the energy per coulomb. Field strength is the potential gradient: E = -dV/dr - the field points down the potential slope. Graphically, V against r for a point charge is a curve falling as 1/r from large values at small r; the gradient at any r gives -E. Equipotential surfaces are spheres of constant V around a point charge (parallel planes between plates): moving a charge along one does no work (ΔV = 0), and field lines cross them at right angles - the two diagram facts always tested. Between parallel plates, equipotentials are evenly spaced planes because E is uniform. Comparison table with gravity (standard six-mark synthesis): force inverse-square in both; field strength force per unit charge/mass; potential zero at infinity in both; E/g = -dV/dr in both; gravity always attractive (V_g = -GM/r always negative) while electric potential has either sign; electric field can be shielded by conductors, gravity cannot. Worked example: potential and work done Find the potential 0.30 m from a +5.0 μC point charge, and the work done moving a +2.0 μC charge from 0.50 m to 0.30 m.
