Real-world: the Soft Drinks Industry Levy (2018; 18p/24p per litre, raised in 2025) cut sugar content as firms reformulated; the UK carbon price floor (£18/tonne since 2015) plus EU ETS linkage prices carbon in power generation. Evaluation: the output effect depends on PED — cigarette demand is addictive and inelastic, so a large tax cuts output little while raising revenue mostly from consumers (regressive, hitting low-income smokers hardest); government faces an information gap in measuring MEC; and illicit trade is an unintended consequence (illegal tobacco is estimated at a double-digit share of the UK market). Subsidies for positive externalities (education, vaccination, renewable energy) shift supply right, raising output towards Q*; evaluation: cost to the taxpayer, opportunity cost, and deadweight loss if the subsidy over-corrects. Tradable pollution permits (cap-and-trade): a cap on total emissions; firms with low abatement costs sell permits to firms with high abatement costs, so reduction is achieved at minimum total cost; the cap guarantees the environmental outcome, unlike a tax which guarantees price but not quantity. Real-world: the EU Emissions Trading Scheme (permit prices peaked above €80 in 2023); phase 1 saw prices collapse to near zero because the cap was set too generously — the information-gap failure. Regulation (bans, standards, quotas): simple and certain, but blunt — no incentive to abate beyond the minimum standard, high enforcement costs. Price controls: a maximum price (ceiling) set below equilibrium causes shortage → rationing by queues, waiting lists or black markets (e.g. rent controls — evidence from San Francisco and Berlin shows reduced rental supply and deteriorating quality); a minimum price (floor) set above equilibrium causes surplus — e.g. the failed alcohol minimum unit pricing proposal in the UK was resisted before Scotland introduced it in 2018, and EU agricultural price floors created butter mountains. Nudges (behavioural economics): choice architecture — default pension enrolment, salience, framing — changes behaviour without banning options or changing prices; cheap but effects are modest and can be gamed. State provision and information provision (labels, public campaigns) complete the toolkit: name the policy, show the diagram, then evaluate with elasticity, information gaps, administrative cost and unintended consequences. Government failure occurs when intervention worsens the allocation of resources compared with the free market — net welfare falls. The five recognised causes (AQA 4.1.6.3, Edexcel 1.4.2): information gaps — governments cannot measure MEC, MEB or optimal output accurately, so taxes/subsidies/caps are set too high or too low (EU ETS phase 1 permits collapsing to near zero); administrative and compliance costs — enforcement exceeds the welfare gain (costly regulation of small firms); regulatory capture — the regulator comes to serve the industry it regulates (revolving-door appointments, industry lobbying shaping rules); unintended consequences — black markets, rent controls reducing housing supply, buffer-stock agencies running out of funds; and rent-seeking — resources diverted to lobbying for protection or subsidies rather than productive activity (grandfathered permits giving windfall gains to incumbents). Real-world examples for evaluation: rent controls in Berlin and San Francisco reduced rental supply and worsened shortages — intervention disabled the price mechanism's rationing and incentive functions; the EU Common Agricultural Policy's price floors created overproduction (“butter mountains”, “wine lakes”) at huge budgetary cost; biofuel mandates (US corn ethanol) raised food prices while delivering questionable emissions gains; and the UK 2022 energy price guarantee capped bills but muted the incentive to cut consumption, adding to the fiscal cost of the shock. The evaluation frame examiners reward: (1) identify the market failure and its size — is intervention justified at all?; (2) assess the chosen instrument against alternatives (a tax vs regulation vs permits vs nudge) using elasticity, information, administrative cost and political acceptability; (3) consider government failure — can the government actually implement it well?; (4) conclude with a judgement that weighs the size of the market failure against the risk of government failure. The classic A* line: intervention should correct the failure without creating larger ones — the comparison is not “market vs perfect government” but “imperfect market vs imperfect government”.

topics.name: Macroeconomics: AD-AS and Objectives
topics.subject: economics
topics.searchText: economics Economics Macroeconomics: AD-AS and Objectives Calculate real GDP and the GDP deflator from nominal data, and evaluate GDP as a measure of living standards Explain the circular flow of income, injections and withdrawals, and derive the multiplier Analyse the determinants of C, I, G and (X − M) with accurate chains of reasoning Draw SRAS, classical LRAS and Keynesian LRAS, and shift each correctly in response to cost and demand shocks Determine macroeconomic equilibrium and interpret negative and positive output gaps State the four main macroeconomic objectives with current UK data Evaluate conflicts between macroeconomic objectives using spare capacity, elasticities and credibility GDP The total value of goods and services produced within an economy in a period, measurable by expenditure, income or output methods. Real GDP Nominal GDP adjusted for inflation using the GDP deflator: (nominal ÷ deflator) × 100. GDP deflator (Nominal GDP ÷ real GDP) × 100: the implicit price level of all domestically produced output. Aggregate demand (AD) Total planned spending on domestic output at each price level: AD = C + I + G + (X − M). Aggregate supply (AS) Total planned output of firms at each price level; SRAS slopes up because some costs are sticky, LRAS reflects productive capacity. Circular flow of income The flow of income and spending between households and firms, with injections (I, G, X) and withdrawals (S, T, M); equilibrium where injections = withdrawals. Multiplier The ratio of the final change in real GDP to the initial change in an injection: k = 1/(1 − MPC) or 1/MPW. Negative output gap Actual output below potential output: spare capacity, demand-deficient unemployment, downward pressure on inflation. Full-employment output (Yf) The level of output at which the labour market is at the natural rate of unemployment; the classical LRAS is vertical here. Sticky wages Nominal wages that adjust slowly downwards because of contracts, minimum wages, morale and union resistance — the basis of the upward-sloping SRAS and Keynesian LRAS. GDP — the total value of goods and services produced in an economy in a period — can be measured three ways, which must equal by construction: the expenditure method (C + I + G + (X − M)), the income method (wages, rents, interest, profits), and the output method (value added by sector). Real GDP = (nominal GDP ÷ GDP deflator) × 100 — it strips out inflation to measure volume. The GDP deflator = (nominal ÷ real) × 100; the worked example below shows the calculation. GDP per capita adjusts for population; GNI adds net income from abroad (important for Ireland, where GDP overstates living standards because of multinational profit flows). Limitations of GDP as a measure of living standards (a guaranteed essay/data-response theme): it ignores the hidden/shadow economy (undeclared work); non-market activity (housework, volunteering); income distribution (average vs typical — median income can fall while mean rises); quality and composition of output; externalities (pollution, congestion are not deducted); leisure ; and it is a flow not a stock — a country can raise GDP by depleting resources. Alternative/complementary measures: HDI (see the International topic), Green GDP adjustments, measures of subjective wellbeing (the ONS four wellbeing questions), and the OECD Better Life index. Data anchors: UK nominal GDP is roughly £2.7 trillion (2024); real GDP fell about 11% in 2020 (the largest peacetime collapse on record) and regained its pre-pandemic level only in 2022; growth since has been sluggish (roughly 0.3–1% a year), well below the pre-2008 trend of 2–2.5%. Exam technique: when given nominal and real figures, always compute the deflator and interpret it as the implicit price level — then link to CPI divergence if asked about inflation measurement. The circular flow of income : households supply factors of production to firms and receive factor incomes, which they spend back on firms' output. Withdrawals (leakages) : saving (S), taxation (T), imports (M). Injections : investment (I), government spending (G), exports (X). National income is in equilibrium when injections = withdrawals; if injections exceed withdrawals, income rises (expansion); if withdrawals exceed injections, income contracts. This frame explains why the multiplier works and why trade deficits drain demand. AD = C + I + G + (X − M) — total planned spending on domestic output at each price level; AD slopes downward because of the wealth effect (higher price level cuts real balances), the interest-rate effect (higher prices raise money demand and rates) and the exchange-rate effect (higher prices cut competitiveness). UK composition (approximate): C ≈ 60–63% of GDP — the largest and most stable component; I ≈ 17% — the most volatile (accelerator effects, confidence); G ≈ 18–20% (current plus capital spending); (X − M) is a small net figure but both flows are large (exports ≈ 30% of GDP). Determinants of each component (memorise the chains): C — disposable income, wealth (house prices), interest rates (saving return vs borrowing cost), confidence, credit availability; I — profit expectations/“animal spirits” (Keynes), interest rates (hurdle rate), accelerator (demand growth), corporation tax, spare capacity, credit; G — fiscal policy decisions; X − M — real exchange rate, world income, relative inflation, non-price competitiveness and quality. Diagram description: axes price level (vertical) and real output (horizontal); AD downward-sloping; a fall in any component shifts AD left from AD1 to AD2, moving equilibrium down the SRAS curve — lower price level, lower real output, a negative output gap and rising cyclical unemployment. SRAS is upward-sloping because some input costs (notably wages on fixed contracts, and other contracted prices) are sticky in the short run: a higher price level raises firms' margins, so output expands. SRAS shifts left when costs rise (oil, imported inputs, a depreciation raising import prices, wage settlements above productivity) and right when costs fall or productivity improves. The classical LRAS is vertical at the full-employment level of output (Yf): in the long run wages and prices are fully flexible, markets clear, and output returns to Yf regardless of AD — the economy is self-correcting ; extra AD raises only the price level. The Keynesian LRAS is reverse-L-shaped or upward-sloping: at low output (deep recession) it is flat, because spare capacity lets output rise without inflation; at high output it turns vertical as capacity binds. Keynesians argue wages are sticky downwards (contracts, minimum wage, morale, union resistance), so a fall in AD causes prolonged demand-deficient unemployment rather than instant wage/price adjustment. Diagram descriptions to memorise: (1) Classical: axes price level/real output; vertical LRAS at Yf; AD1→AD2 right shift moves equilibrium up LRAS — price level rises, output unchanged. (2) Keynesian: flat LRAS at low output; AD right shift raises output with little or no price rise (spare capacity absorbed); near the vertical section the same shift is mostly inflation. (3) SRAS left shift: costs rise (oil shock) → SRAS1→SRAS2 left → higher price level, lower output — stagflation. Assessment (which view fits the evidence?): the Keynesian view explains the medium run better — after 2008 and again after 2020, output gaps and elevated unemployment persisted for years, inconsistent with rapid classical self-correction; policy at the zero lower bound failed to restore full employment quickly. The classical view has force in the very long run: output did eventually recover as wages adjusted relatively and capital was reallocated; and stimulus near full capacity causes inflation rather than output (2021–22). Most economists accept a hybrid: the speed of self-correction depends on wage/price flexibility — this “depends on” judgement is the A* conclusion. Macroeconomic equilibrium : where AD intersects AS (SRAS in the short run; LRAS in the long run). If equilibrium output Y1 sits below potential output Yf there is a negative output gap — spare capacity, demand-deficient (cyclical) unemployment, downward pressure on inflation. If Y1 > Yf there is a positive output gap — overheating, demand-pull inflation, pressure on the current account as imports rise. Diagram description: mark Yf with a vertical dashed line; equilibrium left of it = negative gap (shade the distance); right of it = positive gap. Gaps close via self-correction (wage/price adjustment shifting SRAS) or policy (shifting AD). The four main UK macro objectives (AQA 4.2.1, Edexcel Theme 2.6): (1) sustainable economic growth — rising real GDP consistent with capacity, roughly 2–2.5% trend historically, though potential growth is now estimated near 1.5% by the OBR; (2) low and stable inflation — the 2% CPI target ±1 percentage point, set by HM Treasury and pursued by the Bank of England; (3) low unemployment — full employment at the natural rate (frictional + structural only), UK unemployment around 4–4.5% in 2024–25; (4) equilibrium in the balance of payments — broadly, a sustainable current account (the UK has run deficits of roughly 3–4% of GDP, financed by financial inflows). Secondary objectives: equitable income distribution, sound government finances, balanced regional growth, environmental sustainability. Conflicts between objectives (the core evaluation theme): growth vs inflation (AD expansion into capacity → demand-pull inflation — the Phillips-type trade-off); inflation vs unemployment (disinflation raises unemployment in the short run); growth vs the current account (income growth pulls in imports); growth vs government finances (stimulus raises borrowing; austerity slows growth); growth vs the environment (GDP growth raises emissions absent decoupling). Exam technique: 25-mark essays on objectives almost always ask you to weigh a benefit against a conflict — structure as “objective A improved, but at the cost of objective B, and the size of the trade-off depends on [elasticities, spare capacity, credibility]”. The multiplier (k) is the ratio of the final change in real GDP to the initial change in an injection: k = 1 / (1 − MPC) in the simple two-sector model, or more fully k = 1 / MPW where MPW (the marginal propensity to withdraw) = MPS + MPT + MPM. Process: an initial £50bn injection is paid to construction firms and workers, who spend 80% (with MPC = 0.8); those recipients spend 80% of that, and so on in a geometric series converging to £250bn (see the worked example below). The reverse also holds — the reverse multiplier: withdrawal of spending (fiscal austerity, a fall in exports) shrinks GDP by a multiple of the initial change, which is why 2010–13 Eurozone austerity deepened recessions. Size in practice: the UK's open economy has large leakages (high MPM, progressive taxation), so OBR central estimates of fiscal multipliers are around 0.6–1 (higher — above 1 — when the economy has spare capacity and monetary policy is accommodative; lower near full employment when the Bank of England offsets the stimulus). The simple 1/(1−MPC) formula overstates: it ignores imports, taxes, crowding out, time lags and capacity constraints. Uses in essays: the multiplier magnifies the effect of any AD shock — oil price rises, confidence collapses, export slumps — and magnifies policy responses; it interacts with the accelerator (investment responds to the growth of demand, not its level, so a slowing multiplier can trigger an investment slump). Evaluation points to deploy: the multiplier is larger when MPC is high (lower-income recipients spend more — targeting transfers at low-income households raises k), when spare capacity exists, and when leakages are small; it is smaller in open economies, near capacity, and if households save transfers (Ricardian-style caution) or the central bank offsets. Data anchor: UK MPC around 0.6–0.9 depending on income group; MPM is high enough that the open-economy multiplier is well below the closed-economy formula.

topics.name: Inflation, Unemployment and Growth
topics.subject: economics
topics.searchText: economics Economics Inflation, Unemployment and Growth Explain how CPI is constructed and evaluate its limitations as a measure of the cost of living Analyse the costs of inflation and deflation, including redistribution, fiscal drag and uncertainty Draw and shift AD/AS diagrams for demand-pull and cost-push inflation with full chains of reasoning Explain the short-run Phillips curve trade-off and why the long-run curve is vertical at the natural rate Evaluate the Phillips curve using the 1970s stagflation and the 2022–25 UK evidence Distinguish frictional, structural, seasonal and cyclical unemployment, and explain hysteresis Distinguish actual from potential growth and evaluate the UK productivity puzzle with data Inflation A sustained rise in the general price level; measured in the UK by CPI with a 2% target ±1 percentage point. CPI Consumer price index: a weighted basket of roughly 700 goods and services tracked by the ONS to measure consumer inflation. Demand-pull inflation Inflation caused by excess aggregate demand shifting AD right into the capacity-constrained region of AS. Cost-push inflation Inflation caused by rising costs of production shifting SRAS left (energy shocks, wage claims, imported inputs, depreciation). Phillips curve The short-run inverse trade-off between inflation and unemployment; the long-run Phillips curve is vertical at the natural rate (no permanent trade-off). Natural rate of unemployment (NRU/NAIRU) Frictional plus structural unemployment — the rate at which the labour market clears; only supply-side policy can lower it. Frictional unemployment Short-term unemployment from search and matching between jobs, caused by information gaps. Structural unemployment Long-term unemployment from a mismatch between workers' skills/location and available jobs, caused by industrial, technological or global change. Cyclical (demand-deficient) unemployment Unemployment caused by insufficient aggregate demand in a downturn; maps to the negative output gap. Hysteresis Cyclical unemployment becoming structural as the long-term unemployed lose skills and labour-force attachment, raising the natural rate. Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level; disinflation is a fall in the inflation rate; deflation is a sustained fall in the price level. CPI : the ONS surveys a basket of roughly 700 goods and services, weights each by its share of average household spending (updated annually), and tracks the price change of the weighted basket; weights are based on household expenditure surveys. RPI differs mainly by including mortgage interest payments and some housing costs, and by using an arithmetic-average formula that biases it upwards — the UK stopped using RPI as an official inflation measure in 2030-linked reforms and regulators have migrated to CPIH (CPI plus owner-occupier housing costs). Limitations of CPI (a standard data-response question): the basket is an average that misrepresents groups with different spending patterns (pensioners, renters vs owners); quality changes are imperfectly adjusted (hedonic adjustments); new products enter with a lag; and regional variation (London vs the North East) is masked. Costs of inflation : menu costs (repricing), shoe-leather costs (holding less cash), redistribution — from savers to borrowers when inflation is unexpected, and regressive effects when prices of essentials rise; fiscal drag — unindexed tax thresholds pull taxpayers into higher bands (frozen income tax thresholds to 2028 pushed millions into higher-rate bands); reduced international competitiveness — higher relative inflation makes exports dearer; uncertainty — planned investment falls, long contracts are avoided; and menu of distortions in business planning. Costs of deflation are often worse: consumers postpone purchases expecting lower prices, debt burdens rise in real terms (debt-deflation spiral — the 1930s and the Eurozone 2014–16), and the zero lower bound blocks monetary stimulus. Data anchors: UK CPI peaked at 11.1% in October 2022 (a 41-year high), returned to the 2% target in mid-2024, then rose above 3% in 2025 driven by energy, water and administered price rises — always quote the target (2% ±1) and a real figure in data responses. Demand-pull inflation : excess aggregate demand pulling the price level up — AD shifts right into the vertical (classical LRAS) or steep (Keynesian) region of AS. Diagram description: axes price level/real output; vertical LRAS at Yf; AD1→AD2 right shift moves equilibrium up LRAS — price level rises from P1 to P2 with output unchanged (at full capacity). Causes: any AD component rising faster than AS — tax cuts, low interest rates, wealth gains, booming world demand. Cost-push inflation : rising costs shift SRAS left — oil and energy shocks, imported input costs (including a depreciation), wage settlements above productivity growth, or administered price rises (regulated energy and water tariffs). Diagram description: SRAS1→SRAS2 left shift — price level rises, real output falls (stagflation). The monetarist view (quantity theory) : MV = PQ, so with V (velocity) and Q (output) stable in the long run, sustained money-supply growth translates into sustained inflation — “inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon” (Friedman). This underpins inflation targeting: control money growth/AD and inflation follows. Wage-price spiral and expectations : higher prices trigger wage demands; higher wages raise costs and prices further — expectations-augmented inflation. Imported inflation : a depreciation raises import prices directly (input costs → SRAS left) and via pass-through to consumer prices. Real-world application (the 2021–24 UK episode — an ideal essay case): the inflation surge was both demand-pull and cost-push — pandemic fiscal and monetary stimulus (furlough ~£70bn, QE to £895bn, Bank Rate 0.1%) met supply-side constraints (energy shock after Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, post-Brexit and pandemic supply frictions, labour shortages); the OBR and Bank of England judge that roughly half was imported energy shock and half excess demand. The disinflation of 2023–24 came from tightened monetary policy (Bank Rate to 5.25%), falling energy prices and easing supply chains — a chain-of-reasoning gift for evaluation paragraphs. The short-run Phillips curve (SRPC) shows an inverse relationship between inflation and unemployment: lower unemployment (a positive output gap) is associated with higher inflation, as excess demand tightens labour markets and raises wage settlements. Diagram description: axes inflation (vertical) against unemployment (horizontal); downward-sloping SRPC; a movement along it (e.g. from 5% inflation/3% unemployment to 2%/6%) shows the trade-off; shifts of SRPC (caused by expectations or supply shocks) move the whole curve. The expectations-augmented and long-run Phillips curve (LRPC) : monetarists (Friedman, Phelps) argue the trade-off is only temporary. Workers base wage demands on expected inflation; if unemployment is pushed below the natural rate (NRU/NAIRU) , actual inflation exceeds expected inflation, wages chase prices, SRPC shifts up, and unemployment returns to the NRU with higher inflation. Repeated attempts keep unemployment below NRU produce accelerating inflation. Hence the LRPC is vertical at the NRU : no permanent trade-off exists — only supply-side policy can lower the NRU. Diagram description: vertical LRPC at the natural rate (say 4%); successive SRPCs at higher expected inflation; a point moving up the vertical line shows inflation rising with unemployment stuck at NRU. Evidence and evaluation (A* material): the 1970s stagflation (oil shocks + wage-price spirals; UK inflation 24% in 1975 with unemployment rising) shattered the simple Phillips trade-off and supported monetarism. The 2022 UK episode supports a downward-sloping but flattening SRPC: inflation hit 11.1% with unemployment only ~3.6% (a strong trade-off on the demand side), but in 2023–25 inflation fell from 11% towards 3% while unemployment rose only to ~4–4.5% — a flatter trade-off than the 1970s, consistent with better-anchored inflation expectations (independent central bank, credible target) and weaker union power. The flatter the SRPC, the more output must be sacrificed to disinflate — and the more valuable central bank credibility becomes. Judgement frame: the short-run trade-off exists but its steepness depends on expectations credibility, labour-market flexibility and whether shocks are demand-side or supply-side; the long-run curve is vertical, so the sustainable way to cut unemployment is supply-side, not demand-side. Measurement : the ILO/Labour Force Survey counts as unemployed those without work, available to start and actively seeking — UK unemployment around 4–4.5% in 2024–25; the claimant count (claiming unemployment-related benefits) is cheaper to collect but understates (not all seekers claim) and overstates (some claimants are not genuinely seeking); economic inactivity (~21–22% of working-age adults — students, carers, long-term sick) sits outside both. Underemployment (workers in jobs below their skills or hours) is a further hidden measure. Types of unemployment : frictional — search and matching time between jobs (information gaps); structural — a mismatch between workers' skills/location and available jobs, caused by industrial change, technological change and globalisation (coal, steel, textiles; regional concentration); seasonal — agriculture, tourism, retail peaks; cyclical (demand-deficient) — insufficient AD in a downturn (negative output gap). The natural rate = frictional + structural — the unemployment rate at full employment, when the labour market clears. Diagram description (cyclical unemployment): AD1 intersecting SRAS at Y1 Hysteresis : cyclical unemployment becomes structural — the long-term unemployed lose skills, morale and attachment to the labour force (discouraged workers move into inactivity), and firms' capital is scrapped, so potential output falls and the natural rate rises. Evidence: the UK and much of Europe after the 1980s recessions saw persistently elevated unemployment for a decade — the key argument against letting recessions self-correct slowly (a direct criticism of the pure classical view). Costs of unemployment : lost output (the output gap itself), fiscal costs (benefits, lost tax revenue), scarring/hysteresis, social costs (crime, health), and regional divergence. Data anchors: UK unemployment peaked at ~11.9% in 1984 and ~8.5% in 2011; post-pandemic it stayed low (~3.6–4.5%) while inactivity rose — a useful nuance: low unemployment masked high inactivity, so the labour market was tighter than the headline rate suggested. Actual growth is the percentage change in real GDP — driven by AD (components C, I, G, X − M moving output towards capacity). Potential growth is the growth of productive capacity — driven by AS-side factors: labour (size, skills, participation), capital investment, technology and productivity. The economic cycle : boom (positive output gap, inflationary pressure), recession (two or more quarters of falling real GDP), recovery. Diagram description: a trend line of potential output with the actual path oscillating above (booms) and below (recessions) it; alternatively the AD/AS diagram with equilibrium swinging either side of Yf. UK cycle data: output fell ~11% in 2020, rebounded strongly in 2021, then stagnated (roughly 0.3–1% growth a year in 2022–24) — a rare prolonged stagnation rather than a classic V-shaped cycle. Causes of growth (chains): AD-driven recovery — lower rates, fiscal stimulus, export booms; potential-driven — investment in capital and infrastructure, education and training (human capital), immigration expanding the labour force (UK net migration peaked above 900,000 in 2023, easing labour shortages but straining housing and services), R&D and technological diffusion. The productivity puzzle (the UK's central growth issue): labour productivity growth has averaged under 0.5% a year since the 2008 financial crisis, versus over 2% before — the OBR judges the crisis left a permanent hole in potential output; explanations include weak business investment (post-Brexit and post-financial-crisis), regional disparities, low R&D intensity, and capital misallocation. Benefits of growth : higher living standards, employment, tax revenue (the fiscal dividend), and improved public services; costs : inflationary pressure near capacity, environmental damage (emissions rise with GDP absent decoupling), inequality if gains are unevenly shared, and balance-of-payments pressure as imports rise. Evaluation frame: distinguish actual from potential growth in every answer — demand-side policy can close an output gap but cannot raise the trend; only supply-side policy raises potential growth, and it works with long lags (see the Policy topic). The UK's stagnation since 2022 illustrates both: demand support stabilised employment, but trend growth requires the supply side.

topics.name: Policy: Fiscal, Monetary and Supply-Side
topics.subject: economics
topics.searchText: economics Economics Policy: Fiscal, Monetary and Supply-Side Distinguish discretionary fiscal policy from automatic stabilisers and explain the current budget position and national debt Evaluate fiscal policy using the multiplier, crowding out, time lags and the Laffer curve Explain the five channels of the monetary transmission mechanism with full chains of reasoning Analyse QE and QT and evaluate monetary policy at the zero lower bound and against supply-side shocks Classify supply-side policies as market-based or interventionist and evaluate each with time lags, cost and equity Identify conflicts between macroeconomic objectives and explain how the policy mix manages them Construct justified judgements on policy effectiveness using credibility, elasticities and the state of the cycle Fiscal policy The use of government spending and taxation to influence aggregate demand; expansionary (G↑/T↓) or contractionary (G↓/T↑). Automatic stabilisers Progressive taxation and welfare payments that dampen the economic cycle automatically, without new policy decisions. Budget deficit Government spending exceeding tax revenue in a year; adds to the national debt. UK roughly 4–5% of GDP in 2024–25. National debt The accumulated stock of past budget deficits; UK public sector net debt near 100% of GDP. Crowding out Government borrowing raising interest rates and squeezing private investment; stronger near full employment and with high debt. Monetary policy Central bank management of Bank Rate, quantitative easing/tightening and the money supply to meet the inflation target. Bank Rate The Bank of England's policy rate set by the MPC; transmits to market rates, consumption, investment, the exchange rate and asset prices. Quantitative easing (QE) Central bank purchase of bonds with central-bank money at the zero lower bound, lowering yields and easing credit conditions; UK balance sheet peaked ~£895bn. Transmission mechanism The channels through which Bank Rate affects AD: market rates → consumption, investment, exchange rate, asset prices and expectations. Supply-side policy Policies raising productive potential by shifting LRAS right: market-based (tax incentives, deregulation) or interventionist (education, infrastructure, R&D). Fiscal policy is the use of government spending (G) and taxation (T) to influence aggregate demand. Expansionary (G↑ and/or T↓) shifts AD right to boost growth and employment; contractionary (G↓ and/or T↑) shifts AD left to cut inflation. Discretionary policy — deliberate new decisions (a Budget package) — differs from automatic stabilisers : progressive taxation and welfare payments dampen the cycle without new decisions (in a recession, tax receipts fall and benefits rise automatically, cushioning disposable income and the multiplier). Diagram description: AD1→AD2 right shift from expansionary policy; the final output effect depends on the multiplier and spare capacity (flat vs vertical AS region). The budget position : a budget deficit (spending exceeds revenue; the UK's current budget deficit was roughly 4–5% of GDP in 2024–25) adds to the national debt (the stock of accumulated deficits; UK public sector net debt near 100% of GDP). Cyclically adjusted balance strips out the automatic stabilisers to reveal the underlying stance. Fiscal rules : the UK's current rules target debt falling as a share of GDP in the medium term and borrowing to cover only day-to-day spending by the end of the forecast horizon — rules anchor credibility but are tested by forecasts. Data anchor (the 2022 mini-budget — the textbook case): the September 2022 unfunded tax-cut package (£45bn) triggered a gilt-market crisis — yields spiked, the pound fell to near $1.03, pension funds using liability-driven investment faced margin calls, and the Bank of England intervened to restore orderly markets. Lesson: fiscal credibility matters; markets punish unfunded expansion near 100% debt-to-GDP. Recent UK fiscal policy: the Autumn 2024 Budget raised employer National Insurance contributions from 13.8% to 15% and cut the secondary threshold to £5,000 (raising ~£25bn a year), plus capital gains and inheritance changes — a tax-raising, spending-boosting package under new fiscal rules. The multiplier : the final change in GDP is a multiple of the initial injection — k = 1/(1 − MPC) in the simple model; k = 1/MPW in the open economy where MPW = MPS + MPT + MPM. UK OBR central estimates are around 0.6–1 (higher with spare capacity and accommodative monetary policy; lower near full employment). Crowding out : government borrowing raises demand for loanable funds, pushing up interest rates and squeezing private investment — the classical objection; crowding out is stronger near full employment and with high debt, weaker with spare capacity and at the zero lower bound (when the central bank is not offsetting). Ricardian-equivalence caution : households expecting future tax rises to repay debt may save transfers rather than spend them, shrinking the multiplier. Time lags : recognition lag (identifying the gap), implementation lag (Budget cycles, planning permission for infrastructure), impact lag (multiplier rounds take 1–2 years) — fiscal policy is slow relative to shocks; the 2020 furlough scheme shows policy can be fast when the machinery exists. The Laffer curve : beyond some tax rate, higher rates reduce revenue as incentives, avoidance and emigration respond — relevant to top-rate income tax and capital gains debates; the revenue-maximising rate is unknown, so tax elasticity is an empirical judgement. Sustainability and evaluation frame: with debt near 100% of GDP, the cost of borrowing (gilt yields) matters — a debt spiral (r > g) is the risk if markets doubt credibility; but austerity in a slump shrinks GDP via the reverse multiplier (the Eurozone 2010–13 experience). The A* judgement: fiscal policy is powerful when targeted at high-MPC households, when spare capacity exists, and when credibility is maintained; it is weak (crowded out, inflationary, slow) near capacity — so its effectiveness depends on the state of the cycle, the design of the package, and the credibility of the fiscal framework. Monetary policy : the central bank (Bank of England's nine-member MPC) sets Bank Rate to meet the 2% CPI target. The transmission mechanism (memorise the five channels): (1) higher Bank Rate raises commercial bank funding costs and market rates; (2) consumption (C) falls — saving returns rise, mortgage and credit costs rise, discretionary income falls; (3) investment (I) falls — hurdle rates for capital projects rise; (4) the currency appreciates (hot-money inflows seeking higher yields), making exports dearer and imports cheaper, so (X − M) falls; (5) asset prices (houses, equities) fall, adding wealth and collateral effects; plus expectations — credible policy anchors inflation expectations, reinforcing the effect. Net result: AD shifts left, dampening demand-pull inflation. Timing: long and variable lags — 12–18 months to affect inflation; the MPC therefore acts on forecasts. Quantitative easing (QE) : when Bank Rate is near zero (the zero lower bound), the central bank buys bonds (gilts, corporate bonds) with central-bank money: bond prices rise, yields fall, portfolio rebalancing pushes investors into riskier assets, credit conditions ease, and the currency may depreciate — AD shifts right. UK QE took the Bank's balance sheet to ~£895bn (2020 peak); quantitative tightening (QT) — running down the portfolio (from February 2022) — reverses these effects. Current stance (the data anchor): Bank Rate rose from 0.1% (Dec 2021) to 5.25% (Aug 2023) to fight the inflation surge, then was cut in stages to 4% by August 2025 as inflation fell towards target and growth weakened — the MPC balancing the inflation target against the output/stability objective. Evaluation: monetary policy cannot fix supply-side shocks (it faces the stagflation conflict — raising rates deepens the output fall); it is weak when confidence is low (liquidity trap — 2009–16, 2020); distributional effects (asset-price gains favour the wealthy; mortgage costs hit leveraged households); and independence from government insulates the target from political cycles — the credibility dividend that flattened the Phillips curve (see the Inflation topic). Supply-side policies aim to raise productive potential by shifting LRAS (and LRMC) right: higher potential output, a lower equilibrium price level, growth without inflation — and a lower natural rate of unemployment. Market-based policies (work through incentives): cutting corporation tax (the UK rate rose from 19% to 25% in April 2023 — the reverse direction, raising revenue but weakening incentives); full expensing (made permanent in the Autumn 2023 Statement) allowing immediate capital write-off, boosting investment; welfare reform to improve work incentives (cutting benefits raises the incentive gap but may increase poverty); labour-market flexibility (weaker employment protection — job creation vs job insecurity); privatisation and deregulation (competition vs negative externalities); trade liberalisation. Interventionist policies (state direct action): education and training investment (human capital — apprenticeships, Skills England); infrastructure (roads, rail, broadband, energy grid — the OBR estimated planning-reform measures could add measurable output by the end of the decade); R&D support (tax credits merged into a single R&D relief; the £20bn+ annual public R&D budget); childcare expansion (30 free hours from nine months, rolled out from 2024) to raise parental labour-force participation; regional policy (investment zones, devolution deals). Diagram description: LRAS (vertical line at Yf) shifts right to Yf2; with AD fixed, the price level falls and potential output rises; with AD also rising, growth occurs without inflation. Evaluation (the A* frame): time lags — a generation of schooling is needed before human capital raises productivity; infrastructure takes 5–15 years — supply-side policy cannot solve short-run demand-deficient unemployment; cost and opportunity cost — infrastructure spending raises borrowing (opportunity cost against health or debt reduction); uncertainty — tax cuts may be saved rather than invested (confidence-dependent); equity — benefit cuts increase inequality; deregulation can weaken environmental and labour protections; complementarity — LRAS shifts right only raise actual output if AD is sufficient to absorb the extra capacity. Evidence: East Asian growth was built on state-led investment in education and infrastructure plus export discipline; the UK's productivity puzzle (under 0.5% a year since 2008) shows the cost of under-supply-side effort. Judgement: supply-side policy is the only sustainable route to higher long-run growth and a better inflation–unemployment trade-off, but it works as a long-term programme with stable demand management — not a quick fix. Conflicts between objectives and instruments (the core 25-mark theme): (1) inflation vs growth/unemployment — contractionary policy to meet the 2% target raises unemployment and cuts growth (the short-run Phillips trade-off; Bank Rate 5.25% in 2023–24 deepened the growth slowdown); (2) growth vs government finances — stimulus raises deficits and debt (market credibility risk — the 2022 mini-budget); austerity cuts growth (Eurozone 2010–13); (3) growth vs the current account — income growth pulls in imports; depreciation helps net exports but is inflationary (the J-curve logic); (4) growth vs the environment — GDP growth raises emissions absent decoupling; carbon taxes restrain growth in carbon-intensive sectors; (5) equity vs efficiency — high redistribution may weaken incentives (Laffer logic), but inequality itself can depress human-capital investment. The policy mix (how conflicts are managed): assign instruments to objectives — monetary policy to inflation (independent central bank), fiscal policy to growth and the cycle (with rules for credibility), supply-side policy to potential growth and the natural rate. Stagflation example (the hardest case): a supply shock (2022) raises inflation and cuts output simultaneously — monetary tightening faces a direct conflict (rates to 5.25% fought inflation but deepened the slowdown); the standard resolution: tighten against inflation while protecting the most vulnerable (targeted fiscal support), and let supply-side measures address the underlying cost structure. Recession example: monetary and fiscal expansion are complements (no conflict when inflation is below target) — rate cuts plus infrastructure spending in 2020–21. Trade-offs and evaluation technique: every policy has at least one cost — the A* structure names the benefit, the cost, the factor that determines the size of the trade-off (elasticities, spare capacity, credibility, lags), and a justified judgement. Evaluation factors to deploy across all policies: time lags (monetary 12–18 months; supply-side years); size of the multiplier (spare capacity, MPC of recipients); credibility and expectations (independent central bank, fiscal rules); openness (leakages, exchange-rate feedback); distributional effects ; and government failure (information gaps, capture). Judgement template: “The policy achieves [objective] at the cost of [conflict]; the size of the trade-off depends on [factor]; on balance, [judgement] given the current state of the cycle and the credibility of the framework.”

topics.name: International Trade and Development
topics.subject: economics
topics.searchText: economics Economics International Trade and Development Calculate opportunity-cost ratios, identify comparative advantage and explain the gains from trade and the terms-of-trade window Evaluate comparative advantage theory using its assumptions: constant costs, transport costs, mobility and dynamic advantage Draw the tariff diagram in words, marking consumer loss, producer gain, government revenue and the two deadweight losses Evaluate the arguments for and against protectionism with real examples (US 2025 tariffs, EU EV duties, Smoot–Hawley) Distinguish trade creation from trade diversion and evaluate trade blocs including Brexit and the UK's CPTPP accession Explain floating, fixed and managed exchange rate systems, the Marshall–Lerner condition and the J-curve effect Analyse the balance of payments structure and evaluate development strategies: export-led growth vs import substitution, aid, FDI and debt relief Absolute advantage A country can produce more of a good with the same resources than another country. Comparative advantage A country can produce a good at a lower opportunity cost than another country — the basis for specialisation and trade (Ricardo). Tariff A tax on imports, raising the domestic price, cutting consumption, raising domestic production and government revenue, and creating deadweight losses. Trading bloc A group of countries reducing trade barriers between themselves — free trade area, customs union, common market or monetary union. Trade creation Joining a bloc replaces high-cost domestic production with lower-cost production from members — an efficiency gain. Trade diversion Joining a bloc replaces lower-cost imports from non-members with higher-cost imports from members — an efficiency loss. Marshall–Lerner condition A devaluation improves the current account only if the sum of the price elasticities of demand for exports and imports exceeds 1. J-curve effect After a devaluation, the current account initially deteriorates (fixed contracts, inelastic short-run demand) before improving as elasticities rise — tracing a J shape. Balance of payments The record of all transactions with the rest of the world: current account (goods, services, income, transfers), capital and financial accounts; the accounts sum to zero. Human Development Index (HDI) The UNDP index (0–1) combining life expectancy, education (mean and expected years of schooling) and GNI per capita (PPP). Absolute advantage : a country can produce more of a good with the same resources. Comparative advantage : a country can produce a good at a lower opportunity cost — the basis of trade (Ricardo). Gains from trade : specialisation according to comparative advantage raises total world output; both countries can consume beyond their production possibility frontier (PPF) through trade at terms of trade between the two opportunity-cost ratios. Worked example (real exam-style calculation): Country A: 10 labour hours produce 1 unit of cloth or 5 of wine; Country B: 6 hours produce 1 cloth or 4 wine. Opportunity costs — A: 1 cloth = 2 wine (10/5), 1 wine = 0.5 cloth; B: 1 cloth = 0.67 wine (6/4), 1 wine = 1.5 cloth. B has the comparative advantage in cloth (lower opportunity cost, 0.67 Mark-scheme logic: [AO1] define comparative vs absolute advantage; [AO2] compute opportunity-cost ratios accurately; [AO3] explain specialisation and the terms-of-trade window. Assumptions and limits (the evaluation engine): the theory assumes constant opportunity costs (linear PPFs) — real PPFs are concave, so complete specialisation is never optimal; no transport costs ; perfect factor mobility within countries but immobility between them (structural unemployment from specialisation — the classic cost); no exchange-rate complications ; perfect information ; and it ignores dynamic comparative advantage — advantage can be created (South Korea moving from textiles to electronics through investment, not endowment). Patterns of trade : the rise of China and emerging economies (China ≈ 15% of world goods exports), commodity exporters' dependence on primary products, and intra-industry trade (similar goods traded both ways within the EU) driven by economies of scale and product differentiation — which the simple theory cannot explain. Evaluation frame: trade raises world output but its distribution within countries creates winners (consumers, exporters) and losers (import-competing workers) — the source of the protectionist backlash (see the next section); and the terms of trade determine how the gains are shared. Protectionism — restricting free trade — uses: tariffs (taxes on imports), quotas (quantity limits), subsidies to domestic producers, voluntary export restraints (VERs) , administrative barriers (standards, customs delays), and exchange-rate manipulation . Diagram description (tariff): partial equilibrium — axes price/quantity; the world price Pw is a horizontal line (the country is a price taker); domestic demand D and supply S. At Pw: domestic demand Qd, domestic supply Qs, imports = Qd − Qs. A tariff shifts the effective import supply up to Pw + tariff: domestic price rises; Qd falls to Qd1, Qs rises to Qs1; imports shrink to Qd1 − Qs1. Welfare: consumer surplus falls (areas A + B + C + D); producers gain A; government gains tariff revenue C (tariff × import volume); B (production distortion) and D (consumption distortion) are deadweight losses — welfare destroyed with no offsetting gain. Evaluation: the size of the DWL depends on elasticities (the more elastic demand and supply, the larger the loss); the tariff is regressive (essentials hit low-income households hardest); retaliation is likely and shrinks export markets; the large-country case — a big economy's tariff can lower the world price, shifting part of the burden to foreign producers (optimal tariff argument) — but only for large economies. Real-world anchors: the US tariff escalation of 2025 (25% on steel and aluminium from March 2025; 10%+ “reciprocal” tariffs from April 2025), the EU's duties on Chinese electric vehicles (up to ~45% combined, from October 2024), and the classic cautionary tale of the Smoot–Hawley tariff (1930), which deepened the Depression through retaliation. Arguments for protectionism (know both sides): infant industry — temporary protection lets new industries reach the scale to compete (dynamic comparative advantage created); anti-dumping — countering below-cost exports; employment protection — shielding import-competing jobs (politically powerful); revenue — tariffs fund governments with weak tax systems (historically the US's main revenue source); national security — strategic industries (defence, semiconductors, energy); current account correction — reducing imports. Arguments against: DWL and higher prices for consumers; retaliation and trade wars; reduced competition → X-inefficiency in protected firms; regressive incidence; and global inefficiency — production shifts from low-cost to high-cost producers. The A* judgement: the case for protection depends on the infant-industry argument being credible (temporary, exit-credible protection) and on retaliation being avoided — both empirically fragile; the Smoot–Hawley precedent shows the systemic risk. Types of trade bloc (increasing integration): a free trade area (tariffs removed between members, external tariffs set nationally — EFTA); a customs union (common external tariff — the EU Customs Union); a common market/single market (free movement of goods, services, capital and labour — the EU's four freedoms); an economic and monetary union (shared currency and monetary policy — the Eurozone, 20 members). Other blocs: USMCA (2020, replacing NAFTA), ASEAN, and CPTPP — the UK acceded and it took effect from December 2024. The WTO sets trade rules, administers dispute settlement (binding panels), and promotes liberalisation (the Doha Round stalled — multilateral liberalisation has given way to regional deals). Trade creation vs trade diversion (the core analysis, Viner): joining a bloc creates trade when high-cost domestic production is replaced by lower-cost production from a member (efficiency gain); it diverts trade when lower-cost production from a non-member is replaced by higher-cost production from a member (efficiency loss — the external tariff does it). Chain of reasoning: customs union formed → internal tariffs fall → member goods cheaper → imports from members rise (creation); but the common external tariff makes non-member goods relatively dearer → imports shift from efficient non-members to less efficient members (diversion). Net welfare depends on which dominates — determined by the height of the external tariff and cost differences between members and non-members. Real-world evaluation anchors: Brexit — the OBR judges the UK–EU trade arrangements will reduce long-run productivity by roughly 15% relative to remaining in the EU (trade diversion plus higher frictions: customs checks, rules-of-origin, services barriers); the UK's CPTPP accession (effective December 2024) partially diversifies trade (CPTPP covers ~15% of world GDP); the EU single market's four freedoms deliver scale economies and intra-industry trade, but monetary union without fiscal union produced the 2010–13 Eurozone crises (Greece, Ireland, Portugal). The A* judgement: deeper blocs raise trade among members but the welfare effect depends on trade creation dominating diversion; the EU's single market created trade, while Brexit arrangements diverted it — and the distribution of gains within countries (left-behind regions) drives the politics of trade. Exchange rate systems : floating — the market determines the rate (the pound since 1992; the UK left the ERM on “Black Wednesday”, 16 September 1992, after defending a peg proved unsustainable); fixed — pegged to another currency (the Hong Kong dollar peg; the CFA franc); managed (dirty) float — market-determined with occasional central-bank intervention. Determination in a floating system : demand for the currency (exports, FDI inflows, hot money seeking yields) vs supply (imports, outflows); a rise in UK interest rates attracts hot money, appreciating the currency. Purchasing power parity (PPP) : identical goods should cost the same in a common currency in the long run — deviations signal over/undervaluation (the Big Mac index); PPP holds poorly in the short run. Effects of an appreciation : exports dearer, imports cheaper — (X − M) falls, AD shifts left; inflation falls (import prices); growth slows; the current account worsens if elasticities are adequate. Effects of a depreciation : exports cheaper, imports dearer — AD shifts right, but imported inflation raises input costs, shifting SRAS left: growth with a price rise. The Marshall–Lerner condition : a devaluation improves the current account only if PEDx + PEDm > 1 (demand for exports and imports is elastic overall). The J-curve effect : after devaluation the current account initially deteriorates (contracts fixed, quantities respond slowly — inelastic short-run demand), then recovers and improves as elasticities rise in the long run — tracing a J shape. Diagram description: axes time (horizontal) and current account balance (vertical); the line dips below its starting level, troughs, then rises above it — the J; annotate the Marshall–Lerner condition holding only after the trough. Real-world anchor: sterling fell ~10–15% after the June 2016 referendum; the current account did not improve as hoped (services and investment income effects), and inflation rose ~1–2 points — Marshall–Lerner held weakly. The balance of payments records all transactions with the rest of the world: the current account (trade in goods, trade in services, primary income — investment income, secondary income — transfers); the capital account (small: capital transfers); and the financial account (FDI, portfolio investment, reserve assets). The accounts must sum to zero: a current account deficit is financed by financial inflows. UK data anchor: the UK runs a persistent current account deficit of roughly 3–4% of GDP (it peaked near 5% in 2016), with a large services surplus (the UK is the world's second-largest services exporter) offset by a chronic goods deficit. Evaluation: a deficit is not automatically bad — if financed by FDI (productive capital) it funds growth; if financed by hot money it is fragile (sudden stops); persistent deficits signal uncompetitiveness or overconsumption. Disequilibrium under fixed rates forces painful internal adjustment (austerity, deflation — the Eurozone periphery 2010–13); floating rates adjust automatically but with J-curve lags and inflation costs. Measuring development : the HDI (UNDP, 0–1) combines life expectancy at birth, education (mean and expected years of schooling) and GNI per capita (PPP) — a broader measure than GDP per capita; the UK scores around 0.94 (very high human development), while the lowest-ranked countries score around 0.4. Inequality : the Gini coefficient (0 = perfect equality, 1 = perfect inequality; UK disposable-income Gini ≈ 0.35) and the Lorenz curve (cumulative income share against cumulative population share; the further the bow from the 45° line, the greater the inequality — the Gini is the area ratio between them). The World Bank classifies countries by GNI per capita: low income ≈ $1,145 or below (2025 threshold); the international poverty line is $2.15/day (2017 PPP), recently rebased to $3.00/day (2021 PPP). Barriers to development : primary product dependency — volatile commodity prices and declining terms of trade (the Prebisch–Singer hypothesis: primary exporters' terms of trade deteriorate over time, since manufactured goods' incomes rise faster); savings gap (the Harrod–Domar logic — low incomes → low savings → low investment); foreign currency gap ; debt — unsustainable burdens (the HIPC initiative and subsequent restructurings — Zambia's 2020 default restructured from 2023, Sri Lanka's 2022 default restructured 2024–25); poor infrastructure and institutions ; capital flight ; disease and demographics . Development strategies (the classic essay): import-substitution industrialisation (ISI) — protect infant industries behind tariffs/quotas to replace imports (Latin America, 1950s–70s); export-led growth — promote industries competing in world markets (the East Asian tigers: South Korea, Taiwan; then China). Arguments for export-led: world competition forces efficiency and innovation; economies of scale from a global market; export earnings provide foreign currency for capital goods and debt service; attracts FDI and technology transfer — the tigers grew 8–10% a year for decades while ISI economies stagnated. Arguments for ISI: infant industries need temporary protection to reach competitive scale; reduces dependence on volatile primary exports; preserves foreign exchange and jobs. Other strategies: aid (tied vs untied; the UK's aid target was cut from 0.7% to 0.5% of GNI in 2021 — aid fills the savings gap but risks dependency, distortion and capture); FDI (brings capital, technology and jobs but profits repatriate and enclaves can form); microfinance (small loans to the unbanked — Grameen model; helps marginal enterprise but effects are modest at scale); debt relief (HIPC — frees fiscal space but moral hazard if discipline is absent). Evaluation (the A* frame): ISI frequently failed — protected industries never became efficient (no competitive pressure), small domestic markets limited scale, and lobbying entrenched rent-seeking; but export-led growth has risks — dependence on world demand (2008 hit hard), suppressed wages and undervalued exchange rates, and the East Asian success also reflected strong state investment in education and infrastructure, not exports alone. Judgement: the evidence favours export-led growth for most developing economies, provided it is supported by human-capital investment, macroeconomic stability and institutions — the East Asian model is a package, not a single lever.

topics.name: Social Influence
topics.subject: psychology
topics.searchText: psychology Psychology Social Influence Explain and evaluate the three types of conformity and the dual-process explanations NSI and ISI (AQA 4.1.1) Describe Asch's research and situational variables affecting conformity, with AO3 evaluation (AQA 4.1.1) Outline Milgram's baseline obedience study and situational variables; explain agency theory and legitimacy of authority (AQA 4.1.1; Edexcel Topic 1) Explain resistance to social influence: social support and locus of control; authoritarian personality (AQA 4.1.1) Describe and evaluate Moscovici's minority influence research and the role of influence processes in social change (AQA 4.1.1) Evaluate social influence research: ethics, lab methods, cultural bias, demand characteristics (OCR Component 2) Conformity: compliance (public only, NSI), identification (group membership), internalisation (true belief, ISI); Asch: 75% conformed at least once, 32% on critical trials Asch variables: group size (plateaus at 3 confederates), unanimity (dissenter drops conformity to ~5%), task difficulty (harder = more ISI) Obedience: Milgram (1963) 65% to 450V, 40 male volunteers, Yale, prods; agency theory (agentic vs autonomous state), legitimacy of authority, gradual commitment, buffers Situational variables in obedience: proximity (same room 40%, touch 30%), location (run-down office 47.5%), uniform (65% lab coat vs 20% ordinary clothes) Resistance: social support (ally breaks unanimity; Gamson 88% rebelled in groups), locus of control (internals resist); authoritarian personality (Adorno F-scale; Elms & Milgram) Minority influence: consistency, commitment (augmentation), flexibility (Nemeth); Moscovici 8.4% of trials with consistent minority; snowball effect, social cryptomnesia Social change: Suffragettes and civil rights show minority influence; Milgram's obedience research explains why resistance is hard; NSI via social norms (Nolan et al. 2008 energy conservation) Conformity A change in a person's behaviour or opinion as a result of real or imagined group pressure (majority influence). Compliance Publicly conforming to the majority while privately keeping one's own views - a superficial, temporary change driven by normative social influence. Identification Conforming to the role or group we value and adopting its views publicly and privately while we remain a member of the group. Internalisation Accepting the group's views both publicly and privately - the deepest, most permanent form of conformity, driven by informational social influence. Normative social influence (NSI) Conforming in order to be liked and accepted by the group (an emotional process), producing compliance; fear of rejection drives it. Informational social influence (ISI) Conforming because we are uncertain and assume the majority is correct (a cognitive process), producing internalisation; most likely with ambiguous or difficult tasks. Agentic state Milgram's mental state in which we see ourselves as an agent of an authority figure, allowing them to act as a moral proxy and reducing our sense of responsibility for harm (moral strain). Legitimacy of authority The extent to which an order from a person with higher status or position is perceived as justified - strengthened by institutions (e.g. universities, uniforms). Locus of control (Rotter, 1966) The sense of control we have over our own outcomes: internals believe they control events and are more resistant to social influence; externals believe outcomes are due to luck or powerful others. Augmentation principle In minority influence, when a minority is willing to make personal sacrifices for its position (e.g. hunger strikes), observers assume the position must be stronger, boosting influence. Conformity is a change in behaviour or opinion as a result of real or imagined group pressure. Kelman (1958) distinguished three types, defined by depth and permanence: compliance (publicly going along with the majority while privately keeping one's own views - superficial and temporary, stopping once group pressure is removed, e.g. laughing at a joke you do not find funny), identification (conforming to the role or group we value and adopting its views while we remain a member - e.g. a new army recruit adopting regimental attitudes) and internalisation (accepting the group's views both publicly and privately - the deepest and most permanent form, e.g. becoming vegetarian after joining an environmental campaign group). Dual-process explanations explain why we conform. Normative social influence (NSI) : we conform to be liked and accepted - an emotional process driven by fear of rejection, producing compliance. Evidence: in Asch's post-experiment interviews many conformers said they did not want to look foolish even though they knew the answers were wrong; Schachter (1951) found those who deviated were rejected by discussion groups. NSI is strongest with strangers (anonymity lets people resist - a variation where responses were written privately reduced conformity) and with friends, where acceptance matters most. Informational social influence (ISI) : we conform because we are uncertain and assume the majority is correct - a cognitive process producing internalisation. Evidence: Jenness (1932) - participants' second estimates of beans in a jar shifted towards the group estimate; Lucas et al. (2006) found ISI was greater for harder maths problems, showing uncertainty increases ISI. The A* distinction: NSI is about being liked , ISI about being right ; both probably operate together in most real conformity. Asch (1951, 1956) tested conformity using line judgments: 123 US male undergraduates sat with 6-8 confederates who deliberately gave wrong answers on 12 of 18 'critical' trials. Findings: 75% conformed at least once ; 32% of critical trials were conformed to; 25% never conformed. Participants who conformed reported doubting their own perception (distortion of judgement) or knowing they were wrong but conforming to fit in. Asch's variables : (1) group size - 1 confederate produced 3% conformity, 2 produced 13%, 3 reached 32%, after which adding more made little difference (unanimity matters more than size); (2) unanimity - the presence of a dissenter (who gave a different wrong answer) dropped conformity to about 5% , showing a single ally liberates independent behaviour; (3) task difficulty - making the line lengths more similar raised conformity, suggesting ISI increased when the task became more ambiguous. Evaluation (AO3): Artificial task: line judgments are trivial - low ecological validity and possibly demand characteristics, as participants knew they were in a study (though conformity was still substantial). Historical/cultural limitations: Perrin and Spencer (1980) repeated the study with UK engineering students in the 1980s and found only one conforming response in 396 trials - suggesting conformity dropped in a less conformist era, though their sample (experts) was also unsuited to the task. Cultural bias: Smith and Bond's (1997) meta-analysis found mean conformity of 31% in individualist cultures (US, UK) versus 53% in collectivist cultures (China, Africa), suggesting Asch's findings are culture-bound and that conformity is adaptive in collectivist societies. Ethics: participants were deceived (confederates, fake trials) and may have experienced distress; Asch debriefed all participants afterwards. Support from Crutchfield (1955): using booths to avoid group face-to-face pressure still produced ~30% conformity, showing social influence operates without direct interaction. Obedience is a form of social influence in which a person follows a direct order, usually from a figure of authority. Milgram (1963) recruited 40 male volunteers (paid $4.50) through a newspaper advert for a supposed study of learning at Yale University. Participants played the 'teacher', delivering what they believed were electric shocks from 15V to 450V each time the 'learner' (a confederate, Mr Wallace) made an error, with four standardised prods such as 'The experiment requires that you continue'. Findings: 65% went to the full 450V ; 100% went to 300V; only 5% stopped at 300V. Milgram also recorded extreme distress - sweating, trembling, three participants had seizures. The study was supposed to show the 'Germans are different' hypothesis was false: ordinary Americans obeyed destructive orders. Situational variables (Milgram's later experiments, 1963-1974): proximity - teacher and learner in the same room dropped obedience to 40%; the teacher forcing the learner's hand onto a shock plate gave 30%; the experimenter giving orders by telephone gave 2.5% at 450V (proximity of the victim and authority both matter, with buffers allowing distance to reduce moral strain). Location - moving the study to a run-down office block in Bridgeport dropped obedience to 47.5%, showing the legitimacy of the institution contributes. Uniform - when the experimenter was called away and an ordinary member of the public (in everyday clothes) took over giving orders, obedience fell to 20%; uniforms (lab coat, police) are powerful symbols of legitimate authority - supported by Bickman (1973), where passers-by were more likely to pick up litter or give coins to a man dressed as a security guard than as a milkman or civilian. Agency theory (Milgram, 1973) explains why people obey: in the autonomous state we behave independently and feel responsible for our actions; under an authority we experience the agentic shift into the agentic state , seeing ourselves as agents of the authority who acts as our moral proxy - so responsibility for harm shifts away from us ( moral strain ). Binding factors (aspects of the situation that keep us in the agentic state) include fear of appearing rude, gradual commitment (foot-in-the-door: 15V increments make each step feel minor) and buffers separating us from the consequences of our actions. Legitimacy of authority : orders from people of higher status are accepted as justified, especially when backed by institutions - explaining the location effect above. The dispositional alternative - the authoritarian personality (Adorno, 1950) : strict, punishing childhood experiences with conditional love create hostility displaced onto weaker people, extreme respect for authority and conventionalism - measured with the F-scale . Elms and Milgram (1966) found that fully obedient participants scored higher on the F-scale than disobedient ones, supporting a dispositional contribution. Evaluation (AO3): Demand characteristics: Orne and Holland (1968) argued participants guessed the shocks were fake because of the unrealistic setup; however, Sheridan and King (1972) found that when participants believed a real puppy was receiving real shocks, 20 of 26 (77%) delivered the maximum - supporting Milgram's conclusion that obedience is genuine. Ecological validity: Milgram's lab was artificial, but Hofling et al. (1966) found 21 of 22 nurses obeyed a doctor's telephone order to give an excessive drug dose (clearly breaching rules), supporting ecological validity in a real hospital setting. Ethics: Baumrind (1964) criticised deception and lack of protection from harm; Milgram responded that participants were debriefed, and 84% later reported being 'glad to have taken part'. Alternative explanation: Haslam and Reicher (2012) used social identity theory - participants obeyed because they identified with the scientific goals of the experiment ('engaged followership'), not because of blind agentic thinking; Reicher and Haslam (2011) showed followership rose and fell with participants' identification with the cause. Methodological strength: highly standardised prods and controls make the procedure replicable and internally valid; replications across cultures (e.g. Meeus and Raaijmakers 1986, 92% of Dutch participants obeying orders to harass a job applicant) support generalisability. Social support helps resist conformity and obedience because the presence of an ally breaks unanimity and provides an independent model. In Asch's dissenter variation, conformity fell to about 5% when one confederate gave the correct answer; if the dissenting confederate defected back to the majority, conformity rose again - showing unanimity rather than the answer itself was key. Allen and Levine (1971) found that a dissenter who wore thick glasses and claimed vision problems was just as effective, showing even invalid support liberates resistance. Gamson et al. (1982) provide real-world support: groups of participants were ordered by a fictional company (Hydro Petroleum) to produce evidence to help a company smear an oil leak on a local beach; in groups, participants could discuss and share responsibility, and 88% rebelled - showing that peer support and shared responsibility undermine legitimate authority. Locus of control (Rotter, 1966) is a dispositional explanation of resistance: internals believe they control their own outcomes (effort determines success), while externals believe outcomes are due to luck, fate or powerful others. Internals are predicted to be more resistant to social influence because they take responsibility for their own actions, are more achievement-oriented and more likely to resist pressure to conform. Evidence: Oliner and Oliner (1988) interviewed over 400 non-Jewish people who protected Jews during the Holocaust and compared them with non-rescuers; rescuers scored higher on internal locus of control and were more likely to have displayed social responsibility. Holland (1967) repeated Milgram-type obedience with internals and externals: 37% of internals did not continue to 450V versus only 23% of externals. Evaluation (AO3): Measurement problem: locus of control is measured by self-report questionnaire (Rotter's IE scale), vulnerable to social desirability and low temporal validity - Twenge et al. (2004) found that young people's locus of control became more external between 1960 and 2002, alongside rises in anxiety and depression, which is inconsistent with the prediction that modern life makes people more internal and resistant. Correlational evidence: most support for locus of control is correlational, so a third variable (e.g. confidence, self-esteem) may drive both resistance and internal scores. Situational power sometimes wins: in strong situations (Milgram, Zimbardo) even high-internal individuals obeyed, suggesting locus of control explains only mild pressure - Asch-type situations - rather than obedience to authority. Practical application: resistance programmes (e.g. smoking resistance training with social support) show that allies reliably reduce peer pressure, supporting the social support explanation. Minority influence occurs when a small group or individual changes the views of the majority. Moscovici et al. (1969) : 172 participants in groups of six (4 real participants, 2 confederates) judged the colour of 36 blue slides in an unambiguous task. Findings: a consistent minority (calling all 36 slides green) influenced real participants on 8.4% of trials , and 32% conformed at least once; an inconsistent minority (calling slides green only 24 times) influenced just 1.25% of trials - consistency is essential. A control group without confederates answered incorrectly on only 0.25% of trials. Three factors determine minority influence: (1) consistency - synchronic (all members agree with each other) and diachronic (agreeing over time); consistency makes others think the minority must have a good reason, suggesting the position is correct (ISI). (2) Commitment - personal sacrifice (e.g. hunger strikes) triggers the augmentation principle : observers assume the minority would not suffer for a weak position, so influence increases. (3) Flexibility - Nemeth (1986) argued that rigid, dogmatic minorities are off-putting; a minority that accepts compromise appears reasonable and cooperative. In Nemeth's mock jury study, when a minority negotiated (proposing to share the compensation payment), influence rose compared with a stubborn minority. The process : the minority draws attention to the issue, creates conflict in the majority (deep processing, unlike the shallow compliance of majority influence), demonstrates commitment via augmentation, and eventually produces the snowball effect (minority becomes majority) - leaving social cryptomnesia , where people remember the change but forget its origins. Social change applies the same processes: the Suffragettes (consistent messages from 1903, commitment via hunger strikes and Emily Davison's death) gradually won women the vote; the US civil rights movement (Rosa Parks's 1955 refusal, Martin Luther King's consistent non-violent campaigning) used augmentation and the snowball effect. Normative influence also drives social change : Nolan et al. (2008) hung messages on Californian doors stating most residents were trying to reduce energy use ('majority of neighbours agree') and caused significant decreases in energy consumption versus messages about the environment alone - showing NSI is a powerful tool for social change. Milgram's gradual commitment explains why obedience to authority can block social change; his own research illustrates that disobedient peers (dissenters) help others refuse. Evaluation (AO3): Artificial task: Moscovici's colour judgment is trivial, unlike real campaigns (e.g. civil rights) where stakes are high and emotions engaged - limiting generalisability (minority influence may be stronger when issues matter). Consistency is necessary but not sufficient: real minorities need resources, organisation and social/political context; research oversimplifies the process. Methodological support: Wood et al.'s (1994) meta-analysis of nearly 100 studies confirmed that consistent minorities were most influential, supporting Moscovici's central claim. Real-world application: Nemeth applied minority influence to legal decision-making (juries), and public health campaigns use the snowball effect and normative messages - showing ecological validity in application. Difference from majority influence: majority influence produces shallow compliance, minority influence deep processing (internalisation) - a distinction examiners reward when explaining social change. Zimbardo (1971-73, Stanford Prison Experiment) : 21 male volunteers (screened as psychologically stable) randomly assigned to guards or prisoners in a mock prison in the basement of Stanford University; the planned two-week study was stopped after six days because prisoners showed extreme distress (hunger strikes, crying) while guards became increasingly brutal. Zimbardo concluded that the situation (roles, uniforms, institutional power), not personality, caused the behaviour - supporting a situational explanation of social influence. However, the 'John Wayne' guard later admitted he had deliberately played a cruel role because he thought it was expected of guards, suggesting demand characteristics ; Zimbardo also took part as the prison superintendent, blurring the line between researcher and participant. Haslam and Reicher (2006, BBC Prison Study) found guards did not spontaneously identify with their roles and refused to impose power, suggesting tyranny requires an identity-based commitment to a role rather than blind situational forces - a direct challenge to Zimbardo. General evaluation of social influence research (AO3) - a bank of points usable across all essay questions: Lab experiments (Asch, Milgram, Moscovici): high control, standardised procedures and replicability; but artificial, low mundane realism, possible demand characteristics and deception. Ethics: deception (confederates), lack of informed consent, protection from harm (Milgram's distressed participants; Zimbardo's prisoners) - all studies would need full debriefing and modern BPS safeguards; the studies nevertheless drove the development of ethical guidelines.
