The PNS splits into the somatic nervous system (voluntary control of skeletal muscles; sensory neurons carry information to the CNS, motor neurons carry commands to muscles) and the autonomic nervous system (ANS) (involuntary control of internal organs: heart rate, digestion, breathing). The ANS further divides into the sympathetic branch (arouses the body - increases heart rate, inhibits digestion, prepares for action) and the parasympathetic branch (calms the body - 'rest and digest', conserves energy). The branches are antagonistic: sympathetic dominance raises heart rate, parasympathetic dominance lowers it back. Neurons transmit electrical and chemical signals. Structure: dendrites (receive signals from other neurons), cell body (contains the nucleus), axon (carries the impulse; wrapped in a myelin sheath for insulation, with nodes of Ranvier where the impulse 'jumps', speeding conduction) and terminal buttons (communicate with the next cell across the synapse). Types: sensory neurons (carry messages from receptors to the CNS; cell body in a dorsal root ganglion, long dendrites), relay/intermediate neurons (within the CNS, connecting sensory to motor neurons; short dendrites and axons) and motor neurons (carry messages from the CNS to effectors - muscles and glands; long axons, short dendrites). Electrical transmission is via the action potential : an all-or-nothing impulse firing down the axon when the threshold (~-55mV) is reached, with resting potential (~-70mV) maintained by the Na⁺/K⁺ pump. The reflex arc is the basic unit of nervous action: stimulus → sensory neuron → relay neuron (in the spinal cord) → motor neuron → effector (muscle). The arc is fast and unconscious because it bypasses the brain entirely (e.g. withdrawing a hand from a hot stove), and it demonstrates the automatic, protective function of the spinal cord. Evaluation (AO3): Strength - biological support: neuroimaging and lesion studies confirm the divisions (ANS arousal measured physiologically - heart rate, skin conductance) and the neuron structure is universally accepted neuroscience. Limitation - simplification: the textbook three-neuron reflex arc is the simplest case; most neural circuits involve interneuron networks and neuromodulation far more complex than the model suggests. Application: understanding the ANS underpins biofeedback therapy (controlling sympathetic arousal in anxiety) and explains stress responses measured in research. Synaptic transmission is chemical communication between neurons. Process: (1) an action potential arrives at the presynaptic terminal button, opening voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels ; (2) Ca²⁺ influx causes synaptic vesicles to fuse with the presynaptic membrane, releasing neurotransmitters into the synaptic cleft by exocytosis; (3) neurotransmitters diffuse across the cleft and bind to specific receptors on the postsynaptic membrane; (4) binding produces an excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP) - depolarising the membrane and increasing firing (e.g. adrenaline, glutamate) - or an inhibitory postsynaptic potential (IPSP) - hyperpolarising and decreasing firing (e.g. GABA, serotonin); (5) neurotransmitters are cleared by reuptake into the presynaptic neuron (the target of SSRI drugs, which block serotonin reuptake) or broken down by enzymes. Summation decides whether the postsynaptic neuron fires: temporal summation (rapid repeated releases from one neuron add up) and spatial summation (simultaneous releases from several neurons) must jointly exceed the threshold. Synapses are unidirectional (vesicles only on the presynaptic side, receptors only postsynaptic). The endocrine system communicates via hormones - chemical messengers released by glands into the bloodstream, slower than neural transmission but longer-lasting. The pituitary gland ('master gland') controls other glands under hypothalamic direction; the adrenal glands release adrenaline (adrenal medulla) and cortisol (adrenal cortex); the pineal gland releases melatonin (regulating sleep); the thyroid releases thyroxine (metabolism). Fight-or-flight response : a stressor is perceived (e.g. threat) → the hypothalamus activates the sympathetic branch of the ANS and the pituitary -adrenal (HPA) axis → the adrenal medulla releases adrenaline into the bloodstream → heart rate and blood pressure rise, breathing quickens, glucose is released for energy, digestion is inhibited, pupils dilate → the body is prepared to fight or flee. Once the threat passes, the parasympathetic branch reverses the changes ('rest and digest'). Chronic activation (ongoing stress) produces prolonged cortisol release, linked to immune suppression and cardiovascular problems - a standard application point. Evaluation (AO3): Strength - drug evidence: SSRIs (blocking serotonin reuptake) and antipsychotics (blocking dopamine receptors) alter synaptic transmission and change behaviour, supporting the chemical basis of psychology. Strength - physiological measurement: adrenaline and cortisol are measurable in blood/saliva, and heart-rate/skin-conductance measures track ANS arousal objectively - supporting research into stress. Limitation - fight-or-flight oversimplified: Gray (1988) proposed freeze as a first response, and Taylor et al. (2000) argued women show tend-and-befriend (protecting offspring, seeking allies) rather than fight-or-flight - the classic account is male-biased and built on animal (rat) research. Limitation - reductionism: explaining behaviour purely by neurotransmitter levels ignores cognitive, social and environmental factors - a standard AO3 point for the biological approach generally (biological reductionism). Localisation of function claims specific brain areas control specific functions (as opposed to the holistic view that the whole brain works together). Cortical areas: motor cortex (frontal lobe - voluntary movement; Penfield's 'homunculus' mapping showed body parts represented in proportion to their dexterity, not size), somatosensory cortex (parietal lobe - touch, pressure, pain from the opposite side of the body), visual centres (occipital lobe - processing from both eyes via the optic chiasm) and auditory centres (temporal lobe - sound analysis). Language centres (usually in the left hemisphere - hemispheric lateralisation): Broca's area (left frontal lobe) controls speech production ; damage causes Broca's aphasia - slow, laborious speech with comprehension intact (Broca's 1861 patient 'Tan' could say only one syllable but understood speech); Wernicke's area (left temporal lobe, adjacent to the auditory cortex) controls language comprehension ; damage causes Wernicke's aphasia - fluent but meaningless speech ('word salad') with poor comprehension. Broca's and Wernicke's areas are connected by the arcuate fasciculus (Wernicke's model of language processing). Split-brain research (Sperry 1968; Gazzaniga) : patients with severe epilepsy had the corpus callosum (the bundle of fibres connecting the hemispheres) severed. Sperry presented stimuli to one visual field (which projects to the opposite hemisphere): when 'RING' was shown to the right visual field (left hemisphere), patients could name it verbally; when shown to the left visual field (right hemisphere), patients could not name it but could select the object by touch with the left hand - the right hemisphere 'understood' but could not speak. Findings support hemispheric lateralisation : the left hemisphere dominates language, the right dominates visual-motor and spatial processing. Evaluation (AO3): Strength - research support for localisation: Tulving's PET scans showed episodic retrieval activates the right prefrontal cortex, semantic the left; Penfield's brain stimulation during surgery mapped motor/sensory functions; case studies (Tan, Phineas Gage) support specific-area damage producing specific deficits. Limitation - language is not fully localised: 98% of right-handed people have language in the left hemisphere, but the equipotentiality principle (Lashley) shows the whole cortex can substitute for damaged areas - high-level functions (learning, memory) are distributed, not localised. Limitation - case study generalisability: 'Tan' and split-brain patients are rare and unusual (surgery for epilepsy); findings may not generalise to normal brains, and later work (Gazzaniga) showed some split-brain patients can name left-field stimuli, weakening Sperry's clean lateralisation claim. Limitation - plasticity (network models): modern neuroscience (fMRI) shows functions arise from distributed networks (Wernicke's model of language processing) rather than isolated spots; plasticity (Maguire's taxi drivers) shows the cortex reorganises, challenging rigid localisation. Practical application: localisation guides neurosurgery (mapping before tumour removal) and stroke rehabilitation (targeting damaged areas); split-brain research informs understanding of hemispheric differences. Plasticity (neuroplasticity) is the brain's ability to change and adapt structurally in response to experience and learning: synaptic connections form, strengthen (long-term potentiation) or wither (synaptic pruning) throughout life. Evidence: Maguire et al. (2000) - London taxi drivers (who must learn 'The Knowledge') had significantly larger posterior hippocampi than controls, and volume correlated with years of driving; Draganski et al. (2006) - learning to juggle increased grey matter in visual-motor areas within three months; Kuhn et al. (2014) - video-game playing increased hippocampal grey matter. Functional recovery after trauma (stroke, injury) works through: axonal sprouting (undamaged axons grow new connections), denervation supersensitivity (receptors become more sensitive to compensate) and recruiting homologous areas (the opposite hemisphere's equivalent area takes over, e.g. Broca's area's mirror region for speech). Recovery is faster in the first few weeks, then slows; it is aided by rehabilitation (movement therapy, electrical stimulation). Ways of studying the brain : (1) fMRI (functional magnetic resonance imaging) - detects blood oxygenation (active areas consume more oxygen): 3D images with high spatial resolution (~1-2mm), non-invasive and no radiation - but expensive, requiring the participant to stay still, with ~5-second lag (poor temporal resolution) and indirect measurement (blood flow, not neural activity). (2) EEG (electroencephalogram) - electrodes on the scalp measure overall electrical activity in the brain: high temporal resolution (milliseconds), useful for sleep research (sleep stages, dreams) and diagnosing epilepsy - but poor spatial resolution (activity from deep structures is hard to localise) and general noise. (3) ERPs (event-related potentials) - EEG data averaged over many trials, time-locked to a specific stimulus: isolates responses to stimuli with high temporal resolution - but requires many trials and background noise must be statistically removed; used in cognitive research (attention, perception). (4) Post-mortem examination - the brain is examined after death (e.g. Broca's 'Tan', Alzheimer's plaques): allows deep-structure study impossible in vivo, historically foundational - but the person is dead (causation unclear - damage may have been pre-mortem illness) and retrospective; ethical consent issues. Evaluation (AO3): Plasticity - strengths: Maguire, Draganski and Kuhn all use controlled comparisons with brain imaging - converging evidence that experience changes brain structure; practical application to stroke rehabilitation and education. Plasticity - limitations: Maguire's taxi drivers are a unique occupational group (generalisability limited), and correlational - differences may predate the job; plasticity research is also partly animal-based (rat studies showing synaptic change). fMRI - evaluation: high spatial resolution and non-invasive (strengths), but poor temporal resolution, expensive, and measures blood flow indirectly - neural activity is inferred. EEG/ERP - evaluation: millisecond temporal resolution (strengths), useful for sleep and epilepsy, but poor spatial resolution and, for ERPs, the need for many averaged trials; no causal claims possible from correlational imaging. Post-mortem - evaluation: deep-structure access and historical importance, but causation is unclear and consent raises ethics; modern imaging largely supersedes it, though it remains valuable for rare conditions. Biological rhythms are cyclical changes in physiology and behaviour. Circadian rhythms (~24 hours): the sleep-wake cycle , body temperature (lowest ~4am, highest ~6pm) and hormone production. Endogenous pacemakers : the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) in the hypothalamus (the 'master clock', receiving light information from the eyes via the retinohypothalamic tract) directs the pineal gland to release melatonin in darkness, inducing sleepiness. Exogenous zeitgebers (external cues) entrain the rhythm: light resets the SCN daily; social cues (meal times, alarm clocks, work schedules) also entrain sleep patterns. Evidence: Siffre (1975, cave study) - spent six months in a Texan cave with no external cues; his free-running sleep-wake cycle settled at ~25 hours rather than 24, showing the endogenous clock runs slightly long and needs light to entrain; Folkard et al. (1985) - participants in an underground bunker free-ran to ~25-27 hours; Aschoff and Wever (1976) - similar findings in a bunker without clocks. Morgan (1959) - SCN-lesioned hamsters lost circadian rhythmicity, which returned when the SCN was transplanted - supporting the SCN as the master clock. Infradian rhythms (>24 hours): the menstrual cycle (~28 days, regulated by oestrogen and progesterone; ovulation mid-cycle) and seasonal affective disorder (SAD, a yearly rhythm linked to melatonin and light). Evidence: Stern and McClintock (1998) - pheromones (released in sweat) from women at the start of their cycles shortened the cycles of women mid-cycle, and vice versa, suggesting menstrual synchrony via exogenous chemical signals; Russell et al. (1980) - similar pheromone findings. Ultradian rhythms ( sleep stages in ~90-minute cycles (NREM stages 1-4 then REM) - Dement and Kleitman (1957) found REM sleep correlated with dreaming; and the basic rest-activity cycle (BRAC) - 90-minute cycles of alertness during the day (Kleitman). Evaluation (AO3): Sleep-wake cycle - strengths: converging evidence (Siffre, Folkard, Morgan) supports the SCN as master clock and light as the key zeitgeber; practical application - shift work, jet lag and light therapy for SAD. Sleep-wake cycle - limitations: Siffre used himself (case study, small sample, his vision deteriorated in the cave, possibly distorting light perception); small volunteer samples in bunker studies may be unrepresentative; individual differences exist (Duffy et al. 2001: 'morning' and 'evening' people have different cycle timings), so a single 'normal' 24-hour cycle is a simplification. Menstrual synchrony - limitations: Yang and Schank (2006) failed to replicate synchrony findings and questioned the statistics; synchrony may be coincidence; pheromone research is difficult to replicate (confounds: diet, stress, partners). Methodological issues: much evidence is animal-based (hamsters, rats) - extrapolation to humans is limited; lab studies remove zeitgebers artificially, so ecological validity is low, though field cave/bunker studies are higher in realism. Interactionist conclusion: rhythms are endogenously controlled but exogenously entrained - exam answers reward noting that neither alone explains timing (the SCN runs ~25 hours; light entrains it to 24).

topics.name: Sociological Theories and Perspectives
topics.subject: sociology
topics.searchText: sociology Sociology Sociological Theories and Perspectives Classify perspectives along the structural/action and consensus/conflict axes (AQA 4.4.1; OCR; Eduqas AC1.1) Set out functionalist, Marxist and feminist accounts of society with named theorists and precise concepts Explain Weber's social action theory, symbolic interactionism, phenomenology, ethnomethodology and Giddens' structuration Evaluate each perspective with counter-theorists, studies and postmodernist critique (AO3) Deploy synoptic theory-and-methods links (MODs) in 10- and 30-mark answers Match theoretical content to command words and reach justified conclusions Functionalism: Durkheim (social facts, solidarity, anomie), Parsons (value consensus, functional fit, socialisation and social control), Merton (dysfunctions; manifest and latent functions). Marxism: Marx (class conflict, exploitation, alienation, ideology), Althusser (ideological/repressive state apparatuses), Gramsci (hegemony); evaluated by Willis (1977). Feminism: liberal (Oakley), radical (Millett, Firestone), Marxist (Ansley), difference and poststructural (Butler's performativity). Action theories: Weber (verstehen, four action types), symbolic interactionism (Becker, Goffman), phenomenology (Schutz), ethnomethodology (Garfinkel), structuration (Giddens). Postmodernism: Lyotard, Baudrillard; counters — it is internally contradictory and understates measurable inequality (Harvey; Best and Kellner). AO3 rule: every claim needs a named study or counter-theory; adjectives alone never earn evaluation marks. Structural theory An approach explaining behaviour through the organisation of society — institutions and social class shaping individuals from above; includes functionalism, Marxism and feminism. Social action theory An approach (Weber) starting from the subjective meanings individuals attach to their actions; society is the ongoing product of interaction rather than a determining structure. Value consensus In functionalism, general agreement in society about norms and values which integrates individuals and underpins social order. Anomie Durkheim: normlessness — the breakdown of social rules during rapid change, leaving individuals without moral regulation; also the starting point of Merton's strain theory. False class consciousness The Marxist claim that the proletariat misperceives its interests because ruling-class ideology presents inequality as natural, preventing revolutionary action. Hegemony Gramsci: ruling-class domination achieved through consent — ideas and institutions win voluntary acceptance — rather than force; contested until a counter-hegemony is built. Patriarchy A structure of male dominance over women operating through institutions (family, work, media); the core concept of feminist theory. Verstehen Weber's empathetic understanding: grasping the subjective meanings actors give to their behaviour before explaining it sociologically. Typification Schutz (phenomenology): shared common-sense categories people use to classify others and organise interaction, so social reality is constituted through them. Structuration Giddens (1984): structure and action are two sides of one process — structures enable and constrain action, while action reproduces or transforms structures. Meta-narrative Lyotard (1979): a grand explanatory story (e.g. Marxism, science-as-progress) claiming universal truth; postmodernists argue such narratives have lost credibility. AQA 4.4.1 (Theory and Methods), OCR H580 and Eduqas AC1.1 expect you to classify every perspective along two axes. Structural vs action: structural theories (functionalism, Marxism, feminism) treat society as an external force shaping individuals from above; action theories (Weber, symbolic interactionism, phenomenology, ethnomethodology) begin with the meanings individuals give to their behaviour. Consensus vs conflict: consensus theories see order resting on shared agreement; conflict theories see order resting on the power of one group over another. Macro/micro: functionalism, Marxism and feminism are macro theories; interactionism, phenomenology and ethnomethodology are micro theories. Why it matters: most 30-mark questions name a perspective; the A* skill is locating it on both axes and letting that drive evaluation — e.g. functionalism is structural-consensus, so it struggles to explain conflict and power. Synoptic link (MODs): structural theories pair naturally with quantitative methods (questionnaires, official statistics) because they seek general patterns; action theories pair with qualitative methods (unstructured interviews, participant observation) because they seek meanings — examiners explicitly reward such links. Functionalism sees society as a system of interdependent parts, each performing functions that maintain order. Durkheim (1893) argued society exists over and above individuals — 'social facts' are external and constraining — and modern societies hold together through organic solidarity, with anomie the danger when regulation collapses. Parsons (1951) added the value consensus, functional fit (institutions adapt as society moves from traditional to modern) and two mechanisms of integration: socialisation and social control. Merton (1938) criticised from within: institutions can be dysfunctional , and functions may be manifest (intended) or latent (unintended). Marxism sees society divided by class conflict. For Marx, the capitalist mode of production rests on exploitation of the proletariat, producing alienation and ruling-class ideology that makes inequality appear natural. Neo-Marxists refined this: Althusser (1971) distinguished Ideological and Repressive State Apparatuses, with education and media transmitting bourgeois ideology; Gramsci (1971) explained durable domination as hegemony — rule by consent — which revolutionaries must contest with a counter-hegemonic bloc. Willis (1977) supplied the classic evaluation: his 12 'lads' formed a counter-school culture, showing working-class pupils partially saw through ideology yet still drifted into manual work. Feminism treats patriarchy as the fundamental division. Liberal feminism (Oakley) seeks reform within the system — equal pay, shared parenting; radical feminism (Millett, Firestone) sees patriarchy as the oldest and deepest structure demanding revolutionary change, including separatism; Marxist feminism (Ansley: women as 'takers of shit' absorbing male frustration) links women's subordination to capitalism; difference and poststructural feminism (Butler) reject a single category of 'women', emphasising diversity and the performativity of gender. Weber operates on two levels: structural factors (class, status, party) set the context, but sociology must use verstehen — empathetic understanding of subjective meanings. He classified action into four ideal types: instrumentally rational, value-rational, traditional and affectual. Meanings and symbols: symbolic interactionism (Blumer, Becker, Goffman) studies how meanings arise in interaction through symbols. Becker (1963) showed deviance is created by audience reaction and labelling, with 'moral entrepreneurs' applying labels; Goffman's dramaturgy analysed how actors manage impressions on a 'front stage'. Phenomenology (Schutz) argues actors experience the world through typifications — shared common-sense categories — so reality is socially constructed. Garfinkel's ethnomethodology (1967) demonstrated how fragile those categories are through breaching experiments, such as students acting as lodgers in their own homes. Synthesis: Giddens' structuration (1984) dissolves the structure-action dualism: structures are both the medium and the outcome of action (the 'duality of structure') — rules and resources enable as well as constrain, and persist only because actors keep drawing on them. AO3: critics argue structuration is too abstract to research empirically; Margaret Archer insists structure and action must be analytically separated because structures pre-exist the individuals who reproduce them. Postmodernism (Lyotard 1979; Baudrillard) argues that in post-Fordist, media-saturated society the meta-narratives — Marxism's class story, functionalism's consensus story, even science-as-progress — have lost credibility; identity is now constructed through consumption and choice rather than class. AO3 response: critics (Harvey; Best and Kellner) argue postmodernism is itself a meta-narrative, is internally contradictory (making universal claims that there are no universal claims) and understates continuing structural inequality — class, gender and ethnic gaps remain measurable and material. Functionalism — where it fails Understates conflict and power; assumes a value consensus that may simply reflect dominant groups; explanations risk teleology ('institutions exist because they have functions') and circularity; Merton's own internal critique concedes dysfunctions. Yet it remains the benchmark for explaining integration and socialisation — e.g. Durkheim on education creating shared values. Marxism — where it fails Economic determinism (Weber: class is one dimension among several; feminists: gender matters too); the predicted revolution never arrived in advanced capitalism; Willis shows pupils resist ideology. Still useful: Althusser and Gramsci explain consent, and neo-Marxism remains the reference point for analysing power. Feminism and action theories — where they fail Radical feminism risks treating all men as uniformly privileged, while difference feminism can fragment into un-theorisable individualism. Action theories ignore structural constraints — a pupil's poverty shapes life chances regardless of meaning. Yet Becker (1963) and Garfinkel (1967) show meanings genuinely shape outcomes, so the strongest answers combine levels (Weber, Giddens). Examiner tip: never evaluate a perspective as merely 'outdated' or 'too simplistic' — name the theorist making the counter-claim and the evidence they would deploy. On AQA 7192 , theory appears in short item questions (4-6 marks), 10-mark 'outline and analyse two...' questions and 30-mark 'outline and evaluate...' essays; OCR asks 'assess'/'evaluate' style questions (up to 30 marks) and Eduqas uses extended 'discuss' essays. AO weighting: 30-mark essays are roughly AO1 8 / AO2 8 / AO3 14 — evaluation carries the most credit. Command word What it demands AO focus Outline and analyse two Two developed points, each applied to the question AO1 + AO2 Outline and evaluate Knowledge plus sustained debate with a reached judgement AO1 + AO2 + AO3 Assess / discuss how far Weigh evidence for and against a claim AO3-heavy 30-mark skeleton: (1) define the perspective with its key concepts and theorists; (2) three or four developed points, each with a named study or application; (3) three or four evaluation points, each with a counter-theorist or study; (4) a conclusion answering the actual question with a weighed judgement — never 'both views have merit'. Timing: 30 marks ≈ 30 minutes: plan for 4, write for 24, check for 2. Common pitfalls: describing theory at length then bolting on one evaluation; confusing Marx and Weber on class; writing 'society says' without naming who; omitting the synoptic theory-and-methods link that AO marks reward.

topics.name: Research Methods
topics.subject: sociology
topics.searchText: sociology Sociology Research Methods Classify research data as quantitative/qualitative and primary/secondary, and match methods to positivism or interpretivism (AQA 4.1.3.1-3) Outline the practical, ethical and theoretical strengths and limitations of each main method (AQA 4.1.3.1) Describe the research process from aim to report, including stratified random sampling, quota sampling and pilot studies (AQA 4.1.3.4) Apply theoretical, practical and ethical considerations to the choice of topic, method and conduct of research (AQA 4.1.3.5) Evaluate positivism and interpretivism with named studies and methodological pluralism (AO3) Deploy methods knowledge in 10-mark, 20-mark and 30-mark answers across AQA Papers 1 and 3 and OCR H580/02 Positivism seeks reliable, representative data for causal laws (Durkheim); interpretivism seeks valid, authentic data for meanings (Weber). Questionnaires and official statistics suit positivists; unstructured interviews and participant observation suit interpretivists. Sampling: random, systematic, stratified random, quota, snowball, opportunity — probability techniques need a sampling frame. Ethics: informed consent, deception, confidentiality, harm, right to withdraw (BSA ethical guidelines). PET/E rule: every method evaluation must name a practical constraint, an ethical issue or a theoretical position — bare lists earn little credit. Positivism The view (Comte, Durkheim) that society is an external reality of social facts which can be studied objectively, like nature, to discover cause-and-effect laws; favours reliable, representative, quantitative data. Interpretivism The view (Weber, symbolic interactionism) that social reality is constructed through meanings, so sociology needs valid, authentic data on actors' interpretations; favours qualitative methods and verstehen. Hypothesis A testable prediction about the relationship between two or more variables, usually used in quantitative, deductive research. Operationalisation Turning an abstract concept (e.g. class, religiosity) into a measurable indicator, such as occupational category or church attendance. Pilot study A small trial run of a questionnaire or interview schedule to test clarity, timing and wording before the main study. Stratified random sampling A probability technique that divides the sampling frame into relevant strata (e.g. class, gender, ethnicity) then selects randomly from each in proportion, maximising representativeness. Quota sampling A non-probability technique where interviewers fill quotas of respondents of particular types until targets are met; faster but open to researcher bias. Snowball sample A non-probability technique where existing respondents recruit further contacts; used for hard-to-reach or deviant groups but unrepresentative. Reliability Whether repeating the research by another researcher would produce the same results; highest for standardised methods like questionnaires. Validity Whether the data gives a true, authentic picture of what is being studied; highest for naturalistic methods like participant observation. Representativeness Whether the sample reflects the characteristics of the wider population, allowing generalisation; depends on sampling technique and response rate. Value freedom The ideal that research should be objective and unbiased; Weber argued values may choose the topic but must not dictate the findings, challenged by Becker's 'whose side are we on?' AQA 4.1.3.1-3 , OCR H580/02 and Eduqas AC2.1/AC2.2 expect you to classify every method along three distinctions before evaluating it. Quantitative vs qualitative: quantitative methods (questionnaires, structured interviews, official statistics, content analysis) produce numbers suitable for measuring patterns and testing hypotheses; qualitative methods (unstructured interviews, participant observation, personal documents) produce words and observation suitable for understanding meanings and motives. Primary vs secondary: primary data is collected first-hand by the sociologist (experiments, questionnaires, interviews, observation); secondary data already exists (official statistics, company reports, diaries, media content) — cheap and accessible, but not designed for the researcher's purpose. Positivism: associated with Comte and Durkheim — society is an external reality of social facts that constrains individuals, so it can be studied objectively to discover cause-and-effect laws; positivists therefore favour methods producing reliable and representative data, above all official statistics and questionnaires. Durkheim's study of suicide (1897) is the classic model: official statistics on suicide rates correlated with levels of social integration. Interpretivism: associated with Weber and symbolic interactionism — social reality is constructed through meanings, so sociology needs valid and authentic data through empathy (verstehen); interpretivists favour unstructured interviews and participant observation. Atkinson's study of coroners' verdicts (1978) shows even suicide statistics rest on the meanings coroners give to a death. Synthesis: the A* point is methodological pluralism or triangulation — combining methods to balance reliability and validity, as Eileen Barker did in The Making of a Moonie (1984), using questionnaires, interviews and observation over several years. Why it matters: 10-mark methods questions usually ask for two advantages or problems of a method; the marks come from development, so each point must be explained in the method's own terms — e.g. questionnaires are reliable because they are standardised, so every respondent answers identical questions and results can be replicated. AQA 4.1.3.1 expects the strengths and limitations of each main method, evaluated through practical, ethical and theoretical (PET) criteria. Learn the methods in pairs of opposites and attach one classic study to each. Method Key strengths Key limitations Lab experiments Reliable, replicable, controlled variables Artificial; Hawthorne effect; small samples Questionnaires Large, cheap, representative; reliable Low response rates; imposition problem; shallow Structured interviews Reliable; quick; trained interviewers Interviewer bias still possible; little depth Unstructured interviews Valid, flexible, in-depth rapport Unrepresentative; costly; hard to replicate Participant observation Valid, naturalistic, access to hidden worlds Unrepresentative; going native; ethics if covert Official statistics Free, large-scale, trends over time Socially constructed; dark figure; definitions change Documents Authentic meanings; personal insight Unrepresentative; credibility problems Experiments — classic studies Lab experiments manipulate variables under controlled conditions: Milgram's obedience experiments (1963) demonstrated the power of authority, but were criticised for deception and psychological harm — a stock AO3 example. Field experiments occur in natural settings: Rosenhan's pseudo-patient study (1973) showed how a psychiatric label overwhelms behaviour, though it was ethically heavy on deception and never repeated. Both illustrate the reliability-validity trade-off: control raises reliability but artificiality cuts validity. Interviews — classic studies Ann Oakley (1981) rejected the detached, formal interview in favour of unstructured interviews with expectant mothers, building rapport that produced far richer data on women's experiences of childbirth — the standard evaluative evidence that interviewing style shapes validity. Dobash and Dobash (1980) used unstructured interviews with women in refuges to expose the reality of domestic violence, a sensitive topic where trust is essential. Observation — classic studies Participant observation ranges from overt (openly known) to covert (undercover). Humphreys' Tearoom Trade (1970) observed men in public lavatories without consent and later identified them through car number plates — the classic ethical critique of covert research, though it produced data no other method could access. Venkatesh's Gang Leader for a Day (2008) shows how observation accesses hidden subcultures, but also its risks: he witnessed violence and had to negotiate his role with a gang leader. Observation produces high validity but low reliability and representativeness. Secondary sources — classic studies Official statistics are cheap, cover whole populations and allow trends over time (e.g. birth rates since 1900), but they are socially constructed: Farrington and Dowds (1986) showed rising recorded crime in one Lancashire area partly reflected police recording practices, not more crime. Victim surveys such as the Crime Survey for England and Wales (developed by Mayhew and colleagues) expose the dark figure of unreported crime. Documents range from public records to personal diaries: Hey (1997) used girls' friendship notes in The Company She Keeps to access authentic meanings, but such sources are unrepresentative and credibility is hard to verify. AQA 4.1.3.4 lists the main stages of the research process — learn them in order and be ready to explain what can go wrong at each stage. Choosing a topic: driven by theoretical interest, practical feasibility, funding bodies and ethical acceptability — sensitive or harmful topics (e.g. child abuse) attract ethical scrutiny from the outset. Formulating aims and hypotheses: an aim states the purpose of the study; a hypothesis is a testable prediction, used mainly in quantitative, deductive research. Interpretivists often work with looser research questions instead. Operationalising concepts: turning abstract ideas into measurable indicators — e.g. measuring religiosity through attendance, or class through occupational category. Poor operationalisation invalidates findings: if attendance does not capture belief, the study measures the wrong thing. Pilot study: a small trial run to check question clarity, timing and response rates before the main study — cheap insurance against wasted fieldwork. Sampling: define the population, obtain a sampling frame (a list of the population), then select. Random and systematic sampling need a full frame; stratified random sampling divides the frame into strata (class, gender, ethnicity) and samples proportionally, maximising representativeness; quota sampling fills quotas of respondent types — faster, but interviewer choice biases the sample; snowball and opportunity sampling suit hard-to-reach groups (offenders, drug users) but are unrepresentative. Selecting and collecting data: apply the chosen method; response rates decide whether a survey is truly representative. Analysing and interpreting data: quantitative data is analysed for patterns, trends and correlations — remember correlation is not causation; qualitative data is coded into themes. Reporting and evaluating the research: findings are published and judged on reliability, validity, representativeness and ethics — the same PET criteria that shaped the design. Examiner tip: 10-mark questions frequently target one stage (e.g. two problems of using quota sampling, or two reasons for using a pilot study). Answer in the stage's own terms with one developed point per reason. AQA 4.1.3.5 requires you to weigh the theoretical, practical and ethical considerations influencing the choice of topic, method and conduct of research — the PET/E framework that underpins every methods evaluation. Theoretical: the positivism-interpretivism divide decides the method: positivists want reliable, representative data (questionnaires, statistics) to test causal laws; interpretivists want valid, authentic data (interviews, observation) to capture meanings. The validity-reliability trade-off means no method maximises both. Value freedom matters here too: Weber argued values inevitably choose the topic but research itself should be objective, while Becker (1967) asked 'whose side are we on?' — arguing sociology should side with the underdog — and Gouldner criticised value-free sociology as a myth that hides the researcher's own assumptions. Practical: time and money limit sample size and method choice; access is decisive — schools and prisons require gatekeepers' permission, and criminal subcultures require special negotiation (Venkatesh 2008); the researcher's own characteristics (age, gender, ethnicity) affect rapport; response rates decide whether a large survey is genuinely representative. Ethical: informed consent (participants must know they are being studied — parents consent for pupils), deception (covert observation involves it by definition), confidentiality and anonymity (Humphreys 1970 broke both), protection from harm (Milgram's 1963 participants suffered stress), and the right to withdraw. The British Sociological Association's ethical guidelines codify these duties. The evaluation dilemma: ethical and practical constraints often cut against validity. Covert observation produces the most authentic data on hidden behaviour but breaches consent; large-scale surveys are ethical and representative but shallow. The strongest answers name this trade-off explicitly rather than treating ethics as a bolt-on list. On AQA 7192 , pure methods appear in the 10-mark 'outline and analyse two...' questions on Papers 1 and 3, and feed the 20-mark Methods in Context question (AQA 4.1.2) and the 30-mark theory-and-methods essays (AQA 4.4.5, e.g. value freedom). OCR assesses methods in H580/02 Section A, where every method point must be applied to researching social inequalities; Eduqas examines quantitative methods (AC2.1) and qualitative methods (AC2.2) separately. Command word What it demands AO focus Outline and analyse two Two developed points, each explained in the method's own terms AO1 + AO2 Assess the usefulness of Sustained weighing of strengths against limits, with a judgement AO3-heavy Explain what is meant by Precise definition with an example AO1 30-mark skeleton (assess the usefulness of X for researching Y): (1) define X and its logic; (2) two or three strengths, each named as practical, ethical or theoretical, each with a study; (3) two or three limitations, likewise; (4) a conclusion weighing usefulness for Y specifically — never a vague 'both have merits'. Common pitfalls: listing strengths without developing them; forgetting to attach the PET dimension to each point; confusing reliability (consistency) with validity (truth); ignoring the positivism-interpretivism pairing examiners reward; omitting named studies — adjectives alone never earn evaluation marks. Timing: 10 marks ≈ 10 minutes; 30 marks ≈ 30 minutes (plan 4, write 24, check 2). Remember that OCR item-based methods questions reward tight application to the given scenario — quote the item's wording in your answer.

topics.name: Methods in Context and Theory
topics.subject: sociology
topics.searchText: sociology Sociology Methods in Context and Theory Apply practical, ethical and theoretical (PET) evaluation to questionnaires, interviews, observations and documents in education settings (AQA 4.1.4; OCR H580/02) Write the 20-mark methods in context answer with sustained application to the named education topic (AQA Paper 1 Q5: AO1 + AO2 only) Anticipate education-specific research problems: classroom access, gatekeepers, safeguarding, the Hawthorne effect and teacher-pupil power Deploy education research studies (Willis, Lacey, Ball, Mac an Ghaill, Gillborn and Youdell) as applied evidence Link method choice to positivism versus interpretivism and to debates over value freedom (AQA 4.4) Plan 30-mark theory-and-methods essays on sociology as a science and value freedom (AQA 7192 Paper 3; synoptic theory essays on OCR H580/03) AQA methods in context (Paper 1 Q5): 20 marks, AO1 + AO2 only — sustained application to the named education topic is what separates levels (AQA 4.1.4). Every PET point must be APPLIED: 'registers give questionnaires a complete sampling frame' beats a generic list of strengths. Education-specific strengths: registers as sampling frames, fixed timetables easing access, anonymous surveys drawing out honest pupil answers. Education-specific limitations: gatekeepers (headteacher, DfE, parents), DBS and safeguarding checks, strong Hawthorne effect with children, teacher-pupil power distorting data. Studies to deploy: Willis (1977) group interviews with the lads; Lacey (1970) Hightown Grammar; Ball (1981) Beachside; Mac an Ghaill (1988) teacher-researcher; Gillborn and Youdell (2000) Rationing Education. 30-mark theory-and-methods essays (AQA 4.4): positivism versus interpretivism underpins method choice; value freedom (Weber, Becker, Gouldner) supplies the evaluation. Methods in context The exam task (AQA 4.1.4): applying knowledge of one named research method to a given education topic, weighted towards AO2 application; assessed similarly in the compulsory methods section of OCR H580/02. PET evaluation Framework for assessing a method by practical issues (time, money, access), ethical issues (consent, confidentiality, harm) and theoretical issues (validity, reliability, representativeness, positivism versus interpretivism). Gatekeeper Anyone controlling access to a research setting or population; in education: headteachers, local authorities, the DfE, ethics committees and parents (who consent on behalf of children). Hawthorne effect Behaviour change caused by awareness of being studied; in classrooms pupils perform for the observer, threatening validity — reduced by long immersion and participant observation, cured only by covert methods. Overt observation Open observation in which those studied know the researcher's identity and purpose; preserves consent but invites the Hawthorne effect. Impression management Goffman's term for the conscious shaping of how one is seen; teachers used to being asked questions may present a professional 'front' in interviews, lowering validity. Performativity Ball (2003): the institutional pressure to measure and display results; makes official education statistics (league tables, exclusions, attendance) potentially distorted by triage and hidden exclusions. Value freedom Weber's ideal that findings be free of the researcher's values, distinct from value-relevance (values legitimately choose the topic); attacked by Becker and Gouldner, who argue some standpoint is unavoidable. Whose side are we on? Becker (1967): complete neutrality is impossible because research is always conducted from a standpoint; sociologists should side with the underdog (pupils rather than schools). Sociology as a science Debate over whether sociology can be scientific: positivists (Comte, Durkheim) say yes via objective study of social facts; interpretivists object; Popper (falsification) and Kuhn (paradigms) qualify the claim; realists (Keat and Urry 1975) offer a middle position via open and closed systems. Both boards test the same skill: applying methods knowledge to a given education topic, not reciting generic strengths. On AQA 7192 this is the compulsory final question of Paper 1 (spec 4.1.4): a short Item on an education topic (labelling, pupil subcultures, class differences) plus a 20-mark demand to evaluate the strengths and limitations of using a named method to investigate it . The 20 marks are assessed through AO1 (knowledge of the method) and AO2 (application to education) only — there is no separate AO3 theory evaluation, which is why examiner reports repeatedly warn against drifting into generic methods lists. On OCR H580/02 (Researching and understanding social inequalities) the compulsory methods section combines item-based short answers with an extended evaluation of a named method applied to a given education or inequality context; application again dominates the marks. The drill: every PET point must name the classroom actors and settings — pupils, teachers, headteachers, parents, registers, timetables — and explain how the method's feature specifically helps or hinders research on this topic. Structure that scores: brief intro (method + topic), 3-4 PET paragraphs each pairing a strength with a limitation, judgement-led conclusion. Application beats volume: four tightly-applied points outscore eight generic ones. Use the Item: quote phrases from it and hang method points on them — that is where AO2 credit sits. Theory lives inside T: positivist versus interpretivist judgements about data quality count as the theoretical limb of PET (AQA 4.4). Level descriptors reward range (several distinct strengths and limitations), application (each point tied to the education context) and quality of argument (an explicit overall judgement). Three common failures: describing the method instead of evaluating it; listing generic strengths with no reference to classrooms, pupils or teachers; and answering a different research focus than the one the item names — re-read the item before planning and quote its exact topic phrase in the intro. Learn the education-specific hook for each method, then the studies that evidence it. Method Practical (education) Ethical (education) Theoretical (education) Questionnaires Cheap for large pupil samples; registers give complete sampling frames; fixed timetables make whole-class administration easy Anonymous, so pupils disclose bullying and attitudes honestly; parental consent needed for minors Reliable and representative (positivist); but young pupils misread vocabulary and joke — low validity; impose researcher's meanings Interviews Unstructured versions time-costly per pupil; teachers are fluent interviewees but busy; group interviews fit the school day Informed consent and safeguarding; sensitive topics (labelling, setting) make teachers fear exposure Unstructured gives valid verstehen of pupil and teacher meanings; group format triggers peer bravado — invalid Observations Timetables make classrooms accessible but need headteacher permission and DBS checks; long fieldwork; researcher may be treated as a spy (Lacey) Overt preserves consent but invites the Hawthorne effect; covert breaches consent and safeguarding with children — rarely justifiable Most valid account of classroom interaction (interpretivist); unrepresentative, unrepeatable, unreliable Documents and official statistics Public documents (prospectuses, league tables, Ofsted reports) instantly available; personal documents rare; pupil records restricted Private records raise confidentiality and Data Protection issues Statistics reliable but socially constructed and performativity-distorted (Ball 2003; Gillborn and Youdell 2000); diaries valid but unrepresentative Questionnaires in schools Schools already run them: Ofsted-style pupil voice surveys and anti-bullying questionnaires. Response rates rise when teachers administer the survey, but that itself biases answers — pupils respond as they think the teacher wants (Goffman's impression management). Positivists prize the reliability and representativeness of large pupil samples; interpretivists reply that answers are artefacts of the instrument — vocabulary a Year 7 cannot read produces data that measures reading age, not attitudes. Interviews with pupils and teachers Willis (1977), Learning to Labour, used group interviews and observation with 12 'lads': the group format let the counter-school culture speak — but peer pressure produces bravado and conformity effects alongside it. Unstructured one-to-one interviews suit sensitive topics and powerful respondents: Ball, Bowe and Gewirtz (1994) interviewed headteachers on marketisation. Costs: time, and guarded 'official' answers from teachers skilled at being observed. Observing classrooms Lacey (1970) Hightown Grammar and Ball (1981) Beachside Comprehensive: overt participant observation by researchers with insider status (Lacey taught at the school). Jackson (1968), Life in Classrooms, non-participant observation of the 'hype' of classroom rewards. The Hawthorne effect is strongest with children, who perform for adult audiences; long immersion (Woods 1979 on pupil strategies) reduces it. Covert observation of pupils is ethically near-impossible: no meaningful consent, safeguarding breached. Documents and official statistics Personal documents (pupil diaries, letters) are rare and hard to authenticate. School documents split into public (prospectuses, websites, league tables) and private (pupil files — access heavily restricted). Official statistics (DfE attainment, exclusions, attendance) are free, up-to-date and cover whole cohorts, but Gillborn and Youdell (2000), Rationing Education, showed league-table pressure producing triage and hidden exclusions: the statistic measures institutional responses as much as pupil behaviour (AQA 4.2.1). Experiments in education Rare in schools but examinable. Field experiments suit the context: Rosenthal and Jacobson (1968) told teachers that randomly selected pupils were about to 'bloom' and measured a self-fulfilling prophecy in later attainment — cheap, natural setting, real classroom behaviour; but teachers were deceived, the sample was one school, and effects were modest. Laboratory-style studies of classrooms control variables well yet are artificial — pupils do not behave normally under controlled conditions, and access plus consent make them rare. Four problems recur in examiner reports because they are unique to, or sharpest in, schools. Revise one applied paragraph on each. Classroom access. Schools are closed institutions: entry needs headteacher (often local authority or DfE) permission, DBS checks and staff cooperation, and timetables fix when research can happen. Insider status helps — Ball and Mac an Ghaill (1988) researched schools they taught in — but creates loyalty conflicts: Mac an Ghaill was simultaneously colleague to the teachers and researcher of their labelling practices. Gatekeepers and consent. Children cannot give legally meaningful consent alone: parents, schools and ethics committees (BSA code of practice) must agree, and any gatekeeper can veto the research or demand changes — for example forbidding questions on ethnicity — that bias the findings. The Hawthorne effect. Children are especially self-conscious before adult observers; classroom behaviour shifts when a researcher is present. Participant observation and long immersion reduce it; covert methods cure it but breach consent. Teacher-pupil power and presentation. Both actors manage impressions: teachers present a professional front in interviews (Goffman); pupils answer as they think the adult wants, or perform for attention — Willis's lads misbehaved regardless of observer control, evidence that some pupil cultures resist the researcher. Classroom power asymmetry means pupils often treat the researcher as just another teacher. Sampling in schools: the register is a near-perfect sampling frame — a rare applied strength worth citing. But random samples still need parental consent forms returned, and response rates are lowest in hard-to-reach households, biasing samples towards cooperative families; the pupils most affected by sensitive outcomes (exclusion, off-rolling, persistent absence) are precisely the hardest to sample. Weigh this against the positivist appeal of large, representative pupil surveys. Theoretical wrap: positivist designs (questionnaires, statistics) struggle with all four because they presuppose cooperation and stable, natural data; interpretivist designs trade reliability for validity precisely by working around them — this contrast is the core T-paragraph of any strong methods in context answer. Methods in context is applied Theory and Methods: the theory half of the AQA spec (4.4) supplies the deep evaluation that lifts answers into top levels. Positivism (Comte, Durkheim): social facts are external and measurable, so questionnaires, structured interviews and official statistics suit education research on patterns — class differences in attainment analysed the way Durkheim analysed Suicide (1897). Strength: reliable, representative, able to test hypotheses. Limitation: data are constructions of the research process (Cicourel 1968) and miss the meanings behind patterns — labelling, subcultures, pupil identities. Interpretivism (Weber's verstehen; symbolic interactionism): education is built through meanings, so validity demands observation and unstructured interviews — Lacey (1970), Ball (1981), Hargreaves (1967). Strength: authentic actor's-eye accounts of classroom processes. Limitation: unrepresentative, unreliable, Hawthorne-prone, small-scale. Value freedom: Weber distinguished value-relevance (values legitimately choose the topic — studying working-class underachievement is itself a value-laden choice) from value-freedom (objectivity in conduct and findings). Becker (1967) 'Whose side are we on?' and Gouldner's attack on the myth of the value-free sociology deny neutrality is possible; funding also shapes agendas — DfE-commissioned and charity-funded education studies (e.g. Sutton Trust reports) reflect their sponsors' priorities. Sociology as a science: Popper's falsificationism says sociology qualifies where it produces testable hypotheses; Kuhn replies that sociology lacks a single paradigm; realists (Keat and Urry 1975) argue classrooms are open systems — no laws, but scientific study of underlying structures is still possible. 30-mark technique (AQA 7192 Paper 3): essays such as 'Evaluate the view that sociology can and should be value-free' or 'Evaluate the claim that sociology is a science' reward AO1 knowledge, AO2 (where an item is provided) and AO3 analysis. Structure: define the key term; three or four evaluative paragraphs (point, named study, counter-position, mini-judgement); an explicit final judgement. Reuse your methods in context PET points as evidence — the Hawthorne effect supports interpretivist claims that neutral observation is impossible; performativity (Ball 2003) supports the claim that official statistics are not objective facts.

topics.name: Families and Households
topics.subject: sociology
topics.searchText: sociology Sociology Families and Households Set out functionalist, Marxist, feminist and personal life accounts of the family with named theorists (AQA 4.2.2.1) Explain the family's relationship to social structure, the economy and state policies (AQA 4.2.2.2) Describe changing patterns of marriage, cohabitation, separation, divorce and child-bearing and evaluate the explanations (AQA 4.2.2.3) Analyse gender roles, domestic labour and power relationships, including domestic violence (AQA 4.2.2.4) Evaluate the nature of childhood and its changing status in family and society (AQA 4.2.2.5) Interpret UK demographic trends since 1900 — birth rates, death rates, ageing, migration — and link them to globalisation (AQA 4.2.2.6) Functionalist: Murdock (1949, four functions), Parsons (primary socialisation, stabilisation of adult personalities, functional fit); New Right update — Murray, Marsland. Marxist: Engels (1884, inheritance of property), Zaretsky (1976, unit of consumption and haven), Ansley (1972, women as 'takers of shit'). Changing patterns: later and fewer marriages, rising cohabitation, around 40% of marriages ending in divorce, births outside marriage at about half of all births (ONS). Domestic labour: Oakley (1974), Boulton (1983), Gershuny (1994) lagged adaptation, Duncombe and Marsden (1995) triple shift, Dobash and Dobash (1980) violence. Childhood: Aries (1960) the invention of childhood, Postman (1994) its disappearance, Palmer (2006) toxic childhood; March of progress vs conflict view. Demography: birth rate fallen from about 28 to about 11 per 1,000 since 1900; ageing population (Hirsch 2005); record net migration reshaping families. Nuclear family A two-generation family of a couple and their dependent children; the unit functionalists treat as universal and central. Extended family A family containing relatives beyond the nuclear unit — vertically (grandparents) or horizontally (aunts, uncles); includes the vertically extended 'beanpole' family. Primary socialisation Parsons: the family's function of teaching children society's shared norms and values, equipping them to become co-operative members of society. Warm bath theory Parsons' image of the family as a place where the (male) breadwinner relaxes and is emotionally stabilised after the strains of work — the 'stabilisation of adult personalities'. Symmetrical family Willmott and Young (1973): the claimed modern family with joint conjugal roles — shared housework, childcare and leisure — typical of richer, home-centred couples. Domestic division of labour The allocation of housework and childcare between partners; feminists (Oakley) show it remains unequal and gendered in practice. Dual burden When a woman performs paid work and remains responsible for most housework; Duncombe and Marsden (1995) add the triple shift of paid work, housework and emotional work. Individualisation Beck and Giddens: in late modernity people construct relationships through personal choice and negotiation rather than fixed obligations, producing family diversity. Pure relationship Giddens (1992): a relationship sustained only because both partners find it emotionally satisfying, not for duty or economic necessity — inherently unstable. Beanpole family A vertically extended family with many living generations but few members in each — a product of longer life expectancy and lower fertility. Dependency ratio The relationship between the working (economically active) population and the non-working population (children, pensioners); shifts as fertility and life expectancy change. Fictive kin Personal life perspective (Smart): people treated as family despite no legal or blood tie — close friends, pets, godparents — showing 'family' means more than structure. AQA 4.2.2.1 (also OCR H580/01 Families and relationships; Eduqas Component 1) expects four competing accounts. Functionalism : Murdock (1949) argued the nuclear family performs four functions everywhere — sexual, reproductive, economic and educational — making it universal. Parsons (1955) updated this for industrial society: the family has undergone functional fit, shedding production to factories and retaining two irreducible functions — primary socialisation of children and the stabilisation of adult personalities (the warm bath). The New Right applies functionalist logic politically: Murray (1994) blames the breakdown of the nuclear family — welfare dependency, lone parenthood — for crime and educational failure; Marsland claims welfare has undermined the family's self-reliance. Marxism : Engels (1884) traced the monogamous nuclear family to the need to pass private property to legitimate heirs; Zaretsky (1976) argued the family offers a private sanctuary from alienating capitalism but is also a unit of consumption absorbing advertising and debt; Ansley (1972) called wives 'takers of shit' — absorbing the frustration male workers bring home, so the family stabilises capitalism rather than individuals. Feminism : liberal feminists (Oakley) seek equal sharing of domestic labour within existing structures; radical feminists (Delphy and Leonard 1992) see the family as the main site of patriarchal oppression — women's unpaid domestic work benefits men; Marxist feminists (Ansley) link women's subordination to capitalism. Personal life perspective (Smart 2007): 'family' means more than blood and law — fictive kin, friends, pets and chosen families (Weeks 1999 on same-sex households) show relationships are what people define as significant. AO3: functionalism is criticised for ignoring conflict and the dark side of family life; Marxism is economically deterministic; radical feminism treats all families as equally oppressive, which personal life research disputes. AQA 4.2.2.2 links the family to the social structure and social change, with particular reference to the economy and state policies. Industrialisation restructured the family: Parsons argued pre-industrial extended families gave way to the nuclear unit that suited geographic and social mobility; Laslett's household-size data (1972) showed the extended family was never universal in pre-industrial England; Anderson (1971) found working-class families in 1850s Preston used extended kin as a mutual insurance system against poverty — evidence the family adapts to economic conditions. State policy shapes family life directly: the Divorce Reform Act 1969 made divorce easier; the Civil Partnership Act 2004 and the Marriage (Same Sex Couples) Act 2013 extended legal recognition to same-sex couples; child benefit, Sure Start and free childcare support child-rearing. Evaluations of policy: the New Right criticises welfare for rewarding lone parenthood and weakening incentives (Murray); Donzelot (1977) argued professionals — doctors, social workers, health visitors — 'police the family' through surveillance targeted at the poor and working class; Fletcher (1976) counters that the welfare state supports the family in performing its functions better. Feminists note policy remains gendered: childcare provision and tax systems have historically assumed a male breadwinner, and Thatcherite policy reinforced women's domestic role. Exam point: a 30-marker on policy needs a perspective debate — functionalists see policy as helping the family perform functions; Marxists see it as relieving capitalism of costs (Donzelot's surveillance protecting the workforce); feminists see it as patriarchal in design and effect — with a weighed conclusion. AQA 4.2.2.3 expects the trends and their sociological explanations. Trends (ONS): the marriage rate has roughly halved since the early 1970s; the average age at first marriage has risen to over 30; cohabitation has risen steeply (over 3 million cohabiting couple families); around 40% of marriages end in divorce; births outside marriage have risen to about half of all births; lone-parent families are around a quarter of families with children, about 90% headed by women; families are smaller and stepfamilies have grown. Secularisation: with church attendance in decline (Wilson), marriage loses its religious status and divorce its stigma — couples see cohabitation as legitimate. Declining stigma and changing attitudes: divorce and lone parenthood are now normalised (Weeks 1999) — media and policy treat them as ordinary. Rising expectations: Fletcher (1966) argued couples expect more from marriage (companionship, romance), so they are less willing to tolerate unhappy marriages — higher standards, more divorce. Individualisation and the pure relationship: Beck (1992) and Giddens (1992) argue late-modern relationships are chosen, negotiated and retained only while they satisfy — divorce becomes a route to new family types (Stacey). Women's economic independence: Wilkinson (1994) called the change a 'genderquake' — women with careers and welfare rights need not tolerate unsatisfying marriages. New Right counter: Murray (1994) blames welfare dependency for rising lone parenthood — a political, not cultural, explanation that feminists dispute (benefits are modest and single mothers face poverty). Consequences — family diversity: Chester (1985) argued the nuclear family remains the dominant arrangement (the neo-conventional family: dual-earner but nuclear); the Rapoports (1982) identified five types of diversity — organisational, cultural, class, life-course and cohort. AO3: the A* answer weighs cultural explanations (secularisation, attitudes) against economic ones (genderquake, welfare) and judges which better explain the data. AQA 4.2.2.4 covers the domestic division of labour, power relationships and resources. Housework: Oakley (1974) treated housework as work — monotonous, unrewarding, done mostly by women and largely dissatisfying. Willmott and Young (1973) claimed the symmetrical family with joint conjugal roles was emerging among home-centred couples; Boulton (1983) rebutted this: men may 'help', but women remain responsible for housework and childcare in practice. Gershuny (1994) found a lagged adaptation — men increase housework as wives enter full-time work, but slowly; Kan (2001) showed the gap narrows with women's earnings but never closes. Dual burden and triple shift: Duncombe and Marsden (1995) found women in paid work carry paid work, housework and emotional work — men neglect the emotional shift. Same-sex households: Dunne (1999) found lesbian couples divide labour more equally, supporting the claim that inequality is gendered, not natural. Decision-making: Edgell (1980) found men dominate important decisions (moving house, finances) and women the routine ones. Money: Pahl (1993) and Vogler showed pooling has grown with dual-earner households, but men usually control it when they are the main earner. Domestic violence: Dobash and Dobash (1980) interviewed 109 women in refuges: violence was systematic male control, often triggered by challenges to male authority; Mirrlees-Black (1999, BCS) found around one in four women had experienced domestic violence — many incidents unreported. AO3: functionalists (Young and Willmott) see growing symmetry; Marxists (Zaretsky) blame capitalism's strains; radical feminists see patriarchy persisting regardless of employment; the personal life perspective asks whose meanings count — e.g. the woman who insists she 'chooses' domesticity. The strongest answers weigh symmetry evidence (Gershuny) against continued responsibility (Boulton) and reach a judgement. AQA 4.2.2.5 — childhood: Pilcher (1995) defines childhood by separateness — a distinct status with its own laws, dress and institutions. Aries (1960), studying medieval paintings, argued childhood is a recent invention: in the 10th-13th centuries children were 'miniature adults' working and mixing with adults from an early age. Childhood varies culturally (Punch 2001 — Bolivian children take adult responsibilities early), so it is socially constructed. Change: the March of Progress view holds childhood has improved — compulsory education, child protection (Children Act 1989; UN Convention 1989), shorter working hours. Conflict and postmodern views disagree: Firestone saw children as oppressed by adult control; Hillman called the control an 'age patriarchy'; Postman (1994) argued TV is blurring the adult-child boundary and childhood is 'disappearing'; Palmer (2006) blames a 'toxic childhood' of screens, junk food and marketisation. Childhood also varies by class, gender and ethnicity — not all children enjoy the same protected status. AQA 4.2.2.6 — demography since 1900: the birth rate fell from about 28 per 1,000 (1900) to about 11 today, with baby booms after the world wars and in the 1960s; total fertility is around 1.5 — well below replacement (2.1). The death rate fell from about 19 to about 9 per 1,000 as sanitation, nutrition (McKeown) and medicine improved; life expectancy rose from under 50 to over 80. Consequences: an ageing population (Hirsch 2005 — rising pension and health costs, changing dependency ratios), smaller families, and migration-driven diversity: record net migration in recent years has produced transnational families and greater ethnic diversity of family forms (globalisation). AO3: link demographic change to theory — ageing supports Hirsch's policy warnings and postmodern accounts of diverse life courses. Exam technique for families essays AQA Paper 2 : each optional topic carries 4- and 6-mark items, a 10-mark 'outline and analyse two...' and a 30-mark 'outline and evaluate...' — roughly AO1 8 / AO2 8 / AO3 14, so evaluation dominates. 30-mark skeleton: (1) define the claim and its key concepts; (2) three or four developed points, each with a named study and date; (3) three or four evaluations with counter-theorists; (4) a conclusion with a weighed judgement answering the exact question. Pitfalls: describing statistics without sociological explanation; citing Murdock's universality claim without evaluating it (polygamy, single-parent households); confusing the symmetrical family claim (Young and Willmott) with its rebuttal (Boulton); omitting the synoptic link to socialisation, education and the economy that 30-markers reward.

topics.name: Education
topics.subject: sociology
topics.searchText: sociology Sociology Education Set out functionalist, Marxist and feminist views of the role of the education system (AQA 4.1.1.1) Explain class differences in achievement through external (material and cultural) and internal factors (AQA 4.1.1.2) Explain ethnic and gender differences in achievement with named studies and dates (AQA 4.1.1.3-4) Analyse relationships and processes within schools: labelling, streaming, pupil subcultures and pupil identities (AQA 4.1.1.5) Evaluate the significance of educational policies from 1944 to the present, including marketisation, parentocracy, privatisation and globalisation of policy (AQA 4.1.1.6) Deploy education content in 10- and 30-mark essays and in the Methods in Context question (AQA 4.1.2) Functionalist: Durkheim (school as society in miniature), Parsons (1961, bridge and meritocracy), Davis and Moore (1945, role allocation). Marxist: Bowles and Gintis (1976, correspondence principle), Althusser (1971, ISA), Willis (1977, lads resist). Class — external: material deprivation (Smith and Noble 1995), cultural capital (Bourdieu 1984; Sullivan 2001); internal: labelling (Becker), streaming (Lacey 1970, Ball 1981). Ethnic: Gillborn and Youdell (2000, educational triage), Coard (1971), Fuller (1984), Mirza (1997), institutional racism (Gillborn 2008). Gender: girls' improvement (Gorard et al 2001; Sharpe 1994), boys' underachievement (Mitsos and Browne 1998), laddish subcultures (Sewell). Policy: 1944 tripartite, comprehensives, 1988 ERA marketisation, parentocracy (Ball, Bowe and Gewirtz 1994), privatisation (Ball and Youdell 2008), PISA policy borrowing (Ball 2008). Meritocracy The claim (Parsons) that education sifts and sorts pupils by ability and effort, so success reflects talent — the 'myth of meritocracy' for Bowles and Gintis. Correspondence principle Bowles and Gintis (1976): school hierarchies, punctuality and reward systems mirror the workplace, reproducing a passive, obedient workforce for capitalism. Cultural capital Bourdieu (1984): the knowledge, tastes and language middle-class parents pass on, which the education system values and rewards, converting class advantage into qualifications. Material deprivation Lack of physical necessities — housing, diet, income — that hinders attainment; statistically linked to free school meals eligibility and class gaps. Labelling Becker: teachers judge pupils against an 'ideal pupil' image (middle-class) and attach labels that shape how pupils are treated and how they respond. Self-fulfilling prophecy Rosenthal and Jacobson (1968): teacher expectations, once communicated, cause pupils to internalise labels and act them out. Streaming Separating pupils into ability groups across subjects; Lacey (1970) and Ball (1981) show it pushes lower-stream pupils into anti-school subcultures. Pupil subculture A group whose members share values and status derived from response to school — pro-school (high stream) or anti-school (low stream) subcultures (Lacey). Marketisation The 1988 Education Reform Act policy of creating an education market: formula funding, league tables, open enrolment and competition between schools. Parentocracy Miriam David's term for the marketised claim that parental choice drives standards; Ball, Bowe and Gewirtz (1994) call it a myth. Ideological state apparatus Althusser (1971): institutions such as education and media transmit ruling-class ideology, reproducing and legitimating class inequality. Ethnocentric curriculum A curriculum centred on one culture (Coard 1971: white, British, Christian) that devalues minority-ethnic pupils' identities and lowers their self-esteem. AQA 4.1.1.1 (also OCR H580/03 Section B) expects competing views of what education is for. Functionalism: Durkheim argued school is 'society in miniature' — teaching shared norms and values creates the social solidarity modern society needs; Parsons (1961) saw school as the focal socialising agency, a bridge between family's particularistic values and society's universalistic ones, operating through meritocracy; Davis and Moore (1945) added role allocation — education sifts and sorts the most able into the most functionally important (best-rewarded) roles. Marxism: Bowles and Gintis (1976) claimed the correspondence principle mirrors workplace hierarchy in school — subservience, motivation by external rewards, fragmentation — producing a passive workforce; the claim that education is meritocratic is a myth that legitimises inequality by making class advantage look like talent. Althusser (1971) called education an Ideological State Apparatus reproducing and legitimating class inequality. Willis (1977) supplied the classic evaluation: his 12 'lads' formed a counter-school culture, partially seeing through school ideology yet still drifting into manual work — resisting, but not escaping, class reproduction. Feminism: education historically channelled girls into domestic subjects; girls still face gendered subject choice and the devaluation of feminine achievement. Evaluation of each view Functionalism: assumes a value consensus that may simply reflect dominant groups; explanations risk teleology ('schools exist because they have functions'); ignores inequality of opportunity. Marxism: economically deterministic — Willis shows pupils resist; the correspondence principle overstates workplace similarity (many jobs are not hierarchical); ignores gender and ethnicity. Interactionism (Becker): focuses on meanings and everyday processes but ignores structure — a pupil's poverty shapes attainment regardless of teacher meaning. AQA 4.1.1.2 splits explanations into external (home and background) and internal (school processes). External — material deprivation: poor housing affects study space and health; Smith and Noble (1995) listed housing, diet and income as barriers to schooling; Tanner et al (2003) showed the cost of books, uniforms and transport burdens low-income families; Flaherty (2004) found free school meals carry stigma that discourages uptake. External — cultural factors: Bernstein (1975) distinguished restricted and elaborated speech codes — schools use and reward the elaborated code middle-class pupils arrive with (criticised by Labov as language difference, not deficit); Douglas (1964) linked parental interest to attainment; Feinstein (2003) showed educated parents' children do better from the earliest years; Bernstein and Young (1967) found middle-class mothers buy more educational toys; Sugarman (1970) identified working-class subcultural values — fatalism, immediate gratification, present-time orientation. Cultural capital: Bourdieu (1984) argued middle-class parents pass on cultural capital (knowledge, tastes, language) which schools reward; Sullivan (2001) measured it — pupils with wider reading and cultural knowledge did better, supporting Bourdieu over pure cultural deprivation theory. Internal — labelling and streaming: Becker (1971) found teachers' 'ideal pupil' image was middle-class; Rosenthal and Jacobson (1968) demonstrated the self-fulfilling prophecy in 'Pygmalion in the Classroom'; Hargreaves (1967) showed differentiation and polarisation — streaming pushes lower-stream working-class pupils into anti-school subcultures; Lacey (1970) found the same in Hightown Grammar; Ball (1981) at Beachside showed even banding (not full streaming) produced the same polarisation. Archer et al (2010) analysed working-class pupil identities — 'Nike identities' — showing schools devalue working-class taste, and pupils respond with symbolic violence. AQA 4.1.1.3 — ethnic differences: external factors include material deprivation and racism in wider society (Rex 1986 — racial discrimination in housing and work); internal factors matter more in exam answers: Gillborn and Youdell (2000) found 'educational triage' — schools under pressure from league tables sort pupils into those who will pass anyway, hopeless cases and borderline A-to-C candidates, with black pupils over-represented in the lower groups; the A-to-C economy drives it. Coard (1971) argued the curriculum is ethnocentric, devaluing black culture and lowering self-esteem; Troyna and Williams (1986) agreed the curriculum gives priority to English and European culture.
