Harm: profit repatriation and tax avoidance (Starbucks-style transfer pricing), the race to the bottom in wages and conditions (Rana Plaza collapse 2013, killing over 1,100 garment workers in a Primark supply chain; Foxconn assembly for Apple), environmental damage (Shell in Nigeria - Ogoniland pollution and the 1995 execution of Ken Saro-Wiwa after protests). Benefit: FDI, employment, technology and skills transfer, and infrastructure - and the NICs industrialised through export manufacturing. Verdict: harms are real but not inherent - where host states negotiate hard (South Korea, Vietnam), benefits outweigh; weak states capture less. Aid works as emergency stabiliser; trade as long-run engine - but only with fair rules and accountable recipients. Aid detail for the 20-marker: distinguish aid types precisely - bilateral (state to state, often tied), multilateral (pooled via the World Bank, IMF or UN agencies) and NGO aid (Oxfam, Save the Children - typically small-scale, bottom-up, needs-led). Note the debate's sharp edge: emergency humanitarian aid is broadly defended even by Moyo, while long-term development aid is where the dependency, corruption and donor-interest critiques bite. On trade, the standard case study is commodity dependence - when world coffee or copper prices collapse, whole export economies contract - which is why fair trade, diversification and value-added processing recur in mark schemes as the policy responses. Environment: global development externalises ecological costs onto the weakest. TNC production relocates to low-regulation states, so pollution is exported - e-waste dumped and burned at sites like Agbogbloshie, Ghana; global commodity demand drives Amazon deforestation (beef and soy exports) releasing carbon and destroying habitats; and climate change hits developing countries hardest - drought, flooding and crop failure - while they contributed least to emissions. AO3: the growth-versus-sustainability tension (Brundtland's 1987 'sustainable development') frames the debate: can the global South industrialise without replicating the North's environmental damage? Green and state crime links apply here (AQA 4.3.1.5): TNC and state complicity in environmental harm, as in Ogoniland. Feminist perspectives: Boserup (1970) showed development planning ignored women - modernisation schemes transferred technology to men, widening gender gaps; WID/WAD/GAD mark the feminist evolution from adding women into development, to reading women's subordination as structured by global capitalism, to transforming the gendered structures of development itself (GAD). Elson & Pearson theorise the feminisation of labour : export manufacturing concentrates women in flexible, low-paid, insecure EPZ assembly work (the Rana Plaza workforce was mostly female), while women still carry subsistence labour - water, fuel, care - and remain excluded from decision-making. AO3: employment also brings independence and bargaining power (Kabeer), and education access has narrowed gaps - so benefits are real but unequal and conditional on class and locality. Postdevelopment (Escobar 1995): 'development' is a Western discourse that constructs the South as backward and authorises intervention - the strongest answers use it to question the question itself, before reaching a judgement: global development has lifted living chances measurably, but its benefits are distributed along core-periphery lines and its costs (environmental, gendered) fall on those with least power. Case anchors for essays: Shell/Ogoniland (state-TNC complicity, Ken Saro-Wiwa 1995) for environmental harm; the Amazon (beef and soy commodity demand) for deforestation; Agbogbloshie, Ghana (exported e-waste) for pollution transfer; Rana Plaza (2013, majority-female workforce) linking TNC labour practices to the feminisation of labour; and the MDGs/SDGs for measurable development progress (extreme poverty falling, girls' school enrolment rising) - the standard evidence that development delivers, used to balance the structural critiques. One or two named anchors per paragraph is enough: the marks come from tying them to theory, not listing them.

topics.name: Business Growth and Objectives
topics.subject: business-studies
topics.searchText: business-studies Business Studies Business Growth and Objectives Explain the nature and purpose of business activity and the common objectives — profit, growth, survival, cash flow, social and ethical — and how the balance of objectives changes between a start-up and an established plc (AQA 3.1.1) Distinguish the main forms of business — sole trader, partnership, private and public limited companies, not-for-profit organisations and franchises — and evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of each form (AQA 3.1.2) Identify internal and external stakeholders, analyse their interests and potential conflicts, and apply stakeholder mapping by power and interest (AQA 3.1.3; Edexcel Theme 3) Compare organic (internal) growth with external growth through mergers, takeovers, joint ventures, strategic alliances and franchising (AQA 3.9; Edexcel 3.2) Assess why growth strategies fail — overtrading, diseconomies of scale, culture clash and cash-flow strain — and the criteria for judging a growth decision Calculate and interpret market share, revenue growth and return on capital employed when evaluating growth options and how they are funded Mission statement A brief statement of the overall purpose and values of an organisation, designed to communicate what the business does and why it exists to stakeholders. Limited liability The legal position where the financial liability of the owners (shareholders) for the debts of a business is limited to the amount they invested; their personal assets are protected. Unlimited liability The legal obligation of a sole trader or partner to pay all debts of the business, potentially requiring the sale of personal assets if the business fails. Organic (internal) growth Growth generated from within the business, for example by opening new outlets, expanding output, developing new products or entering new markets using the firm's own resources. Horizontal integration A merger or takeover of a business operating at the same stage of production in the same industry, for example one supermarket chain buying another. Vertical integration A merger or takeover of a business at a different stage of production in the same industry — backwards towards suppliers or forwards towards distributors and retailers. Conglomerate integration A merger or takeover of a business operating in an entirely different industry, spreading risk across unrelated markets. Joint venture An agreement between two or more businesses to work together on a project, sharing costs, risks and expertise, while remaining separate legal entities. Stakeholder Any individual or group with an interest in, or affected by, the activities of a business — for example shareholders, employees, customers, suppliers, the local community and government. Diseconomies of scale The rise in average unit costs that occurs when a business grows beyond its optimum size, typically through communication failures, coordination problems and de-motivation in large organisations. Businesses exist to satisfy the needs of customers, owners and society by producing goods and services. The mission statement sets the overall purpose and values; from it flow corporate objectives , and from those functional (departmental) objectives. Examiners reward answers that show the hierarchy : mission → corporate objectives → functional objectives → targets, and that objectives must be consistent with each other. The common business objectives are: Profit — profit maximisation is rarely pursued literally; most owners satisfice , targeting a satisfactory return. Profit matters because it rewards risk-takers, funds reinvestment and attracts finance. Growth — sales growth or market share growth increases market power, economies of scale and often managerial rewards; growth may be pursued even at the cost of short-term profit (penetration pricing, heavy investment). Survival — the dominant objective for new businesses and during recessions or crises; roughly a fifth of UK start-ups fail in year one and around half within three years, so cash preservation outranks profit. Cash flow — a profitable business can still fail if it runs out of cash; maintaining liquidity is a genuine objective in its own right. Social and ethical objectives — for social enterprises and increasingly for plc brands, environmental and ethical goals (sustainability targets, fair pay) shape decisions and reputation. Objectives change over time. A start-up prioritises survival and cash flow; an established plc balances shareholder returns (dividends, share price) with growth and reputation. Objectives also conflict: growth financed by debt raises risk; an ethical sourcing policy raises unit costs. Strong evaluation always identifies these trade-offs and judges which objective should dominate in the given context — an objective is only 'right' relative to the business's situation, stakeholders and stage of development. The form of ownership determines liability, access to finance, control and how objectives are set — a core AO1/AO2 distinction across all boards. Sole trader — one owner with unlimited liability . Quick and cheap to set up, full control, keeps all profit and privacy (no accounts published). Weaknesses: unlimited liability, hard to raise finance, no continuity if the owner dies or retires, workload and skill bottlenecks. Partnership — two to twenty owners sharing profit, risk and expertise under the Partnership Act 1890 (a Limited Partnership or LLP gives some partners limited liability). More capital and shared decision-making, but partners are jointly liable and disagreements can paralyse the firm. Private limited company (Ltd) — shares sold privately to known investors; shareholders have limited liability , the business has separate legal identity and continuity. Finance is easier to raise than for a sole trader, but shares cannot be advertised for sale to the public, so growth capital is still restricted. Public limited company (plc) — shares traded on the stock market after a flotation . Access to very large-scale finance and enhanced public profile, but costly to float, subject to regulation and scrutiny, exposed to divorce of ownership and control (professional managers may pursue their own objectives rather than shareholders'), and vulnerable to takeover because shares can be bought openly. Not-for-profit organisations — charities, mutuals and social enterprises whose surplus is reinvested in the cause rather than distributed to owners; objectives centre on stakeholder benefit, and funding comes from donations, grants and trading. Franchise — the franchisor grants the franchisee the right to trade under its brand in return for fees and royalties. For the franchisee: a proven business model, brand recognition and training, at the cost of fees, limited independence and the franchisor's rules. For the franchisor: rapid, low-capital expansion by others. Shareholders own limited companies, receive dividends and typically one vote per share; institutional investors (pension funds, insurers) exert heavy influence on plcs. In exams, link the choice of legal form to objectives and growth: a sole trader converting to an Ltd gains limited liability and capital, but loses some control and privacy — whether that trade-off is worthwhile depends on the scale of growth planned and the owner's appetite for risk. Choosing a form in exams. The assessment angle is almost always judgement : the best legal form depends on objectives, funding needs and attitude to risk. A high-growth technology start-up may stay private to protect control through early losses, then float once brand and profitability de-risk the issue; a community-focused enterprise may stay not-for-profit because shareholder returns would conflict with the mission. Note also that liability drives risk appetite: unlimited liability makes owners cautious — sensible for stability, but it can starve a business of the investment needed to grow, which is why many firms convert to limited companies precisely when they plan expansion. Stakeholders are groups affected by or with an interest in the business. Internal stakeholders include employees, managers and owners; external stakeholders include customers, suppliers, creditors, the local community, government and pressure groups. Each has distinct needs: Shareholders — dividends, capital growth, ethical governance. Employees — fair pay, job security, development, working conditions. Customers — quality, value for money, honest marketing, safety. Suppliers — reliable orders, prompt payment, long-term relationships. Local community — employment, low pollution, investment in the area. Government — tax revenue, compliance with legislation, employment. Stakeholder conflict arises because needs compete: a takeover rewarding shareholders may mean redundancies for employees and reduced choice for customers if a competitor is absorbed; a pay rise pleases employees but raises costs for owners; cost-cutting that pleases shareholders may damage quality for customers. The stakeholder map (power/interest grid) helps managers prioritise: High power, high interest — manage closely (key shareholders, senior managers). High power, low interest — keep satisfied (regulators, major creditors). Low power, high interest — keep informed (employees, local community). Low power, low interest — monitor with minimal effort. In evaluation, note that objectives set by management must reconcile these conflicts — a shareholder-primary approach (Friedman) maximises owner returns but risks reputational damage from ignored stakeholders, while a stakeholder approach builds long-term legitimacy at the cost of some short-term profit. AQA 3.2.3 also treats stakeholder influence on management decision-making: the more powerful and interested a stakeholder group, the more it shapes strategy — use this to explain why a business chose a particular course, not just to list groups. Organic growth expands the business using its own resources: opening new outlets, increasing capacity, developing new products (Ansoff), entering new markets, or franchising the concept. It is slower but lower-risk: financed from retained profit and steady borrowing, it keeps control within existing management and grows culture and capability gradually. External growth acquires scale instantly through mergers (two firms agree to combine) and takeovers/acquisitions (one firm buys a majority stake, sometimes hostile), joint ventures , strategic alliances and franchising . Types of integration: Horizontal — same stage, same industry: market share, removal of a competitor, economies of scale (e.g. supermarket mergers). Risk: Competition and Markets Authority intervention if market dominance results. Vertical backwards — acquiring a supplier: secures inputs, quality and margins; risk of complacency and higher fixed costs. Vertical forwards — acquiring distribution or retail: control of the customer interface and retail margin. Conglomerate — unrelated industry: spreads risk; but no synergy or expertise, which is why conglomerates often underperform. Why grow? Economies of scale (purchasing, technical, marketing), greater market power and pricing influence, reduced risk through diversification, access to new markets and talent, and increased brand recognition. Why external growth fails: research consistently suggests a majority of mergers destroy value — through overtrading (expanding sales faster than cash and capacity allow), culture clash between merged workforces, overpayment in bidding wars, key staff departures, integration costs exceeding synergies, and management distraction. The Greiner growth model adds that growth passes through phases, each ending in a crisis (leadership, autonomy, control) that demands structural change. Worked application: a firm with revenue of £40m in a market worth £500m has market share of £40m ÷ £500m × 100 = 8%; after acquiring a rival with £65m of sales (assuming no market growth), share rises to £105m ÷ £500m × 100 = 21% — quantifying the jump in market power an acquisition delivers is exactly the AO2 application examiners reward. Organic versus external in evaluation. The two routes are not mutually exclusive — many plcs grow organically and acquire selectively. The exam question is which route better fits the context : speed of growth needed, availability and price of targets, existing gearing, management capacity, and cultural compatibility. Organic growth compounds learning (each new store informs the next); external growth imports capability (technology, brands, people) that organic growth could take years to build — but only if integration succeeds. A* answers evaluate growth against explicit criteria rather than asserting benefits. Use financial evidence: Return on Capital Employed (ROCE) = operating profit ÷ capital employed × 100. If the expected ROCE of the growth option exceeds the cost of borrowing (and the current ROCE), it adds value. Worked example: a £25m acquisition funded by a loan at 6% must deliver enough additional operating profit to beat 6% on £25m = £1.5m a year; expected synergies of £2.5m a year clear this hurdle, but only forecasts — hence the need for sensitivity analysis. Gearing = non-current liabilities ÷ capital employed × 100. Debt-funded growth raises gearing; above roughly 50% the business is financially risky because interest is paid regardless of profit, so a downturn amplifies losses. Retained-profit growth avoids this but is slower and may mean missing market opportunities. Cash flow — growth consumes cash before it generates it: stock, premises and recruitment all precede revenue. Assess the cash-flow forecast for the growth period, not just profit projections. Non-financial criteria matter equally in AO4: cultural compatibility in a merger, management capacity to integrate, impact on existing stakeholders (redundancies, customer service), regulatory risk, and whether the growth fits the mission. The strongest conclusions are conditional : 'growth by acquisition is justified if synergies are realistic and cultures integrate; otherwise organic expansion better preserves value'. Finally, link growth back to objectives: growth is a means — judge it by whether it better delivers the objectives (profit, survival, shareholder value, social goals) that the business actually pursues, in its context.

topics.name: Marketing
topics.subject: business-studies
topics.searchText: business-studies Business Studies Marketing Set and justify marketing objectives — sales volume and value, market share, market growth, brand loyalty — and analyse the market using size, growth and share data (AQA 3.3.1) Evaluate market research methods — primary and secondary, quantitative and qualitative — including sampling, cost and the reliability of data in dynamic markets (AQA 3.3.2) Apply segmentation (geographic, demographic, psychographic, behavioural), targeting (mass versus niche) and positioning, including market mapping and USPs (AQA 3.3.3; Edexcel 1.1) Apply and evaluate the extended marketing mix (7Ps) — product, price, place, promotion, people, process, physical evidence — including pricing strategies and distribution channels (AQA 3.3.3; Edexcel 1.2) Analyse the product life cycle, extension strategies and the Ansoff matrix, and the risk gradient between its four strategies (AQA 3.3 and 3.8; Edexcel 1.2) Calculate and interpret price elasticity of demand and use it to inform pricing decisions (AQA 3.3.2) Evaluate digital marketing — SEO, PPC, social media, email and e-commerce — against traditional channels Market segmentation Dividing a market into distinct groups of buyers with common characteristics or needs — geographic, demographic, psychographic or behavioural — so that marketing can be targeted at each group. Market positioning How consumers perceive a product relative to competing products, often analysed on a market map plotting two attributes (for example price against quality). Market mapping A diagram plotting products in a market against two key attributes to identify positioning of competitors and possible gaps in the market. Unique Selling Point (USP) The distinctive feature or benefit of a product that differentiates it from competitors and gives consumers a reason to buy it. Price elasticity of demand (PED) The responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in price: the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price. Penetration pricing Setting a low initial price to gain market share quickly and discourage competitors, usually raising prices once a customer base is established. Price skimming Setting a high initial price for a new or innovative product to maximise revenue from early adopters and recover development costs, lowering the price over time. Product life cycle (PLC) The stages a product passes through — development, introduction, growth, maturity and decline — each with different sales, profit and cash-flow characteristics. Extension strategy Marketing action taken to prolong the maturity stage of the product life cycle, such as new versions, new markets, new uses, repositioning or price changes. Ansoff matrix A two-by-two model of growth strategies plotting existing/new products against existing/new markets: market penetration, product development, market development and diversification (in ascending order of risk). Marketing objectives must derive from corporate objectives. Common ones: sales volume (units) and sales value (revenue), market share (firm sales ÷ market sales × 100), market growth, brand loyalty/awareness and — in some specifications — customer satisfaction. Objectives should be measurable and realistic: 'increase market share from 12% to 15% within two years' allows performance to be judged. Market analysis uses market size, growth rate, market share and trends. A growing market offers easier growth (the tide lifts all boats); a static or declining market makes share gains the only route — which intensifies rivalry and usually requires promotion or price competitiveness. Market research gathers the data behind these decisions: Primary (field) research — data collected first-hand: surveys, questionnaires, interviews, focus groups, observation, test marketing. Up-to-date and specific to the firm's needs, but costly, time-consuming and subject to sample bias. Secondary (desk) research — existing data: government statistics (ONS), market reports, competitor accounts, internet data. Cheap and fast, but may be outdated, generalised or collected for another purpose. Quantitative — numerical data (survey scores, sales figures): easy to analyse statistically but shallow on reasons. Qualitative — opinions and motives (focus groups, interviews): explains why consumers behave as they do, but small samples limit generalisation. Sampling — random, quota or stratified — lets firms survey a representative subset rather than the whole market. Random sampling avoids bias but may miss target customers; quota sampling guarantees representation of key groups but risks interviewer bias. Limitations to evaluate: cost versus value of information, sample size and bias, respondent dishonesty, and — critically — dynamic markets : research is a snapshot in markets where tastes shift quickly (fashion, technology), so data can be obsolete before it is used. The best answers weigh the reliability of the data against the risk of the decision it informs. Segmentation divides the market so that marketing matches buyer needs. Four bases: Geographic — by location: urban versus rural, region, climate (a surfwear brand targets coastal regions). Demographic — by population characteristics: age, gender, income, occupation (premium models target high incomes; family cars target parents). Psychographic — by lifestyle, values and personality: environmentally conscious 'green' consumers, thrill-seekers, status-seekers. Behavioural — by usage and buying behaviour: heavy users, first-time buyers, brand loyalty, benefits sought (convenience versus quality). Effective segments are measurable, accessible, sizeable and distinct. Targeting then chooses which segment(s) to serve: mass marketing (one product for the whole market — economies of scale, but intense competition and generic appeal) versus niche marketing (a specialised segment — less competition, premium pricing, customer loyalty, but limited sales volume and vulnerability if the niche shrinks or attracts larger rivals). Positioning establishes how the product is perceived relative to rivals — typically on a market map (price against quality, or any two attributes). Gaps in the map reveal unmet positions (a gap for 'high quality, low price' may be an opportunity — or may simply show that position is unprofitable). Positioning is delivered through the USP and consistent branding: Volvo owns 'safety', Aldi owns 'value'. Added value — the difference between the price charged and the cost of inputs — is created by branding, quality, convenience and service, and it is what allows premium pricing. Worked application: a new energy drink targeting 18–25 males segments demographically (age, gender), psychographically (active, risk-taking) and behaviourally (gym-goers); pricing at £1.50 penetrates the market; promotion via social media influencers and gym sponsorships reaches the segment cheaply — every element of the mix flows from the segment chosen, which is the analytical point examiners reward. The marketing mix is the combination of marketing decisions — the 4Ps plus three service elements. Consistency matters: a premium price with poor packaging confuses positioning. P Key decisions Example / evaluation point Product Features, quality, design, branding, range, life-cycle stage Brand equity allows premium pricing (Apple); product must deliver the promise promotion makes Price Pricing strategy and tactics See pricing table below; price signals quality and must reflect elasticity and positioning Place Distribution channels: direct (manufacturer to consumer via own website/stores), indirect (wholesalers, retailers, agents), multi/omnichannel Omnichannel integrates online and physical (click-and-collect); channel choice affects cost, control and reach Promotion Above the line (TV, radio, print), below the line (sales promotion, direct mail, PR, sponsorships), digital (SEO, PPC, social, email) Choice depends on budget, target market, competition and product stage — a £2,000 bakery budget rules out ATL People Staff who deliver the service: recruitment, training, appearance, attitude In services the person is the product experience — a rude waiter destroys a premium restaurant's positioning Process How the service is delivered: queues, delivery speed, online ordering, after-sales Amazon's one-click ordering and next-day delivery are process-based competitive advantage Physical evidence Tangible cues: packaging, store décor, uniforms, website design Signals quality and reassures buyers of intangible services (clean gym = competent gym) Pricing strategies — know the mechanics and the risk of each: Penetration — low initial price gains share fast; hard to raise later, may signal low quality, thin margins. Skimming — high initial price harvests early adopters and recovers R&D; attracts competitors, slows volume. Psychological — £9.99 reads as £9; aspirational pricing supports premium images. Competitive — matching rivals' prices; sensible in price-sensitive markets with similar products, but ignites price wars if all follow. Cost-plus — unit cost plus a mark-up; simple and guarantees margin per unit, but ignores demand, competitors and elasticity. Dynamic — real-time adjustment to demand and availability (airline seats, Uber surge, concert tickets); maximises revenue but risks customer resentment. Loss leader — selling below cost to attract footfall that buys profitable items; unsustainable if customers only buy the loss-maker. The product life cycle tracks sales over time: introduction (slow sales, heavy promotion spend, negative or low cash flow), growth (rapid sales growth, rising profit, competitors enter), maturity (peak sales, price competition, strong positive cash flow), decline (falling sales as tastes and technology move on — DVDs, iPods). Cash-flow implications matter for analysis: growth-stage products consume investment; mature products generate the cash that funds them — the logic behind the Boston Matrix. Extension strategies prolong maturity: new versions and flavours, new markets (exporting), new uses, repositioning to a new segment, promotional refresh or price adjustments. Coca-Cola is the classic example — over a century of maturity sustained by continuous extension. The Ansoff matrix maps growth strategies by risk: Market penetration (existing product, existing market) — lowest risk: promotion, loyalty schemes, price tactics to win share from rivals. Limited if the market is saturated. Product development (new product, existing market) — moderate risk: leverages brand loyalty but demands R&D and innovation; failure wastes investment (New Coke). Market development (existing product, new market) — moderate risk: exporting or new segments; leverages the proven product but faces unfamiliar competitors, cultures and regulation. Diversification (new product, new market) — highest risk: no experience of either dimension, but spreads risk across markets; related diversification (synergy) is safer than unrelated (conglomerate). Evaluation: risk rises as the firm moves further from what it knows, because research is less reliable for new products and markets. But low-risk penetration in a declining market can be the worst strategy — risk must be weighed against reward and market conditions, not minimised blindly. The Ansoff matrix also ignores competition: a 'low-risk' penetration strategy in a market dominated by a powerful incumbent may be effectively impossible. Price elasticity of demand (PED) = % change in quantity demanded ÷ % change in price. Worked example: a price rise from £4.00 to £4.40 (a 10% increase) causes sales to fall from 2,000 to 1,700 units (a 15% fall). PED = −15 ÷ 10 = −1.5 — elastic (ignoring the sign, greater than 1). Interpretation: where demand is elastic (|PED| > 1), a price rise reduces revenue (the quantity loss outweighs the price gain) — so cut price to grow revenue; where demand is inelastic (|PED| Uses: PED informs pricing strategy, forecasting revenue effects of price changes, and — for retailers — loss-leader decisions. Limitations: elasticity is an estimate based on past data and assumes other factors are constant (ceteris paribus); it varies over time, along the demand curve and between segments, so a single figure is unreliable. Digital marketing uses online channels to reach and convert customers: SEO (search engine optimisation) — structuring content to rank organically in search results; slow to build but free per click and high-trust. PPC (pay-per-click advertising) — paid search and display ads; instant, measurable and targetable, but costs scale with competition. Social media — organic content and paid campaigns; cheap reach, precise targeting by demographics and interests, influencer partnerships; risks of viral backlashes and platform dependence. Email — direct, personalised, near-zero marginal cost; excellent for retention, but depends on an opted-in list. E-commerce — selling online removes geographic limits, cuts property costs and generates rich behavioural data, but faces intense price comparison, delivery/logistics costs and digital exclusion of some segments. Evaluation: digital offers measurable, targeted, low-cost reach — its data also feeds segmentation (behavioural) and dynamic pricing. But traditional ATL still builds mass brand awareness faster, and the best promotion mixes blend channels by budget, market type and product stage. Strong answers justify the mix against the context : budget, target segment, competition and life-cycle stage.

topics.name: Operations Management
topics.subject: business-studies
topics.searchText: business-studies Business Studies Operations Management Set operational objectives — unit costs, quality, speed of response, dependability, flexibility, environmental impact — and analyse operational performance data (AQA 3.4.1–3.4.2) Calculate and interpret capacity utilisation, labour productivity and unit costs, and evaluate ways of managing under- and over-utilisation (AQA 3.4.2) Compare production methods — job, batch, flow, cell and mass customisation — and analyse the implications of switching methods (AQA 3.4.3; Edexcel 2.4) Evaluate lean production — waste reduction (the seven muda), just-in-time (JIT), kanban, kaizen and 5S — including JIT's supply-chain vulnerability (AQA 3.4.3) Evaluate quality management — quality control versus quality assurance, TQM, kaizen, Six Sigma (DMAIC) and benchmarking — and the costs of quality Analyse supply chain management — procurement, logistics, outsourcing and supplier relationships — and the impact of technology: automation, AI, IoT and Industry 4.0 Capacity utilisation Actual output as a percentage of maximum possible output: (actual output ÷ maximum output) × 100. Low utilisation raises unit costs; excessively high utilisation leaves no slack for maintenance or demand spikes. Labour productivity Output per worker over a period: total output ÷ number of employees. A key measure of workforce efficiency. Lean production An approach that systematically eliminates waste (muda) from production — overproduction, waiting, transport, over-processing, excess inventory, unnecessary motion and defects — to cut costs and improve quality. Just-in-time (JIT) An inventory system in which materials and components arrive exactly when needed in production, minimising stock held; it depends on reliable, flexible suppliers and strong logistics. Kanban A visual signal (card or board) that triggers the replacement of consumed stock, pulling materials through the production process only as they are used. Kaizen Continuous improvement through small, incremental changes suggested and implemented by the whole workforce, central to Total Quality Management culture. Total Quality Management (TQM) A culture in which every employee is responsible for quality, aiming at zero defects by getting things right first time rather than inspecting errors out afterwards. Quality assurance (QA) Building quality into the production process at every stage so defects are prevented; contrast with quality control (QC), the inspection of finished output to detect errors. Six Sigma A data-driven quality methodology (Define, Measure, Analyse, Improve, Control) aiming to reduce defects to 3.4 per million opportunities. Outsourcing Contracting a third-party provider to perform a business function (e.g. IT support, logistics, payroll); sensible for non-core activities, but loses direct control over quality and data. Operational objectives flow from corporate objectives and typically cover: unit costs , quality (defect rates, returns), speed of response and lead times, dependability (on-time delivery), flexibility (product mix, volume) and environmental performance (waste, emissions). Measuring them: Labour productivity = total output ÷ number of employees. Rising productivity lowers unit costs and signals efficient workforce use; falling productivity signals de-motivation, poor training or process problems. Unit costs = total costs ÷ output. The core efficiency measure — lower unit costs allow lower prices or higher margins. Capacity utilisation = (actual output ÷ maximum possible output) × 100. Worked example: a factory with maximum capacity of 1,000 units a week produces 800. Utilisation = 800 ÷ 1,000 × 100 = 80% . Interpreting capacity utilisation is a classic evaluation point. Under-utilisation (say below 85%) spreads fixed costs over fewer units, raising unit costs — but it creates capacity for new orders, maintenance and training, and reduces staff stress. Very high utilisation (approaching 100%) minimises unit costs but leaves no slack: machine breakdowns halt output, staff work under pressure (raising errors), and a demand spike must be met by overtime, outsourcing or lost sales. Ways to improve utilisation: increase demand (promotion, price tactics, new markets), produce stock ahead of seasonal peaks (just-in-case), reduce capacity (sell plant, cut shifts), or subcontract surplus demand to others. Worked calculation — productivity: a firm producing 48,000 units with 60 employees has labour productivity of 48,000 ÷ 60 = 800 units per worker ; if output rises to 52,800 with the same staff, productivity rises to 880 — a 10% gain that directly lowers labour cost per unit and strengthens competitiveness. Always link the measures: high utilisation with falling quality signals over-stretching; low utilisation with high unit costs signals the need for demand-generation or capacity reduction. Method Nature Strengths Weaknesses Example Job One-off items to customer specification Full customisation, premium prices, skilled motivation, flexibility High unit costs, slow, skilled labour needed Bespoke furniture, wedding cakes, shipbuilding Batch Groups of identical items made together Some flexibility between batches, lower unit costs than job Set-up downtime between batches, storage of part-finished work Bakery bread lines, clothing sizes, paint Flow Continuous, standardised, high-volume output on a line Very low unit costs (economies of scale), consistent quality, automation-friendly Huge capital cost, inflexible, deskilling, breakdowns halt the line Soft-drinks bottling, car assembly, oil refining Cell U-shaped workstations, multi-skilled teams making product families Teamwork and motivation, flexible, faster changeovers than flow, lower waste Multi-skilling is costly to train, requires reorganisation Electronics assembly, component manufacturing Mass customisation Flow production + flexibility: standardised base adapted to individual orders Low unit costs and personalisation — technology-enabled (modular design, flexible systems) Requires significant IT investment and sophisticated supply chains Dell PCs, Nike By You trainers The choice of method depends on the nature of demand : customisation versus standardisation, volume and stability of demand, and the value customers place on uniqueness versus low price. Switching methods (a classic analysis question) has consequences across the business. Worked example — a furniture maker switches from batch to flow production: cost — lower unit costs through economies of scale and fewer set-ups, but a heavy capital investment in a dedicated line; quality — more consistent standardised output, but a single defect repeats across large volumes before detection; flexibility — much reduced, since the line makes one product family and customisation becomes harder; workforce — deskilling and possible redundancies damage motivation and industrial relations; inventory — work-in-progress falls if the line is paired with JIT. The method chosen must match the market: applying flow production to a bespoke maker would destroy the premium customisation customers pay for, while running job production for a standardised high-demand product would leave unit costs uncompetitive. Lean production eliminates muda (waste). The seven wastes: overproduction (making more than demand requires), waiting (idle time between processes), transport (unnecessary movement of materials), over-processing (more work than the customer values), inventory (excess stock holding), motion (unnecessary movement of people) and defects (rework, scrap, returns). Lean tools: Just-in-time (JIT) — stock arrives exactly when needed; the pull system produces only to actual demand. Benefits: lower stock-holding costs, improved cash flow (cash not tied up in inventory), less obsolete stock, smaller warehouses, and defects surface quickly because no buffer hides them. Risks: the supply chain becomes vulnerable — a delayed delivery, strike or transport disruption halts production because there is no buffer stock; it demands highly reliable, flexible, local suppliers, accurate forecasts and disciplined logistics. JIT versus just-in-case (JIC) : JIC holds buffer stock for security at the cost of working capital — the choice depends on supply-chain reliability and demand stability. Kanban — a visual card or board signal that triggers replenishment of consumed stock, pulling materials through the process and preventing overproduction at source. 5S — Sort, Set in order, Shine, Standardise, Sustain: workplace organisation that cuts motion waste and makes abnormalities visible. Kaizen — continuous improvement through many small changes suggested by the workforce; cumulatively transformative, and motivating because employees own the improvements. Evaluation of lean: lean cuts costs, improves quality and releases working capital — but its benefits depend entirely on supplier reliability and demand stability. In a crisis (pandemic, supply-chain shocks) JIT firms with no buffer stock suffer more than JIC rivals — strong answers judge lean against the firm's context: supply-chain dependability, demand variability and the cost of holding stock versus the cost of stopping production. Quality control (QC) inspects output at the end of production to detect defects: simple and keeps inspection expertise centralised, but it finds errors after they are made — scrap and rework are costly, and inspection workers bear no responsibility for preventing defects. Quality assurance (QA) builds quality into every stage so defects are prevented at source: every worker checks their own and the previous stage's work (quality chains), improving quality culture, but it requires training and a genuine culture change. Total Quality Management (TQM) — the culture of QA taken furthest: quality is everyone's responsibility, aimed at zero defects and continuous improvement (kaizen). Features: empowerment of employees to stop the line, quality chains between internal customers, and customer-focused standards. Benefits: lower failure costs, strong reputation and fewer returns; costs: extensive training, cultural resistance, and time before results appear. Kaizen — continuous small improvements; cheap, motivating and cumulative, but incremental rather than radical. Six Sigma — data-driven quality aiming at 3.4 defects per million opportunities, through DMAIC : Define the problem and customer requirements; Measure current performance and defect rates; Analyse the data for root causes; Improve the process by removing those causes; Control with monitoring to sustain the gains. Rigorous and measurable, but demanding in data and expertise. Benchmarking — comparing performance and practices with the best in the industry (or another sector) to identify improvement targets; reveals gaps but assumes practices transfer between firms. Costs of quality strengthen analysis: prevention costs (training, process design) and appraisal costs (inspection, testing) are incurred up front; internal failure costs (scrap, rework) and external failure costs (returns, warranty claims, reputational damage) rise when quality fails. QA/TQM shift spending from failure to prevention — the analytical point is that prevention is cheaper than failure, but it requires investment before payback. Evaluation: the right approach depends on the product (a bespoke maker relies on skilled craft; a bottler needs automated inspection and TQM) and on culture — TQM fails where employees see it as management rhetoric rather than genuine empowerment. Supply chain management coordinates the flow from suppliers to customers: Procurement — selecting suppliers and managing purchasing: criteria include price, quality, reliability, flexibility, ethical standards and location (local suppliers enable JIT; distant ones add lead time and risk). Logistics — transport and warehousing: balancing speed against cost, inventory location, and distribution networks that determine dependability. Supplier relationships — long-term partnerships with development support (sharing forecasts, joint improvement) underpin JIT; adversarial, price-only relationships undermine quality and reliability. Outsourcing — contracting third parties for non-core functions. Benefits: lower costs (specialist providers' scale and labour rates), access to expertise and 24/7 cover, freeing managers for core competences. Drawbacks: loss of direct control over quality and data security, communication and time-zone issues, redundancy costs, morale damage and dependence on a single supplier. The decision hinges on whether the function is core or non-core: for a manufacturer, IT support is non-core, so outsourcing is usually sensible; core production would rarely be outsourced in full. Technology in operations (Industry 4.0) transforms capacity, quality and flexibility: Automation and robotics — consistent quality, 24/7 output, lower unit costs at scale; but high capital cost, deskilling, redundancy costs and inflexibility if demand changes. IoT and cyber-physical systems — sensors monitor machines in real time, enabling predictive maintenance (fixing machines before breakdown halts a JIT line) and traceability. Big data and AI — demand forecasting, dynamic scheduling, quality analytics and personalised mass customisation. Additive manufacturing (3D printing) and digital twins — rapid prototyping and low-volume custom production; virtual models of physical systems test changes before committing capital. Evaluation: technology investment raises productivity, utilisation and quality — but the capital cost must be judged with investment appraisal (payback, ARR, NPV), training costs are significant, and staff resist change. The strongest answers weigh the efficiency gains against the investment risk and the firm's demand stability: a high fixed-cost automated line only pays back with high, stable volume — matching capacity investment to demand forecasts is the core of good operations strategy.

topics.name: Finance and Accounts
topics.subject: business-studies
topics.searchText: business-studies Business Studies Finance and Accounts Evaluate internal and external sources of finance — retained profit, asset sales, overdrafts, trade credit, loans, bonds, share capital, venture capital — and the factors determining the choice (AQA 3.5.3; Edexcel 2.1) Construct and interpret cash-flow forecasts, explain why profitable businesses fail from cash shortages, and evaluate remedies (AQA 3.5.2; Edexcel 2.2) Analyse budgets and variance analysis — zero-based versus incremental budgeting, adverse and favourable variances (AQA 3.5.2) Interpret income statements and statements of financial position, and calculate profitability (gross margin, net margin, ROCE), liquidity (current, acid test), efficiency (inventory, receivables, payables days) and gearing ratios with step-by-step workings (AQA 3.5.2; Edexcel 2.3 and 3.5) Perform break-even analysis — contribution, break-even output, margin of safety, target profit — and evaluate its assumptions (AQA 3.5) Apply investment appraisal — payback, average rate of return (ARR) and net present value (NPV) with discounting — and evaluate which technique suits which decision (AQA 3.5; Edexcel 3.3) Retained profit Profit kept within the business after dividends have been paid; an internal source of finance with no interest or dilution, limited by the size of past profits. Working capital The finance available for day-to-day operations: current assets minus current liabilities. Net cash flow Cash inflows minus cash outflows in a period; the closing balance equals the opening balance plus net cash flow. Profit is not cash — a profitable business can fail from a cash shortage. Contribution per unit Selling price per unit minus variable cost per unit — the amount each unit contributes towards fixed costs and then profit. Margin of safety The difference between actual (or forecast) output and break-even output — how far demand can fall before the business makes a loss. Return on Capital Employed (ROCE) Operating profit divided by capital employed (non-current liabilities plus equity) × 100; the key profitability ratio comparing profit with the long-term capital invested. Gearing Non-current liabilities as a percentage of capital employed (or of equity). Above roughly 50% a business is highly geared — interest must be paid regardless of profit, raising financial risk. Acid test ratio Current assets excluding inventory, divided by current liabilities — a stricter liquidity measure than the current ratio because inventory may be slow to convert to cash. Net present value (NPV) The sum of future net cash flows discounted to today's values, minus the initial investment; a positive NPV means the project beats the discount rate (cost of capital). Average rate of return (ARR) Average annual profit divided by average investment × 100; expresses an investment's profitability as a comparable percentage, but ignores the timing of returns. Internal sources generate funds from within the business: retained profit (no interest, no dilution of control, immediate — but limited by past profitability and hoarding cash risks starving investment); sale of assets (no repayment, but a one-off source that may reduce capacity — sale-and-leaseback keeps use of the asset at the cost of ongoing rent); and better working-capital management (tighter credit control, lower stock levels — releases cash but strains supplier and customer relationships). External sources : Short-term: bank overdraft (flexible, quick, interest only on the amount used — but high interest and repayable on demand); trade credit (delay payment to suppliers — effectively free short-term finance, but strains suppliers and forgoes discounts); debt factoring (sell receivables for immediate cash at a discount — improves liquidity but loses part of the debt's value). Long-term: bank loans (large sums, predictable repayments, no dilution — but interest paid regardless of profit, security/collateral required and gearing rises); corporate bonds/debentures (long-term debt instruments for plcs — fixed interest, but similar risk considerations); share capital (issue shares: no repayment or interest, but dilutes ownership and control, dividend expectations grow, and only plcs can offer shares publicly); venture capital/business angels (equity investment plus expertise — for high-risk start-ups, at the cost of significant ownership and influence); crowdfunding (many small investors via platforms — also a marketing test, but success is uncertain and ideas are exposed). Factors determining the choice: cost (interest versus dividends versus fees), control (debt preserves ownership; equity dilutes it), purpose and time period (match short-term needs to short-term finance — matching principle), the firm's existing gearing and risk appetite, size and legal form (a sole trader cannot issue shares), and flexibility (overdrafts flex with need). Strong evaluation: debt is usually cheaper than equity but riskier — interest is paid regardless of profit, so a highly geared business in a downturn faces failure; equity is safer in downturns but permanently dilutes control. The right answer matches the source to the purpose, time horizon and existing capital structure. A cash-flow forecast projects monthly inflows (cash sales, receivables collected, capital injections) and outflows (wages, rent, materials, VAT), then calculates: net cash flow = inflows − outflows; closing balance = opening balance + net cash flow. Profit is not cash — the single most examined finance distinction: profit is revenue minus costs when earned (including credit sales not yet collected, and non-cash costs such as depreciation); cash is money actually available . A business selling on credit with 60-day terms can be profitable on paper yet unable to pay wages — insolvency , not lack of profit, kills firms. Causes of cash-flow problems: overtrading (expanding sales faster than cash and capacity allow — growth consumes cash in stock, wages and premises before revenue arrives), over-investment in fixed assets, poor credit control (slow-paying customers), excessive credit taken by the firm eroding supplier goodwill, seasonal demand, and loss-making trading. Remedies: improve inflows (tighter credit control, factoring receivables, deposits/upfront payments, promotion), reduce outflows (delay non-essential spending, lease rather than buy, negotiate longer supplier terms), arrange an overdraft facility as a buffer, and — structurally — slow growth to a pace the cash can fund. Working capital = current assets − current liabilities. Too little and the business cannot pay its way (risk of insolvency); too much suggests idle cash and inefficient use of funds. Working capital is managed through the operating cycle : inventory days + receivables days − payables days = the days cash is tied up. A supermarket converts stock to cash daily and pays suppliers late, so its cycle is short and even a negative working-capital position can be safe; a manufacturer with slow-moving stock and 90-day customer terms needs far more. Worked example: a business with current assets of £120,000 (including £40,000 inventory) and current liabilities of £80,000 has working capital of £40,000, a current ratio of 1.5, but an acid test of (£120,000 − £40,000) ÷ £80,000 = 1.0 — the gap between the two ratios reveals how much of its liquidity depends on selling inventory. Budgets set financial targets for revenue and cost per department, and serve four purposes: planning (forcing forward thinking), coordination (aligning departments with corporate objectives), motivation (targets give staff goals — though unrealistic budgets demotivate) and control (variances flag where spending deviates from plan). Incremental budgeting — last year's budget adjusted (typically + inflation). Quick and stable, but perpetuates past waste and encourages end-of-year spending to protect next year's budget. Zero-based budgeting (ZBB) — every budget line starts at zero and must be justified from scratch. Eliminates inherited waste and focuses spending on objectives, but time-consuming and demanding for managers — suited to periods of cost pressure or strategic change. Flexible/rolling budgets adjust during the year as conditions change, keeping targets meaningful. Variance analysis compares actual with budget: a favourable variance improves profit (revenue above budget, costs below budget); an adverse variance reduces it (revenue below budget, costs above budget). Worked example: a department budgets £20,000 for marketing but spends £25,000 — an adverse variance of £5,000 (25% over budget). Interpretation matters more than the calculation: an adverse variance is not automatically bad — overspending on marketing that generated sales 40% above budget may be a sound investment; a favourable variance on training may signal under-investment that damages quality later. Strong answers investigate the cause of variances (demand changes, price changes, efficiency, poor forecasting) and judge them against the corporate objective. Evaluation: budgets are only as good as their forecasts — built on past data in dynamic markets — and rigid budget adherence can distort behaviour (budgetary slack: padding budgets to make targets easy). Variance analysis directs management attention; it does not by itself explain performance. The income statement (profit and loss account) measures performance over a period: revenue − cost of sales (COGS) = gross profit ; gross profit − expenses = operating profit ; operating profit − net finance costs − tax = profit for the year . The statement of financial position (balance sheet) is a snapshot: non-current assets (property, plant, equipment) + current assets (inventory, receivables, cash) = current liabilities + non-current liabilities + equity (share capital, retained earnings). Ratio Formula Interprets Gross profit margin (GPM) Gross profit ÷ revenue × 100 Trading margin — pricing power and direct-cost control Net (operating) profit margin Operating profit ÷ revenue × 100 Overall efficiency — includes overhead control ROCE Operating profit ÷ capital employed × 100 Return on long-term capital; compare with borrowing rate and rivals Current ratio Current assets ÷ current liabilities Short-term liquidity; ~1.5–2 typical, below 1 risky unless cash sales are fast Acid test (Current assets − inventory) ÷ current liabilities Stricter liquidity ignoring slow-moving stock Inventory days Inventory ÷ COGS × 365 Days stock sits before sale — lower is leaner Receivables days Receivables ÷ revenue × 365 Days customers take to pay — lower improves cash flow Payables days Payables ÷ COGS × 365 Days taken to pay suppliers — longer helps cash, strains suppliers Gearing Non-current liabilities ÷ capital employed × 100 Dependence on debt; above ~50% financially risky Worked example — profitability ratios: revenue £500,000, cost of sales £300,000, expenses £120,000, capital employed £400,000. Gross profit = 500,000 − 300,000 = £200,000 → GPM = 200,000 ÷ 500,000 × 100 = 40% . Operating profit = 200,000 − 120,000 = £80,000 → operating margin = 80,000 ÷ 500,000 × 100 = 16% . ROCE = 80,000 ÷ 400,000 × 100 = 20% — above a 6% borrowing rate, so the business creates value from its capital. The 24-point gap between GPM and operating margin signals heavy overheads: management should investigate expense control. Liquidity worked example: current assets £120,000 (inventory £60,000), current liabilities £80,000 → current ratio = 1.5; acid test = 60,000 ÷ 80,000 = 0.75 — liquidity depends heavily on selling inventory; if stock is slow-moving, the true position is weaker than the current ratio suggests. Limitations of ratio analysis: ratios are historical (past performance ≠ future), distorted by differing accounting policies between firms (depreciation, valuation of stock), ignore qualitative factors (brand strength, staff, market conditions), and single-year figures can mislead — always compare over time (trend) and against competitors (benchmarking), and pair ratios with qualitative analysis (SWOT, market data). Break-even finds the output at which total revenue equals total cost. Contribution per unit = price − variable cost per unit. Break-even output = fixed costs ÷ contribution per unit. Margin of safety = actual output − break-even output. Output for target profit = (fixed costs + target profit) ÷ contribution per unit. Full worked example: fixed costs £50,000, variable cost £5 per unit, price £15, actual output 12,000 units, target profit £30,000: Contribution = 15 − 5 = £10 per unit . Break-even output = 50,000 ÷ 10 = 5,000 units . Margin of safety = 12,000 − 5,000 = 7,000 units — or 7,000 ÷ 12,000 × 100 = 58% of current output; demand can fall 58% before losses begin. Output for £30,000 profit = (50,000 + 30,000) ÷ 10 = 8,000 units . Assumptions and limitations to evaluate: assumes constant price and variable cost per unit (no economies of scale), fixed costs fixed over the range, output = sales (no stock change), and a single-product (or constant mix) business — real cost and revenue curves are rarely straight lines, so break-even is an estimate. Still valuable: quick, shows margin of safety and the effect of price/cost changes, and supports 'what-if' analysis. Investment appraisal compares capital projects: Payback period — time to recover the initial outlay. Worked example: £100,000 invested; net cash flows £30,000 a year → payback = 100,000 ÷ 30,000 = 3.33 years (3 years 4 months). For uneven flows, accumulate year by year. Strengths: simple, favours liquidity and limits exposure to forecasting error. Weaknesses: ignores cash flows after payback and the time value of money, and says nothing about profitability. ARR — average annual profit ÷ average investment × 100. Worked example: £100,000 invested, total profit over 5 years £75,000 → average annual profit = £15,000; average investment = (100,000 + 0) ÷ 2 = £50,000 → ARR = 15,000 ÷ 50,000 × 100 = 30% . Compares projects as percentages, but uses forecasts and ignores timing. NPV — discounts future cash flows to today's values. Worked example: £100,000 invested; £30,000 a year for 5 years at 10% (discount factors 0.909, 0.826, 0.751, 0.683, 0.621): present value = 30,000 × (0.909 + 0.826 + 0.751 + 0.683 + 0.621) = 30,000 × 3.790 = £113,700 → NPV = 113,700 − 100,000 = +£13,700 . Positive NPV → the project beats the 10% cost of capital and adds value. Strengths: accounts for time value of money and all cash flows. Weaknesses: sensitive to the discount rate chosen and entirely dependent on forecasts. Which technique when: NPV is theoretically superior; payback suits liquidity-constrained or risk-averse firms; ARR suits percentage comparison with other returns. A* answers combine them — a project with a positive NPV but slow payback may still be rejected if cash flow is tight — and stress that all three depend on forecast accuracy.

topics.name: People and Leadership
topics.subject: business-studies
topics.searchText: business-studies Business Studies People and Leadership Evaluate content theories of motivation — Taylor (scientific management), Mayo (human relations), Maslow (hierarchy of needs), Herzberg (two-factor theory), McClelland (achievement, affiliation, power) (AQA 3.6.3; Edexcel 1.4) Apply process theories — Vroom (expectancy: valence × expectancy × instrumentality) and Adams (equity) — as diagnostic tools for managers (AQA 3.6.3) Evaluate financial and non-financial methods of motivation — piece rate, salary, bonus, commission, profit sharing; job rotation, enlargement, enrichment, empowerment, teamwork (AQA 3.6.3; Edexcel 1.4) Analyse leadership styles on the Tannenbaum-Schmidt continuum — autocratic (tells) through democratic (consults) to laissez-faire — plus situational and transformational leadership, and the factors that determine the best style (AQA 3.2.1) Evaluate organisational design — span of control, hierarchy, tall versus flat structures, delayering, centralisation versus decentralisation, matrix structures (AQA 3.6.3; Edexcel 1.4) Analyse HRM — hard versus soft HRM, recruitment and selection methods, training types, appraisal (360°, management by objectives), labour turnover and employee relations (trade unions, collective bargaining, ACAS) (AQA 3.6.1–3.6.3) Motivation The internal drive and external incentives that determine the effort employees put into work — a key determinant of productivity, quality and labour turnover. Hygiene factors (Herzberg) Factors that prevent dissatisfaction but do not motivate — pay, working conditions, company policy, supervision, job security. Their absence causes dissatisfaction; their presence alone does not create motivation. Motivators (Herzberg) Factors that genuinely motivate — achievement, recognition, the work itself, responsibility, advancement and growth. Self-actualisation (Maslow) The highest level of Maslow's hierarchy — reaching one's full potential; only motivates once lower needs (physiological, safety, social, esteem) are satisfied. Expectancy theory (Vroom) Motivation = valence (value of the reward) × expectancy (belief effort leads to performance) × instrumentality (belief performance leads to reward); if any element is zero, motivation collapses. Tannenbaum-Schmidt continuum A continuum of leadership styles running from boss-centred (manager tells, sells) to subordinate-centred (manager consults, joins, delegates) — the best point depends on the manager, subordinates and situation. Span of control The number of subordinates directly reporting to a manager — narrow spans create tall hierarchies; wide spans create flat structures. Delayering Removing layers of management from a hierarchy to flatten the structure, cutting costs and speeding communication, but increasing spans of control and risking overload. Job enrichment Giving employees more challenging, meaningful work with greater responsibility and autonomy — a vertical extension of the job that targets Herzberg's motivators. Labour turnover (Number of staff leaving in a year ÷ average number employed) × 100 — measures the rate at which employees leave; high turnover raises recruitment and training costs. Taylor (scientific management) — workers are motivated primarily by money; measure and standardise tasks, and pay by results ( piece rate ). Useful in mass production (Amazon warehouse targets, call-centre scripts), but modern evidence shows pay alone is insufficient and piece rate can harm quality and safety. Mayo (human relations) — the Hawthorne studies found workers respond to attention, teamwork and social factors more than physical conditions: motivation comes from belonging and being valued — the foundation of teamwork and employee-voice practices. Maslow (hierarchy of needs) — five levels: physiological (pay, conditions), safety (job security), social (teamwork), esteem (recognition, status), self-actualisation (development, challenge). Lower needs must be satisfied before higher ones motivate, so managers secure pay and safety first, then offer recognition and growth. Criticisms: the hierarchy is culturally biased (self-actualisation is a Western concept) and needs are hard to measure or order strictly. Herzberg (two-factor theory) — hygiene factors (pay, conditions, policy, supervision) prevent dissatisfaction but cannot motivate; only motivators (achievement, recognition, responsibility, advancement, the work itself) genuinely motivate. Practical power: raising pay removes dissatisfaction but does not create motivation — motivation requires job enrichment, recognition and responsibility. Criticism: his critical-incident methodology has been accused of attributing good experiences to motivators and bad ones to hygiene factors. McClelland — three acquired needs: achievement (challenging targets, feedback), affiliation (teamwork, harmony), power (influence, leadership roles) — individuals differ in which dominates, so motivating methods should match the person. Exam technique: evaluate theories against each other — Herzberg directly challenges Taylor's pay-based view; Mayo complements Maslow's social level; McClelland explains why one method never fits all. Worked application: a call centre with high turnover applies Herzberg — hygiene first (competitive pay, ergonomic conditions, supportive supervision, fair policies) then motivators (team targets with recognition, employee-of-the-month, job enrichment through team-leader roles, career paths) — because pay alone cannot fix turnover if the work itself is monotonous. Financial methods: piece rate (pay per unit — motivates output, risks quality); salary and time rate (security, but no output incentive); bonus (one-off reward for targets); commission (percentage of sales — strong output incentive for sales staff, risks aggressive selling); profit sharing (aligns employees with business performance — but individual effort is diluted across the firm); fringe benefits (pensions, healthcare, discounts — retention aids). Evaluation: financial methods target Taylor's view, but Herzberg warns most pay is a hygiene factor — pay rises remove dissatisfaction only temporarily; commission schemes work only where valence and instrumentality are high (Vroom). Non-financial methods target Herzberg's motivators: Job rotation — switching tasks: variety, broader skills, less boredom; but no added responsibility. Job enlargement — more tasks at the same level (horizontal): variety without challenge — risk of mere workload increase. Job enrichment — more challenging, meaningful work with responsibility (vertical): targets motivators directly, but not all employees want responsibility and training costs rise. Empowerment — delegating real decision-making authority: motivation and faster decisions; risks inconsistency and requires trust and training. Teamwork — social needs (Maslow/Mayo) and shared purpose; quality circles involve staff in improvement decisions (kaizen link). Process theories as diagnostics: Vroom's expectancy theory — motivation = valence × expectancy × instrumentality. Applied to sales commission: commission motivates only if the reward is valued (valence), staff believe effort produces sales (expectancy — so training and realistic targets are essential; unreachable targets collapse expectancy to zero), and staff trust that hitting targets reliably triggers payment (instrumentality). If any element is zero, motivation collapses — explaining why identical schemes motivate some staff and not others. Criticisms: perceptions are hard to measure, and the rational-calculating assumption ignores emotional and habitual motivation. Adams' equity theory — employees compare their reward-to-effort ratio with others (referent groups); perceived inequity causes demotivation — explaining why pay transparency, unequal bonuses or perceived unfairness damage morale even among well-paid staff. Exam technique: the strongest answers match methods to theories (enrichment → Herzberg motivators; piece rate → Taylor) and judge against the workforce: money-motivated production staff respond to piece rate; professional staff value enrichment and development. The Tannenbaum-Schmidt continuum arranges leadership styles from boss-centred to subordinate-centred: Tells — autocratic: the manager decides and announces; fast decisions, clear direction, useful in crisis or with inexperienced teams — but demotivating for skilled staff and ignores employee ideas. Sells — the manager decides but persuades: still fast, gains some buy-in. Consults — democratic: the manager consults before deciding — better decisions (employee knowledge), higher motivation and ownership, but slower. Joins — the manager and team decide together: maximum ownership and creativity — but slowest and risks indecision. Laissez-faire (delegates) — the team decides with minimal interference: works for expert, self-motivated teams (design studios, research labs) — but with unskilled or unmotivated teams it produces drift and poor coordination. Choosing a style depends on: the manager's own personality and skill, the subordinates' skill and motivation, the situation (crisis favours telling; innovation favours joining) and the organisational culture. Situational leadership (Hersey-Blanchard) formalises this: adapt the style to follower readiness — telling for low readiness, selling for some, participating for moderate-to-high, delegating for high readiness. Transformational leadership — inspiring through vision, intellectual stimulation and individual attention, creating change and extraordinary commitment (contrast with transactional leadership based on exchange: rewards for compliance); transformational leaders suit change situations (turnarounds, digital transformation) but depend on charisma and can mask over-centralisation. McGregor's Theory X and Theory Y underpins style choice: Theory X managers (workers dislike work) lean autocratic; Theory Y managers (workers seek responsibility) lean democratic — self-fulfilling expectations shape how staff actually behave. Exam technique: there is no universally best style — evaluate against the context (urgency, team expertise, culture) and show the consequences of a mismatch: autocratic with experts wastes knowledge and drives turnover; laissez-faire with novices produces chaos. Organisational design structures people, authority and communication. Key concepts: hierarchy (levels of authority), chain of command (the line of authority from top to bottom), span of control (subordinates per manager), delegation (passing authority down — motivating and developing staff, but requires accountability), and authority and responsibility . Tall structures — many layers, narrow spans: tight supervision, clear promotion paths, but slow communication (messages distorted through layers), high management cost and junior staff feel remote. Flat structures — few layers, wide spans: faster communication and decisions, empowerment and lower cost — but managers overloaded, less supervision and fewer promotion prospects. Delayering — removing management layers: cuts cost, speeds decisions, empowers survivors — but increases spans of control, risks overload and lost coordination, and causes redundancy costs and morale damage ('survivor syndrome'). Centralised — decisions made at the top: consistency, control, economies of scale in decision-making; but slow, ignores local knowledge and demotivates lower levels. Decentralised — authority delegated to divisions/branches: faster local decisions, motivation and responsiveness; but inconsistency, duplication and loss of control. Matrix structure — staff report to both a functional manager and a project manager: flexible deployment of specialists, cross-functional communication and innovation — but dual reporting creates conflicting priorities, stress, unclear accountability and slower decisions. Organisational culture (Handy) — power culture (central, charismatic), role culture (procedures, bureaucracy), task culture (project teams), person culture (individuals first) — structure and culture must align; a task-culture firm with a rigid role-culture structure creates friction. Exam technique: link structure to strategy and context — a growing start-up often moves from flat to tall as it scales (more layers for control); a mature bureaucracy delayers to respond faster. Evaluate with consequences: delayering 'saves cost' only if remaining managers can handle wider spans; a matrix 'improves innovation' only with clear roles and conflict resolution — otherwise coordination problems outweigh collaboration benefits. Hard versus soft HRM: hard treats employees as a resource to be deployed and minimised (workforce planning, redundancy as a tool); soft treats employees as assets to develop (development, involvement, long-term commitment). Soft HRM builds engagement and retention; hard HRM controls costs — the trade-off is a classic evaluation point. Recruitment and selection: the process runs from workforce planning to job analysis , producing a job description (duties, responsibilities) and person specification (skills, qualifications, attributes). Internal recruitment (promoting or transferring): cheaper, faster, candidates are known, motivation boost — but no new ideas and creates another vacancy. External recruitment : fresh ideas, wider talent pool — but slower, costlier and riskier (unknown quantity). Selection methods: CVs and applications (cheap but easy to exaggerate); interviews — structured interviews (consistent questions, comparable, more reliable) versus unstructured (flexible but biased); psychometric tests (measure aptitude and personality — objective but imperfect predictors); assessment centres (tasks, group exercises, multiple observers — the most reliable predictor of performance, but expensive and slow). Worked example — a graduate scheme: person specification (degree, analytical skills, teamwork), screening by application and online tests, then an assessment centre with a group exercise and presentation, because the cost of a poor graduate hire (training plus salary) justifies the most reliable method. Training: induction (new starters — reduces early turnover and errors); on-the-job (shadowing, coaching, mentoring — cheap, job-relevant, but quality depends on the trainer and mistakes can affect customers); off-the-job (courses, e-learning — expert delivery and focus, but costly and not job-specific). Benefits: productivity, quality, motivation (Herzberg growth) and retention; costs: direct expense, staff time away from output, and the risk of trained staff leaving (though not training them leaves unskilled staff — the classic dilemma). Appraisal: systematic review of performance against objectives — management by objectives (MBO) (agreed SMART objectives reviewed periodically), 360-degree feedback (multi-source: manager, peers, subordinates, customers — rounded but can become a popularity contest), self-appraisal. Purposes: identify training needs, inform pay and promotion, motivate through recognition and targets; risks: bureaucratic form-filling, defensive behaviour, and appraisals that never translate into action. Employee relations: trade unions represent workers through collective bargaining (pay, conditions); industrial action ranges from strikes and work-to-rule to overtime bans — costly for both sides; ACAS provides conciliation, arbitration and advice to resolve disputes. Good employee relations (consultation, employee voice, fair procedures) reduce conflict, turnover and disruption; adversarial relations raise costs and reputational risk. Worked calculation — labour turnover: a firm employing an average of 400 staff loses 48 in a year: turnover = 48 ÷ 400 × 100 = 12% ; each leaver costs an estimated £5,000 in recruitment and training, so 48 × 5,000 = £240,000 a year — quantifying turnover's cost justifies investment in retention (pay benchmarking, development, engagement), which is exactly the analytical chain examiners reward.

topics.name: Business Strategy
topics.subject: business-studies
topics.searchText: business-studies Business Studies Business Strategy Apply SWOT analysis — internal strengths and weaknesses, external opportunities and threats — and evaluate its limitations as a strategic tool (AQA 3.7) Apply PESTEL analysis to assess political, economic, social, technological, environmental and legal change in the external environment (AQA 3.7; Edexcel Theme 3) Analyse competitive environment and advantage — Porter's five forces, core competences (VRIN criteria) and the sustainability of competitive advantage (AQA 3.7) Evaluate strategic direction and positioning — Porter's generic strategies (cost leadership, differentiation, focus), 'stuck in the middle', Bowman's strategic clock and the Ansoff matrix (AQA 3.8) Apply decision trees with expected values, and investment appraisal (payback, ARR, NPV), and evaluate their usefulness for strategic decisions (AQA 3.2 and 3.7; Edexcel 3.3) Evaluate change management — Lewin's force-field analysis and unfreeze/change/refreeze, Kotter's eight steps, Kotter and Schlesinger's reasons for resistance — and the risk of strategic drift (AQA 3.10; Edexcel 3.6) SWOT analysis A framework auditing internal strengths and weaknesses against external opportunities and threats; strong strategies match strengths to opportunities and correct weaknesses before threats exploit them. Porter's five forces A framework analysing industry profitability through competitive rivalry, the threat of new entrants, the threat of substitutes, buyer power and supplier power. Core competences The unique capabilities that underpin competitive advantage — valuable, rare, inimitable and non-substitutable (VRIN) — such as Apple's ecosystem or Toyota's production system. Cost leadership Porter's generic strategy of achieving the lowest unit costs in an industry, allowing the lowest prices or industry-average prices at above-average margins. Differentiation Porter's generic strategy of offering unique perceived value — through quality, brand, service or innovation — that customers will pay a premium for. Stuck in the middle Porter's argument that firms failing to commit to either cost leadership or differentiation underperform both, because they achieve neither low costs nor distinctive value.
