R v Parmenter fixed the mens rea of s.47 and s.20: recklessness as to some harm suffices; foreseeing GBH is never required R v Woollin: oblique intention requires virtual certainty plus defendant's appreciation — jury may find intention Law Commission report 361 (2015) recommended replacing the OAPA 1861 with a modern statute graded by culpability — use for AO3 Assault A common-law offence (prosecuted summarily under CJA 1988, s.39): any act, word or gesture causing the victim to apprehend the immediate application of unlawful force. Battery The application of unlawful force to another, however slight; no apprehension is required, and contact generally acceptable in everyday conduct (Collins v Wilcock) is excluded. Actual bodily harm (ABH) Harm calculated to interfere with the victim's health or comfort (R v Miller), including recognised psychiatric injury but not mere emotion (R v Chan-Fook); s.47 OAPA 1861, max 5 years. Occasioning The causation word in s.47: the defendant's assault or battery must factually cause the harm; no foreseeability of the harm is needed (R v Roberts). Wound A break in the continuity of both layers of the skin (R v Eisenhower); internal bleeding, bruises and fractured bones are not wounds. Grievous bodily harm (GBH) Really serious harm (DPP v Smith; R v Saunders), which can be the aggregation of injuries assessed against the victim's age and health (R v Bollom); includes serious psychiatric illness (R v Ireland; R v Burstow). Maliciously In s.20 OAPA 1861: intention or subjective recklessness as to some physical harm, not as to GBH itself (R v Mowatt; R v Savage; R v Parmenter). Inflict The s.20 causation word: held not to require a technical assault — inflicting is the same as causing (R v Ireland; R v Burstow). Direct intention The defendant's aim, purpose or decision to bring about the prohibited consequence (R v Mohan). Oblique intention Where the consequence is a virtual certainty of the defendant's act and the defendant appreciated that virtual certainty, the jury may find intention (R v Woollin). Subjective recklessness The defendant foresees a risk of harm and unreasonably goes on to take it (Cunningham approach, adopted for OAPA offences by R v Savage; R v Parmenter). Psychiatric injury A recognised clinical condition (e.g. depression, anxiety states, PTSD) which can constitute ABH (s.47) or GBH (s.20/s.18); mere emotions such as fear, panic or stress do not qualify (R v Chan-Fook; R v Ireland). Assault is a common-law offence, prosecuted summarily under Criminal Justice Act 1988, s.39 (maximum 6 months' imprisonment and/or a fine): any act, word or gesture by which the defendant intentionally or recklessly causes the victim to apprehend the immediate application of unlawful force . The actus reus needs no contact at all — silent telephone calls causing fear can be an assault: R v Ireland; R v Burstow [1998]. Conditional threats still count: R v Martin (1881) — defendant barred theatre exits and told the crowd to hasten or be hurt. Immediacy is applied flexibly: R v Constanza [1997] — letters and a resentful campaign gave the victim well-founded fear that violence might be used at some time not excluding the immediate future. Words can negate apprehension where they make the threat conditional on a lawful act: Tuberville v Savage (1669). Mens rea is intention or subjective recklessness: in R v Lamb [1967] the victim was shot with a revolver the defendant did not know would fire — no assault (no apprehension) and no unlawful act manslaughter because no unlawful act existed. Battery is the application of unlawful force to another , however slight ( Faulkner v Talbot (1981)); touching a skirt hem without more is too trivial ( R v Thomas (1985)). Force can be indirect: pushing a bar door into a fleeing crowd ( R v Martin (1881)); acid spraying from a tampered petrol nozzle ( DPP v K [1990]); punching a mother causing her to drop her baby ( R v Haystead (2000)). Everyday contact — such as generally guiding a person rather than seizing them — is not unlawful: Collins v Wilcock [1984]. Creating a danger then failing to warn can found liability by omission: R v Santana-Bermudez [2003] — defendant told a searching officer there was nothing in his pockets; she was stabbed by a needle. Exam traps: assault and battery Apprehension, not fear: the victim need only be aware force is imminent, not frightened. Battery requires no apprehension and no direct contact; assault requires no contact and may be by words or silence. Charge practice: where there is injury with a lower mens rea, the CPS charges s.39 assault/battery or s.47 ABH rather than s.20 (CPS charging standards) — use for AO3. Mens rea of both offences: intention or subjective recklessness — see R v Parmenter [1991] for the application. s.47 OAPA 1861 (maximum 5 years): an assault or battery occasioning actual bodily harm . Actus reus: a complete assault or battery plus harm — injury calculated to interfere with the health or comfort of the victim ( R v Miller [1954]); it need not be permanent, and scratches, bruising and transient injuries suffice. Psychiatric injury counts if it is a recognised clinical condition beyond mere emotions: R v Chan-Fook [1994] and R v Ireland; R v Burstow [1998] (depressive illness and anxiety from stalking phone calls). Occasioning requires only factual causation between the assault/battery and the harm — the harm need not be reasonably foreseeable: R v Roberts [1971] — the victim jumped from a moving car to escape the defendant's sexual advances; her injuries were still ABH. Mens rea is only the mens rea of the base assault or battery: R v Savage; R v Parmenter [1992] — the House of Lords held that s.47 requires no mens rea as to the harm itself; recklessness as to some unlawful physical contact suffices ( DPP v Spratt [1990] — pellet-gun spraying near passers-by). Why s.47 matters for AO3 Anomaly : s.47 and s.20 carry the same maximum sentence (5 years), yet s.47 requires only the mens rea of a battery while s.20 requires recklessness as to some harm — the Law Commission (2015) treats this as a principal defect of the OAPA 1861. Causation gap : because occasioning requires no foreseeability, an unforeseeable flight reaction can elevate a battery to a 5-year offence. Consent interplay : for serious consensual activity, s.47 charges are used where s.20 would fail for lack of injury — see R v Wilson [1996] (branding initials; consent available where comparable to tattooing). s.20 OAPA 1861 (maximum 5 years): unlawfully and maliciously wounding or inflicting grievous bodily harm . A wound is a break in the continuity of both layers of the skin: R v Eisenhower [1984] — pellet punctures with internal bleeding were not a wound. GBH means really serious harm ( DPP v Smith [1961]; juries today are directed simply with really serious harm — R v Saunders (1985)). Harm can be cumulative : a series of minor injuries aggregated, assessed in light of the victim's age and health ( R v Bollom [2004]; R v Brown and Stratton [2008]). Serious psychiatric illness can be GBH: R v Ireland; R v Burstow [1998] — inflict is satisfied without a technical assault, and for s.20 inflict means cause. Disease transmission can also found s.20 liability where the victim did not knowingly consent: R v Dica [2004] (HIV). Mens rea of s.20: maliciously means intention or subjective recklessness as to some physical harm — not as to GBH: R v Mowatt [1968]; confirmed in R v Savage; R v Parmenter [1992]. The defendant who foresees only a slight injury is still guilty of s.20 if really serious harm results. s.18 OAPA 1861 (maximum life): unlawfully and maliciously by any means wounding or causing GBH with intent to do GBH, or with intent to resist or prevent lawful apprehension or detention. The mens rea is specific intent : direct intention ( R v Mohan [1976]) or oblique intention — where GBH is a virtual certainty of the act and the defendant appreciated that — the jury may find intention ( R v Woollin [1999]). Subjective recklessness is never enough for s.18: the key distinction from s.20. Note the drafting width: s.18 says by any means (so omissions can suffice), while s.20 says inflict. Offence Key AR point Mens rea Maximum Assault / battery (s.39 CJA 1988) Apprehension / unlawful force Intention or subjective recklessness 6 months s.47 ABH Assault or battery occasioning ABH Base offence mens rea only (Roberts; Savage) 5 years s.20 wounding/GBH Wound (Eisenhower) or inflict GBH (Burstow) Intention or recklessness as to some harm (Mowatt; Savage) 5 years s.18 GBH with intent Wound or cause GBH by any means Specific intent only (Mohan; Woollin) Life Consent is no answer where the conduct causes actual bodily harm or worse , except in recognised categories: properly conducted games and sports, horseplay, surgery, tattooing, ear-piercing, and lawful dangerous displays. The baseline rule: R v Brown [1994] — consensual sadomasochistic activities causing injuries were not protected; consent is unavailable for s.47/s.20 assaults beyond the exceptions. Public policy condemns private fights: A-G's Reference (No 6 of 1980) [1981] — a planned fist fight is unlawful, though incidental injury in a spontaneous scuffle is treated differently ( R v Barnes [2004] — sporting consent covers conduct within the rules and what a reasonable player would expect, but not criminal violence off the ball). R v Wilson [1996] allowed a consent defence for branding initials on a wife — activity analogous to tattooing, showing the court's willingness to expand exceptions; R v Richardson and Irwin [1999] allowed consent to dangerous horseplay (dangling a student from a balcony) and took account of what sober participants would have appreciated. Accidental, truly unforeseeable harm during consensual activity may leave no unlawful act: R v Slingsby [1995]; trivial harm with consent is outside the OAPA altogether: R v Donovan [1934]. Using consent for marks Always test consent after establishing the offence — examiners reward order. Link to law reform: the Law Commission (2015) recommended clarifying which consensual activities should remain criminal. Contrast criminal consent limits with civil volenti (see the negligence topic) — knowledge must be real and free in tort too. The non-fatal offences form a ladder matched to culpability and harm : battery/assault (6 months) to s.47/s.20 (5 years) to s.18 (life). The ladder has long been criticised: language — occasioning, maliciously, inflict and grievous are archaic and inconsistently construed; structure — s.47 carries the same maximum as s.20 despite a lower mens rea; wounding — a technical skin rule produces odd results ( R v Eisenhower : internal bleeding worse than a cut is not a wound). The Law Commission report 361 (2015), Reform of Offences Against the Person Act 1861 , recommended a new statute with offences of intentional serious injury, reckless serious injury and intentional/reckless injury, abolishing the distinctions between wounding and other harm; successive governments have not enacted it — a strong AO3 point on law-making inaction. CPS charging standards mitigate some inconsistency by charging the offence that matches culpability. Exam technique. For each suspect act: (1) identify the possible offence from the ladder; (2) work upwards — assault/battery, then s.47, then s.20, then s.18; (3) define AR and MR with one authority per element; (4) apply to facts, including causation; (5) consider consent; (6) conclude on the most likely charge. In evaluation paragraphs, deploy the s.47/s.20 anomaly, the Eisenhower wound rule, Burstow's psychologisation of harm, and the Law Commission recommendations.

topics.name: Tort: Negligence and Occupiers' Liability
topics.subject: law
topics.searchText: law Law Tort: Negligence and Occupiers' Liability Apply the Caparo three-part test for a duty of care and explain the neighbour principle (Donoghue v Stevenson) (AQA 3.3.2; OCR 2.2.2; WJEC/Eduqas Component 2) Assess duty of care for omissions and public bodies, including Robinson v Chief Constable of West Yorkshire, Hill, Michael and Poole Borough Council Evaluate breach against the standard of care, including Bolam v Friern Hospital Management Committee, Bolitho, Nettleship v Weston and Mullin v Richards Apply factual causation (but-for test; material contribution), legal causation, remoteness (The Wagon Mound (No 1); Hughes v Lord Advocate) and intervening acts Distinguish primary and secondary victims for psychiatric injury (Page v Smith; Alcock; White) and the recoverability of pure economic loss (Murphy v Brentwood; Spring v Guardian Assurance) State and apply the common duty of care under the Occupiers' Liability Act 1957 and the s.1(3) conditions of the 1984 Act for trespassers Apply civil defences — volenti non fit injuria, contributory negligence and illegality — with Froom v Butcher, Pitts v Hunt and Revill v Newbery Deploy the structure of a negligence problem answer in 25-mark AQA and 20-mark OCR/WJEC scenario questions Duty of care: Caparo three-part test (foreseeability, proximity, fair/just/reasonable) — but Robinson v Chief Constable of West Yorkshire [2018] reasserted ordinary principles for positive acts, overruling Hill Omissions are generally not actionable (Smith v Littlewoods; Stovin v Wise), even for public bodies (Michael v Chief Constable of South Wales; Poole Borough Council) Breach is fact-sensitive: probability (Bolton v Stone), gravity (Paris v Stepney), precautions vs utility (Latimer v AEC); professions use Bolam with the Bolitho logical caveat; learners and children: Nettleship v Weston; Mullin v Richards Causation: but-for (Barnett); material contribution (Bonnington Castings v Wardlaw); multiple sufficient causes (Fairchild; Barker v Corus); remoteness = foreseeable kind of harm (Wagon Mound; Hughes v Lord Advocate; Jolley v Sutton) Psychiatric injury: primary victims (Page v Smith) vs secondary victims restricted by Alcock; rescuers must satisfy the primary victim rules (White v Chief Constable; contrast Chadwick) Pure economic loss is irrecoverable except where the defendant assumed responsibility, e.g. negligent misstatement (Hedley Byrne; Spring v Guardian Assurance) and some solicitor cases (Ross v Caunters) OLA 1957: visitors, common duty of care, special rules for children (s.2(3)(a)), workers (s.2(3)(b)), warnings (s.2(4)(a)) and independent contractors (s.2(4)(b)) OLA 1984: trespassers protected only where the s.1(3) conditions are met; Tomlinson and Keown show courts refusing duties where the risk arises from the claimant's own activity Defences: volenti is complete but rarely succeeds; contributory negligence reduces damages by a percentage (Froom v Butcher); illegality may bar or reduce (Pitts v Hunt; Revill v Newbery) Duty of care A legal obligation to take reasonable care not to cause foreseeable harm to a neighbour; tested under Caparo Industries plc v Dickman — foreseeability, proximity, fair, just and reasonable. Neighbour principle Donoghue v Stevenson: you must take reasonable care to avoid acts or omissions you can reasonably foresee would be likely to injure your neighbour — persons closely and directly affected by your act. Breach of duty Falling below the standard of the reasonable person: omission to do what a reasonable person would do, or doing what a reasonable person would not (Blyth v Birmingham Waterworks). Causation in fact The but-for test: the damage would not have occurred but for the defendant's breach (Barnett v Chelsea and Kensington Hospital); multiple sufficient causes use the Fairchild exception. Causation in law The breach must be an operative and substantial cause of harm — an intervening act (novus actus interveniens) may break the chain where it is unforeseeable and independent. Remoteness Damage must be of a reasonably foreseeable kind, though the precise manner or extent need not be (The Wagon Mound (No 1); Hughes v Lord Advocate; Jolley v Sutton). Primary victim A person within the zone of physical danger who suffers psychiatric injury; recoverable if physical injury was foreseeable (Page v Smith). Secondary victim A person who suffers psychiatric injury witnessing or hearing of injury to another; recovery restricted by Alcock control mechanisms — ties of love and affection, proximity, perception, sudden shock. Pure economic loss Financial loss unconnected with physical injury or property damage (e.g. a defective product's value, negligent misstatement); generally irrecoverable (Murphy v Brentwood), except negligent misstatement with assumption of responsibility (Hedley Byrne v Heller). Occupier A person with sufficient control over premises (Wheat v Lacon); there may be more than one occupier, each liable for the areas they control. Common duty of care Occupiers' Liability Act 1957, s.2(2): the duty to take such care as in all the circumstances is reasonable to see that visitors are reasonably safe in using the premises for the purposes they are invited or permitted. Volenti non fit injuria A complete defence where the claimant freely and knowingly consented to the risk; knowledge of risk alone is insufficient (ICI Ltd v Shatwell). Contributory negligence Law Reform (Contributory Negligence) Act 1945: where the claimant partly caused their own damage, damages are reduced by the court's assessment of their share of responsibility (Froom v Butcher). Res ipsa loquitur The thing speaks for itself: where the accident is of a kind that ordinarily does not occur without negligence and the defendant controlled the instrumentality, the burden shifts to the defendant to explain. Negligence requires a duty of care , breach and damage caused by the breach, not too remote. The modern starting point is the neighbour principle : Donoghue v Stevenson [1932] — take reasonable care to avoid acts or omissions you can reasonably foresee would be likely to injure persons closely and directly affected. Caparo Industries plc v Dickman [1990] replaced it with a three-part test : harm of a kind reasonably foreseeable; a relationship of proximity or neighbourhood; and that imposing the duty is fair, just and reasonable. Anns v Merton London Borough Council [1978] had used a looser two-stage test, but the House of Lords retreated from it: Murphy v Brentwood District Council [1991] overruled Anns on defective buildings. Public bodies and omissions. The general rule: there is no liability for omissions — Smith v Littlewoods Organisation [1987]; a highway authority could not be liable merely for failing to act: Stovin v Wise [1996]; Gorringe v Calderdale Metropolitan Borough Council [2004]. Hill v Chief Constable of West Yorkshire [1989] had exempted the police from duties for investigative failures; that immunity was overruled by Robinson v Chief Constable of West Yorkshire [2018] — the Supreme Court held the ordinary principles of negligence apply, and a duty was owed where an officer's positive act (a clumsy arrest) injured a passer-by. But Michael v Chief Constable of South Wales [2015] shows the limits: failing to act on a 999 call created no duty; and R (PNB) v Poole Borough Council [2019] refused duties for child-protection failures absent an assumption of responsibility. For the exam: apply Caparo first; use Robinson for positive acts; use Michael/Poole to refuse omissions-based duties. Exam traps: duty of care Robinson did not make police always liable — it removed a blanket immunity; the Caparo test still governs. Omission claims can succeed where there is control or assumption of responsibility (Barrett v Enfield LBC [2001] — care of a child in council care). Rescuers: a duty is owed to the rescuer foreseeably endangered (Chadwick v British Railways Board [1967]). Breach asks whether the defendant fell below the standard of care : Blyth v Birmingham Waterworks (1856) — negligence is doing something a reasonable person would not do, or omitting something a reasonable person would do. The standard is adjusted by who the defendant is: for professions , the defendant meets the standard by acting in accordance with a responsible body of professional practice: Bolam v Friern Hospital Management Committee [1957], subject to the Bolitho caveat: Bolitho v City and Hackney Health Authority [1998] — the practice must withstand logical analysis. Learners are judged against the competent adult driver, not other learners: Nettleship v Weston [1971]. Children are judged against comparable children: Mullin v Richards [1998] (fencing with plastic rulers). The standard is also fact-sensitive through the risk factors : probability — a very small risk need not be eliminated: Bolton v Stone [1951] (cricket ball over a high fence); gravity — serious potential harm demands more: Paris v Stepney Borough Council [1951] (goggles for a one-eyed welder); precautions against utility — only reasonable precautions are required: Latimer v AEC [1953]. Where the accident is of a kind that ordinarily does not happen without negligence and the defendant had control, res ipsa loquitur shifts the evidential burden to the defendant. Factual causation uses the but-for test: Barnett v Chelsea and Kensington Hospital [1969] — the patient would have died regardless of the hospital's failure, so no causation; the breach must also be a foreseeable cause: Cork v Kirby MacLean [1952]. Where multiple causes each contributed, the claimant need only show a material contribution : Bonnington Castings v Wardlaw [1956] (pneumoconiosis dust). Where science cannot prove which of several exposures caused the disease, the Fairchild exception applies: Fairchild v Glenhaven Funeral Services [2002]; Barker v Corus [2006] — liability is shared among the culpable exposures. Legal causation and remoteness. Damage is recoverable only if it is of a reasonably foreseeable kind: The Wagon Mound (No 1) [1961] — oil spill fouling a dock; fire damage unforeseeable. But the manner of the harm need not be foreseeable: Hughes v Lord Advocate [1963] (paraffin lamp in a manhole); Jolley v Sutton London Borough Council [2000] (injuring a boat; the kind of harm was foreseeable even if the mechanism was not). Intervening acts break the chain only where they are unforeseeable and independent: medical negligence generally does not break it: Robinson v Post Office [1977] — the employer who caused the fracture remained liable for the doctor's misdiagnosis; a claimant's own unreasonable conduct may, unless the reaction was within the range of foreseeable responses. Psychiatric injury is recoverable only as a recognised clinical condition. Primary victims — those within the zone of physical danger — recover if some physical injury was foreseeable: Page v Smith [1996]. Secondary victims — witnesses and those who hear of harm — face the Alcock control mechanisms : Alcock v Chief Constable of South Yorkshire [1992]: close ties of love and affection (presumed only for spouses, parents, children); closeness in time and space to the accident or its immediate aftermath; perception through their own unaided senses; and a sudden shocking event. Rescuers must satisfy the primary victim rules to recover: White v Chief Constable of South Yorkshire [1999] — police officers who suffered psychological injury could not recover as secondary victims; contrast Chadwick v British Railways Board [1967], where the rescuer within the danger zone recovered. Pure economic loss — financial loss unconnected with personal injury or property damage — is generally irrecoverable to avoid indeterminate liability: Murphy v Brentwood District Council [1991] (the cost of replacing defective houses). The exception is negligent misstatement with assumption of responsibility: Hedley Byrne and Co Ltd v Heller and Partners Ltd [1964] (with a disclaimer negating the duty there); Spring v Guardian Assurance plc [1995] — a duty of care is owed in giving references. Some special relationships allow recovery: Ross v Caunters [1980] — a solicitor careless in drafting a will owed a duty to the intended beneficiary. Consequential economic loss flowing from physical injury or property damage is always recoverable. Exam traps: psychiatric injury and economic loss Always classify the claimant first: primary or secondary victim, or economic loss — the rules differ completely. Alcock categories are strict: a friend outside ties of love and affection rarely recovers (contrast spouses and parents). For AO3, criticise the arbitrary divide: pure economic loss often matters more to a claimant than minor personal injury. Occupiers' Liability Act 1957 governs lawful visitors (invitees, licensees, those with contractual permission, those with a right of entry by statute). An occupier is the person with sufficient control: Wheat v Lacon and Co Ltd [1966] — more than one occupier is possible. Section 2(2) imposes the common duty of care : such care as in all the circumstances is reasonable to see that visitors are reasonably safe for the purpose of their visit. Children (s.2(3)(a)): the occupier must be prepared for children to be less careful than adults; a warning must be effective for a child too young to read: Laverton v Kiapasha (1967). Workers (s.2(3)(b)): the occupier may expect workmen to guard against risks incident to their trade: General Cleaning Contractors v Christmas [1953]. Warnings (s.2(4)(a)) discharge the duty only if they enable the visitor to be reasonably safe: Roles v Nathan [1963] (chimney sweep fumes). Independent contractors (s.2(4)(b)): the occupier is liable if the contractor was careless, or the work was improper, or the occupier failed to check: Haseldine v Daw [1941] (negligently maintained lift); Ogwo v Taylor [1988] (firefighter injured; occupier liable); but not where the main contractor directed an unsafe system: Ferguson v Welsh [1988]. Occupiers' Liability Act 1984 protects trespassers . A duty arises only if the s.1(3) conditions are met: the occupier is aware of the danger or has reasonable grounds to believe it exists; knows or has reasonable grounds to believe the person is, or may come, in the vicinity; and the risk is one against which he may reasonably be expected to offer some protection. This codified the duty recognised in British Railways Board v Herrington [1972]. Section 1(5) excludes risks the trespasser willingly accepts. The courts read the Act narrowly where the risk arises from the claimant's own activity : Tomlinson v Congleton Borough Council [2003] (no duty for diving into a lake); Keown v Coventry Healthcare NHS Trust [2006] (climbing a drainpipe); Ratcliff v McConnell [1999] (diving into an unlit pool at night after drinking); Donoghue v Folkestone Properties [2003] (seasonal risk). Where the duty applies, breaches still sound in damages — but reduced: Revill v Newbery [1996] (76-year-old with a gun trap; trespasser recovered, damages cut by 75% for contributory negligence). Defences. Volenti non fit injuria is a complete defence but requires free and knowing consent to the risk, not mere knowledge: ICI Ltd v Shatwell [1965]; spectators accept inherent risks ( Hall v Brooklands Auto Racing Club [1933]); rescuers do not consent: Haynes v Harwood [1935]. Contributory negligence reduces damages by the claimant's share of responsibility (Law Reform (Contributory Negligence) Act 1945): Froom v Butcher [1976] — 25% where a seatbelt would have prevented injury, 50% where it would have made a substantial difference; Sayers v Harlow Urban District Council [1958] — 20% split. Illegality (ex turpi causa) may bar claims arising from the claimant's own crime: Pitts v Hunt [1991] (pillion passenger on a stolen bike encouraging reckless riding); but Revill v Newbery shows it usually reduces rather than bars in modern law.

topics.searchText: law Law Defences State and apply the M'Naghten rules (defect of reason, disease of the mind, not knowing the nature and quality of the act or that it was wrong) and the special verdict disposal options (AQA 3.2.5; OCR H418 Component 3) Distinguish sane from insane automatism using the internal/external cause test (R v Quick; R v Hennessy; R v Burgess) and apply the rules on self-induced automatism (R v Bailey; R v Hardie) Apply the Majewski distinction — why voluntary intoxication is no defence to crimes of basic intent but may negative intention for specific intent crimes (R v Sheehan & Moore; R v O'Grady; R v Heard) — and the rules on involuntary intoxication (R v Kingston) State and apply the mistake rules — honest belief negating mens rea (DPP v Morgan; R v Williams) and the honest AND reasonable requirement under the Criminal Damage Act 1971, s.5(2)(a) Apply the two-stage duress test (R v Graham), the relevant-characteristics limits (R v Bowen) and R v Hasan's foreseeability restrictions, and explain why duress is never available for murder (R v Howe; R v Gotts) Apply self-defence and prevention of crime under the common law and Criminal Law Act 1967, s.3 as codified by the CJI Act 2008, s.76 — necessity, reasonableness (R v Owino) and householder force (Crime and Courts Act 2013) Apply the loss of control qualifying triggers (CJA 2009, s.55; R v Clinton; R v Dawes; R v Asmelash) and diminished responsibility elements (Homicide Act 1957, s.2 as amended; R v Golds; R v Dowds; R v Dietschmann) as partial defences to murder (AQA 3.2.2) Insanity (M'Naghten rules) At the time of the offence D laboured under a defect of reason from a disease of the mind such that he did not know the nature and quality of his act, or did not know it was legally wrong; the verdict is 'not guilty by reason of insanity'. Automatism An involuntary act — total destruction of voluntary muscular control caused by an external factor (e.g. a blow to the head, hypoglycaemia from insulin, reflex action); a complete defence to all offences. Self-induced automatism Automatism brought on by the defendant's own fault, such as taking substances knowing of the risk: no defence to crimes of basic intent, but potentially available for specific intent crimes (R v Bailey; R v Hardie). Crime of basic intent An offence satisfied by recklessness (or intention) — the defendant is taken to have been reckless in getting drunk, so voluntary intoxication is no defence (R v Majewski); e.g. assault, s.47, s.20, manslaughter. Crime of specific intent An offence requiring a purpose beyond the act — recklessness insufficient (e.g. murder, s.18, theft, burglary with intent to GBH); evidence of intoxication may negative the required intention (R v Sheehan & Moore). Mistake Not a separate defence but a denial of mens rea: an honest (even unreasonable) mistaken belief in a fact negates the mental element for common-law offences (DPP v Morgan; R v Williams); under the Criminal Damage Act 1971, s.5(2)(a) the belief must be honest AND reasonable. Duress A defence where D commits an offence because of threats of death or serious physical injury which a sober person of reasonable firmness, sharing D's characteristics, would have been unable to resist (R v Graham; R v Hasan). Duress of circumstances Where circumstances (rather than threats from a person) objectively compel D to offend to avoid death or serious injury — e.g. fleeing violence while driving (R v Willer; R v Conway; R v Pommell); the Graham test applies. Self-defence (s.76 CJI Act 2008) D may use such force as is (or as he honestly and instinctively believes is) reasonable in the circumstances as he believes them to be — under the common law and Criminal Law Act 1967, s.3; mistaken beliefs due to intoxication are disregarded. Consent Where V freely consents to the actus reus; generally no defence to actual bodily harm or worse (R v Donovan; A-G's Reference (No 6 of 1980)), subject to public-policy exceptions such as surgery, tattooing, properly conducted sports and accidental injury during lawful activity. Loss of control (CJA 2009, s.54) A partial defence to murder: D's act resulted from a loss of self-control with a qualifying trigger under s.55 (fear of serious violence; things said or done of extremely grave character giving a justifiable sense of being seriously wronged), and a person of D's sex and age with normal tolerance might have reacted the same way; reduces murder to manslaughter. Diminished responsibility (Homicide Act 1957, s.2 as amended by CJA 2009, s.52) A partial defence to murder: an abnormality of mental functioning arising from a recognised medical condition which substantially impairs D's ability to understand his conduct, form rational judgment or exercise self-control, and provides an explanation for the killing; reduces murder to manslaughter. Insanity — the M'Naghten rules (1843). D is insane if, at the time of the offence, he was labouring under a defect of reason from a disease of the mind , such that he did not know the nature and quality of his act, or did not know that it was wrong . Defect of reason — D must be deprived of the power of reasoning, not merely have a momentary lapse: R v Clarke (1972) (brief absent-mindedness; confusion and depression can amount to a defect). Disease of the mind — a legal, not medical, test: any internal condition producing a malfunction of the mind (reason, memory or understanding) with a lasting or recurring source: R v Kemp (1957) (arteriosclerosis); R v Sullivan (1984) (epilepsy); R v Burgess (1991) (sleepwalking); R v Hennessy (1989) (hyperglycaemia from untreated diabetes). Wrong means legally wrong: R v Windle (1952) (D said he supposed they would hang him — knew it was wrong; conviction upheld). The special verdict is not guilty by reason of insanity ; disposal (hospital order, supervision order, absolute discharge) is governed by the Criminal Procedure (Insanity) Act 1964 as amended by the Criminal Procedure (Insanity and Unfitness to Plead) Act 1991. Criticisms: the internal/external line is arbitrary; diabetes, epilepsy and sleepwalking all yield an 'insane' label; D bears the burden of proof on the balance of probabilities. Automatism. An involuntary act — total destruction of voluntary control — negatives the actus reus. It is defined in Bratty v A-G for Northern Ireland (1963) as an act done without the exercise of the mind; where the cause is external (a blow to the head, hypoglycaemia from insulin — R v Quick (1973); a hypnotic drug taken without knowledge of any criminal tendency — R v Hardie (1985); rape trauma — R v T (1990)), it is sane automatism and leads to a full acquittal. Where the cause is internal , the M'Naghten rules apply instead (insane automatism). Self-induced automatism : R v Bailey (1983) (diabetic failed to eat after taking insulin and attacked his ex-lover): if D knew of a risk of automatism, that fault is treated as recklessness and the defence fails for crimes of basic intent; if the state was truly involuntary, the defence succeeds. Critics argue the internal/external distinction is unprincipled and the Law Commission has recommended abolition; examiners reward a clear internal/external table. Quick recall — internal v external causes Internal → insanity: arteriosclerosis (Kemp); epilepsy (Sullivan); sleepwalking (Burgess); hyperglycaemia, no insulin (Hennessy). External → sane automatism: blow to the head; hypoglycaemia after insulin (Quick); Valium without criminal tendency (Hardie); rape trauma (R v T). Insanity elements: defect of reason, disease of the mind, not knowing nature/quality or wrongfulness (M'Naghten; Clarke; Windle). Voluntary intoxication interacts with the basic/specific intent distinction: Crimes of basic intent — recklessness suffices (assault, s.47, s.20, manslaughter): DPP v Majewski (1977): voluntary intoxication is no defence ; the jury simply disregards it — becoming voluntarily drunk is itself treated as recklessness. R v O'Grady (1987): an intoxicated mistaken belief in self-defence is no defence to a crime of basic intent ( manslaughter conviction); R v Hatton (2005): the same bar applies where D claims a drunken mistake that he was being attacked (conviction for s.18 upheld). Crimes of specific intent — a purpose is required (murder, s.18, theft, burglary s.9(1)(a) with intent to GBH): evidence of intoxication may negative the required intention : R v Sheehan & Moore (1975) (drunken petrol-bomb throwers; if so drunk as to be only reckless, murder falls to manslaughter); R v Heard (2007) (drinking for 'Dutch courage' before using a sword — intoxication relevant where the intent was formed before drinking); R v Allen (1988) (intent formed before getting drunk — still liable). Involuntary intoxication — no defence once the mens rea is established: R v Kingston (1995) (drugged and molested a boy; intent formed despite the drug); but evidence of automatism may be admissible where a non-dangerous drug was taken as prescribed: R v Hardie (1985). Justifications for Majewski : getting voluntarily drunk is culpable (a 'mens rea equivalent'); the rule protects the public and simplifies trials. Criticisms : it is illogical to treat the same mental state differently depending on the offence; alcohol dependency raises disease questions ( R v Tandy (1989) — chronic alcoholism can be a disease, but the automatic default must be excluded); the Law Commission (2009) recommended reform, including a possible new offence of 'intoxicated wrongdoing'; examiners reward the link between Majewski and O'Grady, and the point that R v G's fault-based approach sits uneasily with objective disregard of intoxication for basic intent crimes. Quick recall — the intoxication ladder Basic intent: Majewski — no defence; O'Grady/Hatton — intoxicated mistake in self-defence ignored. Specific intent: Sheehan & Moore — may negative intent; Heard — Dutch courage; Allen — intent before drinking. Involuntary: Kingston — no defence once intent formed; Hardie — non-dangerous drug, automatism evidence admissible. Mistake is not a separate defence but a denial of mens rea. The rules: Common-law offences: an honest (even unreasonable) mistaken belief in a fact negates the mental element: DPP v Morgan (1976) (rape; jury must be told an honest belief in consent is a defence even if unreasonable); R v Williams (1987) (self-defence; honest belief suffices). Criminal Damage Act 1971, s.5(2)(a) : the belief must be honest AND reasonable to negative recklessness. Intoxicated mistake: R v O'Grady (1987) and R v Hatton (2005) — a drunken mistaken belief is no defence to a crime of basic intent, and is disregarded for self-defence (s.76(5) CJI Act 2008). Duress — threats of death or serious physical injury which compel D to offend. The two-stage test is R v Graham (1982), restated in R v Hasan (2005): (1) was D compelled to act as he did because he reasonably believed he had good cause to fear death or serious injury? (2) if so, would a sober person of reasonable firmness, sharing D's characteristics , have responded to the threats by acting as D did? Characteristics must be non-self-induced: age, sex, pregnancy, serious physical disability, recognised mental illness ( R v Bowen (1996)); not low IQ, alcoholism or emotional instability. Multiple threats : R v Valderrama-Vega (1985) (threats of death and exposure of homosexuality; monetary threats irrelevant but death/injury threats dominant — duress succeeded). Limits (R v Hasan) : duress fails where the threats were reasonably foreseeable, where D voluntarily associated with others he knew or ought to have known might put pressure on him, or where D was voluntarily intoxicated. Never available for murder or attempted murder : R v Howe (1987) (House of Lords; also for accessories) and R v Gotts (1992) (attempted murder) — the sanctity of life outweighs the defendant's coercion. Duress of circumstances — circumstances, not threats from a person, objectively compel D: R v Willer (1986) (drove off to escape a gang); R v Conway (1988) (taxi driver fled pursuing men); R v Pommell (1995) (took a gun from his brother intending to dispose of it). The Graham/Hasan test applies. Contrast necessity : R v Dudley & Stephens (1884) — necessity is no defence to murder. Quick recall — duress checkpoints Test: Graham (1982)/Hasan (2005) — reasonable belief in death/serious injury + sober person of reasonable firmness sharing characteristics. Characteristics: Bowen (1996) — age, sex, pregnancy, serious disability, recognised mental illness. Limits: Hasan — foreseeable threats, criminal association, voluntary intoxication. No duress: murder and attempted murder (Howe; Gotts); duress of circumstances — Willer, Conway, Pommell. Self-defence arises at common law and under the Criminal Law Act 1967, s.3 (prevention of crime: 'such force as is reasonable in the circumstances as he believes them to be'), now framed by the Criminal Justice and Immigration Act 2008, s.76 . Two questions: 1. Was the force necessary? Turned on D's honest and genuine belief in the need to use force — even if the belief was unreasonable: R v Gladstone Williams (1987); R v Oatbridge (1994). A pre-emptive strike is lawful where an attack is imminent ( A-G's Reference (No 2 of 1983) (1984)). A mistaken belief due to intoxication is disregarded: R v O'Grady (1987); R v Hatton (2005). 2. Was the force reasonable? Measured against the circumstances as D believed them to be — the force must be proportionate to the threat perceived, but need not match it exactly: Palmer v R (1971) (force is 'not measured on golden scales'); R v Owino (1996) (proportionate to the attack believed, not the attack made). Householder cases — s.76(5A), inserted by the Crime and Courts Act 2013: a person defending his dwelling may use force that is disproportionate (but not grossly disproportionate) and still rely on the defence; the provision was held compatible with the ECHR in R (Collins) v Secretary of State for Justice (2016). R v Martin (2001) (Norfolk farmer) prompted the fresh consideration of force used in the home. The burden is on the prosecution to disprove self-defence beyond reasonable doubt once sufficient evidence of it is raised. Consent. Consent can negate the actus reus for the lowest offences, but there is no consent to actual bodily harm or worse : R v Donovan (1934); A-G's Reference (No 6 of 1980) (1981) (consensual fist-fight in the street — unlawful). Public-policy exceptions where consent is effective: Surgery; tattooing and body piercing; R v Wilson (1996) (branding his wife's initials — analogy with tattooing; conviction quashed) — contrast R v BM (2018) (extreme body modification for sexual gratification fell outside the exceptions). Properly conducted games and sports: R v Barnes (2004) (football tackle; mere negligence in sport is not criminal unless beyond what players can reasonably be expected to accept). Injury accidentally caused during lawful consensual activity: R v Slingsby (1995) (wedding ring cut during rough consensual sex); rough horseplay: R v Aitken (1992) (setting fire to a fireproof flying suit). Consent to the risk of transmission: R v Dica (2004) (informed consent can negate grievous bodily harm from HIV) — but the consent must be informed: R v Konzani (2005). Limits : R v Brown (1993) (consensual sado-masochistic acts — no consent to actual bodily harm; the majority privileged the public interest in protecting people over individual autonomy; upheld by the European Court of Human Rights in Laskey v UK (1997)); R v Emmett (1999) (serious-injury acts fell outside the exceptions). Examiners reward the Wilson/Barnes/Slingsby exception list against the Brown limit, and the autonomy v public-interest evaluation. Quick recall — self-defence and consent Force: CLA 1967 s.3 + s.76 CJI Act 2008; honest belief — Gladstone Williams; Oatbridge; proportionality — Palmer; Owino; householder — Crime and Courts Act 2013 (disproportionate allowed, grossly not); Collins compatibility. Intoxicated mistake: O'Grady; Hatton — disregarded. No consent to ABH+: Donovan; A-G's Ref (No 6 of 1980). Exceptions: surgery; tattooing (Wilson; contrast BM); sports (Barnes); accidental injury (Slingsby); horseplay (Aitken); informed consent (Dica; Konzani). Limit: Brown (1993); Emmett; Laskey v UK. Both partial defences apply only to murder and reduce it to voluntary manslaughter , giving the judge full sentencing discretion instead of the mandatory life sentence. Loss of control — Coroners and Justice Act 2009, s.54 (replacing the common-law defence of provocation). Three elements: (1) Loss of self-control — expressly need not be sudden (s.54(2)); R v Jewell (2014): it is a matter for the jury whether there was a loss of self-control. (2) A qualifying trigger (s.55) : (a) fear of serious violence from V against D or another identified person (s.55(3)); (b) things said or done which constituted circumstances of an extremely grave character and gave D a justifiable sense of being seriously wronged (s.55(4)); or a combination. Sexual infidelity is expressly excluded (s.55(6)(c)) — R v Clinton (2012) (infidelity can form part of the background context to other things said or done, but is not itself a trigger); a self-induced trigger is disregarded (s.55(6)(a)-(b)) — R v Dawes (2013) (D who incited or participated in the violence loses the trigger); voluntary intoxication is disregarded — R v Asmelash (2013). (3) The objective test : a person of D's sex and age with a normal degree of tolerance and self-restraint , in the same circumstances, might have reacted in the same way (s.54(1)(c)); R v Jewell : 'normal' tolerance — it need not be high. Once the defence is raised, the burden is on the prosecution to disprove it beyond reasonable doubt. Revenge is excluded (s.54(4)); a considered desire for revenge defeats the defence. Diminished responsibility — Homicide Act 1957, s.2 as amended by the CJA 2009, s.52 . Three elements: (1) An abnormality of mental functioning arising from a recognised medical condition — R v Dowds (2013): acute voluntary intoxication alone is not a recognised medical condition (though chronic alcoholism with associated brain damage can be: R v Tandy (1989)); R v Martin (2001): organic brain damage and depressive illness qualified. (2) Substantial impairment of D's ability to (a) understand the nature of his conduct, (b) form a rational judgment, or (c) exercise self-control — one suffices; 'substantially' means more than trivially ( R v Golds (2016)). (3) The abnormality provides an explanation for D's acts or omissions. Intoxication does not defeat the defence where the abnormality remains a substantial cause: R v Dietschmann (2003) (grief plus alcohol; the jury asks whether the abnormality substantially impaired). The burden is on D on the balance of probabilities (s.2(2)). Evaluation : loss of control removed the 'sudden and temporary' requirement, excluded sexual infidelity and narrowed the triggers, so fewer pleas succeed and gender criticism of the old provocation law (e.g. R v Ahluwalia (1992), decided under the old law) is partly met; diminished responsibility is broad and depends on psychiatric evidence, and Dowds shows the courts resisting pleas built on voluntary intoxication alone. Quick recall — the two partial defences Loss of control: s.54 — loss of self-control (need not be sudden); trigger s.55 — fear of serious violence OR grave things said/done with justifiable sense of being seriously wronged; sexual infidelity excluded (s.55(6)(c) — Clinton); self-induced trigger (Dawes); intoxication disregarded (Asmelash); objective — sex and age, normal tolerance (Jewell); revenge excluded (s.54(4)). Diminished responsibility: s.2 (as amended by s.52 CJA 2009) — abnormality of mental functioning from a recognised medical condition; substantially impairs understanding/rational judgment/self-control (Golds); provides an explanation; intoxication alone insufficient (Dowds; Tandy); Dietschmann — drink does not defeat it. Both reduce murder to voluntary manslaughter; burden on D for DR, on prosecution for loss of control.

topics.subject: law
topics.searchText: law Law Remedies and Sentencing Distinguish the types of damages — general, special, aggravated, exemplary and nominal — and apply them to claim scenarios (AQA 3.1.1; OCR H418 Component 1; WJEC/Eduqas Component 1) Explain injunctions (prohibitory and mandatory; interim and final) and the contempt sanction, including the American Cyanamid test for interim injunctions Explain when specific performance and rescission are available, including the bars to rescission (affirmation, lapse of time, restitutio in integrum, third-party rights) State the five purposes of sentencing under the Criminal Justice Act 2003, s.142 and explain how judges weigh competing aims, including the welfare principle for under-18s (CYPA 1933, s.44) Explain how the minimum term (tariff) is set for murder — the mandatory life sentence, Schedule 21 CJA 2003 starting points and whole life orders — and the role of the Sentencing Council Apply statutory and guideline aggravating and mitigating factors, including the reduction for a guilty plea (Sentencing Act 2020, s.73) and aggravation for hostility (CJA 2003, ss.145-146) Distinguish custodial, community, fine and discharge sentences — their thresholds, limits and relative effectiveness — and evaluate the aims of sentencing in problem and essay answers Damages The primary common-law remedy: a sum of money awarded to the successful claimant, normally compensatory — restoring the claimant to the position as if the wrong had not happened (Livingstone v Rawyards Coal Co (1880)). General damages Non-pecuniary losses assessed by the court because they cannot be precisely calculated — pain, suffering and loss of amenity. Special damages Pecuniary losses provable and calculable up to the date of trial — lost earnings, medical expenses, damaged property. Aggravated damages A compensatory uplift awarded where the defendant's injurious, humiliating or high-handed conduct aggravated the claimant's loss (e.g. Thompson v Commissioner of Police of the Metropolis (1997)). Exemplary (punitive) damages Damages awarded to punish rather than compensate, confined by Rookes v Barnard (1964) to oppressive, arbitrary or unconstitutional action by government servants, and profit made from the wrong (AB v South West Water Services (1993)). Nominal damages A small symbolic sum where the claimant's right was infringed but no loss was suffered (e.g. trespass without damage). Injunction An equitable order requiring a party to do (mandatory) or stop (prohibitory) something; interim (until trial) or final; breach is a contempt of court. Specific performance An equitable order compelling performance of contractual obligations, granted only where damages are inadequate (Beswick v Beswick (1968)) and refused for personal-service or continuously supervised contracts (Co-operative Insurance Society v Argyll Stores (1998)). Rescission An equitable remedy setting a voidable contract aside from the beginning — available for misrepresentation, duress, undue influence or mistake — subject to bars: affirmation, lapse of time, impossibility of restitutio in integrum and third-party rights. Purposes of sentencing (CJA 2003, s.142) For adults: the punishment of offenders (retribution), the reduction of crime (deterrence), the reform and rehabilitation of offenders, the protection of the public, and the making of reparation by offenders. Tariff (minimum term) The minimum term a life-sentence prisoner must serve before the Parole Board may consider release; for murder, set by the judge from the Schedule 21 CJA 2003 starting points (15 years standard; 30 years or whole life order for the most serious). Aggravating and mitigating factors Factors increasing or reducing seriousness: statutory (CJA 2003, ss.143-146 — previous convictions, hostility, bail) and guideline factors; the reduction for a guilty plea is governed by the Sentencing Act 2020, s.73. Damages are the primary common-law remedy: a sum of money awarded to the successful claimant. The compensatory principle is restorative — put the claimant in the position he would have been in had the wrong not been committed ( Livingstone v Rawyards Coal Co (1880)). The types matter for the exam because each answers a different loss: General damages — non-pecuniary losses that cannot be precisely calculated and are assessed by the judge: pain, suffering and loss of amenity (PSLA), plus pre-trial non-pecuniary loss. Future losses are also assessed. Special damages — pecuniary losses provable and calculable up to trial: lost earnings, medical expenses, cost of repairing damaged property. Aggravated damages — a compensatory uplift where the defendant's injurious, humiliating or high-handed conduct increased the claimant's distress: Thompson v Commissioner of Police of the Metropolis (1997) (false imprisonment of a suspected thief; aggravated award for the humiliating strip search). Exemplary (punitive) damages — awarded to punish, not compensate, and rare: only two categories survive Rookes v Barnard (1964) — (1) oppressive, arbitrary or unconstitutional action by government servants (confirmed in Broome v Cassell & Co (1972)); (2) profit made from the wrong ( AB v South West Water Services (1993)). Nominal damages — the claimant's right was infringed but no loss was suffered (e.g. trespass without damage); a small sum vindicating the right. Contemptuous damages — liability is established but the court has no sympathy with the claimant: a token award, sometimes as little as one penny. Other points: remoteness of loss follows the negligence rules (the Wagon Mound test); interim payments may be made before trial; structured settlements spread large awards; damages under the Human Rights Act 1998, s.8 are 'just and appropriate' rather than strictly compensatory. Quick recall — the damages ladder Compensatory: general (non-pecuniary, assessed) v special (pecuniary, proven to trial). Aggravated: injurious/high-handed conduct (Thompson). Exemplary: punish — Rookes v Barnard categories (government oppression; profit from wrong; AB v South West Water). Nominal: right breached, no loss. Contemptuous: right breached, no sympathy. Equitable remedies are discretionary — the court applies the equitable maxims: he who seeks equity must come with clean hands; delay defeats equity (laches). They are flexible and forward-looking, unlike the fixed, backward-looking money award of damages. Injunctions — orders requiring a party to act or refrain from acting: Prohibitory (restrain the defendant from doing something) and mandatory (compel the defendant to undo something, e.g. remove an obstruction causing a nuisance). Interim (interlocutory) — until trial; the test is American Cyanamid Co v Ethicon Ltd (1975): (1) is there a serious question to be tried, (2) does the balance of convenience favour granting the injunction, (3) preserve the status quo until trial. Final (perpetual) — granted after trial where the claimant establishes the right. Breach is a contempt of court — punishable by fine or imprisonment (Contempt of Court Act 1981); common uses: nuisance, harassment (Protection from Harassment Act 1997, s.3), domestic abuse (Family Law Act 1996, Part IV non-molestation orders), breach of confidence. Specific performance — an equitable order compelling performance of contractual obligations. It is granted only where damages are inadequate : Beswick v Beswick (1968) (pension undertaking to a widow; order granted); Sky Petroleum v VIP Petroleum (1974) (rare fuel supply unavailable elsewhere). It is refused for contracts of personal service or requiring continuous supervision: Co-operative Insurance Society v Argyll Stores (1998); and against minors, or where the claimant has acted unconscionably (clean hands). Rescission — sets a voidable contract aside from the beginning (ab initio); both parties are restored to their pre-contract positions. Grounds: misrepresentation (fraudulent, negligent or innocent), duress, undue influence, non-disclosure in contracts of the utmost good faith, and common mistake. Bars to rescission : Affirmation — carrying on with the contract after discovering the vitiating factor. Lapse of time — undue delay defeats equity: Leaf v International Galleries (1950) (misdescription of a painting discovered five years later). Restitutio in integrum impossible — the goods or situation cannot be restored (substantial consumption or change). Third-party rights — a bona fide third party has acquired an interest in the property. Exam link : problem questions usually pair damages with an injunction or a contract remedy; state the remedy, its requirements and its limits, then argue which the claimant would get and why. The Criminal Justice Act 2003, s.142(1) sets the purposes of sentencing adults: (a) the punishment of offenders (retribution); (b) the reduction of crime (deterrence — individual and general); (c) the reform and rehabilitation of offenders; (d) the protection of the public ; and (e) the making of reparation by offenders (compensation orders; restorative justice). Retribution — punishment proportionate to the offence and the offender's culpability; the basis of the tariff system and the 'just deserts' theory. Deterrence — individual (discourage the offender) and general (discourage others); the evidence for general deterrence is weak — reoffending rates are high despite severe penalties. Rehabilitation — changing the offender (drug and alcohol treatment, programmes, education); most effective in the community, undermined by prison. Protection of the public — incapacitation (custody), plus restrictions (driving bans, restraining orders). Reparation — compensation to the victim and apologies/restorative justice conferences. For under-18s, s.142 does not apply — the welfare of the child is paramount (Children and Young Persons Act 1933, s.44), reflected in referral orders and youth rehabilitation orders. The Sentencing Council (established by the Coroners and Justice Act 2009) issues guidelines the courts must follow unless contrary to the interests of justice (CJA 2003, s.125): categories of culpability and harm produce a range and a starting point, promoting consistency across courts. The tariff for murder. Murder carries a mandatory life sentence (Murder (Abolition of Death Penalty) Act 1965). The judge sets the minimum term from the Schedule 21 CJA 2003 starting points: 15 years for standard adult murder; 30 years for particularly high seriousness (e.g. use of a firearm, murder of a police or prison officer in the course of duty); 25 years where a knife or other weapon was taken to the scene; and a whole life order (CJA 2003, s.269 with Sch.21) for the most exceptional cases — two or more murders, sexual or sadistic murder of a child, murder to advance a political, religious or ideological cause, or murder by a previously convicted murderer. Compatibility was upheld in Hutchinson v United Kingdom (2017). The Parole Board may release after the tariff; recall follows any breach of the licence. Quick recall — the aims and the tariff s.142: punishment (retribution); reduction of crime (deterrence); reform and rehabilitation; protection of the public; reparation. Youths: welfare paramount (CYPA 1933, s.44). Sentencing Council: guidelines must be followed (CJA 2003, s.125); culpability + harm. Murder: mandatory life (1965 Act); Sch.21 starting points — 15/25/30 years; whole life order (Hutchinson v UK); Parole Board release; licence. Seriousness is assessed under the Criminal Justice Act 2003, s.143 by (1) the offender's culpability and (2) the harm caused, or risked and foreseeable; previous convictions are relevant (s.143(2)). Statutory aggravating factors : Offence racially or religiously aggravated — CJA 2003, s.145 (maximum penalties increased; guideline uplifts). Aggravation by hostility to disability, sexual orientation or transgender identity — CJA 2003, s.146 . Offence committed while on bail — s.143(2) . Previous convictions, particularly similar ones. Guideline aggravating factors (Sentencing Council): premeditation, use of a weapon, vulnerability of the victim, group action, abuse of trust or position, offence committed in the victim's home, impact on children, failure to respond to previous warnings, offence committed under the influence of alcohol or drugs. Mitigating factors : Guilty plea — the court must state the reduction (Sentencing Act 2020, s.73): the guideline allows up to one-third off for a plea at the first opportunity, sliding down towards one-tenth at the door of the court — rewards efficiency and remorse. Assistance to the prosecution (informing on others) may reduce the sentence. Age and youth; ill health or disability; mental illness or psychological disorder; genuine remorse; previous good character; caring responsibilities; provocation or circumstances beyond the offender's control. Before sentence the court receives a pre-sentence report (probation), medical or psychiatric reports and victim personal statements ; the defence delivers a plea in mitigation. Exam link : apply the factors to the facts in the order culpability, harm, aggravation, mitigation, and link each factor to the aims it serves — aggravation to retribution, a guilty plea and treatment requirements to rehabilitation. Custodial sentences . The threshold: a court must not pass a custodial sentence unless the offence was so serious that neither a fine alone nor a community order can be justified (Sentencing Act 2020, s.230; formerly CJA 2003, s.152). Types: Mandatory life sentence for murder (minimum term from Sch.21 CJA 2003 — above); discretionary life for other serious offences (manslaughter, rape). Fixed-term imprisonment — the court sets the term up to the statutory maximum; the offender is released at the halfway point on licence, which runs to the end of the sentence; extended sentences for dangerous offenders add a licence period. Suspended sentence — a custodial term of 6 months to 2 years may be suspended for up to 2 years (Sentencing Act 2020, s.189); breach of the requirements activates the custody unless it would be unjust. Effectiveness : custody delivers retribution and incapacitation, but official figures show well over half of those serving short custodial sentences reoffend within a year — prison is poor at rehabilitation and expensive. Community orders — one or more requirements (Sentencing Act 2020; formerly CJA 2003, s.177): unpaid work (40-300 hours), supervision , accredited programmes, curfew with electronic monitoring (up to 16 hours a day), exclusion from places, prohibited activities, drug rehabilitation requirement , alcohol treatment requirement , mental health treatment requirement, attendance centre (under 25s) and residence. Breach returns the offender to court for stricter requirements or custody. Effectiveness: lower reoffending and lower cost than custody for comparable offenders, but perceived as 'soft'. Fines — the standard scale (levels 1-5: maxima from £200 to £5,000 in the magistrates' court; unlimited for either-way and indictable offences); means-tested against weekly income; enforcement by attachment of earnings, bailiffs and, ultimately, default. Discharges — conditional (up to 3 years — Sentencing Act 2020, s.79; no punishment unless a further offence within the period, when both offences are resentenced) and absolute (no punishment — trivial cases or where the defendant is technically criminal but blameless). Other orders: compensation orders, restraining orders, driving disqualification, confiscation of assets. Exam technique : AQA 25-mark essays ('Prison does not work' — evaluate) reward the aims tension (retribution and protection v rehabilitation), the statistics (short-sentence reoffending v community-order outcomes), and a judgement: custody is necessary for serious and dangerous offenders, but community orders with treatment requirements better serve rehabilitation for the rest. Scenario questions reward applying the custodial threshold, the factors (s.143), the guilty-plea reduction (Sentencing Act 2020, s.73) and the choice between custody, a suspended sentence and a community order.

topics.name: Contract and Human Rights
topics.subject: law
topics.searchText: law Law Contract and Human Rights Distinguish offers from invitations to treat and apply the termination rules - revocation, rejection, counter-offer, lapse - to a scenario, citing Partridge v Crittenden, Fisher v Bell, Carlill v Carbolic Smoke Ball and Hyde v Wrench (AQA 3.4.1; OCR H418 Component 3, contract option) Apply the postal rule in Adams v Lindsell and its exceptions - wrongly addressed letters (Household Fire v Grant), post not reasonable or excluded by the offeror (Holwell Securities v Hughes), instantaneous communications (Entores; Brinkibon) Apply the rules of consideration - sufficiency not adequacy (Chappell v Nestle), past consideration (Re McArdle), existing duty (Stilk v Myrick; Williams v Roffey), part payment of debt (Foakes v Beer; Pinnel's Case) and promissory estoppel (High Trees; Combe v Combe) Apply the presumptions on intention to create legal relations and their rebuttal (Balfour v Balfour; Merritt v Merritt), and the privity rule with the Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999, s.1 (Dunlop v Selfridge; Prudential Assurance v Ayers) Explain how ECHR Articles 2, 3, 5, 6, 8, 10 and 11 are protected through the HRA 1998 - s.3 interpretation (R v Lambert; Ghaidan v Godin-Mendoza), s.4 declarations of incompatibility (A v SSHD, Belmarsh), s.6 public authorities Apply PACE 1984 police powers - s.1 stop and search, s.24 arrest, detention limits under ss.41-44 and the safeguards (Fox, Campbell and Hartley) - and evaluate the balance between individual rights and effective law enforcement Offer A definite promise to be bound on specified terms, made with the intention that it will become binding on acceptance - as opposed to an invitation to treat. Invitation to treat A statement inviting others to make offers or to negotiate: advertisements (Partridge v Crittenden), shop-window displays (Fisher v Bell), tenders and goods on self-service shelves. Unilateral contract A contract where acceptance is by performance of the offer's terms rather than by a return promise - Carlill v Carbolic Smoke Ball Co (1893); communication of acceptance is waived. Consideration The price of a promise - some benefit to the promisor or detriment to the promisee (Currie v Misa (1875)). It must move from the promisee and be sufficient (but need not be adequate: Chappell v Nestle (1960)). Promissory estoppel An equitable defence (High Trees (1947)) preventing a party from going back on a clear promise, intended to affect legal relations, which the promisee has relied on - a shield, not a sword (Combe v Combe (1951)). Privity of contract Only a party to a contract may sue or be sued on it (Dunlop Pneumatic Tyre Co v Selfridge (1915)); modified by the Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999, s.1. Postal rule Where post is a reasonable or contemplated means of acceptance, acceptance takes effect on posting, not receipt (Adams v Lindsell (1818)) - subject to exceptions for wrongly addressed letters and express exclusion. Declaration of incompatibility Under HRA 1998, s.4, a superior court may declare that legislation is incompatible with a Convention right; it does not affect the validity or continuing enforcement of the legislation - only Parliament can amend it. Public authority Under HRA 1998, s.6(3), courts, tribunals and any body whose functions are of a public nature (government departments, local authorities, police, NHS); s.6(1) makes incompatible acts of such bodies unlawful. Warrant of further detention Under PACE 1984, ss.43-44, a magistrates' court may authorise continued detention beyond 36 hours, up to a maximum of 96 hours in total, for indictable or either-way offences. An offer is a definite promise to be bound on specified terms. The classic battleground is whether a statement is an offer or an invitation to treat - an invitation to others to make offers. In Partridge v Crittenden (1968) an advertisement of wild birds at 25 shillings each was an invitation to treat, so the seller could not be convicted of offering birds for sale. In Fisher v Bell (1961) a flick knife displayed in a shop window was likewise an invitation to treat, not an offer for sale under the Restriction of Offensive Weapons Act 1959 - the shopkeeper escaped liability, and Parliament promptly closed the gap by amending the Act. The key exception is the unilateral offer to the world : Carlill v Carbolic Smoke Ball Co (1893). The company's advertisement promised £100 to anyone who caught influenza after using the smoke ball as directed, and the £1,000 deposited in the bank showed sincerity - an intention to be bound. The Court of Appeal held this was an offer capable of acceptance by performance - using the smoke ball was acceptance, and communication was waived. A* point: in unilateral contracts the contract completes on performance; in bilateral contracts acceptance must be communicated first. An offer can be terminated by rejection, counter-offer , revocation, lapse of time or death. A counter-offer destroys the original offer: Hyde v Wrench (1840) - Wrench offered a farm at £1,000; Hyde countered at £950; Wrench refused; Hyde's later 'acceptance' of £1,000 failed because the offer was already dead. Revocation must be communicated before acceptance ( Byrne v Van Tienhoven (1880)), and an offer lapses after a reasonable time ( Ramsgate Victoria Hotel v Montefiore (1866)). Acceptance must be a mirror image of the offer and must be communicated to the offeror; silence is not acceptance ( Felthouse v Bindley (1862) - the nephew's silence could not bind him). The postal rule : in Adams v Lindsell (1818) acceptance took effect on posting, not receipt - the offeror is taken to accept the risk of postal delay. The rule only applies where post is a reasonable or contemplated means of acceptance, with exceptions: the letter must be correctly addressed and stamped ( Household Fire Insurance Co v Grant (1879) - even an acceptance lost in the post bound the offeror), and the offeror may exclude it ( Holwell Securities v Hughes (1974) - notice in writing required actual communication). For instantaneous communications, acceptance takes effect when and where it is received: Entores v Miles Far East Corp (1955), clarified in Brinkibon v Stahag Stahl (1983). Consideration is the price of a promise: Currie v Misa (1875) - a benefit to the promisor or a detriment to the promisee. It must move from the promisee ( Tweddle v Atkinson (1861) - the groom could not sue on a promise made for his benefit). It need not be adequate but must be sufficient : in Chappell v Nestle (1960) three chocolate wrappers were good consideration because Nestle stipulated for them. Past consideration is no consideration : Re McArdle (1951) - work done before the promise of payment could not support the later promise. Performance of an existing contractual duty is not good consideration : Stilk v Myrick (1809) - sailors promised extra wages simply to complete the voyage after desertions gave nothing extra. The modern approach is Williams v Roffey (1991): a subcontractor's promise to complete on time was supported by a practical benefit to Roffey (avoiding the penalty clause in the main contract). Limits: no economic duress, and the principle does not extend to part payment of a debt. Part payment of a debt : Pinnel's Case (1602), reaffirmed in Foakes v Beer (1884) - payment of a lesser sum cannot discharge the whole debt unless made under a deed, supported by different consideration (early payment, goods, a different place), or equity intervenes. Promissory estoppel : Central London Property Trust (High Trees House) Ltd v University Colleges (1947), Denning J - the landlord's wartime promise to accept half rent bound him while the promise lasted. Elements: a clear and unequivocal promise, intended to affect legal relations, on which the promisee relied. It is a shield not a sword ( Combe v Combe (1951) - no cause of action), it only suspends rights (full rent was payable again after the war), and it applies only where it would be inequitable to go back. Intention to create legal relations turns on rebuttable presumptions. Domestic and social agreements are presumed not intended to be binding: Balfour v Balfour (1919) - a husband's promise of a monthly allowance while he worked abroad was unenforceable. But the presumption is rebutted where the relationship has broken down: Merritt v Merritt (1970) - a separated couple's written agreement about the house was binding; the marriage was effectively over. Commercial agreements are presumed to have legal intention, rebuttable only by clear wording such as an honour clause ( Rose and Frank Co v Crompton (1925)). In problem questions intention is usually decided in a sentence or two - do not spend long on it. At common law only a party to a contract may sue or be sued on it, and consideration must move from the promisee. In Dunlop Pneumatic Tyre Co v Selfridge and Co (1915) Dunlop sold tyres to the wholesaler Dew under a clause fixing resale prices; Selfridge bought from Dew, but Dunlop could not enforce the price clause against Selfridge - Dunlop was not a party and had given no consideration. In Tweddle v Atkinson (1861) the groom could not sue on the fathers' agreement even though it was expressly intended for his benefit. The rule caused injustice, and courts worked around it: agency, a trust of the promise ( Beswick v Beswick (1968) - the widow enforced via specific performance), collateral contracts ( Shanklin Pier v Detel Products (1951)) and assignment. Asymmetrically, a third party could be sued on an exemption clause (the shield) but could not rely on one (the sword): Scruttons Ltd v Midland Silicones (1962), where Lord Reid invited Parliament to act. Parliament did so in the Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999 . Under s.1(1) a third party may enforce a term of the contract if the term expressly provides that he may (s.1(1)(a)) or purports to confer a benefit on him (s.1(1)(b)). The third party must be identified by name, as a member of a class or by description, or be identifiable when performance falls due. By s.1(4) the third party has the same remedies as if he were a party; under s.2 the parties cannot rescind or vary so as to extinguish the third party's entitlement once he has assented, relied and the promisor knows, or reliance is reasonably presumed; under s.3 the promisor keeps all the defences against the promisee. A* detail : Prudential Assurance Co Ltd v Ayers (2007), the 'Twisted Dreams' case - after a fire in premises leased from Prudential by Ayers and occupied by the nightclub Twisted Dreams, the nightclub could rely on the head lease's exclusion clause under s.1(1)(b) despite not being named in it - the Act goes beyond named third parties and cures the Scruttons shield/sword problem. The Act applies only to contracts made after 11 May 2000 - always check the date in the problem. In English law rights are not granted by the state - the starting point is residual liberty : you may do anything the law does not prohibit. Before the Human Rights Act 1998 (in force 2 October 2000), rights were protected only through the common law, statutes and the ECHR in Strasbourg (individual petitions from 1966). The HRA made Convention rights directly enforceable in UK courts without entrenching them - Parliament remains sovereign and can still legislate contrary to them. The Act has vertical effect : it binds public authorities. Horizontal effect is only indirect - courts are themselves public authorities (s.6(3)), so they must develop the common law compatibly. s.6(1) makes it unlawful for a public authority to act incompatibly with Convention rights. s.3 requires primary and subordinate legislation to be read and given effect compatibly so far as possible - a strong interpretive obligation exercised before any declaration is contemplated. In R v Lambert (2001) the reverse burden in s.28(2) of the Misuse of Drugs Act 1971 was read down to an evidential burden to preserve Article 6(2) compatibility. In Ghaidan v Godin-Mendoza (2004) 'living with the original tenant as his or her wife or husband' in the Rent Act 1977 was read to include a same-sex partner - s.3 can go to the very edge of interpretation, but cannot contradict the underlying thrust of the legislation. s.4 : where no compatible reading is possible, a superior court may make a declaration of incompatibility . It does not affect the validity or continuing enforcement of the legislation - only Parliament can change it, though ministers usually respond, potentially by fast-track remedial order under s.10. A v Secretary of State for the Home Department (2004), the Belmarsh case: s.23 of the Anti-terrorism, Crime and Security Act 2001, permitting indefinite detention of foreign terrorist suspects, was incompatible with Article 5(1) (and Article 14); the government responded with the Prevention of Terrorism Act 2005 (control orders) - showing both the limits of judicial power and the persuasive force of declarations. Article Right Key authority and exam link 2 Right to life Procedural duty of independent inquiry into deaths involving state responsibility - R (Middleton) v West Somerset Coroner (2004); positive duty to protect life - Osman v UK (1998) 3 Prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment Absolute - no balancing; R (Limbuela) v SSHD (2005) - leaving an asylum seeker destitute breached Article 3 5 Liberty and security Prompt judicial review of the lawfulness of detention (Article 5(4)) - Fox, Campbell and Hartley v UK (1990); delay without judicial review breached Article 5(3) in Brogan v UK (1988) 6 Fair trial Independent and impartial tribunal, presumption of innocence (Article 6(2) - the basis of R v Lambert ), legal representation; applies to criminal and civil litigation 8 Private and family life, home, correspondence Qualified right; Gillan and Quinton v UK (2010) - blanket s.44 Terrorism Act 2000 stop-and-search lacked safeguards; privacy developed through confidence in Campbell v MGN (2004) 10 Freedom of expression Qualified; protects even offensive or shocking speech ( Handyside v UK (1976)); R (Simms) v SSHD (2000) - prisoners' right to interview journalists upheld as a common law right 11 Freedom of assembly and association Includes trade union membership; ASLEF (No 2) v UK (2007) - union could not be forced to retain a BNP member Police powers under PACE 1984 and its Codes of Practice (A-C) balance effective law enforcement against the Convention rights. s.1 stop and search : in public places, on reasonable suspicion that a person carries stolen or prohibited articles (including bladed items). Safeguards: genuine reasonable grounds, only a jacket, outer coat or gloves may be removed (s.2, Code A), and a written record. The blanket s.44 Terrorism Act 2000 power, usable without suspicion, lacked safeguards and was incompatible with Articles 5 and 8 ( Gillan and Quinton v UK (2010)). s.24 arrest : a constable may arrest without warrant anyone reasonably suspected of committing, having committed or being about to commit an offence, if arrest is necessary for one of the s.24(5) criteria (unknown name or address, preventing disappearance or harm, prompt and effective investigation). Citizens' arrests (s.24A) are narrower - indictable offences and necessity only.
