Kant's test case, the false promise : the maxim 'make a promise I do not intend to keep to escape difficulty' universalised destroys the institution of promising (if everyone lied, no one would believe promises — contradiction in conception); the maxim 'never help others' cannot be consistently willed (contradiction in the will — we all sometimes need help). (2) Humanity as an end : never treat persons merely as means — the false promiser uses the deceived person merely as a means; persons have dignity (priceless worth) rather than price. (3) Kingdom of ends : act as a legislating member of a community of rational agents — the formulations are claimed to be equivalent expressions of one supreme principle. Issues. (1) Clashing duties (Constant's objection, the murderer at the door): 'never lie' and 'do not facilitate murder' cannot both be kept; Kant's own reply — lying to the murderer is wrong, and one may be truthful while the outcome harms — strikes most as unacceptable; a weaker reply: the duties do not genuinely clash if formulated precisely (the maxim against lying is about 'unavoidable falsehood', and lying to facilitate murder fails the humanity formulation). (2) Rigidity : universalisability yields inflexible rules insensitive to consequences. (3) Consequences ignored : an act's rightness is independent of outcomes — intuitively wrong when stakes are catastrophic (lying to save a life). (4) Universalisation is slippery: many wicked maxims universalise without contradiction if carefully worded ('always lie when it benefits me' may not contradict itself in conception). (5) Motives ignored: Kant counts only duty-motivated acts as morally worthy, ignoring love, friendship and kindness as motives with moral value. (6) Morality as hypothetical imperatives (Foot): Kant claims the moral law binds unconditionally, but obeying it itself requires a desired end (to be rational, to avoid blame, to live with oneself) — so morality is, after all, a system of hypothetical imperatives. (7) Animals: Kant holds rational nature is the source of worth, so animals have only indirect worth — mistreating them is wrong because it damages our humanity; contrast utilitarianism (sentience suffices) and virtue ethics (compassion). Eudaimonia and the function argument. The highest good is eudaimonia — flourishing, living well and doing well: complete (desired for its own sake, not as a means), final and self-sufficient. The function (ergon) argument : the good of anything with a function lies in performing that function well; the human function is activity of the soul in accordance with reason (plants have nutrition, animals perception — what is distinctive to humans is reason); so the human good is activity of the soul in accordance with virtue — and, for a complete life, in accordance with the best virtue (contemplation, Aristotle adds). Critique: the inference from 'distinctive capacity' to 'function' to 'good' is contested — a capacity for wickedness is equally distinctive of humans, and a solitary, rational but friendless life hardly looks like flourishing; Aristotle's own account of friendship answers the second point. Virtues and the mean. A virtue is a stable character trait (a hexis) to feel, choose and act well. Doctrine of the mean : each virtue lies between two vices, excess and deficiency, relative to us — courage between rashness and cowardice, generosity between prodigality and meanness, proper pride between vanity and false modesty. Some actions (murder, adultery) admit no mean — they are wrong in any degree. Phronesis (practical wisdom) is the intellectual virtue that perceives the particulars of a situation and deliberates to the mean; it unifies the virtues (one cannot have one fully without the others). Virtues are acquired by habituation : we become just by doing just acts, first with instruction and correction, until feeling and action align. The skill analogy : virtues are like skills — acquired by practice, exercised with judgement, assessed by how well they are done — but unlike skills they involve feelings : the generous person enjoys giving. Voluntariness: we are responsible for voluntary actions and for our characters, since habits are built from choices; involuntary actions (from force or ignorance) are not blameworthy, and non-voluntary actions (done in ignorance the agent could not avoid) attract pity rather than blame. Issues. (1) Circularity (Hursthouse): the right act is what the virtuous person would do; the virtuous person is who does the right acts — a vicious circle? Reply: it is an explanatory circle not a definitional one — virtue and right action are mutually illuminating, as health and healthy organs are. (2) Guidance: 'do what the practically wise person would do' seems to give no action-guidance. Reply: the mean, the virtuous examples and phronesis give substantial guidance — but less mechanical than a calculus or a test. (3) Relativism: 'relative to us' invites cultural relativism. Reply: relativism is about how the mean applies, not whether virtue is objective. (4) Applicability/conflict: what happens when two virtues pull apart (honesty and kindness)? (5) Must a trait contribute to eudaimonia to be a virtue? — if virtues are defined by what makes the individual flourish, the good for the individual and the moral good may come apart; Aristotle answers that the practically wise person sees that a flourishing life is also the morally good one. Note also the eudaimonia–pleasure relationship : pleasure completes virtuous activity 'as the bloom of youth' — eudaimonia is not pleasure alone, but the virtuous life is pleasant to the virtuous person. Three decision procedures. Utilitarianism: maximise aggregate welfare (consequentialist, agent-neutral). Kant: test maxims against the categorical imperative (deontological, intention-focused). Aristotle: ask what the person of practical wisdom would do (aretaic, character-focused). They disagree structurally: on what makes an act right (outcomes vs universalisable intention vs virtuous character), on whether consequences matter, and on partiality (utilitarianism counts everyone equally; Aristotle begins from relationships and communities; Kant from rational agents). Issue Utilitarianism Kant Aristotle Stealing Right iff net utility gained (usually wrong, but can permit it) Wrong: the maxim 'take others' property when convenient' cannot be universalised; theft uses the owner merely as a means Wrong as a matter of justice (no mean); but the virtuous person may face cases where what is owed is complex Eating animals Permitted if animal suffering is outweighed — but factory farming fails the calculus (sentience counts, Bentham) Animals lack rational nature: only indirect duty — cruelty wrong because it damages our humanity Wrong if intemperate (gluttony); the mean and compassion govern treatment — not outright prohibition Simulated killing Right: no one is harmed, and pleasure is gained Problematic: habitual willingness to simulate killing may be impossible to universalise cleanly; virtue of the agent is at stake Habituation matters: repeatedly simulating killing may form bad character — the practice shapes what we enjoy Telling lies Right iff consequences favour it (white lies often permitted) Wrong in principle (false promise/universal law); even the murderer at the door (Kant: on a supposed right to lie) Wrong if from a mean-deficient character; but practical wisdom may permit tact — honesty is not bluntness Why the comparison matters for AO2. 25-markers often ask you to argue that one theory is 'the best' or 'most convincing'. Strong answers do not merely list — they weigh structural features: utilitarianism's fairness problem vs its moral reach; Kant's rigidity vs its protection of persons from being used as means; Aristotle's richer moral psychology vs its weaker action-guidance. Then conclude consistently. Where it lands. Moral philosophy (Specs 3.2.1–3.2.5) is Paper 1 Section B: five questions worth 3, 5, 5, 12 and 25 marks . Short questions are pure AO1; the 25-marker (5 AO1 + 20 AO2) is a quoted claim + 'Evaluate this claim'. Metaethics (Spec 3.2.4) has its own revision page — cross-reference it. 25-mark essay structure. Introduction: define the theory/claim, state your thesis. Argument for your view; best objection; response. Argument against; weak response; strong response. Consistent conclusion, no new ideas. Mark scheme top band (21–25) rewards 'crucial arguments clearly identified against less crucial ones' — e.g. in a utilitarianism essay, the tyranny-of-the-majority/fairness issue is crucial; the calculation issue is less so and can be handled in a line with Mill's rule-utilitarian reply. Common pitfalls and examiner tips (click to expand) Act vs rule utilitarianism: act assesses each act by its consequences; rule assesses rules by the consequences of general acceptance. Mill is best read as moving from act to rule; do not attribute the felicific calculus to Mill. From duty vs in accordance with duty: only the former has moral worth (Kant's shopkeeper). Candidates routinely miss this distinction. Mill's 'proof' is fallacious: know the slide from 'each desires their own happiness' to 'the general happiness is desirable' — an A* answer flags it even while defending utilitarianism. The mean is relative to us: not 'moderation in all things' — courage is not 'a bit of rashness plus a bit of cowardice', and some acts admit no mean. Use applied ethics in evaluation: cases (the murderer at the door, Jim and the Indians, simulated killing) earn AO2 only when used to test a theory, not as decoration. Timing: ~35–40 minutes per 25-marker, ~15 for the 12-marker; with 10 questions in 3 hours, move on when a short answer is complete — extra words on 3/5-markers lose marks.

topics.name: Metaethics: Cognitivism, Realism and Moral Language
topics.subject: philosophy
topics.searchText: philosophy Philosophy Metaethics: Cognitivism, Realism and Moral Language Distinguish the two metaethical axes — cognitivism vs non-cognitivism and realism vs anti-realism — and locate each theory on both axes (Spec 3.2.3). Explain the possible origins of moral principles in reason, in emotion/attitudes or in society (Spec 3.2.3). Explain moral naturalism, including naturalist forms of utilitarianism (Bentham) and of virtue ethics, and evaluate it using Moore's open question argument and the naturalistic fallacy (Spec 3.2.3). Explain moral non-naturalism — Moore's intuitionism and Ross's prima facie duties — and evaluate the challenges from Hume's fork, the is-ought gap and the motivation argument (Spec 3.2.3). Explain Mackie's error theory — the arguments from relativity and from queerness — and assess the nihilism charge (Spec 3.2.3). Explain and evaluate emotivism (Ayer, Stevenson) and prescriptivism (Hare), including whether anti-realism can account for moral reasoning, disagreement and moral progress (Spec 3.2.3). Analyse and evaluate metaethical arguments to form reasoned judgements in 25-mark essays (AO2, 'arguing with intent'). Two independent axes: cognitivism (moral judgements truth-apt) vs non-cognitivism (not truth-apt); realism (mind-independent moral facts) vs anti-realism (none). Every theory sits on both. Moral principles may originate in reason (Moore, Ross), emotion/attitudes (Ayer) or society (Mackie: 'inventing' right and wrong). Naturalism: good = natural property — Bentham: pleasure; naturalist virtue ethics: flourishing. Attacked by Moore's open question argument and the naturalistic fallacy. Non-naturalism (Moore, Ross): good is simple, non-natural, known by intuition; Ross adds plural, self-evident prima facie duties. Attacked by Hume's fork, the is-ought gap, the motivation argument and Mackie's queerness. Error theory (Mackie): judgements aim at objective truth but all fail — arguments from relativity and queerness; nihilism charge. Emotivism (boo/hurrah, persuasion) and prescriptivism (universalisable prescriptions) deny truth-aptness; attacked via embedded contexts, disagreement, the fanatic and moral progress. Cognitivism The view that moral judgements express beliefs, state propositions and are truth-apt: 'murder is wrong' is true or false and can be known. Shared by naturalism, non-naturalism and (in modified form) error theory. Non-cognitivism The view that moral judgements express non-cognitive mental states (emotions, prescriptions) and state nothing, so they are not truth-apt. Emotivism and prescriptivism are non-cognitivist theories. Moral realism There are mind-independent moral properties or facts: some moral judgements are true or false independently of what anyone thinks, feels or prescribes. Moral anti-realism There are no mind-independent moral properties or facts — either because moral judgements were never in the business of stating facts (emotivism, prescriptivism) or because, although they aim at objective truth, they systematically fail (error theory). Moral naturalism Cognitivist realism: moral properties are natural properties, reducible to or identical with properties studied by the sciences — e.g. naturalist utilitarianism (Bentham: good = pleasure, right = maximising it) and naturalist virtue ethics (good = traits enabling human flourishing). Open question argument Moore (Principia Ethica, 1903): for any proposed natural property N, the question 'but is N good?' remains open and significant, not self-answering like 'are bachelors unmarried?'; so good is not identical with any natural property — an argument against all reductive metaethical theories. Is-ought gap Hume: no 'ought' follows validly from premises stating only 'is' — a moral conclusion requires a moral premise, so sets of pure facts never entail obligations. Error theory Mackie (Ethics: Inventing Right and Wrong, 1977): moral judgements purport to state objective, mind-independent facts, but there are no objective values, so every positive moral judgement is false; values are projected, not discovered. Emotivism Ayer: moral judgements fail the verification principle (neither analytic nor empirically verifiable), so they are not truth-apt statements but expressions of emotion — 'stealing is wrong' amounts to 'stealing — boo!' (the boo/hurrah theory); Stevenson adds emotive meaning and a persuasive function. Prescriptivism Hare (The Language of Morals, 1952): moral judgements are universalisable prescriptions — imperatives ('do this!') that commit the speaker to prescribing the same for any relevantly similar situation, including their own. Second-order questions. First-order ethics asks 'Is abortion wrong?'; metaethics (AQA 7172 Spec 3.2.3) asks what such a judgement itself is: does it state a fact and aim at truth, or express an attitude and issue a command? Two independent axes organise the theories; a strong answer locates each theory on both. Axis 1 — cognitivism vs non-cognitivism. Cognitivism : moral judgements express beliefs , assert propositions and are truth-apt — 'murder is wrong' is true or false and can be known. Non-cognitivism : moral judgements express non-cognitive states (emotions, prescriptions); they state nothing and are not truth-apt . Both camps agree moral sentences look declarative; the debate is what the utterance does . Axis 2 — realism vs anti-realism. Moral realism : there are mind-independent moral properties or facts, so some moral judgements are objectively true. Moral anti-realism : there are none — either because moral judgements were never in the truth business (emotivism, prescriptivism) or because, though they aim at truth, they systematically fail (error theory). Origins of moral principles. The spec opens 3.2.3 with this question: principles may originate in reason (self-evident truths grasped a priori — Moore, Ross), in emotion and attitudes (approval projected onto the world — Ayer, Mackie) or in society (invented conventions — Mackie's Ethics: Inventing Right and Wrong ). The answer fixes whether moral judgements can be true at all. Cross-classification. The axes combine into a diagnostic grid: Cognitivist (truth-apt) Non-cognitivist (not truth-apt) Realist — mind-independent moral facts Moral naturalism (Bentham; naturalist virtue ethics); non-naturalism / intuitionism (Moore, Ross) — Anti-realist — no mind-independent moral facts Error theory (Mackie) Emotivism (Ayer, Stevenson); prescriptivism (Hare) Examiner-flagged confusions (click to expand) Mackie is not a non-cognitivist: error theory keeps the truth-aim and says it fails. Non-cognitivism is not anti-realism: they answer different questions — semantics vs metaphysics. Moral naturalism. Good, bad, right and wrong are natural properties : reducible to, or identical with, properties studied by the sciences. Two spec-favoured versions. (1) Naturalist utilitarianism (Bentham) : 'good' means pleasure, 'right' means maximising it — moral facts are natural facts about pleasure and pain, discoverable and countable like any other facts (the felicific calculus). (2) Naturalist virtue ethics (Aristotle; Foot): 'good' means what enables a living thing to flourish as the kind of thing it is — good traits are those a well-developed member of the species displays, as good roots draw water. Attractions: it explains moral objectivity (moral claims true or false like scientific ones), moral knowledge (observation of pleasure and flourishing — no special faculty) and moral motivation (natural desires move us). Moore's open question argument. Principia Ethica (1903): 'good' is simple and unanalysable — like 'yellow', it can only be pointed at, not defined. Any proposed natural definition N leaves ' but is N good? ' open : significant, substantive, not self-answering. 'Is pleasure good?' is a genuine question (cruel pleasures seem bad); 'is a bachelor unmarried?' is closed. If good meant pleasure, 'pleasure is good' would be as trivial as 'pleasure is pleasure' — so good is not identical with any natural property. The argument targets all reductive metaethical theories — Bentham's, Foot's, any reduction. Defining good in natural terms is the naturalistic fallacy : deriving value from fact. Critiques. (1) The argument begs the question : the question is open only on the assumption that good is unanalysable — what the naturalist denies. (2) Synthetic identities are open before science closes them: 'is water H2O?' was once a good question, yet water is H2O — natural properties can be discovered , so openness is compatible with identity. (3) Moore's own analysis ('that which we desire to desire') fares no better — the argument proves too much, undermining every definition including his. (4) At most it shows that 'good' and N differ in meaning , not in reference — and the fallacy charge needs the latter. Moore's non-naturalism (intuitionism). If good is simple and unanalysable yet we make true moral judgements, moral properties must be non-natural : simple properties of the world, reducible to no natural property and not studied by science, known by intuition — direct, self-evident, a priori grasping, like seeing that 2+2=4. Ross extends the view: we intuit plural prima facie duties (fidelity, reparation, gratitude, justice, beneficence, non-maleficence, self-improvement), each holding 'unless overridden'; no formula resolves conflicts — judgement decides which duty is most stringent here. Critiques: non-natural properties are metaphysically queer (Mackie, below); a shared faculty of intuition sits badly with persistent disagreement (abortion, capital punishment); intuitions track upbringing, not truth — slavery once seemed 'self-evidently' acceptable; and 'self-evident to whom?' risks subjectivism about the verdicts. Hume's fork and the is-ought gap. Hume's fork (Spec 3.1.3, redeployed): substantive knowledge is either relations of ideas (a priori, analytic, necessary) or matters of fact (a posteriori, contingent). Moral judgements are neither: denying 'murder is wrong' involves no contradiction, yet no wrongness is observable in the act. In the Treatise (Book III, Part 1) Hume notes that writers move from 'is' to 'ought' without explanation: no ought from is — a moral conclusion requires a moral premise, so pure facts never entail obligations. Significance: the naturalist can add a value premise ('pleasure is good'), but then naturalism does not derive value from nature — it presupposes it. Hume's motivation argument. Beliefs are representational and reason alone is inert : 'reason is, and ought only to be, the slave of the passions' — belief cannot by itself move us. But moral judgements are reliably motivating : judging 'I ought to repay the debt' characteristically issues in repayment. So moral judgements are not beliefs — beliefs alone could not motivate us; they involve non-cognitive desire: the classic argument for non-cognitivism. Cognitivist responses: (1) Externalism : motivation needs belief plus desire, and Hume shows only that belief alone is insufficient — the desire can be independent of the belief, present in the normally-constituted and absent in the amoralist who judges 'torturing the child is wrong' and feels nothing; (2) motivational power is no test of truth — we can be moved by false judgements; (3) desire-driven action can be irrational or immoral, so being motivating is no mark of genuine moral judgement. Mackie's error theory. Ordinary moral thought presupposes objective values : categorical, universally binding 'to-be-pursuedness' woven into the fabric of the world. Mackie ( Ethics: Inventing Right and Wrong , 1977): that presupposition is an error — moral judgements aim at objective truth but systematically fail , so every positive moral judgement is false. His positive story is projectivism : we project our desires and attitudes onto the world, as colour-perception projects redness onto the tomato. The nihilism charge: if all positive judgements are false, nothing is morally right or wrong — moral practice looks pointless. Responses: error theory concerns truth , not meaning — moral language still makes sense and attitudes are untouched; and Mackie's title signals the constructive turn: morality should be invented and used as an agreed, useful convention. Counter: nobody can live the theory — deliberating, blaming and promising presuppose that 'wrong' sometimes applies; 'morality as invention' re-describes rather than saves morality. Argument from relativity. Moral codes vary radically and persistently — monogamy, slavery, caste, abortion — and the variation tracks different ways of life , not perceptual conditions. The best explanation of scientific disagreement is misperception of objective facts (hence convergence); the best explanation of moral disagreement is that people approve differently because they live differently ; so objective values are a poor hypothesis. Responses: much moral disagreement is about facts (does the foetus feel pain?); convergence on core prohibitions (murder, betrayal of trust) is real; and persistent disagreement in frontier science has never licensed anti-realism about science. Argument from queerness. Objective values would be metaphysically queer : 'qualities or relations of a very strange sort, utterly different from anything else in the universe', carrying intrinsic to-be-pursuedness — a 'should' built into the world as no natural property is. And epistemologically queer : knowing them would require a special faculty of moral intuition unlike perception, memory or reasoning. Parsimony says they do not exist. Responses: we already accept strange features — consciousness, intentionality — so intrinsically normative properties are less isolated than Mackie suggests; and Moore and Ross accept the faculty, so for them nothing is queer to explain away. Emotivism (Ayer, Stevenson). Ayer ( Language, Truth and Logic , 1946) applies the verification principle : a statement is cognitively meaningful only if analytic or empirically verifiable. Moral judgements are neither — no observation verifies 'murder is wrong' — so they assert nothing and function to express emotions and arouse them: the boo/hurrah theory — 'Stealing is wrong' amounts to 'Stealing — boo!'. Stevenson ( Ethics and Language , 1944) refines this: moral terms carry emotive meaning and a persuasive function — they work to redirect the hearer's attitudes ; and moral reasoning is possible: we cite empirical beliefs as reasons to change attitudes — persuasion by reasons, not proof. Critiques: (1) the embedded-context problem (Frege–Geach): in 'If stealing is wrong, getting your little brother to steal is wrong', the unasserted antecedent expresses no emotion, yet the argument is plainly valid — unasserted moral claims must retain truth-apt meaning ; (2) the disagreement critique : 'Capital punishment is wrong' vs 'Capital punishment is justified' presents itself as genuine contradiction backed by reasons — not two incompatible cheers; (3) the verification principle is self-refuting — itself neither analytic nor verifiable. Prescriptivism (Hare). Hare ( The Language of Morals , 1952): moral judgements are universalisable prescriptions : their meaning is practical — to command and guide action ('do this!') — and their logic is universalisability : whoever prescribes 'ought' for one situation is committed to the same prescription for any relevantly similar situation , including one in which they are the victim. Universalisability makes moral reasoning genuine (prescriptions must be backed by relevant similarities and evidence) and rules out special pleading . Critiques: (1) prescriptions are not truth-apt either, so the embedded-context and disagreement problems return; (2) the fanatic objection: a racist can consistently universalise 'no equal treatment for them' — Hare must insist the fanatic has failed to imagine himself in the victim's position, but universalisability alone does not force that; (3) moral judgements are statements that report , not imperatives that order — 'murder is wrong' can be embedded in arguments and said idly, as commands cannot; (4) moral progress : if judgements only express attitudes, the shift from approval of slavery to its condemnation is a change of fashion, not the discovery of a truth — yet 'progress' is how we describe it.

topics.name: Metaphysics of God: Divine Attributes, Arguments and Religious Language
topics.subject: philosophy
topics.searchText: philosophy Philosophy Metaphysics of God: Divine Attributes, Arguments and Religious Language Explain and evaluate the definitions of God as omnipotent, eternal and omniscient, including the paradox of the stone, Descartes vs Aquinas/Kenny, and Boethius vs Swinburne on eternality (Spec 3.3.1). Explain and evaluate the ontological argument — Anselm (Proslogion 2 and 3), Descartes and Malcolm — with Gaunilo's perfect-island reply and Kant's 'existence is not a predicate' (Spec 3.3.2). Explain and evaluate the teleological argument — Paley's watch, Swinburne's regularity — with Hume's critiques and Darwin's theory of evolution (Spec 3.3.2). Explain and evaluate the cosmological argument — Aquinas' Three Ways, the Kalam argument, Leibniz's principle of sufficient reason — with Hume's and Russell's critiques (Spec 3.3.2). Explain and evaluate the logical problem of evil (Mackie's inconsistent triad, Plantinga's free will defence) and the evidential problem (Rowe's fawn, Hick's vale of soul-making) (Spec 3.3.3). Explain and evaluate religious experience (James, Swinburne's credulity and testimony, Flew's verification challenge) and religious language (via negativa, Aquinas' analogy, Ayer, Hare, Hick) (Specs 3.3.4–3.3.5). Use AQA command words correctly: pure AO1 explanation on 3/5/12-mark questions; 'arguing with intent' and balanced evaluation only on 25-mark essays. Omnipotence (Aquinas/Kenny): every power it is logically possible to have — the stone task is self-contradictory, not a genuine limit; Descartes: God can do the logically impossible, having created the eternal truths. Boethius: God is timeless — 'the whole, simultaneous and perfect possession of unending life'; foreknowledge becomes timeless seeing, imposing only conditional necessity on free acts. Ontological (Anselm Proslogion 2/3, Descartes, Malcolm) vs Kant: existence is not a real predicate (100 thalers) — the crucial debate is whether necessary existence escapes Kant. Cosmological: Aquinas' Three Ways (per se regress), Kalam (no actual infinities), Leibniz (sufficient reason); Hume (fallacy of composition) and Russell ('the universe is just there, and that's all'). Evil: Mackie's triad answered by Plantinga (free will defence + transworld depravity); Rowe's fawn answered by theodicy (Hick) or sceptical theism. Flew's falsification challenge answered by Hare's bliks and Hick's eschatological verification. Paradox of the stone Can an omnipotent God create a stone too heavy for God to lift? If yes, God cannot lift it; if no, God cannot create it — either way a limitation. Aquinas/Kenny: the task is self-contradictory, so not genuinely possible and no limit on power. Boethius' eternity God's eternity is 'the whole, simultaneous and perfect possession of unending life' (Consolation V) — God is timeless, outside time, beholding past, present and future in a single eternal present. Everlasting God Swinburne/Wolterstorff: God is not timeless but everlasting — existing at every moment of time, knowing at each time everything it is then logically possible to know (including past and present, but not future free choices). That than which nothing greater can be conceived Anselm's definition of God (Proslogion 2) — even the fool understands it; since existing in reality is greater than existing in the understanding alone, God must exist in reality as well. Necessary existence Existence that cannot be lacked without incoherence — that which cannot be conceived of as non-existent (Anselm, Proslogion 3). Malcolm: necessary existence cannot be contingent, so God's existence is either impossible or necessary. Existence is not a predicate Kant's critique: 'is' adds no property to a concept, it only asserts that the concept is instantiated (100 real thalers and 100 imagined thalers share one concept) — so defining God as having existence, or counting existence among the perfections, is illegitimate. Principle of sufficient reason Leibniz: everything has a sufficient reason for why it is so and not otherwise; the reason for a contingent thing lies outside it, so the whole series of contingent things requires a sufficient reason outside itself — a necessary being. Per se ordered causal series Aquinas: a series where each member has no independent causal power but only derivatively (hand–stick–stone). Such a series cannot be infinite without a first member; this grounds the First and Second Ways, as opposed to a merely temporal (per accidens) series. Inconsistent triad Mackie ('Evil and Omnipotence'): (1) God is omnipotent, (2) God is wholly good, (3) evil exists — these cannot all be true together, since a wholly good being eliminates evil as far as it can and an omnipotent being can eliminate it entirely. Free will defence / transworld depravity Plantinga: a defence (showing God and evil are logically consistent), not a theodicy. Transworld depravity: it is possible that every creaturely essence goes wrong in at least one action in any world God could actualise, so God cannot create significantly free creatures who never sin. Vale of soul-making Hick (Evil and the God of Love): evil is instrumental — a lawlike world at 'epistemic distance' from God is the environment in which genuinely free persons develop virtues (courage, compassion), with universal salvation ultimately remedying suffering. Principles of credulity and testimony Swinburne: credulity — if it seems to S that X is present, then probably X is present, absent special considerations (known illusions, unreliable witness); testimony — others' reports of their experiences are probably accurate. Religious experience is therefore prima facie evidence of God. Omnipotence and the paradox of the stone. Can an omnipotent God create a stone too heavy for God to lift? Either answer shows a limit: if yes, God cannot lift it; if no, God cannot create it. Aquinas/Kenny: omnipotence is having every power it is logically possible to have — 'a stone an omnipotent being cannot lift' is self-contradictory, not a genuine task, so no limitation (Kenny: God has 'every power which it is logically possible to possess'). Descartes: God can do the logically impossible — God freely created the eternal truths (2+2=4) and could have made them otherwise, so logic does not bind God. Critique: then claims about God cease to be coherent assertions, and the paradox re-runs (can God make himself non-omnipotent?) with no principled answer; for AQA, Aquinas/Kenny is the mainstream line, Descartes the extreme. Eternality: outside time or everlasting? Boethius (Consolation, Book V): God's eternity is 'the whole, simultaneous and perfect possession of unending life' — God is timeless , beholding all times in one eternal present. Swinburne/Wolterstorff: God is everlasting — existing at every moment of time. Against timelessness: a timeless God cannot know tensed truths ('it is now raining'), act at a moment, respond to prayer or relate personally — not the God of worship (Kretzmann, Wolterstorff). Against everlastingness: a God in time changes (learns) as events occur — change implying imperfection — and knows at each time only what is then knowable. Omniscience and free will. Kenny-style definition: God knows everything it is logically possible to know. The problem: if God infallibly knows I will choose tea tomorrow, I cannot do otherwise — not free; if I am free, God lacked the knowledge — not omniscient. Boethius' solution: no fore -knowledge — from outside time God sees my free choice occurring, as I see a friend walking now; and God's seeing does not make it happen. Necessity is conditional , not absolute: if God sees me walk, then I walk — fixing nothing, just as your watching me walk now does not compel me. Response: this trades on timeless knowledge with the problems above; the everlasting alternative (Swinburne) lets God lack knowledge of future free choices — not yet there to be known — but a God who learns is not the immutable, perfect being of classical theism. Either solution buys compatibility with freedom at a cost. Ontological (a priori). Anselm (Proslogion 2): (1) even the fool understands ' that than which nothing greater can be conceived '; (2) it exists in the understanding; (3) existing in reality is greater; (4) if God existed only in the mind, a greater being — God in reality — could be conceived: contradiction; (5) so God exists in reality. Proslogion 3: God cannot be conceived not to exist — necessary existence is greater than contingent. Gaunilo: the same logic 'proves' a most perfect island. Anselm's reply: the form works only where the definition is coherent — for islands a greater is always conceivable; the status is God's alone. Descartes: existence is a perfection — a supremely perfect being lacking it is as incoherent as a triangle without three angles. Malcolm: necessary existence cannot be contingent, so God's existence is either impossible or necessary — and the concept is coherent, so necessary. Kant: existence is not a (real) predicate — '100 real thalers' and '100 imagined thalers' share one identical concept; 'is' only asserts instantiation, so building existence into God's essence as a 'perfection' begs the question. Malcolm's rejoinder: Kant targets contingent existence; necessary existence — not causally dependent — may be a genuine predicate. This Malcolm-vs-Kant exchange is the crucial A* debate. Teleological (a posteriori). Paley: a watch on a heath — parts co-adjusted for purpose — compels a watchmaker; nature shows design qua purpose (the eye) and qua regularity (planetary order) in far greater degree, so its author is a vastly greater intelligence: God. Hume's critiques (Dialogues, pre-Darwin): the analogy is weak — the universe is unique, more organism than machine; even if designed, the effect matches only the cause, licensing a finite, imperfect, possibly plural designer, not the infinite God; order may be internal to the universe itself. Darwin: natural selection explains apparent design (eye, wing) without a designer, undercutting design qua purpose. Swinburne's reply: Darwin explains spatial order, not the temporal regularity of natural laws; regularity 'cries out' for explanation, and theism — one being, simple properties — is the simplest explanation of the whole regular universe. Cosmological (a posteriori). Aquinas' Three Ways (Summa Theologiae I q.2 a.3): First Way — whatever is moved is moved by another, and in a per se series (hand–stick–stone) members have no independent causal power, so the series cannot be infinite: first unmoved mover; Second Way — nothing is its own efficient cause, so a first efficient cause; Third Way — if everything were contingent, at some time nothing existed and nothing would exist now; so there is a necessary being: God. Hume: fallacy of composition — every part having a cause does not give the whole one; the universe itself may be the necessary being; regress is not shown contradictory. Kalam (al-Ghazali, Craig): (1) whatever begins to exist has a cause; (2) the universe began — an actual infinite cannot exist (Hilbert's Hotel) or be traversed by successive addition; (3) the cause is timeless, spaceless, powerful and, freely choosing to create, personal: God — though quantum events lack determinate causes and the Big Bang need not begin time. Leibniz: by the principle of sufficient reason , the series of contingent things needs a reason outside itself: a necessary being. Russell (v Copleston, 1948): the principle is not self-evident, and explaining the parts need not explain the whole — 'the universe is just there, and that's all'. Logical problem (Mackie). Inconsistent triad: (1) God is omnipotent; (2) God is wholly good; (3) evil exists — a wholly good being eliminates evil as far as it can, an omnipotent being can eliminate it entirely, yet evil exists: the three cannot all be true. Solving the logical problem requires only showing the set is consistent. Free will defence (Plantinga): significantly free creatures are a great good; freedom excludes causal determination, so God cannot guarantee free creatures whose free actions are all good. Mackie's counter — why not create people who freely always choose good? — is met by transworld depravity : it is possible that every creaturely essence performs at least one wrong action in any world God could actualise; if so, God could not actualise a world with free creatures and no evil. Conclusion: God and evil are logically consistent — the logical problem fails. Note: a defence shows consistency; a theodicy gives God's actual reasons. Evidential problem (Rowe) and soul-making (Hick). Rowe's fawn: burned in a forest fire, it dies in agony unseen by any human; no apparent good could require such suffering. An omnipotent, wholly good God would prevent pointless evil, so the abundance of apparently gratuitous suffering makes God's existence improbable — a probabilistic, not logical, challenge. Hick's vale of soul-making: a lawlike world at 'epistemic distance' from God is the environment in which free persons develop virtues — courage, compassion — through real challenges; evil is instrumental to soul-making, with universal salvation ultimately remedying suffering. Critiques: dysteleological evil — the fawn, animal suffering before humans, horrendous evils (Phillips) — seems to exceed any soul-making value; and a world with less evil but equal virtue-building seems possible, which Hick must deny. Religious experience. Spec types: corporeal and intellectual visions, voices, the sense of presence. James (Varieties): mystical states are ineffable, noetic, transient and passive; validity is pragmatic — 'by their fruits ye shall know them, not by their roots': transformed, morally serious lives count as evidence. Swinburne: the principle of credulity — if it seems to S that X is present, probably X is present, absent special considerations; the principle of testimony — others' reports are probably accurate. So religious experience is prima facie evidence of God. Flew's verification challenge: Wisdom's explorer's gardener becomes invisible, intangible and scentless through successive 'qualifications' until the claim asserts nothing — 'death by a thousand qualifications'; likewise an 'experience of God' surviving every disconfirmation describes nothing, so it cannot justify belief. Responses: Hare's blik and Hick's eschatological verification (below); and Swinburne's principles, which put the burden on the sceptic to show special considerations apply. Via negativa. Pseudo-Dionysius (Mystical Theology) and Maimonides : God transcends every positive predicate; speak only by denial — 'God is good' means 'God is not evil', protecting transcendence and avoiding anthropomorphism. Critique: negation without affirmation tells us almost nothing — an imperfect being is also 'not evil' — and if no positive claim is legitimate, God-talk fails to identify anything. Examiners reward naming this limit. Aquinas' analogy. Univocal language (same sense) fails: God is not 'wise' as Socrates — anthropomorphic. Equivocal language (entirely different sense) fails: 'God is good' then conveys nothing. Aquinas: religious language is analogical — terms apply proportionately : as 'healthy' is predicated of medicine and urine only by relation to the animal's health (analogy of attribution), God's goodness and wisdom are predicated by relation to God's nature (analogy of proportion). God-talk is meaningful and non-literal. Critique: unclear how much the analogy tells us — 'proportionate to a nature we cannot conceive' may explain too little (Black: analogy 'tells us nothing'). Verification, falsification and bliks. Ayer's verification principle: a statement is meaningful only if analytic or empirically verifiable (in principle); 'God exists' and 'God loves me' are neither — religious language is not false but meaningless . Critiques: the principle is itself neither analytic nor verifiable — self-refuting — and universal scientific laws fail strong verifiability. Hick's eschatological verification: the pious and sceptical lives diverge after death — heaven verifies theism — so religious claims are verifiable in principle, though this is weaker verification than Ayer demands. Hare's bliks: the paranoid and the trusting student see the same dons' behaviour differently; a blik is an unfalsifiable interpretive stance, and religious language expresses bliks, not world-assertions — so Flew's challenge misfires. Critique: Hare concedes religion makes no factual claims, and offers no clear test (beyond pragmatism) for sane vs mad bliks. Exam technique: Paper 2. Paper 2 (3 hours, 100 marks): Section A Metaphysics of God, Section B Metaphysics of mind — five questions per section worth 3, 5, 5, 12 and 25 marks. Everything except the 25-marker is pure AO1 : define terms, set out the argument, illustrate — evaluation on 12-markers is redundant and loses marks . The 25-marker (5 AO1 + 20 AO2) quotes a claim and demands evaluation: argue with intent — thesis in the introduction, best objection met with a weak then a strong response, conclusion with no new ideas. Learn definitions verbatim (Boethius' eternity, Kenny's omnipotence, Mackie's triad) and keep the named debates separate. Common pitfalls and examiner tips (click to expand) Logical vs evidential: the logical problem needs a consistency answer (Plantinga's transworld depravity); the evidential problem (Rowe) needs a probability assessment — do not answer Rowe's fawn with transworld depravity. Ontological ≠ design: the ontological argument is a priori; teleological and cosmological are a posteriori — never answer a 'from reason alone' question with Paley. Boethius precision: quote 'the whole, simultaneous and perfect possession of unending life' and distinguish conditional from absolute necessity before evaluating. Kalam ≠ Aquinas: Kalam argues a temporal beginning (no actual infinities); Aquinas argues per se causal dependence — the critiques differ accordingly. Religious language quad: Ayer = meaninglessness (verification); Flew = empty assertions (falsification); Hare = non-assertive bliks; Hick = eschatological verification.

topics.name: Metaphysics of Mind: Dualism, Physicalism and Functionalism
topics.subject: philosophy
topics.searchText: philosophy Philosophy Metaphysics of Mind: Dualism, Physicalism and Functionalism Explain the mind–body problem and define mental properties via qualia and intentionality (Spec 3.4.1). Explain and evaluate Descartes' conceivability and divisibility arguments for substance dualism, and Elisabeth of Bohemia's interaction objection with the causal closure argument (Spec 3.4.2). Explain and evaluate property dualism via Chalmers' zombie argument, including conceivability-vs-possibility and masking critiques (Spec 3.4.2). Explain and evaluate logical behaviourism (Hempel, Ryle's category mistake) and its circularity, pretence and qualia critiques (Spec 3.4.3). Explain and evaluate type identity theory (Place, Smart), the multiple realizability objection, and eliminative materialism (Churchlands) with the self-refutation critique (Spec 3.4.3). Explain and evaluate functionalism (Putnam) via inverted qualia, philosophical zombies and absent qualia (Spec 3.4.4). Use AQA command words correctly: pure AO1 explanation on 3/5/12-mark questions; argue with intent on 25-mark essays. Qualia Intrinsic, subjective properties of experience — the felt hurtfulness of pain, the redness of red; 'what it is like' to undergo an experience, knowable only from the first person. Intentionality The 'aboutness' or directedness of mental states — beliefs, desires and fears are about things; Brentano's mark of the mental. Substance dualism Descartes' view that mind and body are distinct substances: the mind a thinking, unextended, indivisible thing; the body an extended, divisible, non-thinking one. Property dualism The view that mental properties are non-physical properties had by physical substances (brains): the mind supervenes on the body (Chalmers' naturalistic dualism). Causal closure (of the physical) Every physical event that has a cause has a sufficient physical cause — so immaterial mental causes would violate the closure of physics or the mind is epiphenomenal. Epiphenomenalism The view that mental states are caused by physical states but have no causal power of their own — qualia are causally idle by-products of brain processes. Philosophical zombie A being physically and behaviourally identical to a human but lacking qualia — no inner experience, 'all is dark inside'. Category mistake Ryle: representing items as if they belonged to one logical category when they belong to another — treating 'mind' as a thing alongside the body, like the tourist asking where the University is after seeing all the colleges. Logical (analytical) behaviourism Mental-state statements are translatable without remainder into statements about behaviour (Hempel's hard version) or denote dispositions to behave (Ryle's soft version). Type identity theory Place and Smart: mental-state types are identical with brain-state types — a scientific identity like 'lightning is an electrical discharge', not a mere correlation. Multiple realizability One mental-state type can be realized by many different physical types (human, octopus, silicon) — Putnam's objection to type identity, built into functionalism. Functionalism Putnam: mental states are functional states, individuated by causal role — typical inputs, relations to other mental states and behavioural outputs — realizable in any medium. The problem. Mental properties (belief, desire, pain, seeing red) seem unlike physical properties (mass, charge, neural firing): they are private, qualitative and about things. The mind–body problem asks how the two relate — is the mind a separate substance (dualism), a set of purely physical properties (physicalism), or states to be defined by what they do (functionalism)? Keep substance dualism (two substances) distinct from property dualism (one substance, two kinds of property): examiners report candidates conflating them. Qualia. The intrinsic, subjective properties of experience — the felt hurtfulness of pain, the redness of red, 'what it is like' to see green (Nagel's bat). Qualia seem knowable only from the first person: no third-person description of neural firing appears to capture the feel itself. They power the whole anti-physicalist programme. Intentionality. The 'aboutness' or directedness of mental states: a belief is about Paris, a fear about spiders. Brentano took intentionality as the mark of the mental — no purely physical item is intrinsically about anything (a picture is about Paris only through a mind's use: derived intentionality). Physicalists owe an account of how brain states acquire aboutness. The tests. Every theory below must accommodate qualia, intentionality and mental causation (pain causes wincing) — measure each theory against all three. Substance dualism (Descartes). Mind and body are distinct substances: the mind a thinking, unextended, indivisible thing; the body an extended, divisible, non-thinking one. Conceivability argument ( Meditations VI): (P1) I can clearly and distinctly conceive of myself as a thinking, non-extended thing; (P2) what I clearly and distinctly conceive as separate can be made to exist separately (by God); (C) mind and body are really distinct. Divisibility argument: (P1) every body is by nature divisible; (P2) the mind is not — amputate a limb and nothing is subtracted from the mind; (C) by Leibniz's law (identical things share all properties), mind is not body. Elisabeth of Bohemia's interaction objection (1643 letters). How can an unextended, immaterial mind causally move an extended body? Causation between bodies requires contact and impulsion; a non-spatial thing has no surface to push with. Descartes' reply: the mind is 'intermingled' with the body — a real union, not mere concatenation — acting through the pineal gland; 'mind–body union' is a primitive notion grasped through everyday experience (hunger, pain), not by the pure intellect. Critics reply the defence concedes the point: if interaction needs the brain, the mind is not independent of it. Causal closure. The modern version of Elisabeth: every physical event that has a cause has a sufficient physical cause. Immaterial mind-to-body causation would violate conservation of energy; so either mental causes are physical (physicalism) or the mind is an epiphenomenon — caused by the brain but causally idle, unable to move bodies or exercise free will. Dualists must either reject closure or accept epiphenomenalism. Masking critique of conceivability. Conceivability is a poor guide to possibility: pre-chemistry one could conceive of water that is not H₂O, yet water is necessarily H₂O; conceiving mind as separable may mask an identity. Descartes' reply: he claims complete (clear and distinct) understanding of the mind, not partial — only partial conceivability is unreliable. Property dualism (Chalmers). Mental properties are non-physical properties of physical substances (brains): the mind supervenes on the body. Zombie argument: philosophical zombies are physically and behaviourally identical to us but lack qualia — 'all is dark inside'. Zombies are conceivable; what is conceivable is metaphysically possible; if zombies are possible, physical facts do not fix conscious facts; so physicalism is false. Critiques: (1) conceivability is not possibility (Kripke's necessary a posteriori truths; Dennett: a behaviourally identical being making all our consciousness reports would thereby be conscious — zombies are incoherent); (2) the physicalist denies premise 2: that zombies are impossible is physicalism, so the argument begs the question; (3) interaction problems return — Chalmers' psychophysical laws leave qualia causally idle. Appeal: property dualism explains qualia and leaves science intact, but inherits the interaction problem. Logical (analytical) behaviourism. Mental statements translate without remainder into statements about behaviour. Hempel (hard): 'X is in pain' means X winces, groans, says 'ouch' and reports pain when asked. Ryle (soft): mental concepts denote dispositions to behave (if burned, X would flinch), and Descartes' 'ghost in the machine' rests on a category mistake : treating the mind as one more thing alongside the body when mental vocabulary describes ways bodies behave — like the tourist who, shown the colleges, libraries and labs, asks 'but where is the University?'. Critiques: (1) circularity : dispositions must be defined using other mental terms (desire, belief); (2) perfect actors and super-spartans : behaviourally identical subjects can differ — real pain vs flawless pretence, or pain felt while showing nothing — so behaviour does not exhaust the mental; (3) qualia: behaviourism cannot state what pain feels like, missing the qualitative character of experience. Type identity theory (Place, Smart). Mental-state types are identical with brain-state types — a scientific identity like 'lightning is an electrical discharge' (Place), not a mere correlation. Strengths: parsimony (one substance); interaction solved (pain is C-fibre firing, so mental causation is trivial); science-friendly. Multiple realizability (Putnam): the same mental type is realized by different physical types — pain in humans (C-fibres), octopuses (different wiring), perhaps silicon; by Leibniz's law, pain cannot be identical with any single brain-state type. Responses: token identity (each pain token is some brain state) or species-specific identities; counter: reduction then covers only humans and will not generalize to artificial minds. Eliminative materialism (the Churchlands). Folk psychology (belief–desire explanation) is a radically false empirical theory whose categories — belief, desire, pain — will be eliminated and replaced by mature neuroscience, as phlogiston and caloric fluid were. Evidence: folk psychology fails on sleep, intelligence, memory and mental illness, and has stagnated for 25 centuries. Critiques: (1) self-refutation : 'folk psychology is false' is asserted as a belief, presupposing what it denies; the Churchlands reply that this begs the question — like a phlogiston theorist insisting 'but I believe in phlogiston'; (2) folk psychology is successful : it predicts everyday behaviour superbly, unlike phlogiston; reply: its successes are shallow — it fails precisely where understanding matters. Functionalism (Putnam). Mental states are functional states : individuated by causal role — typical causes (inputs: bodily damage), relations to other mental states (belief that something is wrong; desire to escape) and typical effects (outputs: wincing, saying 'ouch'). A state is pain in virtue of playing the pain role, whatever its material — brains, silicon, or (Putnam's original) the states of a Turing machine. Strengths: builds in multiple realizability (answers type identity's main objection); keeps inner states distinct from behaviour (answers behaviourism's circularity and pretence problems); compatible with scientific psychology. Inverted qualia. Two subjects functionally identical — same inputs, outputs and organization — yet their colour experiences qualitatively inverted. If possible, functional role does not fix qualitative character, so functionalism misses qualia. Functional response (Chalmers' fading/dancing qualia): invert qualia gradually while holding functional organization fixed — the subject could not notice, yet conscious experience cannot systematically fade or flicker without functional change; so inverted qualia are impossible. Counter: the argument assumes phenomenal change requires functional change — exactly what the objection denies. Absent qualia (Block's China brain). A billion Chinese citizens, each playing one 'neuron' and linked by two-way radio, implement the functional organization of a human brain. The functionalist must attribute pain to the nation; intuitively there is no unified conscious subject — so functional organization does not suffice for consciousness. Responses: intuitions about alien systems are unreliable; functionalism need not claim the system is conscious exactly as we are. Zombies: a functional duplicate of you with no inner life is conceivable — functional organization leaves out qualia (with the conceivability caveats from dualism). Exam technique: AQA 7172 Paper 2 Section B (click to expand) Paper 2: Section A Metaphysics of God, Section B Metaphysics of mind — five questions per section worth 3, 5, 5, 12 and 25 marks ; all AO1 except the 25-marker (5 AO1 + 20 AO2, 'Evaluate this claim'). 3/5/12-markers: explanation only — define terms, set out the claim, argument or objection, illustrate. Evaluation is redundant and loses marks. 25-marker top band (21–25): define key terms, state a thesis, develop one or two debates in depth (crucial arguments vs less crucial), give weak then strong responses to objections, finish with a consistent conclusion and no new ideas. Highest-yield 25-marker debates: zombies vs physicalism/functionalism; interaction problem vs dualism; multiple realizability vs type identity; inverted qualia vs functionalism.

topics.name: La Famille en Voie de Changement
topics.subject: french
topics.searchText: french French La Famille en Voie de Changement Describe all contemporary French family structures (nucléaire, monoparentale, recomposée, homoparentale) with accurate INSEE statistics (AQA 7652 3.1.1; Edexcel 9FR0 1.1) Trace the legal milestones that reshaped the family, from the loi Neuwirth (1967) to the mariage pour tous (2013) and the PMA pour toutes (2021) Explain sociologically why attitudes to marriage, cohabitation and divorce have changed (sécularisation, individualisme, autonomie économique des femmes) Evaluate the roles of men and women within the couple, citing evidence on chore division, pay gap and congé paternité Argue for or against the thesis that the French family is in crisis, using statistics as AO2 evidence rather than assertion Deploy topic-specific vocabulary (concubinage, union libre, beau-parent, demi-frère) accurately in essays and speaking La famille nucléaire The classic model: two married parents and their children under one roof; dominant in France until the 1960s, now only one household type among many. Le PACS Pacte civil de solidarité: a civil partnership created by the law of 15 November 1999, offering couples (heterosexual or same-sex) rights and duties without marriage; roughly 209,000 were signed in 2021. Le concubinage (union libre) Cohabitation without any legal formalities; once stigmatised, now the statistical norm before or instead of marriage. La famille monoparentale One-parent family: about two million in France, and in roughly four out of five cases headed by the mother; a key poverty risk group. La famille recomposée Blended family: a couple raising at least one child from a previous union, with demi-frères and demi-sœurs; around 9% of families with children. Le mariage pour tous The Taubira law of 17 May 2013 opening marriage and joint adoption to same-sex couples; opposed by La Manif pour Tous, now accepted by a large majority. L'autorité parentale conjointe Joint parental authority: since the 1970 reform both parents hold equal legal authority over children, replacing the father's legal supremacy. Le congé paternité Paternity leave: two weeks since 2002, extended in 2021 to 28 days, seven of them obligatory — evidence for evolving male roles within the family. Le point d'ancrage du thème. Ce thème demande d'expliquer en quoi la famille française est « en voie de changement » : vous devez nommer les structures, les chiffrer et les relier à des causes sociales et juridiques. AQA (thème 3.1.1 La famille en voie de changement) et Edexcel (9FR0, thème 1.1 La famille) récompensent exactement la même démarche : faits précis, chiffres datés, opinion nuancée. Pour Eduqas/WJEC (thème Être une personne jeune dans une société francophone) et CCEA (AS, unité Les relations), les mêmes données servent aux questions de compréhension et à la discussion orale. Dans tous les cas, le barème distingue deux niveaux : le candidat qui décrit (la famille a changé) et celui qui explique (pourquoi elle a changé, avec quelles conséquences) — c'est ce second niveau qui obtient les notes maximales. Le modèle hérité. Pendant les Trente Glorieuses (1945-1975), la famille nucléaire régnait : un couple marié, un père pourvoyeur, une mère au foyer, des enfants légitimes. Ce modèle reposait sur le Code civil de 1804, qui subordonnait l'épouse au mari (obligation d'obéissance, autorité paternelle exclusive, incapacité civile de la femme mariée). Trois révolutions l'ont démantelé : la contraception (loi Neuwirth, 1967), qui a dissocié sexualité et procréation ; l'émancipation économique des femmes (loi de 1965 : une femme mariée peut travailler et ouvrir un compte sans l'autorisation du mari) ; et la sécularisation, le mariage cessant d'être un sacrement social obligatoire pour devenir un choix parmi d'autres. À cette triple cause s'ajoute un facteur matériel : la prolongation des études et la précarité d'entrée dans la vie active retardent l'installation — on ne fonde pas de famille avant d'avoir un emploi stable et un logement. Les chiffres à connaître (INSEE, ordres de grandeur). Mariages : environ 394 000 en 1970, environ 220 000 en 2022 — un recul massif, avec une pointe atypique de 155 000 en 2020 (Covid). L'âge moyen au premier mariage est passé d'environ 25 ans à 35 ans pour les hommes, de 23 à 33 ans pour les femmes : on se marie plus tard, souvent après avoir vécu ensemble et parfois eu des enfants. PACS : créé en 1999 ; environ 209 000 PACS conclus en 2021, soit autant que les mariages la même année. Le PACS a normalisé l'union sans mariage, d'abord chez les jeunes couples, puis à tous les âges — y compris chez les personnes divorcées et chez les retraités, pour des raisons patrimoniales. Naissances hors mariage : environ 10 % en 1970, environ 63 % aujourd'hui. Le mariage n'est plus le cadre obligé de la parentalité : la majorité des enfants français naissent de couples non mariés, sans que cela nuise à leur statut juridique (l'autorité parentale conjointe s'applique dès la reconnaissance). Divorce : environ 90 000 par an ; on estime qu'environ 45 % des mariages finissent en divorce. Depuis 2017, le divorce par consentement mutuel est déjudiciarisé : avocats communs, dépôt chez le notaire, juge uniquement en cas de désaccord ou d'enfant demandant à être entendu. Familles monoparentales : environ 2 millions, soit une famille avec enfants sur cinq ; dans environ 82 % des cas, la mère élève seule. Ces foyers cumulent les risques : pauvreté (près d'un tiers sous le seuil), temps partiel subi, logements trop petits, coût de la garde. C'est le cœur du sous-thème AQA sur la monoparentalité, les risques et les sacrifices. Familles recomposées : environ 9 % des familles avec enfants, soit plus de 700 000 foyers mêlant beau-parent, enfant d'une précédente union, demi-frères et demi-sœurs — la notion de « belle-famille » s'est élargie, le beau-parent a gagné en droits et en visibilité. Ménages et solitude : plus d'un tiers des ménages sont des personnes seules ; la taille moyenne des ménages est tombée de 3,1 personnes (1968) à environ 2,2 — la « famille » ne recouvre plus tout l'espace domestique. Fécondité : environ 1,7 à 1,8 enfant par femme, sous le seuil de renouvellement de 2,1, mais parmi les taux les plus élevés de l'Union européenne. Paradoxe utile en dissertation : la famille se diversifie sans que la France cesse de faire des enfants. Variations sociales et territoriales. Ces tendances ne sont pas uniformes. Le niveau de diplôme compte : plus les femmes sont diplômées, plus elles retardent le premier enfant et le mariage — mais plus leur couple est stable à long terme. Le territoire compte : dans les DOM, la famille monoparentale et la famille élargie (les grands-parents, les oncles et les tantes) restent beaucoup plus fréquentes qu'en métropole ; dans les zones rurales, le mariage résiste mieux. La génération compte : chez les moins de trente ans, le mariage est perçu comme une option symbolique et coûteuse (plus de 10 000 euros de dépenses moyennes), alors que la majorité des aînés l'avait vécu comme un passage obligé. Enfin, la religion compte : le mariage religieux recule partout, mais il reste minoritairement important chez les catholiques pratiquants, les musulmans et les juifs — un point de comparaison utile avec le Royaume-Uni, où le mariage civil et religieux se sont effrités selon la même logique. Année Mesure Portée pour la famille 1965 Droit du travail et du compte bancaire pour les femmes mariées sans autorisation du mari Fin de la tutelle matrimoniale ; autonomie économique 1967 Loi Neuwirth (contraception) Dissociation sexualité/procréation ; maîtrise des naissances 1970 Autorité parentale conjointe Égalité juridique des parents 1975 Loi Veil (IVG) ; divorce par consentement mutuel Sortie du mariage imposé de fait 1999 PACS Union légale hors mariage 2002 Congé paternité ; loi sur la résidence alternée Père plus présent ; après-divorce repensé 2013 Mariage pour tous (loi Taubira) Mariage et adoption ouverts aux couples de même sexe 2021 Loi de bioéthique PMA pour toutes ; filiation établie pour les couples de femmes Analyse (AO2) : pourquoi ces mutations ? Trois moteurs reviennent dans tous les corrigés. Premièrement, l' individualisme : l'épanouissement personnel pèse plus que le devoir institutionnel — on quitte un couple insatisfaisant au lieu de le supporter. Deuxièmement, l' autonomie des femmes : une femme qui gagne sa vie n'a plus besoin du mariage pour survivre ; le divorce cesse d'être un naufrage économique. Troisièmement, la sécularisation : le mariage religieux perd son monopole symbolique, et l'État a dû inventer un cadre légal (PACS) pour des unions que l'Église ne reconnaît pas. Ajoutez le contexte économique : précarité du travail, prix du logement, retard de l'installation — on fonde une famille plus tard parce qu'on s'installe plus tard. Pour la comparaison AQA/Edexcel avec le monde anglophone : les mêmes moteurs opèrent au Royaume-Uni (cohabitation, familles recomposées), mais la France se distingue par le rôle moteur de l'État (PACS, politique familiale) et par un taux de fécondité plus élevé. Comment exploiter ces chiffres dans un essai (méthode) Ne cumulez pas les statistiques : une par paragraphe suffit, suivie immédiatement de son interprétation. Exemple : « En 2021, environ 209 000 PACS ont été conclus, soit autant que de mariages — preuve que le mariage n'est plus le passage obligé du couple, mais une option parmi d'autres. » Toujours : chiffre → interprétation → mini-conclusion nuancée (« toutefois, le mariage reste… »). Les correcteurs sanctionnent la statistique nue, ils valorisent la statistique analysée. Glissez au moins une structure complexe par paragraphe : un subjonctif après bien que (« bien que le PACS offre des droits, il ne garantit pas… »), un conditionnel de nuance (« le mariage pourrait redevenir… »), un passif (« le PACS a été adopté massivement »). Transition. Ces structures ne sont pas tombées du ciel : elles ont été produites par un arsenal législatif que le paragraphe suivant reconstitue — c'est la matière première de tout essai sur « l'évolution des attitudes envers le mariage ». Le mariage, de l'obligation au choix. Sous l'Ancien Régime comme dans le Code civil de 1804, le mariage était une institution quasi obligatoire, réglée par le chef de famille. Le vingtième siècle l'a transformé en contrat libre. Étapes clés : 1965, les femmes mariées obtiennent le droit de travailler et de gérer leurs biens sans l'autorisation du mari ; 1970, l'autorité parentale conjointe remplace la puissance paternelle ; 1975, le divorce par consentement mutuel entre dans la loi — le lien devient dissoluble d'un commun accord, sans devoir prouver une faute. Résultat statistique : le nombre de mariages annuels a été divisé par presque deux entre 1970 (environ 394 000) et aujourd'hui (environ 220 000), tandis que l'âge au mariage grimpait d'une dizaine d'années. Mariage civil, mariage religieux, remariage. Depuis la loi de séparation des Églises et de l'État (1905), seul le mariage civil a valeur juridique : le mariage religieux est optionnel et ne peut précéder le civil. Environ un mariage sur six aujourd'hui unit un conjoint étranger ou binational (mariages mixtes), chiffre qui nourrit à la fois la francophonie et certains débats sur les mariages de complaisance. Le remariage représente environ un mariage sur cinq, conséquence directe du divorce et de l'allongement de la vie : on fonde désormais plusieurs familles au cours d'une même existence — d'où la progression des familles recomposées. Ces angles secondaires font la différence dans une copie : ils montrent que vous maîtrisez le thème au-delà du cliché « on divorce beaucoup ». Le PACS (1999) : l'union civilisée sans mariage. La loi du 15 novembre 1999 crée le pacte civil de solidarité, pensé d'abord pour les couples de même sexe à qui le mariage était interdit, mais adopté massivement par les couples hétérosexuels. Le PACS offre : obligations mutuelles d'aide matérielle, imposition commune après trois ans, droits successoraux améliorés, statut de « pacsé » sur les formulaires officiels. Il laisse de côté : la filiation automatique du conjoint, le nom de famille, la pension de réversion complète. Après un démarrage timide (environ 20 000 en 2000), le PACS a dépassé régulièrement les 200 000 par an, rivalisant avec le mariage — un cas d'école de la norme juridique qui crée la norme sociale. Attention à la nuance qui rapporte des points : le PACS est aujourd'hui conclu par deux générations — les jeunes couples qui le voient comme une étape avant le mariage, et les couples plus âgés ou remariés qui le préfèrent définitivement pour sa souplesse patrimoniale. Le divorce aujourd'hui. Environ 45 % des mariages finissent par un divorce, soit environ 90 000 par an. Trois voies : le consentement mutuel (de loin le plus fréquent, déjudiciarisé depuis 2017 — plus de juge, acte d'avocats contresigné et déposé chez un notaire) ; le divorce accepté (désaccord sur les conséquences mais accord sur le principe) ; le divorce pour faute ou pour altération définitive du lien. La faute, motif quasi unique avant 1975, recule : les Français divorcent plus pour insatisfaction que pour scandale — autre marque de l'individualisme. Conséquences sociales à citer : résidence alternée des enfants (loi de 2002), pensions alimentaires impayées (environ 300 000 familles concernées, d'où l'Aripa créée en 2020 pour avancer les pensions), et paupérisation féminine après divorce — le même homme voit son niveau de vie augmenter après la séparation, la même femme le voir baisser : chiffre-choc parfait pour l'oral. Mariage PACS Concubinage Fiscalité commune Immédiate Après trois ans Jamais Succession Époux héritier réservataire Partenaire protégé (legs obligatoire) Aucun droit automatique Filiation du couple Présomption de paternité Reconnaissance nécessaire Reconnaissance nécessaire Sortie de l'union Divorce (procédure) Déclaration simple Déménagement Le mariage pour tous (loi Taubira, 17 mai 2013). Après treize ans de PACS, le mariage et l'adoption conjointe sont ouverts aux couples de même sexe. Le débat fut d'une violence exceptionnelle : centaines de milliers de manifestants pour La Manif pour Tous, fronde parlementaire, débats passionnés dans les médias, mais aussi mobilisation massivement favorable. Chronologie utile : vote de l'Assemblée nationale en avril 2013, promulgation le 17 mai 2013, premier mariage homosexuel à Montpellier le 29 mai 2013. Arguments opposés à connaître pour l'essai : pour les adversaires, l'enfant aurait besoin d'un père et d'une mère, et la filiation biologique serait « naturelle » ; pour les partisans, l'égalité des droits prime, et l'amour parental compte plus que le genre des parents. Dix ans après, le sujet est sorti des radars politiques : environ trois quarts des Français approuvent le mariage homosexuel, et l'argument « mesure du changement des mœurs » est indispensable en conclusion. La suite : PMA et GPA. La loi de bioéthique d'août 2021 ouvre la PMA (procréation médicalement assistée) à toutes les femmes, mariées ou non, hétérosexuelles ou lesbiennes ; l'ouverture de la GPA (gestation pour autrui) reste refusée, jugée incompatible avec l'indisponibilité du corps humain. Cette frontière PMA oui/GPA non est un excellent material d'évaluation : elle montre que la libéralisation a des limites affirmées, et qu'en France le débat familial se règle en termes d'égalité, non de libéralisme généralisé. L'État famille : la politique familiale française. Distinctive par rapport au Royaume-Uni : la France mène une politique familiale ancienne et assumée — allocations familiales, quotient familial dans l'impôt, PreParE (congé parental rémunéré), crèches subventionnées, carte famille nombreuse. Cette politique explique en partie le taux de fécondité élevé ; elle montre aussi que, pour un Français, fonder une famille reste une affaire publique, pas seulement privée — argument de conclusion inattendu qui distingue une copie A*. Vocabulaire d'examen du chapitre juridique + plan d'essai Vocabulaire : le conjoint / la conjointe (spouse) ; le partenariat enregistré (registered partnership) ; la déjudiciarisation (taking a process out of the courts) ; le consentement mutuel (mutual consent) ; la pension alimentaire (maintenance payment) ; la résidence alternée (shared custody) ; l'adoption plénière (full adoption) ; l'indisponibilité du corps humain (the human body cannot be traded) ; la filiation (legal parent-child link) ; la réversion (survivor's pension). Plan d'essai (AQA, 250 mots) : Le mariage, une institution dépassée ? I. Ouverture paradoxale : on se marie moins, mais on se marie mieux (âge 33-35 ans, mariage choisi). II. Oui, dépassée comme obligation : PACS autant que mariages ; 63 % des naissances hors mariage ; divorce déjudiciarisé. III. Non, réinventée comme symbolique : retour des mariages post-Covid ; appétit des jeunes pour la cérémonie ; égalité désormais ouverte à tous. IV. Synthèse : le mariage a perdu son monopole, pas son prestige. V. Ouverture : l'institution que la France a réellement inventée, c'est le PACS — et c'est elle qui a sauvé le mariage. Piège classique (AQA Paper 1, Edexcel Paper 1). Ne confondez pas mariage pour tous (2013, mariage et adoption) et PMA pour toutes (2021, accès à l'assistance médicale). Ce sont deux lois, deux dates, deux combats ; les mélanger coûte des points de précision et affaiblit l'argument. Sous-thème AQA explicite. Le point 3.1.1 de l'AQA intitulé « les rôles des hommes et des femmes au sein du couple » exige plus que des statistiques démographiques : il faut décrire la répartition réelle des rôles, la mesurer, et l'évaluer. Même exigence côté Edexcel (relations au sein de la famille, sous-thème 1.1) et à l'oral CCEA/Eduqas où la question « la famille est-elle encore patriarcale ? » tombe régulièrement. La stratégie d'examen : opposer systématiquement égalité légale et égalité réelle — c'est le contraste qui structure la meilleure copie. Le travail domestique : le « second shift ». Malgré l'égalité juridique, les femmes consacrent en moyenne près de deux fois plus de temps que les hommes aux tâches ménagères et à la garde des enfants (environ 3 h 30 contre 2 h par jour, INSEE), et l'écart se creuse à l'arrivée du premier enfant — les hommes déclarent plus souvent partager, les données du temps réel disent le contraire. Ce « second shift » (le second emploi de la femme, le soir) a un coût mesurable : carrières ralenties, temps partiel subi (environ quatre temps partiels sur cinq sont féminins, et la majorité d'entre eux sont choisis faute de garde, non par préférence), absence des postes de direction. Complétez avec les chiffres de l'inégalité professionnelle : un écart de salaire de l'ordre de 15 à 22 % selon les méthodes de mesure, un plafond de verre documenté, et un écart de pension de retraite d'environ 40 % qui prolonge toute la carrière inégale. L'argument d'essai gagnant : l'égalité légale a devancé l'égalité réelle — la loi change plus vite que les mœurs, et la famille est l'endroit où ce retard se voit le mieux. Les politiques qui poussent le père vers l'enfant. Le congé paternité (2002 : deux semaines ; 2021 : 28 jours dont sept obligatoires et indemnisés comme un salaire) vise à rééquilibrer la parentalité dès la naissance : l'État impose sept jours, car l'expérience montre que les pères ne prennent que ce qui est obligatoire. La résidence alternée (loi de 2002) fait du père un parent à temps plein après divorce, non un visiteur du week-end. Les crèches et la revalorisation des aides à la garde permettent le retour rapide des mères à l'emploi. Le congé parental (PreParE), lui, reste massivement féminin : environ 97 % des bénéficiaires sont des mères, avec un coût de carrière considérable — nuance parfaite pour démontrer que la politique familiale a des effets contraires à ses intentions. Évaluation honnête : les dispositifs fonctionnent, mais la norme sociale (le père pourvoyeur, la mère référent) survit à la loi ; le « nouveau père » existe dans les médias et dans les couples diplômés des villes, moins dans les données statistiques. La violence dans le couple : l'angle sombre. Chiffres à maîtriser pour l'oral et l'essai argumenté : environ 220 000 victimes de violences conjugales par an, environ quatre cinquièmes des femmes ; environ une centaine de féminicides par an ; réforme de 2021 sur la protection des enfants témoins, bracelet anti-rapprochement, dépôt de plainte facilité. Depuis #MeToo (en France, #BalanceTonPorc, 2017), la parole s'est libérée et la législation s'est durcie. Utilisez ce volet avec sobriété : deux chiffres exacts et une idée (la famille peut être un lieu de danger, pas seulement de protection) valent mieux qu'une liste — et ils retournent l'argument romantique « la famille, refuge du monde ». Les familles homoparentales. Depuis 2013 (mariage et adoption) et 2021 (PMA), les couples de même sexe fondent des familles pleinement reconnues : adoption conjointe, filiation établie d'emblée pour les couples de femmes (la mère biologique et sa femme sont toutes deux parents), reconnaissance du parent d'intention. L'argument d'évaluation que les correcteurs attendent d'un candidat A* : l'enquête sociologique n'établit aucun déficit de développement des enfants de couples homosexuels ; les difficultés signalées viennent surtout du regard social (école, entourage), pas de la structure familiale — renversez la charge de la preuve : ce n'est pas à la famille homoparentale de prouver qu'elle fonctionne, c'est au scepticisme de prouver qu'elle échoue, et il n'y parvient pas. Les grands-parents et la solidarité familiale.
