Zeitplan über zwei Jahre: Das IRP lebt vom Vorlauf: im ersten Jahr Thema wählen und Quellen sammeln (Notizen systematisch), im Sommer vor dem Prüfjahr die Präsentation strukturieren (Unterfragen, Stichwort-Karten), im Prüfjahr üben (Aufnahme, Selbstkorrektur, Zeitcheck) und die Redemittel einüben (Konjunktiv I für Berichte, Konjunktiv II für Hypothesen). Wer im letzten Monat alles erarbeitet, verliert die Tiefe – die Diskussion lebt von vorbereiteten Unterfragen, die Zeit brauchen. Für CCEA und WJEC/Eduqas gilt derselbe Zeitplan – nur die Formate variieren. Die letzten zwei Wochen vor der Prüfung: Der Endspurt gehört der Übung, nicht dem Stoff: Präsentation fünf Mal laut sprechen (mit Stoppuhr), Aufnahme und Selbstkorrektur (Tempo, Aussprache, Füllwörter), Redemittel laut einüben (Konjunktiv I für Berichte, Konjunktiv II für Hypothesen), sechs erwartbare Rückfragen mit Antworten durchspielen (mit Partner oder allein), und die Präsentation ohne Stichwort-Karten testen (ein Mal mit, ein Mal ohne). Wer im Endspurt Stoff hinzufügt, verliert die Tiefe – wer übt, gewinnt die Interaktions- und Aussprachepunkte. Die Prüfung belohnt Souveränität: Struktur, Redemittel, Konjunktiv – nicht Stoffmenge.

topics.name: Unseen Prose Translation
topics.subject: latin
topics.searchText: latin Latin Unseen Prose Translation Apply a translation method to an unseen prose passage (vocab triage, main verbs, clause structure) Identify and translate subjunctive clauses, participles and indirect statement in context Manage unseen vocabulary by recognising derivatives and compound verbs Allocate exam time correctly and produce a fluent, accurate translation Subjunctive The mood of hypothesis, purpose, result and reported thought; in unseen prose its main uses are purpose, result, indirect questions and cum-circumstantial clauses. Indirect statement Accusative + infinitive after verbs of saying, thinking and perceiving; the infinitive's tense is relative to the main verb (present = same time, perfect = before, future = after). Participle A verbal adjective: present (-ns, active), perfect (-tus/-sus, passive), future (-turus/-surus); translate as a clause ('when/after/because X had been...') where a literal rendering fails. Ablative absolute A noun + participle in the ablative expressing attendant circumstances, cause or time: 'when X had been done...' — always translate as a separate clause. Gerundive The passive verbal adjective in -ndus; with esse it expresses obligation ('must be done'); in the gerundive of obligation the gerundive agrees with the noun. Historic infinitive An infinitive standing alone in narrative ('to march and to fight...'), expressing vivid continuing action. First pass: the shape of the sentence. Latin prose (adapted Livy, Cicero, Caesar) is highly periodic: the main verb often comes LAST. Do not translate word by word from the start. Instead: (1) read the sentence to its end; (2) find the main verb(s) and the subject (nominative); (3) bracket the subordinate clauses (quod/ut/cum/si + indicative or subjunctive); (4) mark the participles and ablatives absolute — each becomes a separate clause in English; (5) only then translate, from the main clause outwards. Vocabulary triage. In the OCR unseen, roughly 5-10% of words are glossed; the rest you should know or recognise: (1) compounds : adversus (ad + versus), appropinquare (ad + prope); (2) derivatives : expugnare → to fight out fully = to storm; (3) the core function words (nam, igitur, tamen, quidem) carry the argument's logic — translate them first for the sentence's drift. Never spend two minutes on one word: mark it, guess from context, move on, return at the end. Time management. The unseen translation paper allows roughly 1.5-2 minutes per line. Budget: first pass 30% of the time, translation 60%, checking 10%. Write the translation in fluent English — a literal rendering that produces non-English loses the accuracy marks; examiners mark for sense conveyed accurately. Trap How to spot it How to translate it Purpose clause ut/ne + subjunctive, no main-verb tense dependency 'in order that...', 'so that... not' Result clause ut + subjunctive, TAM/talis/sic in the main clause 'with the result that...', 'so... that' Indirect question question word (quis, ubi, cur, num) + subjunctive 'asked where/whether/why...' — backshift the tense Cum-circumstantial cum + subjunctive (imperfect/pluperfect) 'when/while/after...'; cum + indicative = 'since/although' Indirect statement accusative + infinitive after dico, puto, scio, video 'that X was/would be...' — tense relative to the main verb Ablative absolute noun + participle in the ablative, unconnected 'when/after/since X had been...' Gerundive of obligation -ndus + form of esse 'must be...', 'needs to be...' Conditions si/nisi + indicative or subjunctive open ('if X happens'), future less vivid ('if X were to happen'), unreal ('if X had happened, would have...') Participles in detail. The perfect passive participle with a preceding noun usually needs a time clause: 'urbe capta' = 'when the city had been captured'. The present participle is continuous ('while doing'); the future participle is intention ('about to do', or purpose with a verb of coming). The ablative absolute is the most common unseen-prose structure — find them all before translating. Worked mini-example (adapted Livy): 'Urbem sine pugna tradidissent hostes, ni consul, spe victoriae adductus, copias in castris recitavisset.' Method: (1) main verbs — tradidissent (pluperfect subjunctive, 3rd plural) and recitavisset (pluperfect subjunctive); (2) the structure: ni + subjunctive = unreal condition; ablatives absolute: 'spe victoriae adductus'? — no: 'adductus' modifies consul (nominative); (3) translation: 'The enemy would have surrendered the city without a fight, if the consul, led on by hope of victory, had not drawn up his forces in camp.' Check: the subjunctives agree (unreal condition in past time), the ablative ('spe victoriae') is cause ('led on BY hope'), the word order reversed for emphasis. Exam technique. (1) Read the passage's first and last sentences for its subject matter; (2) identify the narrative's subject (a general? an embassy?) and keep pronouns resolved; (3) translate in fluent, natural English — prefer 'the enemy surrendered' to 'the enemies they surrendered'; (4) mark unknowns with a dash and return; (5) check number/person agreement and tense backshift in indirect speech at the end. OCR marks: 45 marks for the translation, marks lost per error category (tense, case, sense) — accuracy of SENSE beats literalism every time.

topics.name: Unseen Verse Translation and Scansion
topics.subject: latin
topics.searchText: latin Latin Unseen Verse Translation and Scansion Scan a Latin hexameter line correctly (feet, elision, ictus) Apply scansion to resolve ambiguities in translation Translate Ovidian and Virgilian verse with awareness of word order and style Recognise verse style markers (chiasmus, hyperbaton, golden line) Hexameter The epic metre: six feet, each dactyl (long-short-short) or spondee (long-long), the fifth usually a dactyl, the sixth always a spondee (or trochee). Dactyl A foot of one long plus two short syllables (−∪∪); the hexameter's most common foot. Spondee A foot of two long syllables (−−); slower and weightier, used for emphasis and solemnity. Elision A vowel or -m at a word's end is elided before a word beginning with a vowel or h: 'ave atque' scans 'av' atque'; the elided syllable does not count. Caesura A word-break within a foot, usually after the first syllable of the third foot (penthemimeral); the line's sense-break point. Golden line A hexameter patterned A-B-A-B (adjective-noun-verb-adjective-noun); a Virgilian style marker. The foot pattern. A Latin hexameter = six feet: feet 1-4 dactyls (−∪∪) or spondees (−−), foot 5 usually a dactyl, foot 6 always two longs (−− or −∪ with the final syllable counted long — the trochee). Syllable quantity : a syllable is long by nature (a long vowel or a diphthong) or by position (a short vowel followed by two or more consonants, or by x/z). Elision : a word ending in a vowel or -m loses that syllable before a vowel-initial (or h-) word — 'atque' before 'omnes' scans as one elided unit; a monosyllable ending in -m sometimes resists (the rare 'ecthlipsis'). Scanning method. (1) Mark all elisions first; (2) mark long-by-nature syllables (diphthongs: ae, oe, au; long vowels); (3) mark long-by-position (vowel + 2 consonants); (4) fill the remaining feet from the left: each foot = − or −∪∪, with the fifth dactyl and the sixth spondee forced; (5) mark the caesura (usually the third foot's break). If the pattern breaks, check for an missed elision or a misjudged quantity — the metre is a self-checking system. Word order. Verse word order is free — the metre's requirements rearrange the syntax. Translate from the MAIN VERB outwards as in prose, but expect: hyperbaton (separated adjective-noun pairs: 'magnanimum... Aenean' split across the line), chiasmus (A-B-B-A patterns), the golden line (A-B-A-B). Identify the verb and its subject first, then rebuild the sentence in English word order. Style markers as translation aids. Ovid's style (Metamorphoses, Amores): witty, balanced, antithetical — expect paired phrases and rhetorical questions; his elegiac couplets (the Amores) alternate hexameter + pentameter. Virgil's style (Aeneid): elevated, solemn — expect spondaic lines at moments of weight, the golden line, enjambment (the sense running past the line's end). Enjambment matters for translation: the sentence's sense may complete in the NEXT line — always translate in sentence units, not line units. Worked mini-example (adapted Virgil): 'Arma virumque cano, Troiae qui primus ab oris | Italiam fato profugus Laviniaque venit | litora.' Scansion: line 1 — Ar-ma (−∪) vi-rum-que (−∪) ca-no (−−)... the elision check: no elisions; the penthemimeral caesura after 'cano'. Translation: 'I sing of arms and the man who first came from the coasts of Troy to Italy and the Lavinian shores, an exile by fate' — the hyperbaton ('fato profugus' inserted) and enjambment ('litora' completing the sense in line 3) rebuilt in English order. Exam technique. (1) Scan the line FIRST — the metre confirms quantities and reveals elisions; (2) find the main verb and subject; (3) translate in sentence units (not line units — enjambment); (4) mark the style markers (chiasmus, hyperbaton) and rebuild in English order; (5) check quantities at the end (a 'long' vowel misjudged distorts the foot). OCR marks: the verse unseen = translation (c. 30 marks) + scansion (c. 10) + comprehension; accuracy of metre confirms the translation's correctness — the two feed each other.

topics.name: Grammar and Accidence
topics.subject: latin
topics.searchText: latin Latin Grammar and Accidence Recall the case uses and their governing constructions Decline and conjugate across all groups, including deponents and irregulars Identify and translate every major subjunctive use Master the gerund, gerundive, indirect statement and conditionals Nominative The subject's case; also the complement after esse ('rex est' = he is king) and the predicated noun. Accusative The direct object's case; also motion towards ('ad urbem'), duration of time ('duas horas'), extent of space ('duo milia passuum') and the indirect statement's subject. Genitive Possession ('rex regis'); also description ('vir magnae virtutis'), the partitive whole ('pars urbis'), value ('magni pretii'), and with verbs of remembering/accusing. Dative The indirect object ('regi dat'); also possession with esse ('mihi nomen est'), the agent with gerundives ('regi faciendum est'), reference ('mortalibus'), and with compound verbs ('adfuisse rei publicae') and adjectives ('fidus regi'). Ablative Separation ('urbe discedere'), instrument ('gladio occidere'), manner ('magna celeritate'), means/cause, agent with a passive ('a/ab + person'), time ('tertia hora'), place where (with in), and the ablative absolute. Deponent verb Passive in form, active in meaning (hortari = to urge, sequi = to follow, proficisci = to set out); the perfect participle is passive in form AND meaning (secutus = having followed). Indirect statement Accusative + infinitive after verbs of saying/thinking/perceiving; the infinitive tense is relative to the main verb. Subjunctive The mood of the hypothesis: main uses = hortatory/jussive, purpose, result, indirect questions, cum-circumstantial, conditions (less vivid/unreal), potential (optative/deliberative). Case Core use Extended uses to know Nominative Subject Complement after esse; predicated noun Vocative Direct address Same form as nominative in most declensions (marpe: 'Marce' for Marcus) Accusative Direct object Motion towards (ad/in + acc); duration of time; extent of space; Greek accusative (respect); indirect statement Genitive Possession Description/quality; partitive; value; with memini/obliviscor, accuso/incuso, interest/refert Dative Indirect object Possession with esse; agent with gerundives; reference; with compounds (adsum, praefero); purpose (auxilio = for help); adjectives (fidus, similis + dat) Ablative Separation/instrument Manner; means; cause; agent (a/ab + person, person only); time; comparison; ablative absolute; place where (in/ab + abl) Time and place rules. Time HOW LONG = accusative ('duas horas' = for two hours); time AT WHICH = ablative ('tertia hora' = at the third hour); place TO WHICH = accusative (ad/in + acc); place FROM WHICH = ablative (ab/ex/de + abl); place WHERE = ablative (in + abl); names of towns and domus/rus/humus take no preposition: location = locative ('Romae' = at Rome; 'domi' = at home), motion to = accusative ('Romam'), motion from = ablative ('Roma'). Regular conjugations (1-4: -are, -ere, -ere, -ire): know all six tenses (present, imperfect, future, perfect, pluperfect, future perfect) active + passive. Deponents (passive form, active meaning): hortari, sequi, proficisci, pati, loqui, utor, fruor, fungor, potior, vescor (the PUFFVE verbs take the ablative/GENITIVE objects: utor + ablative, potior + ablative or genitive). Semi-deponents (audere, fido, gaudeo — perfect forms passive in appearance, active in meaning: ausus est = he dared). Irregulars : sum/esse/fui, possum, eo, fero, volo/nolo/malo, fio. Subjunctive uses — the complete list with their markers: Use Marker Translation Hortatory/jussive Present subjunctive, main clause 'let us...', 'should...' (1st/3rd person) Purpose ut/ne + subj. 'in order that...' Result ut + subj. with tam/ita/talis 'so... that' (SEQUENCE OF TENSE applies) Indirect question question word + subj. 'where/whether/why...' (backshift) Cum-circumstantial cum + subj. 'when/while/after...' Cum-causal/concessive cum + indic. 'since/although...' Conditions si/nisi + subj. (less vivid/unreal) 'if X were to/were/had...' Potential subj. alone 'would/might...' (possim, debeam) Optative/deliberative subj. alone 'would that...!' / 'what am I to do?' Fear clause ne/ut + subj. after timeo/vereor 'fear THAT... (ne)' / 'fear THAT NOT... (ut)' Sequence of tenses. Primary main tenses (present, future, future perfect, perfect with present force) take primary subjunctives (present = same time, perfect = before); secondary (imperfect, perfect historic, pluperfect) take secondary (imperfect = same, pluperfect = before). The result clause and indirect question both follow it — the most common unseen error is a misbackshifted indirect question. Gerund (verbal noun, -ndi/-ndo/-ndum/-ndum): 'ars scribendi' = the art of writing; with ad + acc for purpose ('ad scribendum' = for writing); with caus (because of) + abl. Gerundive (verbal adjective, -ndus): with esse = obligation ('faciendus est' = he must do it — 'the thing must be done'); the agent in the DATIVE ('mihi scribendum est' = I must write); alone as a passive necessity ('leges servandae' = laws to be kept). The gerundive ATTRACTION: in purpose clauses, a gerund with an object may become a gerundive ('ad pacem petundam' for 'ad petendam pacem'). Conditionals — the full set: (1) Open (si + indicative): 'if X happens, Y happens' — real possibility, any time; (2) Future less vivid (si + present subj., main + present subj.): 'if X were to happen, Y would happen'; (3) Unreal present (si + imperfect subj., main + imperfect subj.): 'if X were happening, Y would be happening'; (4) Unreal past (si + pluperfect subj., main + pluperfect subj.): 'if X had happened, Y would have happened'. Mixed conditions exist (past condition, present result) — translate accordingly. Miscellany worth marks: indirect reflexives (se = the subject of the main verb in indirect speech); attractive relative pronouns (qui = the antecedent's case: 'cuius... patrem' for 'eius pater'); dum + present for historic present ('while he is doing'); the predicative dative ('auxilio esse' = to be a help); numerals and time expressions; the comparison of adjectives (quam with comparative = 'than'; ablative of comparison without quam); satis/idoneus constructions.

topics.name: Set Texts
topics.subject: latin
topics.searchText: latin Latin Set Texts Know the set prose and verse texts and their contexts Analyse key lines with literary technique and effect Apply context (author, audience, purpose) to set-text analysis Write set-text essays to the mark scheme: knowledge, analysis, evaluation Set text The prescribed passage of Latin (prose and verse) examined in translation and analysis; OCR prescribes prose (Cicero/Ovid/Livy) and verse (Ovid/Virgil/Catullus) options. Aeneid Virgil's epic (12 books, c. 29-19 BC) on Aeneas' flight from Troy and the founding of Rome; the A-level verse set text (books prescribed per year). Elegiac couplet The Ovidian metre: hexameter + pentameter alternating; the elegy's form (Amores, Tristia, Metamorphoses-era usage). Rhetorical period Ciceronian prose architecture: the tricolon, the periodic sentence, the parallelism and balance of the courtroom speech. Ekphrasis A literary description of a work of art (Virgil's shield of Aeneas, Book 8); a set-text essay staple. Prose (OCR options, rotating by year): Cicero. The courtroom and political speeches (In Verrem, Pro Milone, the Philippics, In Catilinam): the rhetorical period's architecture — tricolon ('veni, vidi, vici' pattern), parallel clauses, the periodic suspension; the rhetorical questions; the moralising. Context: the Late Republic's courts (the senatorial jury, the bribery), Cicero's novus homo position, the speeches' publication (edited for readers, not verbatim). Verse (OCR options): Ovid. The Metamorphoses (mythological epics in hexameters) and the Amores/Tristia (elegiac couplets): witty, antithetical, the transformation's irony. Virgil's Aeneid. The epic's books (1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 12 prescribed in rotation): Aeneas' piety (pius Aeneas), the Dido affair (Book 4's tragedy), the underworld (Book 6), the shield (Book 8's ekphrasis), the ending's fury (Book 12). Learning the lines. For each set text: 5-8 key passages, each with (1) the Latin's technique (device + effect), (2) the context (what precedes/follows), (3) the translation's nuance. The A-level essays (c. 20 marks) ask for knowledge + analysis + evaluation: quote the Latin (or reference the line numbers), analyse the technique's effect, evaluate its contribution to the text's themes. In Virgil: the ekphrasis (Aeneas' shield, Book 8: Rome's future history in the shield's metal — the epic's themes in art); the similes (the hunt, the storm, the ants — epic similes as thematic commentary); the gods' machinery (Juno's opposition, Venus' aid — the divine plan vs human suffering); Dido's curse (Book 4 — the Punic Wars' aetiology); the ending (Aeneas' furor — Turnus' killing, the piety question). In Ovid: the transformation's wit (Daphne's laurel, the metamorphoses as irony and punishment); the antithesis and the couplet's balance; the narrator's playfulness. In Cicero: the tricolon and anaphora (the courtroom's rhythm); the rhetorical question (the jury's engagement); the ethopoeia (character portrayal — the opponent's vice); the periodic build (the sentence's suspense). Essay frames. The set-text essay: (1) thesis (the passage's contribution to the theme); (2) two or three analytical points (technique + effect, with the Latin quoted or referenced); (3) context (the author's purpose, the audience); (4) evaluation (the passage's significance). The unseen-style technique (grammar + sense) applies to the SET text too — the essays reward precise linguistic knowledge. The OCR set-text paper (Verse Literature / Prose Literature): comprehension questions on the passages (the text printed with notes) + an essay (c. 20 marks) on a theme or passage. Technique: (1) read the passage twice (the notes' glosses first); (2) answer the comprehension questions with the TEXT's evidence (quote the Latin); (3) the essay: thesis, technique + effect with the Latin, context, evaluation; (4) time: the comprehension first (marks per minute), the essay planned in the margin. The set texts reward preparation: 5-8 key passages per text, known for technique and context.

topics.name: Literary Technique and Essay Writing
topics.subject: latin
topics.searchText: latin Latin Literary Technique and Essay Writing Recognise the major stylistic devices in Latin prose and verse Analyse each device's effect on the reader/audience Write Latin literature essays to the mark scheme Use essay frames for technique-driven answers Anaphora Repetition of a word or phrase at the start of successive clauses — emphasis through rhythm ('non... non... non...'). Tricolon Three parallel phrases or clauses with increasing force — 'veni, vidi, vici' pattern; the rhetorical crescendo. Hyperbaton Separation of linked words (adjective from noun) for emphasis — the reader holds the pair apart until the line's end. Chiasmus A-B-B-A word order (crossing); balance with reversal — the ABBA pattern of emphasis. Alliteration and assonance Initial-consonant repetition (alliteration) and vowel-sound repetition (assonance) — sound patterning for effect. Polysyndeton and asyndeton Repeated conjunctions (polysyndeton: 'et... et... et...') for accumulation; their omission (asyndeton) for pace and force. Zeugma One verb governing multiple objects in different senses — economy and wit in a single construction. Litotes Affirmation by negating the opposite ('non ignoro' = I know very well) — understatement for emphasis. Device Pattern Effect Anaphora Word/phrase at successive clause-starts Emphasis, building rhythm (Cicero's 'non... non... non...') Tricolon Three parallel units, rising Crescendo, completeness ('veni, vidi, vici') Hyperbaton Separated adjective-noun Emphasis through suspension (Virgil's epic style) Chiasmus A-B-B-A Balance with reversal; the crossing mirrors meaning Alliteration/assonance Sound repetition Aural texture, mood (sibilance = hiss) Polysyndeton Repeated 'et' Accumulation, abundance Asyndeton No conjunctions Pace, force, breathlessness Zeugma One verb, varied objects Wit, economy (Ovid's favourite) Litotes Negated opposite Understated emphasis ('non ignoro') Golden line A-B-A-B hexameter Virgilian elegance; the verb central Historic infinitive Lone infinitive in narrative Vivid continuing action Metaphor/simile Figurative comparison Theme made concrete (epic similes as commentary) Analyse the EFFECT, not just the label. The mark scheme pays for the device's contribution: 'the tricolon compresses Caesar's speed into three verbs, its asyndeton mirroring the pace' — label + pattern + effect. A device named without its effect is half a point. Cicero (prose) : the rhetorical period — tricolons, anaphora, balance (parallelism of clauses), the periodic build, rhetorical questions, ethopoeia (character portrayal); his courtroom speeches (In Verrem, Pro Milone) perform persuasion. Virgil (verse) : elevated epic — golden lines, hyperbaton, enjambment, spondees at weight, the epic simile, the ekphrasis; his Aeneid marries Homer's models with Roman politics. Ovid (verse) : witty, antithetical — zeugma, the couplet's pointe, the transformation's irony, rhetorical playfulness; his elegiac couplets (Amores) and hexameters (Metamorphoses) trade on surprise. Recognising the AUTHOR's style is a short cut: expect Cicero's balance, Virgil's suspension, Ovid's wit. The technique essay (c. 20 marks, OCR): (1) thesis — the passage's style serves its theme (one sentence); (2) two or three analytical points: device + pattern + effect, with the Latin quoted; (3) the context (the author's purpose, the genre's conventions); (4) evaluation — the style's contribution. Example frame: 'The passage's anaphora (quote) hammers the theme of loss; the tricolon (quote) completes it; the asyndeton (quote) denies the reader rest — the style enacts the emotion the theme describes.' Latinate analysis in English essays. The A-level essays are written in ENGLISH about the Latin: quote the Latin (short phrases), analyse in English, cite line numbers. The comprehension questions (the passage printed with notes) reward precise linguistic knowledge; the essay rewards the technique's analysis. Preparation: know each device's Latin pattern (the anaphora's repeated word, the tricolon's three units), so the recognition is instant.

topics.name: The Personal Investigation (Component 1)
topics.subject: art-and-design
topics.searchText: art-and-design Art and Design The Personal Investigation (Component 1) State the structure and mark demands of AQA Component 1 (7202/C): a practical investigation plus a 1,000-3,000 word written element, 96 marks, 60% of the A-level, no time limit, marked by the centre and moderated by AQA. Identify a focused, independently chosen starting point (an idea, issue, concept or theme) and shape it into an investigation that sustains a line of reasoning from first starting point to final realisation. Plan portfolio evidence against AO1-AO4, knowing each AO carries 24 of the 96 marks and that the component is judged as one integrated whole across practical and written material. Structure the written element so it clarifies the focus, demonstrates critical understanding of contextual sources, substantiates decisions and connects visual and written elements. Compile a bibliography identifying contextual references and acknowledge every source that is not your own. Recognise the difference between AQA (7202/C, 96 marks), OCR (Component 01, 120 marks) and Pearson Edexcel (9AD0/01) Personal investigation requirements. Personal investigation Component 1 of AQA A-level Art and Design (7202/C): a practical investigation into an idea, issue, concept or theme, supported by written material, leading to a finished outcome or a series of related finished outcomes; 96 marks, 60% of the A-level. Non-exam assessment (NEA) Work set and marked in the centre and moderated by the board rather than sat in a written exam; both AQA Art and Design components are NEA, so the qualification is coursework-based. Sustained line of reasoning The coherent development of the investigation from an initial starting point through research, experimentation and refinement to a final realisation, where each piece of work visibly leads to the next. Related finished outcomes A set of final works produced as one resolved body - for example a triptych, a print series or an installation - rather than one isolated piece. Written element The 1,000-3,000 word extended response of continuous prose (a single passage, or linked shorter passages incorporated within the practical work) that documents the investigation and confirms understanding of creative decisions. Critical/contextual sources The artists, movements, texts, exhibitions and other research that inform the investigation; the spec requires the work to be informed by an aspect of contemporary or past practice of artists, photographers, designers or craftspeople. Moderation AQA's visit to the centre (normally in June) to check that centre marking of Component 1 is accurate and consistent; moderated marks can move up or down. Candidate record form (CRF) The form completed for each student on which the teacher records a separate mark for each AO (out of 24) and a total out of 96. Say it first: A-level Art and Design is a coursework-based qualification - there is no written examination paper. Both AQA components are non-exam assessment (NEA). Component 1, the Personal investigation (7202/C) , is the larger: 96 marks, 60% of the A-level , with no time limit . It is set and marked by your centre and moderated by AQA during a visit that normally takes place in June. Because the weighting dwarfs Component 2 (40%), every decision you make about the Personal investigation is an A* decision - a two-band swing on a single AO here is worth more than any amount of exam-hall revision. Revision in this subject therefore means something different from other A-levels: you are revising the specification's evidence requirements against a portfolio that already exists, auditing it for gaps, and preparing to close them - not memorising content for a hall. The component has two inseparable parts. First, a practical investigation into an idea, issue, concept or theme whose focus must be identified independently by you and which must lead to a finished outcome or a series of related finished outcomes . Second, written material : a coherent, logically structured extended response of between 1,000 and 3,000 words of continuous prose , presented either as one passage or as a series of shorter, linked passages incorporated within the practical work. The spec is explicit that the component is assessed as a whole : evidence of all four assessment objectives must appear in both the practical and the written material . A brilliant sketchbook with a bolted-on essay, or an elegant essay with thin practical work, caps your mark in every band. The spec also frames the component as synoptic assessment : you must draw together the knowledge, understanding and skills learned across the whole course - contextual study, media technique, observational recording, presentation - and apply them to one sustained enquiry of your own, responding to a stimulus, issue or theme you chose yourself. The four assessment objectives, set by Ofqual and identical across all boards, are: AO1 - Develop ideas through sustained and focused investigations informed by contextual and other sources, demonstrating analytical and critical understanding. AO2 - Explore and select appropriate resources, media, materials, techniques and processes, reviewing and refining ideas as work develops. AO3 - Record ideas, observations and insights relevant to intentions, reflecting critically on work and progress. AO4 - Present a personal and meaningful response that realises intentions and, where appropriate, makes connections between visual and other elements. Each component is marked out of 96 with the AOs equally weighted: a maximum of 24 marks per AO . Six bands are provided, each worth four marks, and within a band the qualifiers just , adequately , clearly and convincingly fix the exact mark - the lowest mark in a band means you have just met its descriptor, the highest that you have convincingly met it and only just failed the band above. Know the band language - it tells you exactly what A* looks like: Band (marks per AO) Descriptor Vocabulary 21-24 (A*) Exceptional ability Fluent use of appropriate specialist vocabulary 17-20 Confident and highly developed Assured use of specialist vocabulary 13-16 Consistent ability Consistent use of specialist vocabulary 9-12 Reasonably consistent Reasonably consistent vocabulary 5-8 Some ability Limited specialist vocabulary 1-4 Minimal ability Little or no specialist vocabulary Each AO has its own top-band phrase, and they are worth memorising because they double as a checklist for your portfolio. AO1 top band: an exceptional ability to develop ideas through sustained investigations informed by contextual and other sources , with exceptional analytical and critical understanding . AO2: an exceptional ability to explore and select appropriate resources, media, materials, techniques and processes , reviewing and refining ideas in a confident and purposeful manner as work develops . AO3: an exceptional ability to record ideas, observations and insights relevant to intentions and to reflect critically on work and progress . AO4: an exceptional ability to present a personal and meaningful response , successfully realising intentions and making connections between visual, written and other elements , with exceptionally clear, coherent and accurate use of language . In Component 1 terms this translates as: AO1 lives in your artist-analysis pages and the contextual thread running through your experiments; AO2 lives in media trials and the visible decisions between them; AO3 lives in observational drawing, photography and the critical notes after each phase; AO4 lives in the planning studies, the finished outcome(s) and the curation of the whole. Note that AO1 rewards sustained and focused investigation - both words matter: sustained means depth over time, focused means every page serves one line of enquiry. Note also that the AOs sit on top of a quality of making requirement: handling materials effectively, skilfully and safely underpins all four, because confident technique is what lets intentions reach the outcome. How the AOs actually get judged: your teacher marks each AO separately on the Candidate record form after internal standardisation (the centre's process for checking all its marking is consistent), then AQA's moderator reviews a sample and can adjust marks in either direction. Because you will not be there to explain the portfolio, every piece of evidence must be legible, sequenced and self-explanatory. Before submission, audit the work AO by AO: for each objective, name the page where its evidence is strongest, the page where it is weakest, and what you will add or annotate to close the gap. This audit - thirty minutes with the assessment criteria grid and the spec's own band descriptors - is the single highest-value revision task in the subject, because it converts a vague sense of is my work good? into a specific list of fixable evidence gaps. Raw marks are scaled: Component 1 (96) is multiplied by 3 to give 288 of the 480 total scaled mark; Component 2 (96) by 2 to give 192. Component 1 therefore carries 60% of the final outcome, which is why centres expect the investigation to be substantially complete before the Externally set assignment paper arrives on 1 February of Year 13. Assessment is to the standard of a full A-level course - 360 guided learning hours - so work is judged at A-level standard, not GCSE-plus. Your teacher marks each AO separately on the Candidate record form after internal standardisation; AQA's moderator then reviews a sample and can adjust marks in either direction, so evidence must be legible, sequenced and self-explanatory without you in the room. Other boards are built on the same coursework logic. OCR (H601 Fine Art) : Component 01 Personal investigation, 120 marks, 60% , comprising the practical portfolio plus a related study (an extended written element of roughly 1,000-3,000 words); Component 02 Externally set task, 80 marks, 40%, 15 hours supervised. Pearson Edexcel (9AD0) : Component 1 Personal Investigation, 60%, self-initiated, internally marked and externally moderated; Component 2 Externally Set Assignment, 40%, with 15 hours supervised time. WJEC/Eduqas follows the same pattern: a coursework personal investigation at 60% and an externally set assignment at 40%. The percentages, the Ofqual AO wording and the coursework basis are common to all boards; only mark totals and administrative detail differ, so this revision transfers directly. Because you must identify the focus independently, the first assessed act of Component 1 is choosing well. AQA asks for an investigation into an idea, issue, concept or theme - not a subject. Portraiture is a subject; how identity is fragmented and reassembled in contemporary portraiture is an investigation. The classic narrowing sequence works in three steps: broad theme, to a personal angle, to a question the work will answer. For example: Nature narrows to the relationship between humans and the coast , which narrows to erosion and memory on the Holderness coastline - a question that can drive a body of work combining photographic records, eroded monoprint surfaces and a final installation of suspended translucent panels. Each narrowing multiplies the connections you can make and sharpens the artists you can legitimately research. Equally, a personal angle - your commute, a family archive, cultural heritage, local politics, a medical experience - almost always produces better evidence than a generic theme, because AO4 rewards a response that is personal and meaningful , and authenticity is difficult to fake. Beware the opposite failure too: a focus so narrow that research dries up. The test is whether at least three or four substantial artists genuinely speak to your question. Test a candidate title against four questions before committing: Access - can you gather strong primary material (first-hand observation, photography, collected objects) for it? Contextual depth - are there at least three or four substantial artists whose practice you can analyse in relation to it? Media range - does it invite experimentation across several processes rather than one? Outcome potential - can you visualise a finished outcome, or a series, that answers it? A theme that fails two of these will strangle the investigation by February. Avoid titles that are really artist studies ( The work of Lucian Freud ) - the spec requires your idea investigated through critical/contextual material, not a biography; and avoid outcome-first choices ( I want to paint a big canvas of the sea ) because an outcome without a line of reasoning cannot show development from initial intentions. Also avoid themes chosen purely for what you think examiners like: moderators read thousands of identity and mental health investigations and reward the ones with genuine evidence, not the ones with fashionable words. Structure is what turns material into a sustained line of reasoning. The spec demands a coherent, in-depth study that demonstrates the ability to construct and develop a sustained line of reasoning from an initial starting point to a final realisation , showing clear development from initial intentions to the final outcome . In practice the portfolio should read in a deliberate order: Starting point and intent - the chosen focus stated, mind-mapped, with initial visual responses and first primary observations. Contextual research - gallery, museum and site visits; artist analysis pages that go beyond copying: analysing methods, contexts and ideas, with your own transcriptions and studies made in response to the work. Experimentation - media, technique and process trials linked explicitly to the research: what you took from each artist's approach and why. Review and refinement - annotated evaluation of what is working, decisions to pursue, modify or discard, and second-generation experiments shaped by those decisions. Recording from observation throughout - drawing and photography that feed the developing idea, not a separate drawing unit bolted on for AO3. Realisation - planning studies, maquettes or compositional drafts leading to the finished outcome or related outcomes, followed by a critical evaluation against initial intentions. A worked sketch of that architecture in action - focus how clutter and consumption bury the domestic interior : page one states the question and shows a mind-map plus photographs of a family kitchen; pages two to four analyse, say, the assemblages of Cornelia Parker and the interiors of Vilhelm Hammershoi, each analysed for method, context and idea with a transcription study in response; pages five to eight trial collage, cast objects and monoprint, each page ending with a decision; pages nine and ten review - one route abandoned with reasons, one escalated; pages eleven to twelve plan the final installation with compositional drafts; the last page evaluates the realised installation against the opening question. Every page answers what next , so the line of reasoning never breaks. Gallery and museum visits are primary research, not decoration. The spec's written-element requirements name studies of others' work made during a residency, or on a site, museum or gallery visit as legitimate contextual references, and AO1 rewards first-hand engagement above screen-scrolling. Work a visit properly: study one work in person for twenty minutes and record what a reproduction cannot show (scale, surface, brushwork, installation logic); sketch in situ, however briefly; photograph labels and wall texts; note the curation - what hangs next to what, and why. Then convert the visit into portfolio pages within a week: a transcription study in response to a named work, an analysis of its method, context and ideas, and one experiment that applies what you learned. Postcards, catalogues and exhibition guides then feed the bibliography. A single well-worked visit generates more assessable AO1 evidence than fifty saved Instagram images. Timing matters because the ESA paper arrives on 1 February of Year 13 and its preparatory period then takes over your working week. A realistic schedule: summer of Year 12 - first observations and reading, provisional theme; September-October - focus finalised, contextual research begun; November-January - experiments and refinement, written element drafted; January-February - final outcome completed, written element polished, work selected and presented for moderation. Students who leave the realisation until after February split their attention at exactly the wrong moment, and the Component 1 outcome suffers for it. Development, not repetition , is the examiner's watchword. Ten competent pages that each restart the idea score lower than six pages that visibly escalate it. Every page should end by answering two questions: what did I learn, and what happens next? If you cannot answer, the page is decoration. Equally, do not delete the failures - rejected experiments with a reasoned annotation are precisely the reviewing and refining evidence AO2's top band demands. Run critique cycles with peers or your teacher at each phase transition and record the outcome: after the critique I abandoned X because... and tested Y instead is exactly the reflexive language the top bands reward. The spec notes there is no restriction on the scale of practical work and that you should carefully select, organise and present your work so it is well structured - curation is assessed. A portfolio of fifty unsorted sheets buries the line of reasoning; a portfolio of thirty-five sequenced sheets, with larger resolved pieces supporting the flow, proves it. Common pitfalls, all visible in moderator reports every year: theme too broad or purely descriptive; contextual research that is copying without analysis; media trials disconnected from intentions; a final outcome that appears with no planning trail; a written element that narrates ( then I did... ) rather than argues; and sources not acknowledged. Each pitfall maps to a lost band. The remedy in every case is the same discipline: every piece of work must lead to the next and, as the spec puts it, relate in meaningful ways to relevant critical/contextual materials . Choose formats deliberately. The spec allows sketchbooks, workbooks, journals and mounted sheets to underpin the work, and each has a different assessment personality. A sketchbook carries the investigative flow - dated, chronological, annotated on the page; a workbook suits layered experiments with tests taped in and evaluated; a journal handles the extended written passages and contextual analysis; mounted sheets present the polished and the large. Most successful investigations mix two or three: the sketchbook as engine, mounted sheets as showcases for the strongest developments, larger canvases or constructions as the realisation approaches. Whatever the mix, the sequencing must survive the moderator's cold read: if a stranger cannot reconstruct your line of reasoning from the order of the pages alone, the structure is not yet finished. The written material is not an add-on essay; it is one half of the evidence. AQA lists exactly what it must do - it must confirm understanding of creative decisions, providing evidence of all four assessment objectives by: clarifying the focus of the investigation; demonstrating critical understanding of contextual and other sources; substantiating decisions leading to the development and refinement of ideas; recording ideas, observations and insights relevant to intentions by reflecting critically on practical work; making meaningful connections between visual, written and other elements. It must also include specialist vocabulary appropriate to the subject matter , include a bibliography that identifies contextual references from books, journals, websites, studies made during a residency, or on a site, museum or gallery visit, and be legible with accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar . You may present it as a single continuous passage or as a series of shorter, linked passages incorporated within the practical work - the embedded-passage model often scores better because the writing sits beside the work it analyses and the examiner sees the connections live, which is precisely what AO4's connections between visual and other elements means. Structure the essay as an argument, not a diary. A reliable shape for 1,000-3,000 words: an introduction (roughly 150-250 words) that states the focus, your line of argument and how the investigation unfolds; three to five thematic body sections (roughly 400-500 words each), each pairing contextual analysis with your own practical response - after studying Hockney's joiners I layered fractured photographic perspectives; this failed because..., which led me to... ; and a conclusion (150-250 words) that returns to the initial intentions and judges how the final outcome realises them. A sweet spot of around 2,000-2,400 words usually leaves room for analysis without padding: examiners consistently reward density of insight over length, and anything drifting towards 3,000 risks thinning the argument and breaching the spec limit. A paragraph skeleton that scores, with the moves labelled: (claim) Hockney's joiners offered a model of time compressed into a single plane; (evidence) his 1980s photographic collages stitch dozens of viewpoints so the viewer's eye wanders rather than fixes; (analysis) the method treats memory as spatial rather than sequential, which matched my intention to layer several moments of the same street; (application) I overlapped twelve photographs of the same junction, then intensified the overlaps in acrylic; (judgement) the trial succeeded in destabilising viewpoint but flattened colour, so the next experiment transferred the composition to translucent layers that could be hung apart. Every paragraph in your essay should contain that final judgement move - it is what separates analytical and critical understanding (top bands) from description (middle bands). Write in first person where it carries judgement - I selected oil glazes because... - but keep the register academic: no conversational filler, precise terminology (impasto, intaglio, gesso, compositional space, negative space) and critical verbs ( subverts, synthesises, echoes, rejects, distils ). The top band of AO4 explicitly requires exceptionally clear, coherent and accurate use of language , and AO1 requires fluent use of appropriate specialist vocabulary - so SPaG is a marks issue, not just a presentation issue. Quote sparingly and always attribute; paraphrase other people's analysis in your own voice; never submit an online commentary or AI-generated text as your own critical understanding. Evidence requirements across the whole component. Both practical and written work must show all four AOs, so plan the essay to cover what the sketchbook cannot easily prove, and vice versa: AO Best evidenced by practical work Written element's job AO1 (24) Artist analysis pages, gallery studies, contextual links made visible inside experiments Critical understanding in prose: analysis of artists' methods, contexts and ideas; synthesis of influences AO2 (24) Media trials, sampling, rejected routes, refinement pages Substantiating why media and processes were selected, reviewed and refined AO3 (24) Observational drawing, photography, annotated reflection on progress Recording insights; critical reflection on what the practical work shows and where it must go AO4 (24) Planning studies, final outcome(s), presentation and curation Connecting visual and written elements; judging how intentions were realised Sources and integrity. The spec states plainly: students must identify and acknowledge sources which are not their own . Keep a live bibliography from day one - books (author, title, publisher, year), journal and web sources (with access dates), and gallery visits recorded as primary research. A consistent minimum format: author surname, initial, year, title , publisher or site, and for websites the URL with the date you accessed it. Quote sparingly and always attribute; paraphrase analysis in your own voice; never submit a transcription of an online commentary as your own critical understanding. Moderators sample for exactly this, and unacknowledged sources put the award of the whole component at risk. Common written-element failures, and the fixes. First, narration without argument - the essay that reads then I did X, then I did Y : fix by ending every paragraph with a judgement move (what worked, what failed, what happens next). Second, description of artists without critical analysis - a biography of the movement instead of an argument about what its methods contribute to your work: fix by pairing every artist claim with your own practical application. Third, disconnection between writing and work - the essay analyses artists that never appear in the portfolio, or the portfolio contains experiments the essay never mentions: fix by cross-referencing explicitly ( as page seven shows... ). Fourth, vocabulary collapse - the essay written in conversational register with no specialist terms: fix by drafting a terminology bank (fifteen to twenty terms from your media and movements) and checking each one appears where relevant. Fifth, a conclusion that introduces new material instead of judging the outcome: fix by returning to the introduction's question and answering it. Finally, present like a curator. The spec asks you to carefully select, organise and present the Personal investigation so it is well structured and provides evidence meeting all four objectives. Mount sheets in sequence, label larger works, embed the linked written passages where they belong, and add a contents page or divider cards for the moderator. Photograph 3D and fragile work before transport, keep the Candidate record form with the submission, and rehearse a two-minute walk-through of the investigation's storyline before moderation day. The last impression the assessor gets should be of a study that was designed, not accumulated - and the first impression, on page one, should already announce the question the whole portfolio exists to answer. A model opening paragraph, at the standard the top band expects: This investigation asks how erosion reshapes memory of place on the Holderness coastline. It grew from weekly photography of a cliff path I have walked since childhood, and from noticing that the maps no longer matched the ground. The investigation is informed by two strands of practice: land artists who treat landscape as material rather than view, and painters of memory whose surfaces encode loss. The first section analyses how these artists' methods and contexts shaped my initial experiments; the middle sections substantiate the media decisions - monoprint, photographic layering, cast plaster - through which the idea developed; the conclusion judges the final installation of suspended translucent panels against my initial intention to make absence visible. One paragraph, and the assessor already knows the focus, the influences, the media route and the outcome - which is exactly the clarity the written element exists to provide.

topics.name: The Externally Set Assignment (Component 2)
topics.subject: art-and-design
topics.searchText: art-and-design Art and Design The Externally Set Assignment (Component 2) State the structure and rules of AQA Component 2 (7202/X): eight starting points, one selected, preparatory period from 1 February plus 15 hours of unaided supervised time, 96 marks, 40% of the A-level. Select a starting point strategically and convert it into preparatory work that evidences all four assessment objectives before supervised time begins. Plan the 15 supervised hours against a time budget, knowing the first three hours must be consecutive and preparatory work may be referred to but not amended. Work independently within the specified time constraints, developing a personal and meaningful response that leads to a finished outcome or series of related outcomes. Apply the conduct rules correctly: stopping prep before supervised time, keeping work secure, acknowledging sources, and the no-internet condition. Externally set assignment (ESA) Component 2 of AQA A-level Art and Design (7202/X): a question paper set by AQA offering eight starting points, from which you select one; assessed through a preparatory period plus 15 hours of supervised time, 96 marks, 40% of the A-level. Starting point One of the eight questions or themes printed on the ESA paper, used as the beginning of your response; the paper is a prompt for an independent personal response, not a brief to illustrate. Preparatory period The period from receipt of the paper on 1 February (or as soon as possible after) until supervised time begins, in which research, planning and preparatory studies are produced in any suitable format. Supervised time The 15 hours of unaided, supervised work in which the finished outcome or related outcomes are produced; the first three hours must be consecutive. Unaided work Work produced without assistance from teachers or peers during supervised time; teachers may give general supervisory guidance but not practical or creative help. Maquette A small-scale preparatory model of a three-dimensional or installation outcome, used to test form, scale and construction before the supervised hours. Time plan A written schedule for the 15 supervised hours allocating hours to composition, main making and resolution, usually annotated onto the final preparatory sheet. JCQ instructions The Joint Council for Qualifications document 'Instructions for the conduct of examinations', whose guidelines must be followed during the supervised time. Remember the frame: A-level Art and Design is a coursework-based qualification - there is no written exam paper, and Component 2 is still non-exam assessment. The Externally set assignment (7202/X) is worth 96 marks, 40% of the A-level , and it is set by AQA, marked by your centre and moderated by AQA during a visit normally in June. What is external is the question paper: AQA prints a separate paper for each endorsed title (Fine Art is 7202), each offering a choice of eight questions to be used as starting points , and you select one . Papers are provided on 1 February , or as soon as possible after. Everything after that - the research, the trials, the outcome - is coursework logic, not invigilated silence. The component runs in two phases: Preparatory period - from 1 February. You consider the eight starting points, select one, and build preparatory work in any suitable format: mounted sheets, design sheets, sketchbooks, workbooks, journals, models and maquettes. Supervised time - 15 hours. Unaided, supervised work in which you produce a finished outcome or a series of related finished outcomes, informed by your preparatory work . The first three hours must be consecutive . Preparatory work and the supervised-time work are assessed together, as a whole, against all four assessment objectives - the same 24-marks-per-AO structure as Component 1, with six bands of four marks and the qualifiers just, adequately, clearly, convincingly. The spec adds a distinctive emphasis for this component: you are assessed on the ability to work independently, working within the specified time constraints, and developing a personal and meaningful response . Independence and time discipline are therefore examined behaviours, not just admin. The AOs translate into ESA practice as follows: AO1 - contextual research into artists relevant to the chosen starting point, analysed critically and used to inform the response; AO2 - media trials during prep and confident, purposeful handling in the supervised hours; AO3 - observational recording and reflective annotation throughout; AO4 - a resolved, personal final outcome that answers the starting point and connects with the preparatory evidence. The conduct rules are mark-critical and easy to lose marks against: Stop prep when supervised time starts. You must stop work on preparatory work as soon as the first period of supervised time begins. You may refer to preparatory work in the supervised hours, but it must not be added to or amended . Security. Preparatory work and supervised work must be kept secure between sessions of supervised time, and all submitted work kept secure at the end of the 15 hours. Identification. The work produced during supervised time must be clearly identified as such - label it, because the moderator must be able to see what was made when. Sources. You must identify and acknowledge sources which are not your own , in prep as in Component 1. No internet in the 15 hours. You must not have access to the internet during supervised time. Access to web-based applications (for example Adobe Creative Cloud) is permitted, but all other internet access must be disabled - so download references, fonts and textures before the first session. Unaided. The 15 hours are unaided and follow the JCQ 'Instructions for the conduct of examinations'. Annotation. Annotation and notes during supervised time should use appropriate specialist vocabulary and be legible with accurate use of language. Raw marks scale by 2: Component 2's 96 becomes 192 of the 480 total scaled mark, against Component 1's 288. Other boards mirror the structure: OCR (H601) Component 02 Externally set task - 80 marks, 40%, 15 hours supervised; Pearson Edexcel (9AD0/02) - externally set assignment, 40%, with 15 hours supervised time; WJEC/Eduqas - externally set assignment, 40%, 15 hours. The eight-question paper format and 1 February release are AQA's specifics; the 15-hour supervised structure is common to the boards. Note the contrast with GCSE, where supervised time is typically 10 hours - the A-level gives you half as much again, and expects a more developed outcome within it. The strategic consequence of 60/40 is easy to state and easy to forget in spring: Component 1 is worth one and a half times Component 2. A common Year 13 error is to over-invest in ESA prep from February and let the Personal investigation's final outcome drift. The ESA is time-boxed and rules-bound; the Personal investigation is open-ended. Finish the open-ended one first. What the ESA is really testing is transfer. The spec frames both components as synoptic: Component 2 asks you to draw together everything learned across the course - contextual analysis, media control, observational recording, curation - and apply it to a stimulus you did not choose, under constraints you cannot negotiate. That is why the strongest ESA submissions come from students who reuse their Component 1 skillset deliberately: the same analysis framework applied to new artists, the same media-audit discipline applied to the starting point, the same annotation method carried into supervised hours. Treat the ESA as Component 1 compressed - the personal voice must survive the compression, which is why the board emphasises a personal and meaningful response . How marking works within the component. Your centre marks preparatory work and supervised work together against the four AOs, each out of 24, using the same six-band grid as Component 1; AQA's moderator samples and can adjust. Two marking consequences follow. First, prep is not 'practice' - it is half the evidence, so a thin preparatory period caps every AO before you sit down. Second, because the supervised work must be clearly identified as such , the moderator must be able to reconstruct what was made when; label sessions, keep the work secure between them, and make the storyline - research to trials to plan to outcome - readable from the sequence of pages alone. Use past ESA papers as your main practice material. AQA publishes previous years' eight-question papers, and they are the closest thing this coursework-based subject has to a past paper. Work them as a timed exercise: given one hour, read all eight starting points of a previous year, run the four-part test, choose one, and sketch a one-page plan - artists, media, compositional direction, outcome, 15-hour time budget. Repeat across three or four years and the selection skill becomes reflexive, which is precisely what the first week of February demands. The papers also reveal the house style of starting points: single words, short quotations and open questions that invite personal interpretation rather than illustration - a pattern worth knowing before the paper arrives. The preparatory period is where ESA marks are won or lost, because the 15 supervised hours can only execute what prep has already planned. The spec says students should consider the starting points and select one - so begin with a deliberate choice, not a reflex. Read all eight questions on day one. For each, run the four-part test you used for the Personal investigation: access (can you gather strong primary material in the six to eight weeks available?), contextual depth (are there artists you already understand who genuinely speak to it?), media range (does it invite your strongest processes?), outcome potential (can you visualise a resolved outcome a moderator would recognise as finished?). Choose the question you can evidence most completely, not the one that sounds most interesting - and choose fast, because every week of prep is a week of evidence. Convert the chosen starting point into a personal interpretation . An ESA question such as fragments or layers is a trigger, not a title; the moderator is assessing whether you developed a personal and meaningful response . Write your interpretation in one sentence at the top of your first prep sheet - I will investigate how layered translucency records the experience of revisiting a demolished place - and let every subsequent prep page serve it. Mind-map visually rather than verbally: the map should generate imagery, artists and processes, not synonyms. Prep must do four jobs, one per AO, before the first supervised hour: AO1 - research. Two to four artists relevant to the starting point, analysed for methods, contexts and ideas, with transcription studies and experiments in response . Gallery visits if possible; otherwise high-quality reproductions with acknowledged sources. AO2 - trials. Media and process experiments that test the approaches you intend to use in the outcome, with review notes deciding what the outcome will be made in and how. AO3 - recording. First-hand observational drawing and photography of primary material relevant to the starting point, plus critical reflection on what the recordings suggest. AO4 - planning. Compositional studies, colour studies, maquettes or design sheets that resolve the outcome's format, scale and structure - and a written time plan for the 15 hours. The time plan is the single highest-value prep sheet. It allocates the 15 hours in advance: for example, hours 1-2 composition and ground; hours 3-7 main development; hours 8-11 detail and secondary passages; hours 12-13 layering and adjustment; hours 14-15 resolution, edges, signature area and final annotation. Annotate it onto the last prep sheet where the moderator can see it, because it demonstrates the working within the specified time constraints the spec explicitly assesses. Rehearse against it: know what you will be doing in hour eight before you sit down. Prep formats are flexible - mounted sheets, design sheets, sketchbooks, workbooks, journals, models and maquettes - and most successful submissions combine them: a sketchbook for flow and reflection, mounted sheets for the strongest studies, a maquette if the outcome is 3D or installed. What matters is that the prep tells a continuous story ending in a plan the supervised hours can execute. Sequence it, date it, and end it with a page that says: this is what I will make, in this media, at this scale, in this order . The stopping rule is absolute: preparatory work stops the moment the first supervised session starts. Anything added afterwards is a conduct breach and risks the component's award. In practice this means the last week of prep is closure, not expansion: finish the time plan, finish the compositional studies, photograph and print any references you will need (the no-internet rule means nothing can be downloaded in the 15 hours), prepare grounds and stretch paper where the centre permits, and pack a kit list. Common prep failures, all mapped to lost bands: choosing a starting point late and thinning the research; copying artists rather than analysing them; trials that explore media with no decision about the outcome; no compositional resolution, so the first supervised hours are spent hesitating; and no time plan, so the 15 hours are spent evenly rather than strategically. Each is fixable in the six to eight weeks the preparatory period gives you - if you treat it as the exam, because in this subject, it is. Analysing artists under time pressure. The prep window is short, so compress the analysis framework rather than skipping it. For each artist, force four sentences: method (what materials and processes, handled how); context (when, where, for whom - what the work responded to); idea (what the work is about, and how the method carries the idea); application (what you take from it, and the trial that follows). Two artists analysed this way, with transcription studies and experiments in response, generate more AO1 evidence than six artists pasted with commentary. Select artists fast using the Tate's collection and art-terms pages, gallery exhibition listings, or monographs - and pick artists whose methods you can actually trial in the centre, because the strongest AO1-AO2 link is an experiment that visibly applies an analysed method. The mind-map should generate work, not words. Verbal mind-maps produce synonyms; visual ones produce artists, processes and imagery. From the chosen starting point, branch into: primary material you can gather; artists per branch; processes per branch; and compositional possibilities. Keep the map in the portfolio - it is the visible record of the independent selection the spec rewards - and date the branches so the moderator can see decisions accumulating. Run prep to a week-by-week schedule. A realistic model across eight weeks: week one - read the paper, select the starting point, write the sentence of intent, mind-map; week two - primary recording (photography, observational drawing, collected objects) and first artist analysis; week three - second and third artist analysis with transcription studies and experiments in response; week four - media trials round one, with review notes; week five - refinement of the strongest trial routes, second-generation experiments; week six - compositional studies, colour studies or maquettes resolving the outcome; week seven - the time plan, kit list, grounds prepared, references printed; week eight - closure: final prep pages, labelling, secure storage, and a rehearsal walk-through of the planned 15 hours. Students who freestyle the preparatory period consistently arrive at supervised time with research but no plan - and the 15 hours then convert a plan-shaped deficit into a mark. Primary sources beat secondary ones in prep, as in Component 1. The starting point usually connects to something you can access first-hand - objects, places, people, archives - and first-hand material feeds stronger AO3 evidence than screen-scraped images. Photograph your primary material well (light, scale reference, multiple viewpoints), draw from it directly, and note what the photographs cannot show. Where a gallery visit is possible, work it as primary research: one work studied in person for twenty minutes beats fifty thumbnails. Secondary sources - monographs, gallery websites, journals - then supply context the primary material cannot, with sources acknowledged from the first week so the bibliography assembles itself. The 15 hours are unaided, supervised , and the first three must be consecutive - plan that opening session like a launch. Before it: grounds prepared, references printed, materials counted, kit list checked, time plan memorised. In it: settle the composition. The classic failure of supervised time is spending the first session redrawing the plan; the moderator expects to see the outcome's structure established in the first three hours because prep already resolved it. Hours 1-3 are for transferring the chosen composition, setting scale, blocking the ground and fixing the format - so that every later hour adds, rather than searches. Run the remaining 12 hours against the time plan, but know where the flex is. A workable pattern for a painted outcome: hours 4-8 main development - the largest, most demanding passages while concentration is fresh; hours 9-12 secondary passages, detail, texture and adjustment; hours 13-14 layering, glazing or reworking weak areas; hour 15 resolution - edges, unifying passages, the final annotation. For a constructed or installed outcome, front-load construction (materials and joins fail slowly) and reserve the final hours for surface and presentation. For a print or photographic outcome, front-load the technical work - exposure, processing, proofs - because failures there consume recovery time you will not have. The principle in every medium: risk early, refine late . An hour spent troubleshooting in hour three is recoverable; the same hour in hour fourteen is not. Hour models by medium, for the time plan: Hours Painted outcome Constructed/installed outcome Print/photographic outcome 1-3 (consecutive) Composition transferred, ground, blocking Armature and main structure Shooting/processing, proofing 4-8 Main development, largest passages Construction, joins, stability Test prints/exposures, selection 9-12 Secondary passages, detail, texture Surface treatment, finishing Final editions, sequencing 13-15 Layering, glazing, unifying, edges Installation logic, presentation, annotation Presentation, mounting, final annotation Annotation during supervised time is worth reclaiming minutes for. The spec requires that annotation and notes use appropriate specialist vocabulary and be legible with accurate language, and AO3 explicitly rewards recording insights and reflecting critically on work and progress. Three disciplined notes per session - what was attempted, what changed, what the next session must achieve - cost five minutes and give the moderator the independent decision-making evidence this component is distinctively assessed on. Write them as judgements, not logs: the glaze flattened the form, so I scraped back and rebuilt with an impasto neutral shows reflection; applied glaze shows only activity. Keep a small annotation sheet in the kit list so the habit survives fatigue in hour eleven. You may refer to preparatory work, but not add to or amend it - so the boundary is visible: prep is evidence of planning, supervised work is evidence of independent realisation. Label all supervised work clearly identified as such ; annotating it with the session number and hour helps the moderator, and that annotation itself should use appropriate specialist vocabulary and be legible. Brief reflective notes during supervised time - session 3, hours 7-9: glaze too saturated; scraped back and rebalanced with complementary neutral - are worth marks under AO3 and cost minutes. The no-internet rule needs practical planning: you must not have access to the internet during the 15 hours, though web-based applications such as Adobe Creative Cloud are permitted with all other internet access disabled. If you work digitally, export everything - reference images, brushes, fonts, previous files - before the first session and work offline throughout. If you work traditionally, print your references in colour at the scale you will need. Nothing in the rules prevents referring to printed materials; what is prohibited is live access. What the moderator is looking for in the supervised work mirrors the AO bands: confident, purposeful execution (AO2); a resolved outcome that visibly realises the prep's plan and answers the starting point (AO4); recording and reflection continuing inside the hours (AO3); and independent decision-making under constraint (the component's distinctive emphasis). The outcome must be informed by preparatory work - a final piece that ignores the prep breaks the storyline the two are assessed as; equally, a final piece that merely photocopies the prep's strongest study wastes the 15 hours. The strongest submissions develop beyond the plan: the composition holds, but scale, surface or colour resolve further than the studies managed, and the final annotation explains those decisions. Do the arithmetic on what 40% means. Two bands on one AO in Component 2 is 8 raw marks, which scale to 16 of 480 - roughly 3.3% of the qualification, close to a typical grade boundary. Conversely, because the AOs are equally weighted, a candidate strong in three AOs but capped by a weak final outcome loses exactly a quarter of the component. This is why the final hour matters as much as the first: AO4's 24 marks are awarded to the response that realises intentions , and an unresolved edge or an unfinished passage reads as unrealised intentions. Budget resolution time with the same seriousness as making time. Common supervised-time failures: treating the hours as ten silent hours plus five for panic; re-composing in session one; running out of a key material in hour nine; leaving resolution to minutes that do not exist; forgetting to label supervised work; and amending prep during a break between sessions - a conduct breach that risks the whole component. The countermeasures are all in the prep: the time plan, the kit list, the compositional resolution, and the discipline of finishing. At the end of the 15 hours all submitted work is kept secure and then presented - prep and outcome together, in sequence, with the supervised work identified - for centre marking and AQA moderation. Your last hour is not for the artwork; it is for the evidence. Digital candidates need an offline workflow. Because internet access must be disabled during the 15 hours (web-based applications such as Adobe Creative Cloud are permitted), everything must be exported in advance: reference images at working resolution, fonts, brushes, textures, and every file version the outcome depends on. Practice the export before the first session, keep files named by session and hour - esa_outcome_s4.jpg - and annotate digitally in the same specialist vocabulary required on paper. Save incrementally; a corrupted file in hour ten is not an excuse the board recognises, and version history is your only undo. Presentation closes the component. At the end of the 15 hours all submitted work is kept secure, then presented for centre marking and AQA moderation: preparatory work in sequence, the supervised outcome(s) clearly identified, annotations legible, sources acknowledged, and the Candidate record form completed. The final presentation should let the moderator read the entire storyline - starting point, interpretation, research, trials, plan, outcome - from the order of the work alone. Mount the prep sheets in the order they were made, label the supervised work, and place the time plan where it can be seen. In a coursework-based subject the presentation is not packaging; it is the last assessed page.

topics.name: Critical and Contextual Study
topics.subject: art-and-design
topics.searchText: art-and-design Art and Design Critical and Contextual Study Place the major art movements from the Renaissance to the contemporary in a timeline, and articulate for each the social, cultural, political and technological context that shaped it. Analyse any artist's work through the four-part framework - form, process, content, context - demonstrating the analytical and critical understanding AO1 requires. Explain continuity and change between movements, genres and traditions, including European and non-European examples, as the AQA 7202 spec demands. Construct a critical-study essay with a thesis, thematic body sections pairing contextual analysis with your own practical response, and a judgement-bearing conclusion. Cite and acknowledge all sources accurately in a bibliography that identifies books, journals, websites and gallery or museum visits. Critical and contextual study Sustained analysis of artists, movements and artefacts in relation to their methods, contexts and ideas - the evidence base for AO1; within AQA 7202 it lives inside the Personal investigation's written element, while OCR offers it as a standalone A-level (H606). Formal analysis Analysis of the visual components of a work - line, tone, colour, texture, shape, form, space, composition, scale - as the first layer of any critical reading. Iconography The study of the subjects and symbols within an artwork and what they meant to their original audience - for example the lily as purity in Annunciation scenes. Patronage The system of commissioning art by church, state or wealthy individuals, which shaped subject matter, scale, media and display from the Renaissance to the modern gallery and art market. Chiaroscuro The dramatic contrast of light and dark modelling form; Caravaggio pushed it to tenebrism - figures emerging from near-darkness - in the service of Counter-Reformation immediacy. Avant-garde The military metaphor for art that leads and challenges - movements from Impressionism to Conceptual Art that broke with academic convention and redefined what art could be. Primary source First-hand evidence: the artwork itself, gallery and museum visits, artist interviews and manifestos - weighted more heavily than secondary commentary in critical study. Continuity and change The AQA 7202 knowledge requirement that you explain what a movement inherited from what preceded it and what it altered - tradition as a chain of revisions, not a sequence of breaks. The AQA 7202 spec requires knowledge of historical and contemporary developments and different styles and genres , and of how images and artefacts relate to social, environmental, cultural and/or ethical contexts, and to the time and place in which they were created - plus continuity and change between traditions, and it insists on European and non-European examples .
