Impulse Force multiplied by the time over which it acts (force-time); impulse changes the momentum of a body, so extending force application time or increasing force changes velocity. Moment of inertia The resistance of a rotating body to a change in its angular motion, calculated as the sum of each particle's mass multiplied by the square of its distance from the axis of rotation (I = sum mr squared); mass distribution matters more than mass itself. Angular momentum The quantity of angular motion of a body, calculated as moment of inertia x angular velocity; it remains constant while airborne (no external torque), so changing the body shape trades one for the other. Bernoulli principle Where a fluid flows faster, its pressure is lower; an aerofoil shape or a pressure differential between airflow sides creates a force (lift) perpendicular to the flow. Magnus effect The deviation of a spinning ball in flight: the spinning surface drags a boundary layer of air, creating a pressure differential (faster side = lower pressure) producing a force that makes the ball swerve or dip. Centre of mass The point at which the body's mass is concentrated and about which it balances; it can lie outside the body (e.g. the arched Fosbury flop position) and its height and position determine stability. Drag The resistance force opposing motion through a fluid, comprising surface drag (friction between fluid and surface) and form drag (resistance created by the shape/cross-sectional area presented); reduced by streamlining. Newton's laws underpin every biomechanics explanation. First law (inertia) : a body stays at rest or moves at constant velocity until an external force acts - a sprinter remains motionless in the blocks until the applied force exceeds inertia; a heavier rugby player has more inertia and is harder to stop or start. Second law : the acceleration of a body is proportional to the force applied and inversely proportional to its mass - F = ma (force in newtons, mass in kg, acceleration in m/s squared); a netball pass accelerates more when more force is applied over the ball's small mass. Third law : for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction - the sprinter pushes back and down on the blocks and the blocks push forward and up on the sprinter; a swimmer pushes water backwards and is propelled forwards; a ball is struck with a force equal and opposite to the force the ball applies to the racket. Exam logic: state the law in full, then give one precise sporting example - the marks are for the application, not the recitation. Levers consist of a fulcrum (pivot), load (weight/resistance) and effort (force applied by the muscle). First class : fulcrum between load and effort - nodding the head (atlanto-occipital joint as fulcrum, head weight as load, neck muscles as effort) or triceps extension at the elbow. Second class : load between fulcrum and effort - plantar flexion/heel raise (ball of the foot is the fulcrum, body weight through the ankle is the load, calf muscles through the Achilles are the effort); second-class levers always give mechanical advantage (effort moves a larger load with less force) but a small range and slow movement. Third class : effort between fulcrum and load - biceps curl (elbow fulcrum, biceps insertion effort, weight in hand load) and most limb movements (knee extension, elbow flexion); third-class levers operate at a mechanical disadvantage (large effort needed for a small load) but produce great speed and range of movement - the classic trade-off the exam wants. Mechanical advantage = effort arm / load arm (distance from fulcrum to effort versus fulcrum to load). Application: most sporting limbs are third class because speed of racket, boot or fist matters more than economy of force - hence biceps and quadriceps insert close to the joint. Linear motion is movement of the body (or parts) in a straight or curved line where all parts move the same distance, direction and speed in the same time. Distinguish the pairs precisely: distance (path length, scalar) versus displacement (straight-line change of position from start to finish, vector - a 400 m runner on one lap has 400 m distance but zero displacement); speed (distance/time, scalar) versus velocity (displacement/time, vector with direction, m/s); acceleration = change in velocity / time taken (m/s squared). Momentum = mass x velocity (kg m/s): the quantity of motion a body possesses; in a collision (tackle) momentum is conserved in the combined bodies unless an external force acts - a heavier, faster player has more momentum and is harder to stop. Impulse = force x time : impulse changes momentum - the greater the impulse, the greater the change in velocity. Applications score the marks: increasing time of contact reduces peak force (a cricketer or netball player draws the hands back when catching - cushioning; landing with bent knees spreads the force); increasing force and/or time increases momentum change (a long jumper drives hard through a long last-contact; a discus thrower's long pull; follow-through in striking actions). Impulse also explains negative impulse (braking forces in the early stance of running - the first half of ground contact decelerates, the second accelerates). Force-time graphs link directly to impulse: the area under the curve = impulse . Exam graphs typically show ground reaction forces in sprinting or landing: identify the peak force , explain that the same impulse can be generated by a smaller force acting for longer (why good landings look soft), and note the negative (braking) and positive (propulsive) phases of the running contact. In jump analysis, a larger area under the vertical force-time curve means a greater take-off impulse and therefore greater take-off velocity and jump height. Worked calculations - the exam sets numericals, so rehearse the four: (1) Force : a 75 kg sprinter accelerating at 4 m/s squared produces F = 75 x 4 = 300 N ; (2) Momentum : an 80 kg player moving at 8 m/s has momentum of 80 x 8 = 640 kg m/s ; in a tackle the combined mass moves with the conserved momentum of the pair; (3) Velocity : 100 m covered in 12.5 s gives velocity = 100 / 12.5 = 8 m/s (state the direction for the vector mark); (4) Impulse : an average force of 200 N applied for 0.25 s gives impulse = 200 x 0.25 = 50 Ns , the change in momentum produced. Show units in every calculation - missing units is the most common lost mark. Friction completes the force picture: static friction acts between surfaces at rest and is essential in sport - sprint blocks, football studs and climbing shoes all rely on static friction to create the grip that makes the third-law reaction force possible (a boot slipping on wet grass produces no useful reaction); kinetic friction acts between moving surfaces and is usually resistive - skiers wax bases and cyclists use narrow, smooth-rolling tyres to cut it. Friction can therefore be necessary or resistive depending on the task - a discrimination point: athletes want maximum friction at the shoe-surface interface (grip) and minimum friction at the body-fluid interface (streamlined suits). Combine with drag: both are resistive forces the performer manipulates - the exam rewards naming the force, stating its direction, and explaining the performer's manipulation of it. For impulse numericals on force-time graphs, remember the area under the curve method: estimate the area of each rectangle/triangle region and sum it - that area is the impulse and hence the momentum change. Distance, displacement and the games application - the worked example that scores: a 400 m runner on a standard track runs a distance of 400 m but a displacement of zero (start and finish coincide) - the classic discrimination; velocity can therefore be zero while speed is high, and velocity can be negative (deceleration, or motion in the opposite direction - a defender back-pedalling). Acceleration is positive when speeding up, negative when slowing down (deceleration in the run-up), and zero at constant velocity (top-speed sprinting between 60-80 m in a 100 m race) - quote one of each in linear motion answers. In games, displacement matters more than distance: a midfielder's total distance covered (10+ km) is quantitative workload, but the displacement of a pass (straight-line direction and length) determines whether it reaches the intended receiver - the vector qualities (direction + magnitude) are what the exam rewards. Lever dimensions in the body - the numbers behind mechanical disadvantage: in a knee extension (third-class lever), the patellar tendon inserts roughly 4-5 cm from the knee joint (effort arm) while the load (lower leg plus any resistance) acts roughly 30-40 cm from the joint (load arm) - the quadriceps must generate roughly 8-10 times the load force to extend the knee, but the foot travels 8-10 times faster and further than the muscle shortens. This is the complete trade-off sentence the exam wants: third-class levers sacrifice force economy for speed and range - hence the body's design for rapid limb movement (kicking, throwing) rather than lifting heavy loads. Second-class levers invert it: the heel raise moves the whole body weight with a calf force well below body weight, but the heel lifts only a few centimetres - force economy at the cost of range. Application: weight-lifting movements that load third-class joints (biceps curl) feel heavy because the muscle works at a mechanical disadvantage - the reason muscles are so strong relative to the loads they move. Exam logic: define the quantity, give the equation, then apply to the named performer - e.g. impulse questions reward time-force trade-offs in both directions (cushion a catch, lengthen a throw). For levers, always identify fulcrum-load-effort in order, name the class, then state the mechanical advantage consequence. Angular motion is rotation of a body or segment around an axis (real or imaginary). It is produced by torque (moment of force) = force x perpendicular distance from the axis to the line of action of the force (newton metres) - the further the force acts from the axis, the greater the rotation produced, which is why gymnasts swing long levers. Angular equivalents mirror linear quantities: angular displacement (angle turned, radians or degrees), angular velocity (angle turned per unit time, rad/s), angular acceleration (change in angular velocity per unit time). Moment of inertia (I) is the resistance of a rotating body to a change in its angular motion: I = sum of (m x r squared) - the sum of each particle's mass times the square of its distance from the axis. Two implications the exam always wants: (1) it depends on mass and, critically, its distribution - the same mass held further from the axis gives a much larger moment of inertia (r is squared); (2) because r is squared, changing body shape (tucking) changes I dramatically without changing mass. Angular momentum = moment of inertia x angular velocity . When a performer is airborne there is no external torque , so angular momentum is conserved (constant) - it can only be redistributed between I and angular velocity. This is the core principle of aerial sports: take-off determines total angular momentum; shape changes then trade it. Tucking pulls mass towards the axis, decreasing I, so angular velocity must increase - faster somersault. Extending for the landing increases I, so angular velocity decreases - slower rotation, controlled landing. Applications: a trampolinist or diver generating a strong pike/tuck to complete multiple somersaults then extending to land; an ice skater spinning faster as the arms are drawn in; a gymnast in a straight somersault rotating slower than in a tucked one. Note for precision: the performer cannot add angular momentum in the air - only vary its distribution - a discrimination point in evaluate questions. Projectile motion : any body released into the air and subject only to gravity and air resistance follows a curved ( parabolic ) path. Three factors affecting the trajectory , in order of importance: (1) speed of release (the greater the release velocity, the further and faster the projectile travels - the dominant factor, which is why force production and technique focus on it); (2) angle of release ; (3) height of release (relative to landing height). For release and landing at the same level, the optimum angle is 45 degrees - equal horizontal and vertical velocity components give maximum range. When the projectile is released above landing height (shot put, javelin, ski jump), the optimum angle is less than 45 degrees - elite shot putters release at roughly 36-38 degrees because the extra release height means less vertical component is needed. When released below landing height (e.g. a chip over a keeper), the optimum is greater than 45 degrees. Horizontal and vertical components are independent: horizontal velocity stays (approximately) constant; vertical velocity changes under gravity - quote this for A* precision when explaining why a projectile's shape is a parabola and why maximum range is not always at 45 degrees in real sport (air resistance shifts it for a javelin or badminton shuttle). Applications to rehearse: long jump (optimum angle ~18-22 degrees in practice because speed cannot be fully converted - a realistic evaluation point), shot put (release height and velocity dominate), golf drive and football punt (angle-speed trade-offs), ski jump (using aerodynamics to extend flight - links to fluid mechanics). Exam logic: state the three factors in the correct order of influence, give the 45 degree rule with its modification for release height, and finish with a performer-specific justification. Angular calculations and units : angles are measured in radians or degrees; 1 radian is approximately 57.3 degrees and a full turn is 2 x pi radians (approximately 360 degrees). Angular velocity = angle turned / time: a gymnast completing a full 360-degree somersault in 0.5 s turns at approximately 12.6 rad/s (6.28 / 0.5). Worked moment-of-inertia logic: if a performer tucks and reduces I to a third of its extended value, angular velocity must triple (momentum conserved: halving or thirding I multiplies angular velocity by the same factor) - quote this inverse proportionality in numerical questions; converting to a pike position reduces I less than a tuck, so angular velocity rises less - know the shape hierarchy: straight (largest I, slowest rotation), pike (intermediate), tuck (smallest I, fastest rotation). Real-sport release angles - the applied detail that separates A* answers: long jump - optimum in practice is only ~18-22 degrees because the take-off leg cannot convert all horizontal speed into vertical velocity without destroying run-up speed; speed of release dominates, so elite long jumpers trade angle for velocity - a textbook evaluation of the 45-degree rule. Shot put - ~36-38 degrees, below 45 because the shot is released above landing height (less vertical component needed). Javelin - released at ~30-35 degrees with a small angle of attack (angle between the implement and the airflow) so the aerofoil shape generates lift that extends flight; air resistance makes the flight path asymmetric rather than a true parabola. Ski jumping - the jumper leans forward over the skis to maximise lift and minimise drag, extending the flight far beyond a ballistic path. Exam logic: for projectile questions, state the three factors in order of influence, give the 45-degree rule and its release-height modification, then finish with the real-sport justification - the marks are for explaining why the optimum shifts, not for reciting 45 degrees. Torque calculations and take-off generation : torque = force x perpendicular distance - a gymnast applying 500 N at 0.4 m from the hip axis generates 200 Nm of torque; the same force at 0.2 m generates only 100 Nm - the reason long levers (straight legs, extended arms) and wide grips generate more rotation. Generating angular momentum at take-off is the detail the conservation questions assume: the performer creates torque while still in contact with the ground - by asymmetric arm actions (one arm up, one down), a lean at contact (trampolinist contacting the bed off-centre), or a hyperextended take-off position (diver's hurdle step) - and the reaction force then supplies the rotation; once airborne, no new torque can be added, only redistributed. State both halves: contact-phase torque generation, then airborne conservation - the two-phase logic that full-mark angular answers follow. Linear and angular combine in most sporting movements - the synthesis the exam rewards: running is angular rotation of the limbs (hip, knee, ankle) producing linear motion of the centre of mass; a throw combines angular rotation of the trunk and arm (increasing the speed of the distal end through the kinetic chain) with linear drive of the legs; a golf swing is angular motion of the body around the spine axis imparting linear velocity to the club head. The general rule: angular velocity of a rotating limb produces linear velocity of its end point proportional to the radius (v = omega x r) - a longer lever moving at the same angular velocity gives the end point greater linear speed, which is why throwing implements (javelin, hammer) are held at the end of extended arms. Quote one combined example per biomechanics answer - the examiners reward linking the two motion types rather than treating them in isolation. Drag is the resistance opposing motion through air or water. Two types, both nameable for a mark: surface drag (friction between the fluid and the surface of the body - reduced by smooth skinsuits and shaving legs in swimming/cycling) and form drag (resistance created by the shape and cross-sectional area presented to the flow - reduced by streamlining : the cyclist's crouched aero position, the swimmer's horizontal body line, the bobsleigh's shape). Drag increases with the square of velocity (doubling speed quadruples drag - why aerodynamics matter most at elite speeds), with cross-sectional area, and with less streamlined shape. Application: sprint cyclists adopt an aero tuck and use disc wheels; swimmers wear textured suits to cut surface drag while keeping the body flat to cut form drag; a sprinter deliberately does not streamline (upright running posture) because generating force matters more than reducing drag at those speeds - a strong discrimination point. The Bernoulli principle : where fluid velocity is higher, pressure is lower. An aerofoil shape (curved upper surface creating a longer path) forces air to travel faster over the top, lowering pressure above relative to below - the pressure differential produces lift perpendicular to the flow. Applications: the discus held at a slight negative angle of attack experiences lift, extending flight; a ski jumper spreads the skis and leans forward, creating lift that prolongs the flight phase; downhill skiers and F1 cars use inverted aerofoils to create downforce (grip). Exam logic: name Bernoulli, state the velocity-pressure inverse relationship, identify the aerofoil/pressure differential and the direction of the resulting force. The Magnus effect applies Bernoulli to spinning balls - a guaranteed explain question. When a ball is struck with spin, the spinning surface drags a thin boundary layer of air around with it. On the side where the surface moves with the airflow, local air velocity increases and pressure falls (Bernoulli); on the opposite side the surface moves against the airflow, velocity falls and pressure rises. The pressure differential creates a force perpendicular to the flight path, deviating the ball . Direction of spin determines direction of force: topspin produces a downward force so the ball dips early (tennis topspin, a dipping football free kick) but bounces forward; backspin produces an upward force so the ball floats (golf wedge shots, a chip that stops); sidespin swerves the ball left or right (banana free kick). Applications to rehearse: Cristiano Ronaldo's knuckleball-free-kick contrast (minimal spin = unpredictable - optional depth), tennis topspin allowing higher net clearance with the ball still dropping in, golf dimples reducing surface drag to enhance the spin-lift interaction. Centre of mass is the point at which the body's mass is concentrated and about which it balances - in an upright standing human roughly behind the navel, but it moves as body position changes and can lie outside the body : in the Fosbury flop the arched back places the centre of mass below the bar while the body clears it - a guaranteed application. In a sprint start the centre of mass is low and forward over the hands (facilitating horizontal propulsion); in a high jump take-off it is driven upward. Stability (resistance to disturbance of equilibrium) is maximised by four factors, a guaranteed 4-mark list: (1) greater body mass ; (2) larger base of support (feet apart, multiple contact points); (3) lower centre of mass (crouch); (4) line of gravity falling within the base of support (and more stability when the line is central). Applications: a gymnast landing bends the knees (lowers COM, enlarges base), plants feet apart and holds arms out; a rugby prop in the scrum crouches with a wide stance so the line of gravity stays central; a sprinter in the blocks is deliberately unstable forward - instability can be desirable when fast movement is needed - the balance-versus-readiness trade-off is a top-band evaluation point. Static stability also improves when the performer is stationary and symmetrical; dynamic balance during movement is maintained by adjustments keeping the line of gravity within the moving base. Buoyancy and flotation (Archimedes' principle) extend fluid mechanics to water: upthrust equals the weight of fluid displaced , so a body floats when its density is lower than water. The swimmer's centre of buoyancy (centre of the displaced water, near the chest/air-filled lungs) sits above the centre of mass (hips and legs, denser muscle and bone), so the body rotates until the two align - the legs sink and the swimmer kicks to raise them, keeping the body horizontal to minimise form drag. Water is roughly 800 times denser than air , so drag dominates swimming: technique, streamlining and the reduced bow-wave all matter more than in land sports - the reason swimming has the highest technique-to-strength ratio of any sport and why shaving down and skinsuits cut surface drag. Applications: front-crawl body roll reduces the cross-sectional area presented; streamlining off the push-off (long, narrow, arms locked) exploits minimal form drag; the breaststroke glide positions the body in the lowest-drag shape. Sport Principle Application Sprint cycling Form drag / streamlining Aero tuck, disc wheels, skinsuit - minimises the cross-section presented Swimming Surface + form drag; buoyancy Horizontal body line, shaved skin; kick raises legs to align centre of buoyancy with centre of mass Discus Bernoulli lift Slight negative angle of attack generates lift, extending flight Ski jumping Bernoulli lift + drag Forward lean over skis maximises lift, prolonging flight Football free kick Magnus effect Sidespin creates pressure differential, swerving the ball Tennis / golf Magnus effect Topspin dips the ball early; backspin floats it Gymnastics landing Stability + impulse Wide base, low centre of mass; knee flexion extends contact time, reducing peak force Dynamic balance is the final stability depth: in movement the base of support constantly changes, so balance is maintained by keeping the line of gravity within the moving base through postural adjustment - a sprinter leans forward with the centre of mass deliberately ahead of the base at the drive phase (controlled instability converting into horizontal propulsion), then brings the line of gravity back over the feet at top speed. The exam rewards the trade-off framing: stability is desirable for landing and contact sports; instability is deliberately engineered for acceleration and change of direction - quote one example of each. Exam logic: fluid questions want the named principle (Bernoulli/Magnus), the velocity-pressure relationship and the performer-specific consequence; stability questions want all four factors plus an applied performer; centre-of-mass questions want the Fosbury flop point. For force-time graphs, always state that the area under the curve equals impulse and link it to momentum change.

topics.name: Skill Acquisition
topics.subject: physical-education
topics.searchText: physical-education Physical Education Skill Acquisition Classify skills on the continua: open-closed, gross-fine, discrete-serial-continuous, self-externally paced, and justify the classification (AQA 3.4; OCR 2.1; Edexcel Topic 3) Justify types and methods of practice (part, whole, whole-part-whole, progressive part, massed, distributed, variable) and explain positive, negative and bilateral transfer (AQA 3.4; OCR 2.1) Compare theories of learning: operant conditioning (Skinner), cognitive theory, social learning theory (Bandura) and constructivism, with coaching applications (AQA 3.4; OCR 2.1) Describe information processing models (Whiting, Welford), selective attention and memory (AQA 3.4; OCR 2.1) Explain reaction time: simple and choice, Hick's law, the single-channel hypothesis and the psychological refractory period (AQA 3.4; OCR 2.1) Evaluate types of guidance (visual, verbal, manual, mechanical) and feedback (intrinsic/extrinsic, positive/negative, KR/KP, concurrent/terminal) (AQA 3.4; OCR 2.1) Skill classification is a continuum, not a category: open-closed (environment), gross-fine (muscle size), discrete-serial-continuous (structure), self-externally paced (control) Methods of practice: whole/part/whole-part-whole/progressive part (structure), massed vs distributed (time), variable practice for open skills Theories of learning: operant (reinforcement shapes S-R bonds), cognitive (insight, whole learning), social learning (Bandura ARMD - attention, retention, motor reproduction, motivation), constructivist (learner builds understanding, guided discovery) Information processing: input - STSS - perception - STM/LTM - decision - effector - output - feedback (Welford); Whiting simplified it to receptor, translatory and effector mechanisms Hick's law: reaction time rises with choice number; psychological refractory period = single-channel delay after a feint; anticipation shortens RT Guidance: visual/verbal for most, manual/mechanical for safety and shaping; feedback: intrinsic vs extrinsic, positive vs negative, KR vs KP, concurrent vs terminal Open skill A skill performed in an unstable, unpredictable environment that changes during execution, requiring the performer to adapt (e.g. a pass in football); opposite of a closed skill, performed in a stable, predictable environment (e.g. a free throw). Transfer The effect that the learning and performance of one skill has on the learning and performance of another: positive (aids), negative (hinders), bilateral (between limbs) or proactive/retroactive (forwards or backwards in time). Operant conditioning Skinner's trial-and-error theory of learning: the stimulus-response bond is strengthened by reinforcement (positive rewards, negative removal of an unpleasant stimulus) and weakened by punishment; skills are shaped by reinforcing successive approximations. Single-channel hypothesis The brain processes one stimulus at a time; a second stimulus arriving before the first is processed must wait, producing a delay in reaction time. Hick's law Reaction time increases logarithmically as the number of response choices increases; reducing choice (fewer options, anticipated cues) shortens reaction time. Psychological refractory period The delay in responding to a second stimulus caused by the single-channel bottleneck when a first stimulus is still being processed (e.g. a feint in basketball delaying the defender). Knowledge of results (KR) Extrinsic feedback about the outcome of the movement (was the shot successful?), as opposed to knowledge of performance (KP) - feedback about the technique used. Selective attention Filtering relevant cues from irrelevant information in the display so the limited-capacity short-term memory processes only decision-relevant stimuli; trainable through focus cues and experience. Skill is the learned ability to bring about predetermined results with maximum certainty and often minimum outlay of time and energy (Knapp's definition - quote it when asked to define skill). Skills are classified on continua , and the exam rewards placing a named skill with justification: (1) open-closed : an open skill is performed in a stable environment that changes during execution (a football pass under pressure), a closed skill in a stable, predictable one (a dart throw, vault); (2) gross-fine : large muscle groups with little precision (a tackle) versus small muscles with fine precision (snooker bridge hand); (3) discrete-serial-continuous : brief single movement with clear beginning and end (penalty flick), a series of discrete skills linked (triple jump = hop-step-jump), or no defined beginning/end and repeated (cycling, swimming); (4) self-paced-externally paced : performer controls start and speed (serve) versus the environment dictates timing (goalkeeper's save); (5) low-high organisation : simple separated subroutines (tumbling sequence) versus highly integrated subroutines that lose their meaning if split (cartwheel). Justification logic: place the skill on each continuum and give the reason from the environment or movement structure - never just name a category. Types and methods of practice follow from the classification. For structure : whole practice - the skill taught in its entirety, suited to high-organisation, fast, ballistic or open skills (cartwheel, dive) where subroutines cannot be separated and the feel (kinaesthesis) of the whole movement matters; part practice - subroutines taught separately then linked, suited to low-organisation, complex or dangerous skills (trampoline routine components, judo breakfall before throw); whole-part-whole - perform the whole, isolate the weak subroutine, return to the whole (netball pass); progressive part - subroutines added one at a time in sequence, suited to complex serial skills (triple jump built hop, then hop-step, then hop-step-jump). For time : massed practice - long sessions with few rests, suited to motivated, fit performers and closed skills, but risks fatigue and boredom; distributed practice - short sessions with rest intervals (rest can include mental rehearsal), suited to beginners, complex/dangerous skills and open skills, allowing feedback and recovery. Variable practice - practising a skill in many conditions/environments, developing schema and adapting open skills (passing drills with moving defenders); fixed/drill practice - repeated in a stable environment, suited to closed skills (diving entry drills). Matching method to classification and performer is the standard A-level application question. Transfer is the effect of learning one skill on another - a guaranteed define-and-apply item. Types: positive (one skill aids another - throwing a javelin aids throwing a ball), negative (one skill hinders another - a badminton wrist flick disrupting a tennis drive, bad habits interfering), bilateral (learning with one limb transfers to the other - football practice with the weak foot), proactive (an old skill aids a new one - netball chest pass before a basketball pass) and retroactive (a new skill affects a previously learned one). To optimise positive transfer (a standard 4-mark list): make practice realistic and game-like (transfer-appropriate practice); teach the underlying principles of the movement; ensure the original skill is well learned (overlearning); point out the similarities between skills; use variable practice across contexts. To limit negative transfer, avoid teaching contradictory skills back-to-back and highlight the differences. Exam logic: define transfer, classify the type with an example, then give two or three strategies the coach uses. Fitts and Posner's three stages of learning frame every practice decision and are a guaranteed knowledge item: (1) cognitive (beginner) - the learner builds a mental picture of the skill; movements are unrefined, errors frequent, and conscious thought is consumed by the movement itself; the coach uses demonstration (visual), simple key points (verbal), and manual/mechanical guidance for safety; feedback is extrinsic, positive and limited to one or two points; (2) associative (intermediate) - practice refines the movement; errors decrease and the learner begins to detect and correct their own errors (intrinsic feedback develops); motor programmes form; the coach shifts to more detailed verbal feedback and variable practice; (3) autonomous (expert) - performance is automatic : the movement runs without conscious thought, freeing attention for tactics, opposition and environment (dual-task capacity); the coach provides fine detail (knowledge of results, statistics, video) and keeps motivation high. The stage determines the practice method: cognitive learners get fixed/distributed part practice; associative learners get whole-part-whole with variability; autonomous performers get variable, game-realistic practice under pressure - match the stage to the method for the application mark. Subroutines underpin the whole/part decision: a skill can be broken into component parts (subroutines) - the triple jump splits into hop, step and jump; a tennis serve into grip, toss, backswing, contact and follow-through. Low-organisation skills have subroutines that can be practised separately without losing meaning (a gymnastics routine); high-organisation skills have subroutines so integrated that splitting them destroys the pattern (cartwheel) - so high-organisation skills get whole practice, low-organisation get part or progressive part. The decision rule the exam wants: complexity x organisation x danger determines the method - complex and dangerous gets part (safety), high-organisation gets whole (kinaesthesis), open skills get variable practice (adaptability). For massed versus distributed, evaluate both directions: massed suits fit, motivated performers and closed skills but risks fatigue (practice quality collapses when tired - poor technique gets practised) and boredom; distributed suits beginners and complex skills (rest allows feedback processing and mental rehearsal) but slows progress and needs scheduling discipline. Drill versus problem-solving practice sharpens the methods decision: drill practice repeats a set pattern under controlled conditions - suited to closed skills and safety-critical technique (diving entry, golf swing path); problem-solving practice sets the performer a task to solve within constraints (3v2 overload games, modified rules, smaller areas) - suited to open skills and tactical understanding, developing decision-making and transferable schema. Fixed practice (repetition in a stable environment) hardens closed skills because the environment never varies; variable practice (the same skill in many conditions) builds the schema that open skills demand - the theoretical basis (schema theory: varied practice builds generalised motor programmes that adapt to new conditions). Transfer pairs to rehearse - the examples that score: positive - a netball chest pass transferring to basketball; throwing a javelin aiding a cricket throw; negative - a badminton wrist-and-finger flick interfering with the flatter, longer tennis drive (racket sports are the classic negative-transfer family); a squash player's short swing disrupting a tennis swing; bilateral - practising with the weaker foot in football improving the stronger foot; swimming breathing practised to both sides. Proactive/retroactive - learning netball first (proactively aids) the basketball pass; learning the tennis drive later (retroactively disrupts) the badminton clear. The strategies for maximising positive transfer, applied: make practice game-realistic (variable practice with defenders), teach the underlying principles (weight transfer, follow-through), ensure the original skill is overlearned before introducing a related one, and explicitly point out similarities and differences between the two skills - the last point prevents the performer applying a skill where it does not fit. Learning is a relatively permanent change in behaviour or performance resulting from practice or experience (distinguish it from a temporary performance fluctuation - fatigue). Four theories are examined: operant conditioning, cognitive theory, social learning theory and constructivism. Operant conditioning (Skinner) : learning by trial and error - the performer tries responses and the environment reinforces the successful ones, strengthening the stimulus-response (S-R) bond . Positive reinforcement (reward - praise, selection) strengthens the bond; negative reinforcement (removing an unpleasant stimulus once correct - stopping the drill) also strengthens it; punishment weakens incorrect responses but should be used sparingly (risk of demotivation - Thorndike's law of effect : responses followed by satisfaction are strengthened). Supporting laws: law of exercise (repetition strengthens bonds) and law of readiness (learning happens when the performer is prepared). Shaping reinforces successive approximations towards the target skill (rewarding a partial somersault before the full rotation). Coaching application: games drills where the environment (not the coach) reinforces correct decisions - e.g. a drill where correct passes earn a point; players learn by trial and error within the designed environment. Evaluation: works well for closed, simple skills and fitness but can be slow, does not explain insight, and risks learning wrong responses without coaching. Cognitive theory of learning (Gestalt) : learning through understanding and insight - the performer problem-solves the whole situation rather than chaining responses; whole learning with the problem organised as one, and past experience (intervening variables) helping interpretation. The learner sees the relationship between parts (insight) and applies understanding to new situations, which aids transfer. Coaching application: guided discovery - asking questions (what happens if you step with the wrong foot?) and using whole demonstrations for open, high-organisation skills. Evaluation: suited to intelligent, experienced performers and complex open skills where understanding tactics matters; less effective for novices who lack the experience base for insight. Social learning theory (Bandura) : learning by observing and copying (modelling) significant others , with vicarious reinforcement (seeing others rewarded increases the likelihood of copying). Bandura's four stages ( ARMD ): Attention (the demonstration must catch and hold attention - accurate, relevant, from a significant other or elite model); Retention (the model must be remembered - mental rehearsal, cues, repetition); Motor reproduction (the learner must be physically able to reproduce it - appropriate to ability level); Motivation (the learner must want to copy - praise, success, rewards). Coaching application: demonstrations, video analysis of elite performers, highlighting one key point per demonstration. Bandura's Bobo doll study (children copying observed aggression) is the classic evidence citation - quote it when asked for a study. Evaluation: powerful for teaching technique quickly and for juniors, but the model must be correct (copying poor technique), the learner must be capable, and it does not guarantee understanding. Constructivist theory : the learner actively builds (constructs) understanding through interaction with the environment and others rather than passively receiving it; problem-solving tasks, exploration and scaffolding (support withdrawn as competence grows - Vygotsky's zone of proximal development: what the learner can do with guidance now becomes independent). Coaching application: small-sided games and problem-solving constraints (play 3v2 and work out how to create the overlap), with coach support faded. Evaluation: develops adaptable, tactical understanding and decision-making; slower and less prescriptive, needing design skill from the coach. The learning plateau is the applied phenomenon every theory question connects to: performance improves rapidly at first, then levels off despite continued practice . Causes (a guaranteed explain list): demotivation/boredom (repetition loses challenge - link to the overjustification effect and reward structures); fatigue (physical limit - practice quality declines); poor technique becoming fixed (the current method has reached its limit - the plateau IS the ceiling of the learned technique); targets reached (no new goal to chase); insufficient coaching (no new cues to process). Remedies : set new, higher goals (goal setting - restart motivation); variable and new practice methods (break the fixed technique - whole-part-whole restructuring); rest and recovery (fatigue); new guidance or a new coach (fresh cues); mental rehearsal and imagery (renewed focus); raise the physical limit with fitness training (a physiological ceiling lifts the skill ceiling). Link the plateau to the theories: operant conditioning explains it as a stale reinforcement schedule (rewards stopped adding value); cognitive theory as insight not yet reached; the remedies are the exam's application marks. Theory Theorist Mechanism Coach role Best suited to Operant conditioning Skinner (Thorndike's laws) Trial and error; reinforcement shapes the S-R bond Designs the environment; reinforces correct responses Beginners, closed and simple skills, fitness drills Cognitive theory Gestalt Insight and understanding of the whole problem Guided discovery; whole demonstrations; questioning Advanced, open, tactical situations Social learning Bandura (ARMD) Observation and copying of models; vicarious reinforcement Accurate demonstrations; cues; motivation Juniors; fast, safe technique learning Constructivist Vygotsky (scaffolding) Building understanding through interaction and problem-solving Sets problems; fades support Tactical understanding; adaptable decision-making Exam logic for theory comparisons: the table is the skeleton, but marks come from the contrast sentences - operant lets the learner discover (slow, errors possible), social learning shows the correct template (fast, safe, but copy-dependent); cognitive and constructivist develop understanding but need experience. The strongest answers pick the theory that fits the performer in the stem, then justify with the stage of learning (Fitts and Posner) and the skill classification - three-way synthesis that reliably reaches the top band. Reinforcement schedules deepen operant conditioning: continuous reinforcement (reward every correct response) builds the S-R bond quickly but extinguishes fast when rewards stop; partial reinforcement (rewarding some correct responses) builds more slowly but is more resistant to extinction - the reason coaches fade praise as learning progresses rather than stopping abruptly. Punishment detail: punishment weakens responses but should be immediate, proportionate and paired with an alternative (state what TO do) - pure punishment breeds resentment and fear of failure (link to NAF). Social learning detail : the model must be significant to the learner (elite performer, coach, older sibling, peer) - the more significant, the stronger the copying; demonstrations can be live (richer, interactive, can be repeated on request) or video (pause, slow motion, frame analysis - better for technique detail); the demonstration should highlight one key point at a time (bandwidth - beginners process few cues) and be matched to the learner's stage. Constructivist detail : the constraints-led approach is its modern coaching form - modify the rules, space, equipment or numbers (smaller pitches, fewer players, modified scoring) so the learner discovers the solution through play rather than instruction; the coach manipulates constraints and asks questions, scaffolding support that is faded as competence grows (Vygotsky's zone of proximal development: what the learner can do with guidance today becomes independent tomorrow). Insight example : a netball player realises, after guided questioning, that the circle entry creates the overlap - the sudden understanding that transfers to new situations without re-teaching, the defining feature of cognitive/constructivist learning. Exam logic: for theory questions, name the theorist, state the mechanism (reinforcement, insight, observation, construction), give the coaching application and one evaluation point. For compare questions, contrast the role of the coach: operant designs the environment, cognitive questions the learner, social learning demonstrates, constructivist sets problems. Information processing models explain how the brain converts a display into a response. Welford's model : sensory input from the display enters the short-term sensory store (STSS) (all information, held ~0.25-1 s); selective attention filters relevant from irrelevant cues; perception interprets the filtered information using long-term memory (comparison with stored experiences); the decision is made in the short-term memory (STM) (capacity ~7 plus or minus 2 items, duration ~30 s without rehearsal - chunking information into groups extends both); the effector mechanism sends the signal to the muscles and the output is performed; feedback loops back in, updating memory. Whiting's model is the simplified version to know by name: display - receptor systems - translatory mechanism - effector system - output - feedback data (input, decision-making in the brain, output). AQA/OCR also reward Schmidt's schema theory as the explanation of how skills are produced and adapted: recall schema (initial conditions + response specifications - what to do) and recognition schema (sensory consequences + outcome - how it felt and what happened); variable practice builds schema, which is why varied practice improves open skills - link it back to practice methods for top marks. Reaction time (RT) is the time between stimulus presentation and the start of the response: simple RT (one stimulus, one response - sprint start) versus choice RT (several possible stimuli and responses - goalkeeper facing a penalty). Hick's law : choice RT increases logarithmically as the number of choices increases - more options mean slower reactions, so reducing choice (coaching positional play, reading cues) speeds responses. Single-channel hypothesis : the brain processes one stimulus at a time, so a second stimulus arriving before the first has been processed must wait - producing the psychological refractory period , the delay in responding to the second stimulus: the basketball defender reacts to the feint, and the real move that follows is delayed - explain both together, as the exam links them. Anticipation (temporal - predicting when; spatial - predicting where) shortens effective RT, but wrong anticipation (being deceived by a fake) lengthens it. Ways to improve reaction time : practice and experience (cue recognition), selective attention training, anticipation from opponent cues, reducing choice, and optimal arousal (too low or too high slows processing - link to arousal theory). Guidance supports learning and safety; four forms with applications: visual guidance - demonstrations, video, diagrams (most useful for beginners and all learners; the model must be accurate and age-appropriate - link to Bandura ARMD); verbal guidance - instruction, questioning, feedback (best with advanced learners; must be concise - beginners process little information; questioning develops cognitive/constructivist understanding); manual guidance - the coach physically supports or moves the performer (gymnast held through a somersault; builds confidence and kinaesthetic feel, gives safety, but can create dependence and over-protect the true movement); mechanical guidance - equipment/aids (harnesses, armbands, golf nets, cricket nets) for safety in dangerous skills and isolating technique, but limits the real feel of the skill. Matching logic: beginners get visual plus manual/mechanical (safety, shape of movement); intermediates get visual plus verbal; advanced performers get verbal plus video (fine detail). Guidance reduces risk and fear in dangerous skills - a standard application point. Feedback - information about performance used to correct and reinforce; the pairs are the exam: intrinsic (from the performer's own kinaesthetic senses - developed with experience, only meaningful once the skill is learned) versus extrinsic/augmented (from coach, video, statistics - essential for beginners who lack intrinsic awareness); positive (what was done well - motivates and reinforces the S-R bond, best with beginners) versus negative (what was wrong and how to improve - best with experienced performers who can handle criticism and act on it); knowledge of results (KR) (outcome - was it in?) versus knowledge of performance (KP) (technique - the movement itself; KP matters most in closed skills and technical sports); concurrent (during the movement - continuous sports like swimming, but can overload) versus terminal (after the movement - standard coaching feedback; use immediately or the STM fades). Effective feedback is immediate, specific, limited to a few key points, and matched to the performer's stage of learning - the general rule that earns evaluation marks. Exam logic: for guidance and feedback questions, name the type, define it, give a sporting example, and state when it is effective - the four-step structure scores every available mark. Memory completes the information processing chain: information is encoded (stored as visual, verbal or kinaesthetic representations), stored (STM then LTM) and retrieved (compared with incoming display information). The short-term memory holds ~7 plus or minus 2 items for ~30 seconds without rehearsal - so instructions must be chunked (grouping items into meaningful wholes - 'grip, toss, swing' as one unit) to fit capacity; rehearsal transfers information to the long-term memory , which has effectively unlimited capacity and stores motor programmes (the stored plans that produce movements) plus experiences used for perception (comparison with the incoming display). Improving memory (a guaranteed list): chunking information; mental rehearsal/imagery; association with existing skills (linking a new skill to a well-learned one); meaningful labelling and demonstration; overlearning (practising beyond mastery so the programme is fixed); and repetition with feedback. Link to the models: perception uses LTM to interpret the display, so a richer LTM means faster, more accurate decisions - the theoretical justification for experience and practice. Performer stage Most effective feedback Most effective guidance Reason Beginner (cognitive) Extrinsic, positive, terminal, simple KP Visual + manual/mechanical Limited processing capacity; needs the correct template and safety; cannot yet use intrinsic feel Intermediate (associative) Mix of intrinsic and extrinsic; KP and KR Visual + verbal Developing error detection; responds to detailed correction Expert (autonomous) Intrinsic, negative (constructive), concurrent where useful, KR statistics Verbal + video analysis Automatic movement; fine detail needed; handles criticism and acts on it Guidance evaluation depth : manual and mechanical guidance build confidence and safety but create dependence and can distort the true kinaesthetic feel of the movement - so guidance must be faded as competence grows (link to Fitts and Posner: guidance is a cognitive-stage tool, withdrawn by the associative stage). Visual guidance fails if the model is poor or the demonstration is too complex (bandwidth problem - beginners process only a few cues); verbal guidance fails if it overloads the STM (limit instructions to one or two chunked points). The exam rewards the withdrawal principle: effective coaching matches guidance and feedback to the stage of learning and progressively removes support - quote one example of guidance faded (manual support on a somersault removed as the rotation is mastered). Reaction time figures add precision: simple reaction time is typically around 0.2 seconds (auditory ~0.17 s, visual ~0.2 s); choice reaction time lengthens with options (Hick's law); in a sprint start, reactions faster than 0.1 s are treated as anticipatory movement and ruled a false start (the IAAF/World Athletics rule) - a real-world application of anticipation shortening RT. Anticipation types applied: temporal - predicting WHEN (a striker timing a run off the passer's body shape); spatial - predicting WHERE (a keeper reading the penalty's direction from hip and foot angle) - and the risk: wrong anticipation (a feint) lengthens effective response time via the psychological refractory period, so anticipation is a gamble the experienced performer wins more often - link to cue recognition through practice.

topics.name: Sport Psychology
topics.subject: physical-education
topics.searchText: physical-education Physical Education Sport Psychology Compare trait and interactionist theories of personality and apply the triadic model of attitudes, including changing attitudes via cognitive dissonance (AQA 3.5; OCR 2.2; Edexcel Topic 4) Explain intrinsic and extrinsic motivation and achievement motivation theory (Atkinson and McClelland: NACH/NAF) and achievement goal theory (Nicholls) (AQA 3.5; OCR 2.2) Evaluate arousal theories - drive theory (Hull), inverted U (Yerkes-Dodson), catastrophe model (Fazey and Hardy) and peak flow - and apply anxiety management techniques (AQA 3.5; OCR 2.2) Distinguish trait and state anxiety, their measurement, and explain theories and control of aggression (AQA 3.5; OCR 2.2) Explain social facilitation (Zajonc, evaluation apprehension) and group dynamics: Steiner's model, the Ringelmann effect and social loafing (AQA 3.5; OCR 2.2) Apply goal setting (outcome/performance/process, SMART), Weiner's attribution theory with retraining, and Bandura's four sources of self-efficacy (AQA 3.5; OCR 2.2) Personality: trait theory (stable, innate) vs interactionist (Lewin B = f(P,E)); Hollander's layers - psychological core, typical responses, role-related behaviour Attitudes: triadic model (cognitive, affective, behavioural); changed by cognitive dissonance (Festinger) and persuasive communication (source, message, situation, recipient) Arousal: drive theory (linear, dominant response), inverted U (optimal point, lower for complex skills), catastrophe (Fazey and Hardy - high cognitive anxiety plus arousal = sudden collapse), peak flow (complete absorption) Anxiety: trait (stable, Spielberger/SCAT) vs state (situational); cognitive vs somatic; measured by questionnaires, observation, physiological measures Groups: Steiner - actual = potential - losses (faulty processes: motivation, coordination); Ringelmann effect and social loafing countered by identifiable contributions and roles Attribution (Weiner): locus (internal/external), stability (stable/unstable), control; retrain failure to internal unstable controllable (effort); Bandura self-efficacy: performance accomplishments, vicarious experiences, verbal persuasion, physiological states Interactionist theory Lewin's formula B = f(P, E): behaviour is a function of the personality (traits) and the environment (situation); predicts behaviour better than trait theory alone because traits are expressed differently in different sporting situations. Cognitive dissonance Festinger's technique for changing attitudes: creating a conflict (dissonance) between the components of the triadic model so the performer changes beliefs or behaviour to restore consistency. Achievement motivation Atkinson and McClelland's theory: the drive to succeed (NACH) competes with the fear of failure (NAF); high NACH performers seek challenges with moderate uncertainty, low NAF-dependent performers avoid risk. Inverted U hypothesis Yerkes and Dodson's arousal-performance relationship: performance improves with arousal up to an optimal point, then deteriorates; the optimum is lower for complex/fine skills, higher for simple/gross skills. Catastrophe model Fazey and Hardy's model: when cognitive anxiety (worry) is high, further increases in physiological arousal cause a sudden, catastrophic collapse in performance; recovery requires arousal to fall well below the original level, not just a small reduction. Social loafing The loss of individual effort in a group when contributions cannot be identified; it reduces actual productivity below potential and is countered by identifying individual contributions, roles and goals. Attribution retraining Changing a performer's reasons for failure from internal, stable causes (lack of ability) to internal, unstable, controllable ones (effort, strategy), maintaining expectations of future success and preventing learned helplessness. Self-efficacy Bandura's term for a performer's confidence in their ability to succeed in a specific situation; built from four sources - performance accomplishments, vicarious experiences, verbal persuasion and physiological/emotional states. Personality is the characteristic pattern of behaviour, thoughts and feelings that makes an individual unique. Trait theory holds that personality consists of stable, innate characteristics shown consistently across situations: introverts (quiet, prefer individual sports, low optimal arousal - benefit from calm environments) and extroverts (sociable, arousal-seeking, prefer team and high-arousal situations - benefit from loud environments). Trait theory is simple but cannot explain why behaviour changes between situations - a guaranteed evaluation point. The interactionist approach (Lewin) : behaviour is a function of personality and environment - B = f(P, E) - traits are stable but expressed differently depending on the situation; a calm netball captain may become aggressive in a derby. Hollander's personality structure earns depth: three layers - the psychological core (true values, deepest), typical responses (usual behaviour) and role-related behaviour (surface, situation-dependent). Measuring personality: questionnaires and observation; evaluation: questionnaires can be faked and behaviour is not fully predictable - the exam rewards saying that personality alone is a weak predictor of sporting behaviour. Attitudes are evaluations of people, objects and situations expressed in three components - the triadic model : cognitive (beliefs and knowledge - swimming is good for fitness), affective (feelings and emotions - enjoying swimming) and behavioural (actions - swimming twice a week). Attitudes form through socialisation (parents, peers, coaches) and conditioning (association with positive experiences). Changing attitudes : (1) cognitive dissonance (Festinger) - deliberately creating a conflict between components (a swimmer who believes they dislike training but keeps winning races must change one component to restore consistency, typically their beliefs), pushing the performer to re-evaluate; (2) persuasive communication - changing attitudes by the message itself, effective when the source is credible and significant (elite coach), the message is clear, relevant and balanced , the situation is comfortable , and the recipient is ready to change (low resistance). Evaluation: attitudes are hard to change if all three components are strong and consistent; dissonance works best when components are already in tension - a standard evaluation point. Motivation is the internal drive and external pressures that direct and sustain behaviour. Intrinsic motivation (from within - enjoyment, satisfaction, mastery, pride) is more durable and linked to long-term participation; extrinsic motivation (from outside - rewards, prizes, praise, avoidance of punishment) works quickly but can undermine intrinsic motivation if overused - the overjustification effect : tangible rewards (money) can replace enjoyment as the reason for playing, and when the reward stops, participation stops - the guaranteed evaluation of reward schemes. Best practice: use extrinsic rewards initially, then shift to intrinsic satisfaction, making rewards informational (feedback on competence) rather than controlling. Achievement motivation theory (Atkinson and McClelland) : motivation to achieve results is the interaction between the need to achieve (NACH) and the need to avoid failure (NAF) , modified by the probability of success and the incentive value of success. High-NACH performers approach achievement situations, seek challenges with moderate risk (uncertain outcomes raise incentive value) and persist after failure; high-NAF performers avoid risk, choose easy tasks (guaranteed success) or very hard ones (no blame for failure), and give up after failure. Developing achievement motivation : attribute success internally (ability, effort), set challenging but reachable goals, provide reinforcement for approach behaviour - links directly to attribution retraining. Achievement goal theory (Nicholls) adds orientation: task-oriented performers judge success against personal mastery (more resilient, sustained motivation) versus ego-oriented performers judging success against others (vulnerable when outperformed); promoting task orientation (mastery climate) sustains motivation - a top-band application. Exam logic: for motivation questions, define intrinsic/extrinsic, give the overjustification evaluation, then link NACH/NAF behaviour to the performer described in the stem. Type Source Advantages Disadvantages Intrinsic Within - enjoyment, satisfaction, mastery, pride Durable; drives long-term participation; resistant to setbacks Slow to develop; can be undermined by over-reward Extrinsic - tangible Prizes, money, medals Fast, powerful motivation for short-term goals Overjustification effect - can replace intrinsic reasons; motivation dies when reward stops Extrinsic - informational Praise, feedback on competence, selection Builds competence and confidence without controlling behaviour Must be genuine and specific - hollow praise loses value Self-determination theory (Deci and Ryan) is the optional depth that separates A* answers: intrinsic motivation is sustained by three needs - autonomy (choice in how to train), competence (feeling effective - link to self-efficacy) and relatedness (connection to others - link to cohesion); coaching that satisfies the three needs builds durable motivation, while controlling coaching (rewards, punishment, pressure) undermines it - the theoretical basis for the informational-rewards strategy. Attitude change worked example : a junior swimmer believes training is pointless (cognitive) but keeps winning (behavioural success). The coach creates cognitive dissonance by pairing training with enjoyable game-based sets and pointing out the race wins that followed training weeks - the conflict between belief and evidence forces the swimmer to change the belief to restore consistency. Persuasive communication factors applied: the source (a respected, elite coach or performer - credibility), the message (clear, relevant, balanced - not one-sided lectures), the situation (comfortable, low-pressure), the recipient (ready to change - low resistance; a strongly attached attitude resists change). Attitude measurement : questionnaires (quick, scalable, but can be faked) and observation of behaviour (real but subjective and time-consuming) - cite both when asked how attitudes are measured. Exam logic: for attitude questions, name the three components, give the change technique (dissonance or persuasion), then apply to the named performer with one evaluation point (strong, consistent attitudes resist change). Personality applied to sport choice - the trait evidence the exam expects: introverts (lower optimal arousal) prefer individual, fine-skill, low-arousal sports (long-distance running, archery, golf) where concentration dominates and arousal stays controlled; extroverts (higher optimal arousal, arousal-seeking) prefer team, gross-skill, high-arousal environments (rugby, football) where excitement is part of the appeal. The correlation is a tendency, not a rule - repeat the caution (interactionist correction) for the evaluation mark. Measuring personality : questionnaires (e.g. EPI-style trait inventories, POMS mood profiling) - quick and scalable but self-report can be faked; observation of behaviour - real but subjective and time-consuming; neither fully predicts performance, so the exam's evaluation is that personality is a weak single predictor - behaviour is better predicted by the interaction of traits and situation. Motivation applied to task choice - the NACH/NAF behaviour the stem expects: a high-NACH performer takes the risky pass, attempts the difficult trick, seeks competition, and persists after failure (approach behaviour); a high-NAF performer takes the safe option, avoids the spotlight, picks easy tasks (or impossible ones where failure carries no blame) and withdraws after setbacks (avoidance behaviour). The coach develops achievement motivation by attributing success internally (ability and effort - link to Weiner), setting challenging-but-reachable goals (moderate probability of success raises incentive value), reinforcing approach behaviour, and reframing failure as information (attribution retraining) - the synthesis across motivation, attribution and goal setting that full-mark answers chain together. Attitude formation : through socialisation (parents, peers, coaches, media role models), conditioning (association of the activity with positive experiences) and familiarity (repeated exposure breeds liking) - cite socialisation as the primary route, then link to the change techniques (dissonance, persuasion) for the full attitude answer. Arousal is the physiological and psychological readiness (activation) of the performer, ranging from deep sleep to high excitement. Four theories, evaluated in pairs: Drive theory (Hull) : performance = habit strength x drive - as arousal increases, performance increases in a linear relationship, but the dominant response is produced: well-learned (expert) dominant responses are correct, so arousal helps experts; novice dominant responses are wrong, so arousal harms novices. Evaluation: predicts a straight line that real performance data do not support (performance declines past a point), but the expert-novice distinction is genuinely useful. Inverted U hypothesis (Yerkes and Dodson) : performance rises with arousal to an optimal point , then declines gradually - too little arousal (under-activated, unmotivated) and too much (over-aroused, tense) both impair performance. The optimum is lower for complex, fine or novel skills (archery, golf putting) and higher for simple, gross or well-learned skills (weightlifting, sprint start) - the required application. Evaluation: better than drive theory (captures the decline), but treats arousal as one-dimensional and cannot explain sudden collapse - which is where the catastrophe model wins. Catastrophe model (Fazey and Hardy) : performance depends on the interaction of physiological arousal and cognitive anxiety (worry). When cognitive anxiety is low , the inverted U holds; when cognitive anxiety is high , rising physiological arousal produces a sudden, catastrophic drop in performance (choking) rather than a gradual decline. Recovery is asymmetric: arousal must fall well below the original optimal point before performance recovers - a subtle but examinable detail. Peak flow (Csikszentmihalyi's flow state ): the ideal state of complete absorption - total focus, effortless automatic performance, sense of control, intrinsic reward - reached when the challenge of the task matches the skill of the performer with optimal arousal. Controlling arousal : somatic (physiological) techniques - progressive muscle relaxation (tense then release muscle groups), breathing control (slow, deep diaphragmatic breathing), biofeedback (monitoring heart rate/sweat to learn control), warm-up routines; cognitive (mental) techniques - mental rehearsal/imagery (visualising successful performance), positive self-talk , goal setting , mindfulness/meditation , attention control (focusing on relevant cues). Match the technique to the type: somatic techniques lower physiological arousal, cognitive techniques lower cognitive anxiety - the exam links them to the catastrophe model's two variables. Anxiety is a negative emotional state with feelings of worry and apprehension. Distinguish the pair precisely: trait anxiety - a stable, inherited disposition to perceive situations as threatening (measured by the SCAT questionnaire); state anxiety - the temporary, situation-specific level of anxiety right now (measured by the STAI/CSAI-2 questionnaires, which separate cognitive anxiety - worry/negative thoughts - from somatic anxiety - physiological symptoms like raised heart rate and butterflies). Measurement (a guaranteed 3-mark list): (1) questionnaires/self-report (SCAT, STAI, CSAI-2 - quick but can be faked); (2) observation of behaviour (visible signs - quick, subjective); (3) physiological measures (heart rate, galvanic skin response, sweat, blood pressure - objective but expensive and the equipment itself can raise anxiety). High trait anxiety performers show more state anxiety in competition - link the two for the application mark. Aggression is deliberate behaviour outside the rules with the intent to harm ; contrast with assertive behaviour - forceful, goal-directed play within the rules with no intent to harm (a hard but fair tackle is assertive; an elbow after the whistle is aggressive). Types: hostile aggression (deliberate harm, anger-driven, e.g. retaliation) and instrumental aggression (harm used as a means to a goal - a late tackle to stop a scorer, harm accepted though not the aim). Theories : instinct theory (Lorenz/Freud) - aggression is innate, cathartic when released (weakly supported - sport does not reliably reduce aggression); social learning theory (Bandura) - aggression is learned by observing and copying models reinforced for it (the Bobo doll study - children copied observed aggression; cite for the study mark); frustration-aggression hypothesis (Dollard, revised by Berkowitz) - blocked goals create frustration, which can produce aggression (but frustration does not always cause aggression - the revision point). Controlling aggression (a standard list): punishment and sanctions (sin-bin, fines, sending off), codes of conduct and contracts, coach reinforcement of assertive not aggressive play, stress and arousal management, removing performers before frustration escalates, and channelling aggression into assertive effort. Social facilitation is the effect of the presence of others on performance: Zajonc - the presence of others raises arousal and produces the dominant response : helping simple, well-learned skills , hindering complex, novel skills - the same expert/novice logic as drive theory, and the guaranteed application. Triplett's study (cyclists rode faster with co-actors than alone) is the classic evidence citation. Types of presence: co-actors (others performing the same task), passive audience (watching, not judging), evaluative audience - evaluation apprehension (Cottrell) : the presence of others who judge performance raises arousal further and impairs novices most; proximity effect (the closer the audience, the greater the effect). Coping strategies : train with an audience present (habituation), use selective attention to block out the crowd, imagery and positive self-talk, ensure skills are overlearned so the dominant response is correct, and gradually introduce competition pressure - link the strategies back to the dominant-response logic for full marks. Measuring arousal and anxiety - the same toolkit applies to both (arousal is neutral activation, anxiety its negative form): self-report questionnaires (CSAI-2 for competitive state anxiety, separating cognitive and somatic components; STAI for state/trait; SCAT for trait) - quick and cheap but can be faked; observation of behaviour (visible signs - pacing, agitation; quick but subjective); physiological measures (heart rate, galvanic skin response, blood pressure, cortisol) - objective but expensive, and the apparatus itself can raise anxiety (a reactivity evaluation point). Matching arousal strategies to the skill - the applied table the exam links to the inverted U: Skill type Optimal arousal Strategies Complex, fine, novel (archery, golf putt, snooker) Lower - must stay calm and controlled Progressive muscle relaxation, slow breathing, imagery, mindfulness, routine Simple, gross, well-learned (sprint start, weightlifting, rugby scrum) Higher - can be psyched up Music, psych-up self-talk, pep talks, imagery of power, warm-up intensity Expert performing well-learned skills Higher - dominant response is correct Arousal raised; overlearning protects the dominant response Novice performing new skills Lower - dominant response is wrong Calm environment; arousal managed down; simple cues Evaluation apprehension depth (Cottrell): an audience that merely watches raises arousal modestly; an audience that judges (selectors, examiners, scouts) raises it far more - explaining why trials and assessments are the worst-case scenario for novices; the proximity effect (the closer and larger the audience, the greater the effect) and the type of audience (supportive versus hostile) complete the picture. Strategies to combat social inhibition : habituation training (practising with audiences present until the presence stops raising arousal), selective attention (focusing on task cues, blocking the crowd), imagery and positive self-talk, ensuring skills are overlearned (dominant response correct), and gradual exposure to competition pressure. Exam logic: for social facilitation questions, state Zajonc's dominant-response logic, name the audience types (co-actors, passive, evaluative), then match strategies to the performer - habituation and overlearning for novices, selective attention for experts facing hostile crowds. Peak flow characteristics (Csikszentmihalyi) - the detail that completes arousal answers: the flow state combines total absorption in the task, effortless automatic performance, a strong sense of control , distorted time perception, and intrinsic reward - reached when the challenge of the task matches the skill of the performer with optimal arousal and no distraction. The practical implication: flow is engineered by matching challenge to skill (goals slightly above current ability), removing distractions (attention control), and rehearsed routines - link it to goal setting and selective attention for the synthesis mark. Aggression distinctions applied : a two-footed lunge after the whistle is hostile aggression (intent to harm, anger-driven); a late but ball-winning tackle in a cup final is instrumental aggression (harm as a means, the goal the aim); a ferocious but legal 50-50 challenge is assertive behaviour (forceful, within the rules, no intent to harm). The channelled aggression concept completes it: performers with aggressive tendencies (high trait arousal, extroverts) can have their energy channelled into assertive, legal intensity by coaching - the constructive use of aggression that separates good coaching from suppression. Groups and teams : a group is two or more people with a shared goal and interaction; a team adds shared identity, interdependence and collective accountability - a relay squad is a group, a netball seven is a team. Steiner's model explains why teams often underperform: actual productivity = potential productivity - losses due to faulty processes . Potential productivity is the best possible output from the group's resources and the task demands; faulty processes are (1) motivation losses - reduced individual effort (social loafing) and (2) coordination losses - poor interaction, timing and communication (a relay changeover dropped, a defence failing to mark). Application logic: identify whether the losses in the question stem are motivational (effort) or coordination (interaction) - the mark scheme distinguishes them. The Ringelmann effect : as group size increases, individual productivity decreases (Ringelmann's rope-pulling study: individuals pulled less hard in larger groups) - coordination losses grow with size. Social loafing : the loss of individual motivation when contributions cannot be identified (a footballer walking in defence because no one will notice). Strategies to counter losses (a guaranteed list): make individual contributions identifiable (statistics, individual roles), set individual and group goals , assign clear roles and responsibilities, build cohesion , reward individual effort, use video analysis to highlight individual input, and select committed performers. Cohesion is the tendency of a group to stick together and remain united in pursuing goals: task cohesion (unity toward the task - most predictive of team performance) versus social cohesion (unity of relationships - matters for sustained participation). Carron's factors affecting cohesion: personal (individual motivation, satisfaction), team (shared goals, success, ability), leadership (coach style, decision-making), environmental (group size, time together, facilities). Building cohesion (top-band application): team goal setting, role clarification, social activities, reducing group size where possible, uniform and identity. Cohesion relates to performance positively, especially task cohesion in interactive sports - a discrimination point (co-active sports like swimming need less social cohesion). Goal setting directs and sustains motivation. Types : outcome goals (the result - winning the league; motivating but not fully controllable - opponents determine them), performance goals (standards relative to own previous performance - 800 m personal best, 90% first-serve; fully controllable, best for building confidence), process goals (the technique/actions - keep the elbow high in the serve; most useful for correcting technique and maintaining focus). SMART principles: goals must be Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Realistic and Time-bound ; set short-term goals (laddering toward the long-term goal) with regular review. Functions: directs attention to relevant cues, mobilises effort, builds persistence, develops new strategies, and raises confidence through measured success - match the goal type to the performer's need for the application mark. Attribution theory (Weiner) explains how performers explain success and failure, along three dimensions: locus (internal - within the performer, e.g. ability/effort; external - outside, e.g. task difficulty/luck), stability (stable - unlikely to change; unstable - changeable) and control (controllable or not by the performer). The four classic attributions: ability (internal, stable, uncontrollable), effort (internal, unstable, controllable), task difficulty (external, stable, uncontrollable) and luck (external, unstable, uncontrollable).
