Effects on motivation : attributing success to internal, stable causes (ability) sustains confidence and expectation of future success; attributing failure to internal, stable causes (lack of ability) destroys motivation and produces learned helplessness (Seligman) - the belief that failure is inevitable, so effort is withdrawn. Attribution retraining (the guaranteed application): the coach changes failure attributions to internal, unstable, controllable causes - effort and strategy - so the performer retains the expectation that change is possible, maintains motivation, and moves from learned helplessness to a mastery orientation (persisting after setbacks). Self-serving bias (attributing success internally, failure externally) protects confidence short-term - an optional depth point. Self-efficacy (Bandura) : a performer's confidence in their ability to succeed in a specific situation - distinct from general self-confidence; it predicts the tasks chosen, effort, persistence and resilience. Four sources , in order of influence (a guaranteed 4-mark list): (1) performance accomplishments - the most powerful source: actual success builds efficacy (structured success experiences, achievable goals - link to goal setting); (2) vicarious experiences - observing a similar other succeed (watching a comparable player succeed raises the belief that one can too - link to social learning/ARMD); (3) verbal persuasion - encouragement from significant others (credible coaches, positive self-talk); (4) physiological and emotional states - interpreting arousal and feelings positively (butterflies read as readiness rather than fear - link to anxiety management). High self-efficacy performers attempt harder challenges and persist; low self-efficacy performers avoid risk and give up - Vealey's sport confidence adds the trait (trait sport confidence) versus state (competitive orientation) distinction for depth. Exam logic: for attribution and self-efficacy questions, name the theorist, give the dimensions/sources precisely, then apply to the performer in the stem with a strategy the coach uses. The Ringelmann study in detail : individuals pulling a rope alone pulled at 100% effort, but as group size grew the individual contribution fell (to roughly half in groups of eight) - Ringelmann attributed this to coordination losses (pulling is not perfectly synchronised) and motivation losses (effort disperses). This is the classic evidence citation for both the Ringelmann effect and social loafing - quote it when a study is required. Steiner applied to task types : interactive tasks (netball, football - team members depend on each other) suffer most from coordination losses (poor timing, communication, tactics - a dropped relay changeover, a failed defensive line) so the remedies are structural: roles, drills, cohesion, communication systems; co-active tasks (rowing eight, relay, cycling team pursuit - individuals perform alongside each other) suffer most from motivation losses (social loafing - effort disperses because contributions blur), so the remedies are motivational: identifiable contributions, individual goals, individual statistics. The exam rewards matching the loss type to the task type - the most common lost mark is prescribing cohesion drills for a co-active sport. Goal setting worked example : a 400 m runner targeting the county final. Outcome goal : reach the county final (motivating, but not fully controllable - opponents determine it). Performance goal : reduce the personal best by 1.5 seconds within 8 weeks (fully controllable, builds confidence). Process goal : keep the arm action tall and relaxed through the final 100 m (technique focus, corrects the mechanism). All three must be SMART - specific, measurable, achievable, realistic, time-bound - and laddered : short-term process goals feed the mid-term performance goal feeds the long-term outcome goal, with regular review to adjust. Learned helplessness versus mastery orientation (Seligman): learned helplessness is the belief that failure is inevitable (attributed to internal, stable, uncontrollable causes - 'I am not good enough'), so effort is withdrawn; a mastery orientation persists after setbacks (failure attributed to internal, unstable, controllable causes - effort and strategy). Self-serving bias - attributing success internally (ability) and failure externally (luck, officials) - protects confidence short-term but blocks learning: the coach should retrain both success and failure attributions honestly. Exam logic: for attribution questions, dimensions first, then the motivational consequence, then retraining as the application; for group questions, Steiner first, then the loss type matched to the task, then strategies matched to the loss.

topics.name: Socio-cultural Issues in Sport
topics.subject: physical-education
topics.searchText: physical-education Physical Education Socio-cultural Issues in Sport Describe the characteristics of pre-industrial popular recreations and contrast them with rationalised post-industrial sport, including the role of the public schools (AQA 3.6; OCR 3.1; Edexcel Topic 5) Explain rationalisation and codification: governing bodies, leagues, respectability and the spread of sport through universities, the army and the railways (AQA 3.6; OCR 3.1) Evaluate globalisation, commercialisation and the media, including the golden triangle and the effects on performers, sport and spectators (AQA 3.6; OCR 3.1) Explain ethics and deviance: sportsmanship, gamesmanship, contract to win, drug use and the role of WADA, and match fixing (AQA 3.6; OCR 3.1) Explain causes and control of player and crowd violence, and forms of discrimination (sexism, racism, disability) with initiatives (AQA 3.6; OCR 3.1) Outline routes to sporting excellence: talent identification, the performance pyramid, and the roles of UK Sport, TASS and national governing bodies (AQA 3.6; OCR 3.1) Popular recreations: natural/simple, local, occasional, severe, ritual, wagering; caused by poor transport, illiteracy, rural life Post-industrial sport: urbanisation initially damaged sport, then railways, Factory Acts (Saturday half-day) and middle-class leadership enabled rational recreation Public schools: muscular Christianity (playing sport builds character), codification, the melting pot, spread via universities, church, army and railways (old boys) Golden triangle: sport - sponsorship - media interdependence; positives (money, profile, participation) and negatives (scheduling, advertising control, win-at-all-costs) Deviance: sportsmanship vs gamesmanship vs contract to win; drugs explained by pressure/money, controlled by WADA/UKAD testing and the prohibited list Routes to excellence: grassroots - club - county - regional - national; UK Sport funds elite (lottery), TASS supports dual-career athletes, NGBs run talent identification Popular recreation Pre-industrial (pre-1800) village sports and pastimes: natural/simple, local, occasional (holy days and festivals), severe (violent), ritualistic and wagering-based, played largely by the rural lower classes. Rationalisation The transformation of sport from occasional, violent, local popular recreations into organised, codified, regular, national competition under governing bodies and written rules in post-industrial Britain. Golden triangle The interdependent relationship between sport, sponsorship and the media: sport provides content and profile, media pay for broadcasting rights, sponsors buy exposure - each side profits from the other two. Commercialisation The treatment of sport as a business commodity: generating income through sponsorship, advertising, broadcasting rights, gate receipts and merchandising, with success increasingly measured by financial return. Globalisation The worldwide spread of sport through shared codified rules, international governing bodies and events, global media coverage and performer migration, making sport a global cultural commodity. Gamesmanship Winning by whatever means - bending the rules without breaking them (time-wasting, sledging, professional fouls); contrasted with sportsmanship (playing fairly and honourably) and the contract to win (all-out commitment to victory). WADA The World Anti-Doping Agency (founded 1999): writes the World Anti-Doping Code, maintains the prohibited list, coordinates testing and sanctions offenders in partnership with national anti-doping organisations like UKAD. Positive discrimination Policies or targets that deliberately favour under-represented groups (women, ethnic minorities, disabled people) in participation, coaching and leadership to correct historical imbalance. Pre-industrial Britain (before ~1800) : sport took the form of popular recreations - village games and pastimes whose characteristics are a guaranteed 6-mark list: (1) natural/simple - played with natural materials (animal bladders, sticks) and without equipment; (2) local - confined to individual villages with differing rules; (3) occasional - tied to holy days, festivals and wakes rather than regular fixtures; (4) severe - violent and rough (mob football, animal baiting, cudgelling); (5) ritual - linked to religious and agricultural calendar customs; (6) wagering - heavy betting surrounded contests; plus courtly/popular divide : the upper classes pursued exclusive pursuits (real tennis, hunting, fencing) while peasants played village games. Causes of the characteristics (the exam rewards the explanation): limited transport and communications (games stayed local, rules never unified), illiteracy (rules were unwritten, passed by word of mouth), harsh rural poverty and long agricultural hours (sport only on holy days), and class separation (two-tier sport). Classic examples to cite: mob football (village versus village, hundreds of players, minimal rules, damage to property - repeatedly banned by authorities) and mob/bare-knuckle prize fighting with wagering. Post-industrial Britain (1800-1900) : the industrial revolution first damaged traditional sport - urbanisation moved workers into crowded towns with no space or fields; long factory hours (12-hour days, seven-day weeks) destroyed free time; child labour and low wages removed energy and money; the loss of village life killed local traditions; lack of space and squalor limited play. The urban lower classes initially had neither the time, money, space nor health to participate - the standard explain point. Then, through the century, conditions improved and sport was transformed: the Factory Acts and the Saturday half-day (from the 1840s-50s) created regular free time; rising wages and cheap excursions gave money and access; the railways made fixtures between towns possible; middle-class employers and the church encouraged respectability; urban parks and provisions created space. The public schools were the engine of rationalisation and are a guaranteed extended-response topic. Stage the development: (1) bullying and brutality (early 1800s - fagging, mob rule, uncontrolled games); (2) control by trust (headmasters like Thomas Arnold at Rugby used older boys and team games to control energy - games became regulated); (3) athleticism - muscular Christianity : the belief that playing team games developed manly Christian character (courage, leadership, fairness) - playing hard and fair; (4) codification : each school wrote rules for its own version (Rugby football, Eton's Field Game), and the universities then became the melting pot where old boys from different schools agreed common rules - leading to national governing bodies such as the FA (1863) , separating Association football from Rugby; (5) spread : old boys carried codified games into the universities, church (church teams), the army (regimental sport), industry (works teams) and abroad via the empire , plus the railways moving teams - the standard explain sequence for how modern sport spread nationally and internationally. Rational recreation replaced popular recreation with sport whose characteristics mirror and invert the old list: regionally/nationally organised; regular league and cup fixtures; codified under governing bodies with written rules; exclusive (amateur ideals excluding professionals); controlled/disciplined (referees, sanctions); respectable . The amateur-professional divide matters for the class dimension: the middle and upper classes played as gentlemen amateurs (sport for character), the working classes became paid professionals (sport as livelihood); professionalism was initially banned from amateur clubs (a discrimination point that later reversed). The exam frequently sets a popular-versus-rational comparison table - prepare characteristics side by side with the industrial causes behind each change. Characteristic Popular recreation (pre-industrial) Rational recreation (post-industrial) Place Local - individual villages Regional/national - leagues across towns Rules Unwritten, varied by village Codified by governing bodies (FA 1863) Frequency Occasional - holy days, festivals Regular - weekly fixtures and leagues Conduct Severe, violent, unruly Controlled, disciplined, officiated, respectable Class Peasant games; courtly pursuits above Middle-class amateur ideals; working-class professionals Purpose Ritual, wagering, celebration Character building, fitness, organised competition The rationalisation timeline in detail - the dates and bodies that earn precision marks: the Football Association (1863) codified Association football and separated it from handling games; the Rugby Football Union (1871) codified rugby, and the 1895 northern breakaway (the Northern Union, later rugby league) split the professional working-class north from the amateur south over payments for 'broken time' - the clearest class dimension in codification; the Amateur Athletic Club (1866) defined an amateur as one who had never competed for money nor for a prize open to professionals - explicitly excluding manual workers, the gentleman-amateur ideal in law; the LTA (1888) codified lawn tennis. Supporting infrastructure: railway excursion trains carried teams and spectators to cup ties (the FA Cup, from 1871-2, was the first national competition); the Factory Acts (the 1847 Ten Hours Act and the Saturday half-day from the 1850s) created regular leisure time; public parks and public baths legislation provided urban space and swimming provision; church movements (temperance societies, church lads' brigades) promoted sport as respectable recreation, spreading muscular Christianity; works teams (factory-employer clubs, several later becoming league clubs) gave the working classes organised sport. Women's exclusion in Victorian sport is the discrimination link-back: Victorian medical myths claimed exercise harmed female health; restrictive dress (corsetry, full skirts) excluded physical activity; women were barred from clubs, competitions and the professions; acceptable activities were limited to croquet, lawn tennis and archery. The exam links this to modern sexism: the historical exclusion explains today's participation, prize-money and leadership gaps - quote the continuity for the synthesis mark. Amateurism versus professionalism completed the class story: amateurs (middle and upper class) valued taking part and character; professionals (working class) played for a livelihood; amateur bodies banned professionals (the Olympic amateur code persisted until 1980s reform) - the reversal of that ban is the bridge to modern commercialisation: once professionals were admitted, sport became a career, and commercial money followed - a synthesis point that links the two sections of this topic. The 'weekend' and leisure time is the structural change behind rational recreation: the Factory Acts and union pressure created the Saturday half-day (from the 1850s), giving the working classes a regular afternoon of free time - the direct precondition for Saturday league fixtures (the Football League, 1888, built its whole structure on it) and for spectator crowds. Transport detail : railways first moved teams (inter-town fixtures), then spectators (cheap excursion trains to cup ties), then trophies and news (results printed nationally, feeding support and rivalry) - cite all three movements for the transport mark. The church and army as spreaders : church lads' brigades and temperance societies promoted sport as respectable, alcohol-free recreation (muscular Christianity applied to the urban working class); regimental sport spread games through the army (garrisons playing codified sport at home and across the empire); public schools supplied the old boys who ran the new clubs and governing bodies - the full spread network: universities, church, army, industry, railways, empire. Female exclusion detail : lawn tennis and croquet were tolerated as 'suitable' because they required little strength, dress modification or public display; competitive and contact sport was barred - the origin of the participation gap the modern initiatives (This Girl Can, coverage growth) address; quote the continuity for the synthesis mark. Exam logic: for popular recreation questions, list characteristics with examples (mob football) and explain the causes (transport, illiteracy, class); for public school questions, stage the sequence (brutality, control, athleticism/muscular Christianity, codification, melting pot, spread) and name Arnold and the FA; for comparison questions, match each rational characteristic to the industrial change that produced it. Globalisation is the worldwide spread and interconnection of sport: codified rules adopted globally, international governing bodies (FIFA, IOC, World Athletics) regulating worldwide competition, global events (Olympic Games, football World Cup), global media coverage and the migration of performers, coaches and capital across borders. Effects the exam rewards: shared global sporting culture (the same sports, stars and brands everywhere); worldwide talent markets (players move to the best leagues - the Premier League recruits globally); growth of sport in new regions (women's football, T20 cricket); but also negative evaluations : cultural homogenisation (minority national sports squeezed out), the talent drain from developing nations to wealthy leagues, and the dominance of a few sports, leagues and sponsors. Link globalisation to the history: codification and the empire's spread of sport in the 19th century was the first globalisation wave; satellite television and digital streaming made the second - a synthesis point that separates A* answers. Commercialisation is sport run as business: income from sponsorship, advertising, broadcasting rights, gate receipts and merchandising . The golden triangle is the guaranteed diagram-and-explain item: sport (content, performers, profile), media (pays for rights, broadcasts to audiences) and sponsorship (buys exposure to those audiences) - a mutually dependent relationship where each increases the value of the other two. Explain the mechanism: media pay billions for rights because advertisers pay for the audience; sponsors pay clubs and performers for the exposure media deliver; sport reinvests in facilities, wages and technology. Quote realistic figures or examples where possible (Premier League broadcasting deals, shirt sponsorship, the Olympics' TOP sponsorship programme) - precision earns marks. The media - types: television, radio, press, internet, streaming and social media (performers build personal brands directly). Positive effects on sport : massive income and investment (facilities, player wages, grass-roots funding via the Football Foundation model); raised profile and participation (visibility drives uptake - women's sport coverage growth); improved officiating and fairness through technology (VAR, TMO, Hawk-Eye, photo finishes); rule changes for excitement (T20 cricket, tie-breaks); global audience growth. Negative effects : scheduling changes for TV (kick-off times moved for broadcast windows - inconvenience to spectators and performers); breaks in play for advertising (commercialised formats); advertiser control (naming rights, kit obligations); loss of tradition (motorsport street circuits, franchise moves); win-at-all-costs pressure flowing from the financial stakes (linking to deviance); and unequal distribution (media money concentrates on few sports, starving minority and disability sport - the equity evaluation). Effects on performers : dramatically higher incomes (prize money, wages, personal sponsorship); fame and profile through social media; but pressure and scrutiny (24/7 coverage, performance anxiety - link to sport psychology), privacy loss, and being traded/controlled by media value. Effects on spectators : wider access (global broadcast, streaming, highlights); improved viewing technology (multiple angles, statistics); but rising costs (subscription channels - Sky/TNT - versus free-to-air tradition; the listed events rule protecting events like the FA Cup final and Olympics for free TV is a good depth point), ticket price inflation from commercial demand, and kick-off times moved for television. Effects on the sport itself : financial dependence on media money (club finances tied to broadcast deals - a fragility evaluation: if rights income falls, wage bills collapse); rule and format changes; commercialisation of previously amateur events. Affected Positives Negatives Performers High incomes (wages, prize money, sponsorship); global profile via social media; better facilities and support Pressure and scrutiny (24/7 coverage, performance anxiety); loss of privacy; controlled by sponsors and media value; personal brand demanded Sport Investment in facilities, technology and grass roots; raised profile and participation; improved officiating (VAR, Hawk-Eye) Rule and format changes for entertainment; fragile finances tied to rights income; media money concentrated on few sports, starving minority and disability sport Spectators Global access via broadcast and streaming; multiple angles, statistics, highlights; improved coverage of women's sport Subscription costs (paywall migration); ticket price inflation; kick-off times moved for TV windows; loss of the shared free-to-air occasion The listed events rule is the depth point on spectator rights: UK regulation protects certain events (the FA Cup final, the Olympics, the Grand National, the Wimbledon finals) for free-to-air television , preventing them being locked behind paywalls - quote it as the counterweight to full commercialisation. Social media deserves its own evaluation: performers build personal brands and direct income streams (bypassing traditional media); clubs and sports reach younger audiences; but 24/7 scrutiny brings online abuse , pressure to maintain the brand, and distraction from performance - the exam rewards both sides. Globalisation examples to cite: performers migrating to the best leagues (worldwide recruitment into the Premier League); overseas ownership of clubs; global transfer markets and wage inflation; the talent drain from developing nations (athletes and footballers leaving systems that invested in them); worldwide growth of women's football and franchise formats (T20 cricket) - evidence that globalisation spreads opportunity and dilutes tradition in the same movement. The golden triangle applied - the worked example that scores: the Premier League sells broadcasting rights (media pay billions for exclusive coverage); broadcasters sell the audience to advertisers; sponsors pay clubs for shirt and stadium naming rights to reach that audience; the club reinvests in players and facilities (raising the product's quality, raising rights value again) - the self-reinforcing loop of the triangle. The Olympic TOP programme applies the same loop globally: worldwide sponsors (category-exclusive) fund the Games and the governing body, buying global exposure across broadcast windows. Media highlight culture : coverage now privileges spectacular, high-scoring, fast formats - a selection pressure on sport itself (rule changes for excitement: T20 cricket, shootouts, shot clocks) - the media shaping the sport, not just reporting it, is the deepest evaluation point. Paralympic coverage growth is the positive counter-example: Channel 4's coverage since 2012 transformed visibility and participation in disability sport - evidence that media exposure changes participation when it is deliberately targeted; contrast with minority sports still starved of coverage (the equity evaluation in one sentence). Exam logic: for commercialisation questions, draw or describe the golden triangle, then evaluate: positives (investment, profile, participation, technology) against negatives (scheduling, control, inequity, win-at-all-costs), and finish with a judgement (commercialisation has transformed sport's quality and reach, but its benefits are unevenly distributed and its pressures feed deviance). For media questions, separate the effects on sport, performers and spectators - the mark schemes allocate marks across the three, so structuring the answer that way guarantees full coverage. Ethics in sport : sportsmanship - playing fairly, observing the rules and courtesy in victory and defeat; gamesmanship - winning by bending the rules without breaking them (time-wasting, sledging, professional fouls, distracting opponents); the contract to win - the modern expectation that performers give all-out commitment to victory, which critics argue has eroded sportsmanship. Deviance is behaviour outside accepted norms - on a spectrum from acceptable assertiveness to cheating. The exam frames ethics questions on this spectrum: identify where the behaviour sits (sportsmanship, gamesmanship, cheating), explain the cause (pressure to win, financial stakes, role models) and evaluate (some gamesmanship is tolerated by officials and crowds - a realism point). Drugs and doping : reasons performers dope (a guaranteed explain list): the win-at-all-costs ethos and pressure from coaches, nation and self; enormous financial rewards for success; belief that rivals dope (arms-race logic); weak perceived risk of detection; pressure to recover from injury. Types to name: anabolic steroids (muscle mass, strength - health risks: liver damage, aggression), blood doping and EPO (raise red cell count and oxygen carriage - endurance; risks: thickened blood, clots), stimulants (alertness), beta blockers (steady fine-motor skills in precision sports), peptide hormones and gene doping as modern frontiers. WADA (World Anti-Doping Agency, 1999) writes the World Anti-Doping Code , maintains the prohibited list , coordinates testing (random, targeted, in and out of competition; the athlete biological passport) and sanctions (bans, stripped titles) via national bodies - in the UK, UKAD . Evaluation: testing has limits (new substances outpace detection; unequal testing resources between nations), but the biological passport and athlete whereabouts rules have tightened the net - a balanced judgement earns the top band. The legalisation debate is a classic evaluation: for legalisation (levelling the field under medical supervision, ending hypocrisy over permitted enhancements) against (health risks, unfairness to clean athletes, undermines the meaning of sport) - know both sides. Match fixing : fixing outcomes or spot-fixing individual events (no-balls, bookings) for betting syndicates or results advantages; causes: betting markets (in-play betting created new fixing opportunities), low-paid performers in weakly governed leagues, weak regulation and detection; consequences: lifetime bans, criminal prosecution (criminal law has been applied to fixing), erosion of trust in results - name a case type (cricket spot-fixing, tennis betting investigations) for the application mark. Control: stricter regulation, betting-integrity monitoring, education, severe sanctions. Violence : player violence - causes (a guaranteed explain list): instinct theory (Lorenz) - innate aggressive drive released in sport; frustration-aggression hypothesis (Dollard/Berkowitz) - blocked goals (losing, poor refereeing) create frustration that erupts; social learning (Bandura) - copying aggressive role models reinforced for violence (cite the Bobo doll study); plus situational causes - importance of the result, rivalries, crowd provocation, officials' weakness, arousal levels (link to sport psychology - the same dominant-response logic). Crowd violence/hooliganism : historical peak in British football in the 1970s-80s; causes: ritualised and territorial behaviour, group dynamics (deindividuation in crowds), alcohol, segregation failures, media hype of rivalries; control measures: all-seater stadia (post-Taylor Report after Hillsborough), segregation, alcohol bans, CCTV and banning orders, policing, and ticket pricing. Control of player violence: codes of conduct, sanctions (cards, sin-bin, retrospective video punishment), officials' authority, technology (VAR/TMO), coach modelling of assertive play, and arousal management - link psychology and sociology for the synthesis mark. Discrimination : sexism - historical exclusion of women (Victorian medical myths about female frailty), persisting gaps in participation, prize money (pay gaps in many sports), coaching and leadership representation, and media coverage (women's sport historically under-broadcast - though coverage has grown sharply); initiatives: This Girl Can (Sport England), equal prize money at the Grand Slams in tennis, growth of women's leagues. Racism - abuse in stadia and online, stereotyping by position, and under-representation in coaching and boardrooms (the Rooney Rule-style initiatives); initiatives: Kick It Out , Show Racism the Red Card , sanction regimes. Disability - access barriers (facilities, transport, cost), segregation of para-sport from mainstream, coaching provision; initiatives: inclusive fitness equipment, the Paralympic movement's profile effect, disability NGB programmes. Positive discrimination (quotas and targets) is the evaluation battleground: for (corrects embedded imbalance, speeds change) against (merit concerns, tokenism) - a balanced conclusion earns the top band. Routes to sporting excellence : the performance pyramid - grass-roots/foundation (school, primary competition), participation (club, community), performance (county, regional, academy), excellence (national, international). Talent identification (TID) : NGB-run scouting and testing (e.g. football academies from age 8; the EIS/UK Sport power2perform-style profiling), school-club links and the School Games . Key organisations and funding (a guaranteed name-and-role list): UK Sport - distributes lottery funding to elite sport on a no-compromise medal model; Sport England - grass-roots participation; English Institute of Sport (EIS) - sports science and medicine support to elite performers; TASS (Talented Athlete Scholarship Scheme) - supports dual-career athletes (education plus training); national governing bodies (NGBs) - run talent pathways, academies and coaching structures. Exam logic: name the organisation and its role in one line each; for evaluation, note the medal-focus critique (funding concentrated on medal-chance sports starves others) and the dual-career balance point - that pairing reliably completes a 6-mark route-to-excellence answer. Class of substance/method Effect Typical sport/example Stimulants Alertness, reduced fatigue Endurance and combat sports Narcotic analgesics Pain masking (compete through injury) Contact sports Anabolic steroids Muscle mass, strength, faster recovery; risks - liver damage, aggression, hormonal damage Strength/power events Peptide hormones (EPO, growth hormone) Raised red cell count / growth; endurance gains; risks - thickened blood, clots Cycling, distance running Beta blockers Steady hands, lowered heart rate Precision sports - shooting, archery, snooker Blood doping Transfusion raises red cell count and oxygen carriage Endurance sport Masking agents/diuretics Hide other substances; flush the system Used to evade testing Crowd control history in detail : the peak of British football hooliganism (1970s-80s) - ritualised, territorial clashes, group dynamics and deindividuation (anonymity in the crowd reduces personal responsibility - link to social loafing's cousin concept), alcohol, and media hype of rivalries; the Hillsborough disaster (1989) and the Taylor Report produced all-seater stadia , segregation, alcohol bans, CCTV and banning orders - the standard explain-and-control sequence; modern digital abuse extends the issue (online racial abuse of performers - link to discrimination). Discrimination initiatives expanded : This Girl Can (Sport England's participation campaign for women - normalising female sport at every level); Kick It Out and Show Racism the Red Card (education and reporting in football); women's sport coverage growth (dedicated broadcast deals) raising the profile-participation cycle; the Paralympic Games' profile effect (visibility of disability sport driving participation and provision); inclusive facilities programmes. Talent identification in detail : NGB-run academies (football category systems from young ages), performance profiling (testing against event-specific benchmarks), the English Institute of Sport providing science and medicine to funded athletes, TASS supporting dual-career athletes at university, and the School Games feeding the pyramid. Evaluation depth: the medal-focused funding model (UK Sport's no-compromise approach) delivers medals but concentrates money on a few sports - the equity critique that reliably completes a route-to-excellence answer; dual-career support keeps talented performers in education and the system.

topics.name: Performance Data and NEA
topics.subject: physical-education
topics.searchText: physical-education Physical Education Performance Data and NEA Distinguish quantitative and qualitative analysis of performance and explain notational analysis (AQA NEA; OCR EAPI; Edexcel Topic analysis) Explain validity, reliability, normative data and standardised protocols in performance measurement Describe the NEA structure for each board: practical performance plus analysis and evaluation (AQA 3.7; OCR Component 04; Edexcel Components 3-4) and the mark scheme logic Outline the structure of a written/oral performance analysis: strengths, weaknesses, prioritised weakness, theory explanation, development programme Describe fitness testing protocols (aerobic, speed, power, strength, flexibility, agility, body composition) with advantages and limitations (AQA 3.2; OCR 1.2) Explain data collection methods: primary/secondary data, laboratory versus field testing, recording procedures and pre-test safety Quantitative = numerical and objective (times, counts); qualitative = observed quality judged against a technical model - the NEA needs both Validity = measures what it claims; reliability = repeatable results; both require standardised protocols, calibrated equipment and normative comparison NEA weightings: AQA 7582 - practical 15% + analysis and evaluation 15%; OCR H555 - practical 15% + EAPI oral 15%; Edexcel 9PE0 - practical performance and performance analysis/development programme together 30% Performance analysis structure: overview - strengths justified with data - weaknesses - prioritise the main weakness - explain with theory (physiology, skill acquisition, psychology) - periodised development programme with re-test Fitness tests: multi-stage fitness test/Cooper (aerobic), 30 m sprint (speed), vertical jump (power), 1RM/grip dynamometer (strength), sit-and-reach (flexibility), Illinois (agility), skinfolds/BIA (body composition) Laboratory tests: accurate, controlled, standardised but expensive and less sport-specific; field tests: cheap, accessible, specific but less valid - estimated results Quantitative data Numerical, objective data that can be measured and statistically compared (times, distances, scores, notational counts); contrasted with qualitative data - descriptive judgements about quality of performance. Qualitative analysis Non-numerical evaluation of performance based on observation and judgement - video analysis, coaching observation of technique, movement quality - interpreted against a technical model. Validity A test is valid if it measures what it claims to measure (a VO2 max test is valid for aerobic power); validity is compromised by poor protocols and non-specific tests. Reliability A test is reliable if it produces consistent, repeatable results under the same conditions - standardised protocols, calibrated equipment, the same tester and warm-up. Notational analysis Systematic recording of events during performance (passes, shots, possessions, conversion rates) to produce objective quantitative data for match and player analysis, by hand or computer. EAPI OCR H555's Evaluating and Analysing Performance for Improvement: a 10-minute oral NEA response analysing a performance, identifying and prioritising weaknesses, and proposing a development plan linked to theory. Normative data Published average scores for a population (by age and gender) against which a test result is compared to rate the performer's fitness component. Primary data Data collected first-hand by the performer or coach for the specific purpose (fitness tests, video of the performer); secondary data is pre-existing (published research, opposition statistics). Quantitative data is numerical and objective: times, distances, scores, percentages and counts (a pass-completion rate of 78%, a 30 m sprint time of 4.2 s, six unforced errors). Qualitative data is descriptive and judgemental: observations of movement quality judged against a technical model (the ideal pattern of the skill - e.g. the coaching model for a sprint start: drive phase mechanics, body angles). The exam's key distinction: quantitative answers what happened and how much ; qualitative answers how well it was done and why . A* analysis always combines both: a quantitative observation (low first-serve percentage) triggers qualitative diagnosis (the toss and contact point are inconsistent) - the pairing is what the NEA mark schemes reward. Data types and quality criteria : objective data (measured by instrument, not opinion - timing gates) versus subjective data (observer judgement - a coach's rating of effort). Primary data is collected first-hand for the purpose (your own fitness tests, your own video); secondary data is pre-existing (published research, elite benchmarks, opposition statistics). Two criteria decide whether data can support an evaluation - validity (does the test measure what it claims? a sit-and-reach test measures hamstring flexibility, not overall flexibility - a standard validity limitation) and reliability (would the same test repeated give the same result? ensured by standardised protocols : calibrated equipment, the same tester, the same warm-up and conditions, clear instructions). Normative data - published averages by age and gender - converts a raw score into a rating (a 52 ml/kg/min estimated VO2 max is 'good' for an 18-year-old male against normative tables); the exam rewards naming normative comparison as the way results become meaningful. Notational analysis produces the quantitative backbone of performance analysis: systematically recording events during play - possessions, passes, shots, tackles, conversion rates, errors, time in possession - by hand on a tally sheet or by computer/video tagging systems. Uses: match analysis (team patterns - where possession is lost), player analysis (individual pass completion, shot conversion, work rate), opposition scouting (tendencies to exploit), and objective evidence for the NEA's strengths and weaknesses (a striker's shot conversion of 12% is a defensible quantitative weakness). Advantages : objective, comparable across matches, tracks improvement over time; limitations : counts do not explain why (a low conversion rate may be poor technique, poor shot selection or poor service - qualitative diagnosis follows), data collection is time-consuming, and definitions of events must be consistent for reliability. Performance profiling is the structured route from data to a development programme: assess the performer across components - technical (skills), tactical (decision-making, positioning), physical (fitness components), psychological (confidence, arousal control), physiological (energy systems, body composition) - often displayed as a profile chart of rated strengths. The output identifies which weakness to prioritise: the one that most limits performance and is most improvable within the programme's timescale. This matches the NEA structure directly (see below) - the examiners want data-justified prioritisation, not a list of everything wrong. Correlation supports the analysis: a positive correlation (both variables rise together - e.g. training hours and VO2 max), a negative correlation (one rises as the other falls - e.g. body fat percentage and endurance performance) or zero correlation (no relationship). Presented as scatter graphs, correlations justify causal claims cautiously - correlation indicates a relationship but does not prove cause (a classic evaluation point the exam awards): other variables (injury, motivation) may explain the pattern. Use the vocabulary precisely: strong/weak, positive/negative correlation. Presenting data is the examinable skill that turns measurement into analysis: tables for multi-variable comparison (test battery results against norms); bar charts for discrete comparisons (the performer's test scores versus squad norms, component by component); line graphs for change over time (re-test progression across a programme - the visual proof of improvement); scatter graphs for correlation between two variables (training load versus VO2 max, body fat versus endurance time). Every graph needs a title, labelled axes with units, and a stated source - the presentation marks reward correct chart choice as much as correct data: bar charts for categories, line graphs for trends, scatter graphs for relationships. The technical model is the benchmark that makes qualitative analysis objective: the ideal performance pattern for the skill (e.g. the sprint-start model: block angles, drive-phase mechanics, shin angles, arm action), against which video is judged frame by frame. Without a technical model, qualitative analysis is just opinion - the exam rewards naming the model as the standard against which the observed technique is compared. Subjective rating scales support it: Likert-type ratings and the Borg/RPE scale (rate of perceived exertion, 6-20) convert perception into a structured (if subjective) measure of intensity - useful for monitoring training load alongside objective heart-rate data. Reliability of observation is the key evaluation of qualitative data: observation is weaker than instrumentation, so its reliability is raised by structured checklists (predetermined criteria from the technical model), inter-observer agreement (two observers comparing judgements), repeated viewings, and slow-motion/frame-by-frame analysis - quote these when asked how to make qualitative analysis more reliable. Exam logic: for analysis-method questions, define the method, state what it produces (quantitative or qualitative), give the quality criterion (validity, reliability) and the presentation - the four-step chain scores every available mark. Notational sheet structure - the practical detail for data-collection answers: columns for each event (passes attempted, completed, tackles won, turnovers, shots, goals), rows for time periods or players, tallies recorded live or from video afterwards, definitions agreed before recording (what counts as a 'pass completed' - reaching the intended teammate under no pressure) so the data is reliable; totals converted to rates (pass completion percentage, conversion rate) for comparison against squad norms and previous matches. Video evidence in the NEA : record the performer in realistic conditions (competition, not drills - or the data is unrepresentative), capture long clips (several attempts, not one), and edit to the relevant moments; stills from video placed beside the technical model justify the qualitative claims visually. Objective versus subjective examples : objective - timing gates, GPS distance, heart rate, notational tallies; subjective - coach ratings of effort or quality, RPE scores, Likert ratings of confidence - both are used, but objective data anchors the analysis and subjective data explains it. Exam logic: for data questions, define the type (quantitative/qualitative, valid/reliable, primary/secondary), give a sporting example, and state the consequence for analysis - e.g. unreliable data cannot track improvement; invalid data cannot support the chosen conclusion. The most common lost marks are (1) confusing validity with reliability and (2) forgetting that qualitative diagnosis must follow quantitative observation. All three boards assess a non-exam assessment (NEA) worth 30% of the A-level, split into practical performance and a performance-analysis task - know your board's exact shape: AQA 7582 : practical performance in one activity as a player/performer, coach or official (15%), plus the analysis and evaluation of performance - a written piece identifying a weakness in the chosen or a different activity and devising a corrective programme (15%). OCR H555 : practical performance (15%) plus the EAPI - Evaluating and Analysing Performance for Improvement: a 10-minute oral response to unseen video of a performer, analysing strengths and weaknesses, prioritising, and proposing a development plan (15%). Edexcel 9PE0 : practical performance plus the performance analysis and performance development programme (together 30%). The written/oral analysis is marked against the same three objectives as the exams: AO1 (accurate theoretical knowledge), AO2 (application to the performer), AO3 (analysis and evaluation - justification and prioritisation). The universal structure of a full-mark analysis - learn it as a sequence: (1) Overview : the performer, their sport, position/event, level and aims - brief, factual; (2) Strengths : identified through observation, video and data (notational counts, fitness test results) and justified with theory - e.g. a strong aerobic base (above-normative multi-stage fitness test score) underpins the midfielder's repeated sprints; (3) Weaknesses : identified the same way - technical (video shows inconsistent contact point), tactical (notational data shows possession lost in transition), physical (test data below norm), psychological (observation shows anxiety under pressure); (4) Prioritisation : justify which weakness to address first - the one that most limits performance, is most improvable, and is measurable within the programme (the AO3 marks live here); (5) Theoretical explanation : explain the weakness's cause using the specification - a physiological cause (energy system, muscle fibre type, VO2 max), a skill-acquisition cause (information processing, guidance, practice methods, transfer), or a psychological cause (arousal, self-efficacy, attribution) - the theory must be correct and relevant , not decorative; (6) Development programme : a periodised plan (macro/meso/microcycle structure) with specific practices/drills targeting the weakness, measurable targets (SMART goals), and a re-test to evaluate improvement - the closing evaluation loop. What earns the marks (the marking logic that separates A* pieces): data-justified claims at every stage (quote the test score, the notational count, the video observation); theory that is applied, not listed (a weakness explained by anaerobic glycolysis limits plus a targeted interval programme beats a generic 'needs more fitness'); correct prioritisation with justification; and a programme whose exercises clearly target the identified cause with progression. Common mistakes: describing the performer instead of analysing; listing weaknesses without data; theory that does not connect to the weakness; programmes without progression or re-testing; and ignoring the priority question (examiners explicitly reward selecting one weakness and going deep). Board-specific tactics : for AQA , the written analysis rewards depth on one weakness with a full corrective programme - structure your writing with the six stages above and reference theory by topic (energy systems, information processing, attribution); for OCR EAPI , practise the 10-minute oral timing : roughly 2 minutes overview and strengths, 3 minutes weaknesses, 1 minute prioritisation, 4 minutes development plan - the oral is marked on the same criteria as a written piece, so plan headings before speaking; for Edexcel , the development programme is weighted alongside the analysis - give the programme its own periodised structure with weekly detail. In all boards, link the weakness to both a physiological/skill cause and a psychological factor where relevant - the marking criteria reward cross-strategy synthesis (e.g. a technique weakness underpinned by high state anxiety). Practical performance side : assessed in one activity as performer, coach or official (or a combination depending on board rules) against sport-specific criteria - the analysis activity does not have to be the same activity as the practical in all boards (check your board's current rules - AQA allows the analysis on a different activity from the practical). Exam logic: the NEA is the easiest place to bank marks because you control the content - choose a weakness with clear theory links, collect your own data (video, tests, notation), and let every paragraph cite evidence and theory in one sentence each. A worked analysis paragraph - the template to memorise for the NEA (football midfielder example): 'The performer's sprint speed is below the squad norm (30 m: 4.4 s versus the squad's 4.1 s average - quantitative evidence). Video analysis shows the drive phase is upright and the arm action is low (qualitative, against the sprint-start technical model). The cause is physiological: low phosphocreatine stores and limited fast-twitch recruitment in training limit the ATP-PC contribution (theory - AQA 3.1.4); a contributing psychological factor is low self-efficacy in 1v1 situations (Bandura - performance accomplishments lacking). The development programme therefore targets the cause: a 6-week periodised plan (microcycles with progressive overload) combining sprint intervals and plyometrics to raise PC stores and fast-twitch recruitment, with structured success experiences (achievable 1v1 drills) building self-efficacy. SMART target: reduce the 30 m time by 0.2 s within 6 weeks, re-tested with the same timing gates and protocol (reliability).' Every sentence carries data, theory, or the programme - that density is what the marking criteria reward. Practical performance assessment detail : performers are assessed against sport-specific criteria in one activity, as a performer, coach or official (or a combination, depending on board rules); the analysis activity does not have to match the practical activity (AQA permits the analysis on a different activity - check current board rules). The practical side rewards applied skill under conditions similar to competition; the analysis side rewards the six-stage structure. EAPI timing tips : plan headings before speaking; rehearse to the 10-minute limit (roughly 2 minutes overview and strengths, 3 minutes weaknesses, 1 minute prioritisation, 4 minutes development plan); make every sentence evidence-led ('the video shows... the test data shows... the theory explains...'); close with the re-test loop. The oral is marked on the same AO criteria as a written piece - structure is not optional because the format is spoken. Exam logic: the NEA is bankable marks - choose a weakness with clear theory links, collect your own data, and let every paragraph cite evidence and theory in one sentence each. What the OCR EAPI criteria reward - the four command verbs behind the marks: analyse (break the performance into components against the technical model - strengths AND weaknesses, both evidenced), evaluate (judge the significance of each - which limits performance most, with justification), prioritise (select the target weakness and defend the choice - most limiting, most improvable, most measurable), and propose (a corrective practice programme targeting the cause, linked to theory, with progression and a re-test). Balance matters : a full-mark response includes genuine strengths (with evidence) before weaknesses - analysing only weaknesses caps the mark; and the weaknesses must be specific and observable from the video, not generic ('needs more fitness' fails; 'inconsistent contact point on the forehand drive under pressure' scores). Use of stills and data : in the AQA written analysis, still frames beside the technical model and small data tables (test scores against norms) are expected supporting evidence - reference them explicitly in the text; in the OCR oral, describe the moments you would point to. Exam logic: the marking criteria reward the same chain in every board - evidence, theory, programme, re-test - so build every paragraph and every spoken segment around those four links. Fitness testing measures the components of fitness against normative data ; every exam answer should give the protocol, one advantage and one limitation. The core table of tests is a guaranteed knowledge item: Component Test and protocol Advantage Limitation Aerobic endurance Multi-stage fitness test: 20 m shuttles increasing in speed with levels/bleeps until exhaustion; estimated VO2 max from final level. Cooper 12-minute run: maximum distance covered. Yo-Yo intermittent recovery: 20 m shuttles with active recovery - intermittent-sport specific Large groups, cheap, normative data, estimates VO2 max Estimate only (indirect), motivation-dependent, not as valid as gas analysis Speed 30 m or 60 m sprint with timing gates; flying 30 m for max speed Direct measure, reliable with gates Needs accurate timing; influenced by reaction time Power Vertical jump (Sargent): jump height against a wall/board; standing long jump; Wingate test (30 s cycle against resistance) for peak anaerobic power Cheap and quick (jumps); Wingate is a valid lab anaerobic test Jump tests estimate leg power only; Wingate needs lab equipment Strength One repetition maximum (1RM) on a lift; handgrip dynamometer Direct measure of max strength 1RM has injury risk without supervision; grip is not whole-body specific Muscular endurance Sit-up or press-up test: repetitions in a set time Simple, large groups Form degradation affects validity Flexibility Sit-and-reach: forward reach beyond toes from a seated position Cheap, normative data Measures hamstring/lower back only - not overall flexibility (validity) Agility Illinois agility run: cone course with turns completed for time Sport-relevant movement pattern Includes speed - not pure agility (validity limitation) Body composition BMI (mass/height squared - crude), skinfold calipers (sum of sites), bioelectrical impedance (BIA) Quick, field-friendly Skinfold/BIA are estimates with tester error; BMI ignores muscle mass Laboratory versus field tests - the guaranteed compare: laboratory tests (treadmill VO2 max with gas analysis, Wingate cycle, isokinetic dynamometry) are accurate, valid and controlled - direct gas measurement of VO2 max is the criterion measure; standardised conditions give reliability; but they are expensive, need trained staff, are time-consuming and not sport-specific (a treadmill differs from over-ground running). Field tests (multi-stage fitness test, vertical jump, Illinois run) are cheap, accessible, quick and sport-specific (the Yo-Yo test matches intermittent games demands) but produce estimates, depend on motivation and pacing, and are less valid and reliable than lab equivalents. Exam logic: for any evaluate-the-test question, state validity (does it measure the claimed component?), reliability (standardised protocol, calibrated equipment), and the estimate-versus-direct distinction - then judge against the performer's purpose (field tests suffice for team monitoring; lab tests are needed for precision). Data collection procedures : pre-test - informed consent, health screening (PAR-Q), calibrated equipment, standardised warm-up, controlled environment (temperature, surface), clear standardised instructions and demonstrations; during - the exact protocol followed (shuttle timing, recorded attempts - best of three for jumps), the same tester throughout; post-test - cool-down, results recorded immediately, compared with normative data by age and gender, and re-tested on schedule (e.g. every 6-8 weeks) to track adaptation. Quantitative collection methods : fitness testing batteries, notational analysis sheets (tally of passes, shots, errors), timing gates, GPS/accelerometer data (distance covered, sprint counts), heart rate monitors (intensity zones); qualitative collection methods : video analysis judged against a technical model, coach observation with structured checklists, performer self-report (questionnaires - e.g. SCAT for anxiety, satisfaction scales), interviews. Primary versus secondary : primary (your own tests and video - specific, current) versus secondary (published research, elite norms, opposition data - quick and broad but possibly dated or not comparable). Exam logic: for data-collection questions, name the method, say what it produces (quantitative or qualitative), give the procedure (calibration, standardisation, consent, warm-up), and finish with how the data is used (compared with norms, tracked over time, feeding the development programme) - the four-step chain scores every available mark. Direct VO2 max testing - the criterion measure in detail: an incremental test on a treadmill or cycle ergometer to exhaustion, with a gas-analysis mask measuring oxygen uptake and carbon dioxide output breath by breath; VO2 max is identified when oxygen uptake plateaus despite increasing workload (the plateau criterion), with heart rate near maximum and respiratory exchange ratio above 1.0; it is the gold-standard measure of aerobic power but requires laboratory equipment, trained staff and high participant motivation - the standard accuracy-versus-accessibility compare with field estimates. Objective load monitoring extends the toolkit: heart rate monitors - training intensity zones set from maximum heart rate percentages (recovery, aerobic, threshold, anaerobic zones); the HR response tracks effort when pacing and terrain vary; GPS/accelerometer units - distance covered, sprint counts, high-speed running, work:rest ratios in games (the objective backbone of notational analysis in team sports); questionnaires - PAR-Q (health screening before testing), RPE/Borg scales (perceived intensity), satisfaction and anxiety scales (psychological monitoring). Designing a test battery - the sequencing detail the exam rewards: order tests so that fatigue does not contaminate later results - non-fatiguing tests first (body composition, flexibility), then power and strength, then speed and agility, with aerobic endurance last (the most fatiguing); the same warm-up and rest intervals throughout; re-test every 6-8 weeks with identical protocols so adaptation, not test variation, explains change. Interpreting normative data : published tables are population averages by age and gender - a performer's raw score is rated against the norm (above/below average, percentile); but norms are averages, so elite performers exceed them - compare also against squad data and the performer's own previous scores for meaningful evaluation. Exam logic for testing questions: name the test, give the protocol, state validity and reliability, then judge against the performer's purpose - the four-step chain scores every available mark, and the battery-order point is the detail that separates top-band answers. Wingate test detail : a 30-second all-out cycle against a fixed resistance (typically 7.5% of body mass); power output is recorded continuously - peak power (highest 5-second output) and mean power (average across 30 s), with a fatigue index calculated from the decline; it is the standard laboratory measure of anaerobic peak power and capacity (ATP-PC and glycolytic systems) - accurate and controlled but lab-bound, exhausting and motivation-dependent. Sit-and-reach protocol detail : sit with legs extended, soles against the box; reach forward slowly (no bouncing - ballistic reaching invalidates the measure) and hold the furthest point for ~2 seconds; the best of three attempts is recorded in centimetres (past the toes) and compared with normative data; a standardised warm-up precedes the test - the protocol precision that the exam's 5-mark describe questions reward.
