topics.subject: accounting
topics.searchText: accounting Accounting Double Entry and the Ledger Apply the accounting equation and the dual effect of every transaction to decide the correct debit and credit entries for any transaction (AQA 7127, 3.3) (AO1/AO2). Select the correct book of prime entry for each transaction type and post accurately to the ledger using folio references (3.3) (AO2). Prepare and interpret a trial balance, naming the six error types it fails to detect and justifying why it is not proof of accuracy (3.4) (AO1/AO3). Open, use and clear a suspense account through the journal, and assess the effect of each correction on profit for the year (3.4) (AO2/AO3). Prepare sales and purchases ledger control accounts, reconcile them to lists of balances, and reconcile the cash book to the bank statement (3.4) (AO2). Evaluate the benefits and costs of operating a double entry bookkeeping system, using business examples (3.1/3.3) (AO3). Debit: expenses, assets, drawings increase. Credit: liabilities, capital/equity, income increase. Revenue received in advance is a liability, not income. Balanced errors (complete omission, same wrong amount both sides, wrong account, reversal, principle, compensating) never break the trial balance; only one-sided errors do. Only one-sided errors need a suspense account. A correction made with equal debit and credit via suspense never changes profit; corrections touching income or expense accounts do. Prepare control accounts from day books and the cash book only - never from the personal ledgers - so the reconciliation actually tests them. Bank reconciliation: update the cash book first (charges, interest, standing orders, direct debits and credits, dishonoured cheques), then adjust for timing: subtract unpresented cheques, add outstanding lodgements. Accounting equation Assets = Capital + Liabilities, restated internationally as Assets = Equity + Liabilities. It must hold after every transaction because of the dual effect. Capital The owner's claim on the business: opening capital plus profits minus drawings; called equity in company accounts. Book of prime entry The first place a transaction is recorded before posting to the ledger - sales day book, purchases day book, returns books, cash book or general journal. Trade discount A reduction off list price given to trade customers; deducted before the transaction is recorded, so it never appears in the ledger accounts. Settlement (cash) discount A discount for prompt payment, recorded only when taken: discount allowed (expense) for the seller, discount received (income) for the buyer. Trial balance A list of all ledger balances at a date with debit and credit columns; it tests the arithmetic accuracy of double entry only, not completeness or correctness of classification. Suspense account A temporary account holding the difference when the trial balance fails to agree (or when a one-sided error is found before it is corrected); cleared by journal entries and closed before final accounts are prepared. Control account A summary account for trade receivables or trade payables in the nominal ledger, built from day books and the cash book; its balance is checked against the sum of the individual personal accounts. Every transaction has a dual effect : it changes at least two items, and the accounting equation survives each change. If Suneja opens a business with £20,000 from savings, assets (bank) rise £20,000 and capital rises £20,000. If she then buys a van for £6,000 cash, one asset rises and another falls - the equation still balances. If she buys inventory for £2,000 on credit, assets rise £2,000 and liabilities (payables) rise £2,000. The equation is not a formula to memorise for one question: it is the logic that generates every debit and credit. Account category To increase To decrease Assets (non-current and current) Debit Credit Expenses (including purchases) Debit Credit Drawings Debit Credit Liabilities Credit Debit Capital / equity Credit Debit Income (sales, rent receivable, discount received) Credit Debit A four-step routine decides any entry. Step 1: identify the two (or more) accounts affected. Step 2: classify each as asset, liability, capital, income or expense. Step 3: decide whether each increases or decreases. Step 4: apply the table. Test it: pay wages £800 in cash. Wages (expense) increase, so debit wages £800; cash (asset) decreases, so credit cash £800. Receive £500 rent from a sub-tenant: debit bank (asset up), credit rent receivable (income up). Owner takes goods worth £150: debit drawings £150, credit purchases £150 - goods drawn are recorded at cost, credited to purchases, not sales. Worked example: eight transactions through the double entry Transaction Debit Credit Buy goods on credit from Pell Ltd £2,400 Purchases 2,400 Pell Ltd 2,400 Sell goods on credit to Kaur £3,100 (cost £1,900) Kaur 3,100 Sales 3,100 Return goods to Pell £180 Pell Ltd 180 Purchases returns 180 Kaur pays £3,100 by cheque Bank 3,100 Kaur 3,100 Pay Pell £2,220 in full settlement of £2,400, taking discount Pell Ltd 2,400 Bank 2,220; Discount received 180 Owner pays in a second £5,000 Bank 5,000 Capital 5,000 Buy shelving by cheque £1,500 Equipment 1,500 Bank 1,500 Pay rent by standing order £600 Rent payable 600 Bank 600 The Pell settlement shows the settlement discount rule: only the discount actually taken is recorded, split so the payables account is cleared in full. A trade discount, by contrast, would simply mean the purchases were recorded at, say, £2,280 rather than list price. Transactions are first entered in a book of prime entry , which keeps the ledger clean, records supporting details once, and creates an audit trail. The sales day book lists credit sales invoices (total posted to debit sales, each invoice posted to the credit of the individual customer). The purchases day book does the mirror image for credit purchases. Returns inwards and returns outwards books handle credit notes and debit notes. The cash book records all bank and cash movements and is both a book of prime entry and a ledger account, often extended with discount allowed and discount received columns. The petty cash book records small cash payments under analysed heads, using the imprest system: the float is topped up to a fixed amount by the exact value of vouchers, so the petty cashier is automatically checked. The general journal records everything else: opening entries, purchases and sales of non-current assets on credit, corrections of errors, irrecoverable debts written off, and the year-end transfer entries. Sales day book - credit sales invoices; source: copies of sales invoices. Purchases day book - credit purchases; source: suppliers' invoices. Returns inwards / outwards books - credit notes / debit notes. Cash book - receipts and payments; source: till rolls, counterfoils, statements. Petty cash book - small payments; source: petty cash vouchers. General journal - everything not covered above; source: instructions, schedules. The ledger is split for control: the sales (receivables) ledger holds one account per credit customer, the purchases (payables) ledger one per supplier, and the nominal (general) ledger everything else, including the sales ledger control and purchases ledger control accounts. Every posting carries a folio reference (e.g. SL 14, CB 7) cross-referencing book to account. Folios look cosmetic but they are examinable: they prove each entry was cross-checked, they let any figure be traced both ways, and they are part of the internal control story you must be able to tell in extended answers about the benefits and costs of the double entry system (3.1, 3.3). The costs are real: a full double entry system needs trained staff, books or software, and time; for a micro-business with few transactions the cost can exceed the benefit, which is why incomplete records techniques exist (3.14). Command-word discipline matters here. For state or identify , give the entry only. For explain , give the entry and why (account classification plus the dual effect). For prepare the journal entries , show date, accounts, amounts, and a narration - AQA mark schemes award for narrations because they demonstrate the transaction, not the habit, has been understood. Push the dual effect one step further, because examiners love the cases where the equation survives something that looks one-sided. A customer pays £1,200 in December for work to be done in January: bank (asset) rises, but the credit is to deferred income (revenue received in advance) - a liability - because no income has been earned yet. The business receives an electricity bill for £300 but will pay next month: the expense is debited now and the credit sits in accruals, a liability. In both cases the equation holds because a liability absorbs the difference. Candidates who credit sales or debit expenses directly have destroyed the matching that the ledger is supposed to preserve, and the error surfaces in the adjustments section of Paper 1. Similarly, when a non-current asset is bought partly on credit, the debit is the asset but the credits split between bank and the supplier's personal account - two credits against one debit is perfectly valid double entry, since 'two entries' means at least two, not exactly two. Worked example: discounts - trade versus settlement Ridge sells goods list price £1,000 to Doherty, allowing 10% trade discount and offering 2.5% settlement discount. Invoice raised: £1,000 less 10% = £900 . Entry: Dr Doherty £900, Cr Sales £900 - the trade discount is buried in the figure and never appears separately. If Doherty pays within terms, the settlement discount is £22.50 (2.5% of £900): Dr Bank £877.50, Dr Discount allowed £22.50, Cr Doherty £900. Ridge's books show discount allowed £22.50 (expense). From Doherty's side the mirror image: Dr Ridge £900, Cr Bank £877.50, Cr Discount received £22.50 (income). If Doherty pays late, nothing further is recorded - settlement discounts are recognised only when taken, unlike trade discounts which are recognised by never recording them. Posting runs in totals with only the personal accounts getting individual attention. If the sales day book for March lists 40 invoices totalling £46,300, the nominal ledger receives one entry - Dr Sales ledger control £46,300, Cr Sales £46,300, folios referencing SDB 3 and NL 22 - while each of the 40 customers' personal accounts is credited with its own invoice amount. This is why the sales ledger control account in section 3 below can be rebuilt from the day books alone: the control account receives exactly the same totals the day book produced. Understanding this flow answers a classic exam question - state the source of each entry in a control account - and stops candidates inventing entries (such as irrecoverable debts written off) that never pass through the day books but only through the journal. Multiple-choice and short-answer items on 3.3 are usually one-line decisions - state the double entry for paying a supplier by standing order (Dr payables, Cr bank) - so speed comes from classification, not memory. The extended questions reward narrative control: knowing that the cash book doubles as a ledger account, that the journal is the book of corrections, and that every figure in the financial statements can be traced through folio references back to a source document. Hold the whole chain in mind - source document, book of prime entry, ledger, trial balance, financial statements - because every later topic in the specification (adjustments in 3.6, company accounts in 3.16, even the data trail questions on technology) assumes you can move along it in either direction without hesitation. At the reporting date each ledger account is balanced : total both sides, insert the smaller total as balance c/d on the larger side, carry it down as balance b/d on the opposite side. Debit balances (assets, expenses, drawings) and credit balances (liabilities, capital, income) are then listed in a trial balance . Because every transaction was recorded with equal debits and credits, the two columns must agree. If they do not, something is wrong - and the difference is parked in a suspense account so final accounts can be drafted while the error is traced. Suspense is a device, not an account with meaning: a trial balance must agree, and the suspense account must be cleared, before financial statements are finalised. The crucial A* distinction is between the six error types a balanced trial balance cannot detect and the errors it can . All six undetectable types are balanced errors: both sides were recorded, just wrongly. Error type Example Revealed by TB? Complete omission A £400 credit sale never recorded at all No Same wrong amount both sides Sale recorded as £540 instead of £450 in both accounts No Error of commission Debited the wrong customer's account No Error of principle Motor expenses debited to motor vehicles No Reversal of entries Sale debited to sales, credited to customer No Compensating errors Sales overcast £100, wages overcast £100 No One-sided errors (posting one side only; casting one account wrongly) Cash debited, receivables never credited Yes - TB fails So a trial balance that agrees is not evidence that the records are correct: any of the six balanced errors could be sitting inside it. That is why verification continues beyond the trial balance with control accounts, bank reconciliation and physical checks (3.4). Conversely, a trial balance that fails tells you a one-sided error exists but not which - hence the suspense account. Balancing itself is examinable. In the wages account for a month, total debits (wages paid) sit on the left; the balance c/d goes to the right at the period end, and comes back as balance b/d ready to start the next period. Accumulate it over the year and the closing balance transfers to the statement of profit or loss. Permanent accounts (assets, liabilities, capital) carry their balances forward as balance b/d into the next period and appear in the statement of financial position; temporary accounts (income and expenses) are closed off to the statement of profit or loss and start each new period at nil. Knowing which accounts are which tells you instantly where a balance belongs in the final accounts - and it explains why drawings is a debit-balance account deducted from capital rather than an expense. When the trial balance disagrees, open the suspense account with the difference on the side that is short . If debits exceed credits by £100, suspense carries a debit balance of £100, restoring apparent agreement. Then correct each error through the journal. For each correction ask two questions. First, does this error involve an account missing an entry on one side only (or a wrong amount on one side)? If yes, the suspense account absorbs the imbalance. Second, do the correcting entries touch income or expense accounts? If yes, profit for the year changes. Worked example: clearing a suspense account and measuring the profit effect A business's trial balance shows debits £96,000 and credits £95,900, a difference of £100. The suspense account is opened with a debit balance of £100. Three errors are then found: A cheque of £100 received from a credit customer was debited to the bank account but never credited to the customer's account. Correction: Dr Suspense 100, Cr Trade receivables 100. The missing credit is supplied; suspense is cleared. No profit effect - the error sat entirely within balance-sheet items. A credit sale of £400 to D Fell was completely omitted. Correction: Dr D Fell 400, Cr Sales 400. No suspense needed - the error was balanced. Profit increases by £400 (revenue previously understated). Motor expenses of £600 were debited to motor vehicles (error of principle). Correction: Dr Motor expenses 600, Cr Motor vehicles 600. No suspense needed. Profit decreases by £600 (expenses understated, asset overstated). Net effect on profit: +£400 − £600 = −£200. Note the pattern examiners reward: the correction that used the suspense account (error 1) changed no profit figure, because suspense entries are always equal debits and credits by construction. Profit effects come only from balanced errors corrected through the statement of profit or loss accounts. Also state the balance sheet effects: trade receivables were overstated by £100, motor vehicles overstated by £600 before correction. Common one-sided errors to watch for in data: a casting error in a single account (e.g. sales day book totalled £9,860 instead of £8,960, posted as £9,860); a posting made to one side of one account only; two debits with no credit; the wrong figure on one side. Common balanced errors that trap candidates: writing off an irrecoverable debt but crediting the customer's account and forgetting the receivables control account interplay, or treating drawings of goods as at selling price (it is at cost, credited to purchases). Reversals (type 4) are corrected by doubling the wrong entry: if a £250 receipt was reversed, debit and credit the original accounts again with £250 to cancel, then post correctly - a two-step journal worth stating explicitly for full marks. Remember the statement of financial position consequences as well as the profit consequences, because part (b) of these questions almost always asks for both. An uncorrected error of principle (expenses sitting in motor vehicles) overstates both profit and non-current assets; an uncorrected omission of a credit sale understates profit, trade receivables and revenue. And a suspense account must be cleared before the financial statements are published: a suspense balance in a published statement of financial position signals uncorrected records and would prevent the accounts from showing a true and fair view. In exam answers, finish every suspense question by writing 'the suspense account now has a nil balance' - it is a marking point in its own right. For the extended-answer variant - discuss whether a trial balance that agrees proves the accounts are accurate - structure as: (i) purpose of the trial balance (arithmetic check of double entry); (ii) the six undetectable error types with one example each; (iii) what does provide assurance (control accounts reconciled, bank reconciliation, physical stock counts, internal check segregation); (iv) judgement that a balanced TB is necessary but far from sufficient. That fourth move - the justified conclusion - is what separates the top band from mid band in AQA's 25-mark Section C questions. Worked example: the imprest petty cash system Petty cash float £200, restored by imprest. During the week vouchers totalled £87 (postage £34, cleaning £28, stationery £25). The cashier reimburses exactly £87, restoring the float to £200. Check: float £200 = vouchers £87 + cash in box £113. The verification is built in - if cash plus vouchers does not equal the imprest amount, something is missing, and the analysis columns feed the nominal accounts (Dr postage, Dr cleaning, Dr stationery, Cr cash) without cluttering the main cash book. Finally, link the model to the accountant's role (3.1). Double entry is not paperwork for its own sake: it is what allows the trial balance to self-check the books, the financial statements to be prepared from ledger balances rather than reconstructed by guesswork, and managers to interrogate any figure back to its source document. When you are asked to evaluate the double entry system, anchor each benefit to this mechanism and each cost to the resources it consumes - that is the difference between assertion and analysis. Verification goes beyond the trial balance. The three named mechanisms in 3.4 are control accounts , the bank reconciliation and checks on the personal ledgers. Their shared logic: build a figure independently from summary records, then compare it with the detailed records. Any difference must be explained and corrected. In an exam this is one of the highest-yield preparation areas because the formats are fixed and the marks are mechanical. A sales ledger control account summarises everything owed by credit customers; the purchases ledger control account summarises everything owed to suppliers. Critical rule: build them only from the day books, returns books and cash book - never from the individual personal accounts - otherwise the check is circular. Items are posted in totals, with the other side of each entry to the nominal account named in brackets. Dr side (sales ledger control) Source Cr side Source Opening balance b/d Last year's TB Cash and cheques received Cash book (Cr bank) Credit sales Sales day book (Cr sales) Discounts allowed Cash book (Dr discount allowed) Dishonoured cheques Bank statement (Cr bank) Returns inwards Returns inwards book (Dr returns inwards) Interest charged on overdue accounts Journal (Cr interest income) Irrecoverable debts written off Journal (Dr irrecoverable debts) Contra to purchases ledger Journal (Dr purchases ledger control) Closing balance c/d Balance figure The purchases ledger control is the mirror image: debits for payments, discounts received, returns outwards and contras; credits for opening balances and credit purchases. A contra (set-off) arises where the business is both customer and supplier of the same firm: the two balances are netted, Dr Purchases ledger control, Cr Sales ledger control , with no cash movement. Reconciling the control account to the list of personal balances: prepare the control account, list and total the individual balances, then investigate the difference. Typical causes: a transaction omitted from the list of balances but in the control account (or vice versa); a casting error in either; a posting to the wrong personal account (commission - affects the list total, not the control account); or an error in the control account itself. Explain each difference, correct it, and show that both now agree. Control accounts deliver control benefits you should be able to evaluate for AO3: they localise errors (the discrepancy is inside one ledger, not the whole system); they deter fraud because a different clerk maintains the personal ledgers from the one who prepares the control account (internal check through segregation of duties); they give the trial balance a quick receivables/payables figure; and for large businesses they allow the sales ledger to be split across clerks without losing overall control. The cost is duplication of bookkeeping work and the need for competent, independent staff. The bank reconciliation follows the same compare-and-explain logic between the cash book and the bank statement. Always in this order. Step 1: update the cash book for items on the statement not yet in the books - bank charges and interest, standing orders and direct debits, direct credits (customers paying directly), dishonoured cheques, and any bank errors. The corrected cash book balance is the figure that appears in the statement of financial position. Step 2: list timing differences, which need no entry: cheques paid in but not yet credited (outstanding lodgements) and cheques issued but not yet presented. Step 3: start from the updated cash book balance and adjust for timing, or start from the statement balance and work back - both must land on the same number. Worked example: full bank reconciliation Cash book shows a debit balance of £4,320. The bank statement shows £4,880. The statement reveals bank charges £50, a direct credit from a customer of £200, unpresented cheques £1,150, and a lodgement of £740 not yet credited. Updated cash book £ Balance per cash book (Dr) 4,320 Less: bank charges (50) Add: direct credit 200 Corrected (adjusted) balance 4,470 Reconciliation to statement £ Balance per bank statement 4,880 Less: unpresented cheques (1,150) Add: outstanding lodgement 740 Balance per updated cash book 4,470 Mark-scheme pattern: the £50 and £200 go through the cash book with double entries (Dr/Cr bank); the £1,150 and £740 appear in no ledger account at all - they are pure timing. Candidates who 'correct' the cash book for unpresented cheques throw marks away every year. Two reconciliation wrinkles appear regularly. A dishonoured cheque from a customer (insufficient funds, or a technical error) reverses the original receipt: Dr Trade receivables, Cr Bank - the customer owes again, so it appears on the debit side of the sales ledger control account and the customer's personal account. A bank error (for example the bank debiting your account with another customer's direct debit) is corrected by notifying the bank; it appears only in the reconciliation statement, never in your books, until the bank corrects it. Remember too that the figure reported in the statement of financial position is the corrected cash book balance - if that is negative, the overdraft is a current liability. The purchases ledger control account is the exact mirror image, and being able to state its sources is a standard short-answer demand. Dr side (purchases ledger control) Source Cr side Source Payments to suppliers Cash book (Cr bank) Opening balance b/d Last year's TB Discounts received Cash book (Cr discount received) Credit purchases Purchases day book (Dr purchases) Returns outwards Returns outwards book (Dr returns outwards) Contra to sales ledger control Journal Closing balance c/d Balance figure To reconcile either control account with its list of balances: prepare the control account from the summary books; list and total the individual balances from the memorandum ledger; then explain and correct any difference line by line. Typical causes, each with its correcting treatment: a transaction in the control account but omitted from the list (add it to the list); a casting error in one personal account (correct that account); a posting to the wrong personal account - an error of commission - which distorts the list total but not the control account (transfer the amount between the two personal accounts); an entry missing from the control account itself (post it); or a debit balance among the payables (an advance payment) listed as a negative. The discipline of explaining each difference, not just adjusting, is what the mark scheme pays for. Tie it together for the extended question on the benefits and costs of operating a double entry bookkeeping system (3.3, with links to 3.1). Benefits: it self-checks (trial balance), it detects errors and deters fraud through control accounts and reconciliation, it produces reliable financial statements and management information for decisions, it supports tax compliance and audit, and it permits performance comparison over time. Costs: staffing and training; software purchase and maintenance; data security investment; time taken per transaction; risk that over-complex systems generate information nobody uses. The evaluation point AQA rewards: the benefits grow with the size and complexity of the business, so the optimal system differs between a market trader (incomplete records may suffice) and a limited company (full double entry is legally required). Conclude with a judgement, not a list. In Paper 1 this material typically appears as a 20-mark structured question (prepare a control account, then reconcile, then explain one cause of difference) or inside a Section C scenario asking you to evaluate internal control. Whatever the wrapper, the mechanics are identical: know the source of every control account line, know which items enter the cash book and which are pure timing, and be ready to state double entries for the adjustments (dishonoured cheque, contra, write-off). Drill the formats until you can produce a balanced control account in under five minutes - the time saved funds the evaluation paragraphs that decide the top grades.

topics.name: Financial Statements
topics.subject: accounting
topics.searchText: accounting Accounting Financial Statements Prepare a statement of profit or loss and a statement of financial position for a sole trader from a trial balance, correctly classifying cost of sales, expenses and other income (AQA 7127, 3.6) (AO2). Apply the accounting concepts - accruals/matching, prudence, going concern, consistency, business entity, materiality, realisation - and explain their effect on reported figures (3.5) (AO1/AO2). Record year-end adjustments: accruals, prepayments, straight-line and reducing-balance depreciation, disposals, irrecoverable debts and the allowance for trade receivables (3.6) (AO2). Prepare the financial statements of a limited company including share capital, share premium, retained earnings, dividends and the taxation and finance cost lines (3.7/3.16) (AO2). Prepare partnership appropriation accounts, capital and current accounts applying the terms of the partnership agreement (3.15) (AO2). Evaluate the effect on profit and the statement of financial position of omitted or misstated adjustments, and discuss the limitations of historical cost reporting (AO3). Cost of sales = opening inventory + purchases + carriage inwards - closing inventory. Carriage outwards is a selling expense, never in cost of sales. Depreciation is never a cash flow; the cash left at purchase and at disposal. Straight line = (cost - residual)/useful life; reducing balance = % × net book value each year. The MOVEMENT in the allowance for receivables goes to the statement of profit or loss, not the total; a write-off goes straight to receivables and to expense. Company statement of profit or loss: operating profit - finance costs = profit before tax - tax = profit for the year. Dividends are appropriations of profit, not expenses. Partnership: capital accounts usually stay fixed; interest on capital, salaries and residual shares flow through the current accounts; interest on drawings is added back before the residual split. Accrual (accrued expense) An expense incurred but not yet paid at the year end; added to the expense in the statement of profit or loss and shown as a current liability. Prepayment An expense paid in advance of the period it relates to; deducted from the expense and shown as a current asset. Mirror image: accrued income (asset) and income received in advance (liability). Depreciation The systematic allocation of the depreciable amount (cost less residual value) of a non-current asset over its useful economic life; an application of the accruals concept, not a valuation or a cash fund. Net book value (carrying amount) Cost (or revalued amount) of a non-current asset less accumulated depreciation to date. Irrecoverable debt A trade receivable written off as uncollectable; charged as an expense in full in the statement of profit or loss and removed from trade receivables. Allowance for trade receivables An estimate of doubtful debts, shown as a deduction from trade receivables in the statement of financial position; only the increase or decrease in the allowance is adjusted in the statement of profit or loss. Retained earnings Cumulative profits reinvested in the business, less any dividends paid; the main equity reserve of a limited company. Partnership current account The account recording each partner's share of profit, interest on capital, salary, interest on drawings and drawings; it fluctuates and, with the capital account, makes up the partner's equity. The statement of profit or loss measures performance for a period; the statement of financial position reports position at a date. In the exam you are usually handed a trial balance plus adjustments and asked for one or both. Speed comes from a fixed routine, and marks come from classification - most lost marks in these questions are not arithmetic but putting items in the wrong place. Layout drill for the statement of profit or loss. Revenue less cost of sales gives gross profit , where cost of sales = opening inventory + purchases + carriage inwards − closing inventory. Then add other income (commission receivable, rent receivable, profit on disposal, discount received). Then deduct expenses in the order they arrive: selling and distribution costs (carriage outwards, sales staff, advertising), administrative expenses (office salaries, rent and rates, insurance, depreciation), and finance costs if any. The bottom line is profit for the year, transferred to the capital account of the sole trader. In the statement of financial position: non-current assets at net book value (cost less accumulated depreciation), current assets in the order inventory, trade receivables, prepayments, bank, cash; then equity (opening capital + profit for the year − drawings), current liabilities (trade payables, accruals, overdraft, income received in advance) and, if given, non-current liabilities. Item from the trial balance Where it goes Carriage inwards Add to purchases in cost of sales Carriage outwards Selling expense Discount received Other income Drawings (cash or goods) Deduct from capital, never an expense Rent receivable Other income Bank overdraft Current liability Provision for depreciation Deduct from non-current asset cost The concepts (3.5) are not decoration: AQA asks you to state and explain the concept underlying a treatment, and the adjustments in the next section are each an application of one of them. Accruals (matching) : report expenses and income in the period they are incurred or earned, not when cash moves. Prudence : do not overstate assets or income; provide for probable losses (e.g. the allowance for receivables) as soon as anticipated, but recognise gains only when realised. Going concern : assume the business will continue, so non-current assets are held at cost less depreciation rather than break-up value. Consistency : like items treated the same way each period so figures are comparable; changes in policy (e.g. depreciation method) must be disclosed and justified. Business entity : the owner and the business are separate - hence drawings, and hence why the owner's house never appears on the statement of financial position. Materiality : trivial items may be treated expediently (a £5 stapler expensed rather than capitalised and depreciated over years). Realisation : revenue is recognised when earned - goods delivered and title passed - not when ordered or when cash arrives. Worked example: mini statement of profit or loss with adjustments Revenue £240,000; opening inventory £22,000; purchases £121,400; carriage inwards £3,600; closing inventory £25,000; carriage outwards £4,800; wages £38,000; rent £12,000 (accrual of £1,000 outstanding); insurance £2,400 (prepayment of £400); irrecoverable debts written off £1,500; increase in allowance for receivables £400; depreciation of equipment £6,000. £ £ Revenue 240,000 Opening inventory 22,000 Purchases (121,400 + 3,600 carriage inwards) 125,000 Less closing inventory (25,000) Cost of sales (122,000) Gross profit 118,000 Expenses: carriage outwards 4,800; wages 38,000; rent (12,000 + 1,000) 13,000; insurance (2,400 − 400) 2,000; irrecoverable debts 1,500; allowance increase 400; depreciation 6,000 (65,700) Profit for the year 52,300 Every adjustment line is developed in the next section - but note now how the accruals concept drove rent (£13,000 is the period's true cost) and insurance (£2,000 likewise). Closing inventory enters the statement twice and this trips candidates every year: it is deducted in cost of sales (raising gross profit) and added in current assets. Under the prudence concept it is valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value - if some inventory is damaged or obsolete, write it down before the calculation. Watch also for goods on sale or return: they stay in inventory (at cost) until the customer accepts. The final statement of financial position must balance; if it does not, hunt in this order: an adjustment posted once only, depreciation charged but not added to accumulated depreciation, an accrual omitted from current liabilities, or the drawings figure left out of equity. Presentation marks are free marks if you rehearse the format. AQA's international terminology appendix permits balance-sheet names, but train yourself into statement of profit or loss and statement of financial position headings, subtotals at gross profit and profit for the year, and current assets ordered inventory, receivables, prepayments, bank, cash. A question answered as a running list of figures scores presentation marks at best; the same figures in the correct three-column layout (details, £, £) with subtotals score the structure marks. Where a question asks for both statements, they are linked in one place only: profit for the year flows into capital (sole trader) or retained earnings (company). If your two statements disagree, the error is almost always in that transfer - not a failure of the balance itself. Concepts applied: one-line exam scenarios Scenario Concept Treatment Customer orders goods in December; delivered in January Realisation Revenue recognised in January - when earned, not when ordered or paid Owner's private car kept off the business accounts Business entity Only business assets and liabilities are recorded £5 stapler expensed rather than capitalised Materiality Immaterial items treated expediently Allowance for receivables created at year end Prudence Probable loss provided for before it is certain Depreciation method unchanged year on year Consistency Like items treated alike for comparability Assets held at cost less depreciation, not break-up value Going concern Business assumed to continue operating Electricity for December paid in January Accruals/matching Charged to the period that used it For the extended questions, prepare two flexible argument frames. Frame 1 - why adjustments matter: the accruals concept requires them, they prevent profit being a cash-timing lottery, and omitting them misstates both the statement of profit or loss and the statement of financial position (work one example through both statements). Frame 2 - the concepts in tension: prudence pushes towards earlier recognition of losses while consistency forbids switching policies at convenience; historical cost gives objectivity but ignores inflation. AQA's Section C 25-markers reward a judgement that weighs two sides and concludes - not a list of definitions. One further trap: adjustments given in the question are often half-given . 'Rent of £13,000 was paid in the year, of which £1,000 relates to next year' means the trial balance figure of 13,000 must be reduced by 400-style logic - the expense is 12,000 and the prepayment 1,000. 'Rent paid £12,000; rent owing at the year end £1,000' means expense 13,000. Read whether the trial balance figure is the cash paid or the charge required, and annotate the question paper before you touch the answer booklet. Under time pressure, the candidates who score full marks on these questions are the ones who label each adjustment against the statement line it hits before writing anything. Year-end adjustments exist for one reason: the trial balance contains cash-timing noise, and the accruals concept demands period-matching figures. Master the four families of adjustment - accruals/prepayments, depreciation, irrecoverable debts and the allowance, and the miscellany of rent receivable and drawings of goods - and Paper 1's biggest structured question becomes mechanical. Accruals and prepayments. An accrual is an expense used but unpaid (December's electricity bill arriving in January). Treatment: add to the expense in the statement of profit or loss; show as a current liability. A prepayment is an expense paid but not yet used (annual insurance paid in November covering next year): deduct from the expense; show as a current asset. The income mirror images: accrued income (rent earned, not received) is a current asset added to income; income received in advance is a current liability deducted from income. The cleanest technique is a T-account for the expense : put the trial balance figure and the adjustment in, and the statement of profit or loss transfer falls out. Adjustment Double entry Statement of profit or loss Statement of financial position Accrued expense £1,000 Dr Expense, Cr Accruals Expense +1,000 Current liability 1,000 Prepaid expense £400 Dr Prepayments, Cr Expense Expense −400 Current asset 400 Accrued income £500 Dr Accrued income, Cr Income Income +500 Current asset 500 Income received in advance £300 Dr Income, Cr Deferred income Income −300 Current liability 300 Worked example: the rent T-account does the thinking Year 2 rent paid £13,400; at the end of Year 1, £600 was accrued; the charge required for Year 2 is £13,000. Dr Rent payable account £ Cr £ Bank (paid in year) 13,400 Balance b/d (Year 1 accrual) 600 Statement of profit or loss (balancing figure) 12,800 Payment exceeds the required charge, so the balancing figure reveals a prepayment of £600 carried down on the debit side (a current asset). The account does the reasoning: enter what you know, let the statement of profit or loss figure emerge as the balance, and the carried-down balance hands you the statement of financial position item with its correct side. Run every accrual, prepayment and income adjustment through this pattern and direction errors disappear - and in the exam, sketch the T-account in the margin even when only the final figures are required. Depreciation. Straight line spreads the depreciable amount evenly: (cost − residual value) ÷ useful life, with part-years pro-rated by months. Reducing balance charges a fixed percentage of net book value, so charges are large early and smaller later - suited to assets that lose most value in early years (vehicles, IT). Neither method aims to equal market value; both allocate cost, and AQA examiners repeatedly ask you to justify method choice with that point. Depreciation entries: Dr Depreciation expense, Cr Provision (accumulated) for depreciation; the provision is deducted from cost in the statement of financial position. Part-year policies (a full year in the year of purchase but none in the year of sale, or months-based) are stated in the question - read them, do not assume. A disposal runs through four steps: transfer cost out of the asset account (Dr Disposal, Cr Asset, at cost); transfer accumulated depreciation (Dr Provision, Cr Disposal); record proceeds (Dr Bank/Cash receivable, Cr Disposal); the disposal account balance is a profit (credit side larger) or loss (debit side larger) transferred to the statement of profit or loss as other income or expense. Worked example: depreciation and disposal, months-based straight line Machine bought 1 October Year 1 for £54,000; residual value £6,000; useful life 8 years; depreciation charged monthly from date of purchase. Sold 30 June Year 5 for £28,000. Annual charge: (54,000 − 6,000) ÷ 8 = £6,000; monthly £500. Year 1 (October-December, 3 months): £1,500. Years 2, 3, 4 (full years): 3 × £6,000 = £18,000. Year 5 (January-June, 6 months): £3,000. Accumulated depreciation at disposal: £22,500; net book value £54,000 − £22,500 = £31,500. Disposal: proceeds £28,000 − NBV £31,500 = loss on disposal £3,500 , an expense in the statement of profit or loss. Journal summary: Dr Disposal 54,000 / Cr Machine 54,000; Dr Provision for depreciation 22,500 / Cr Disposal 22,500; Dr Bank 28,000 / Cr Disposal 28,000; Dr Loss on disposal 3,500 / Cr Disposal 3,500. Choosing (or changing) method is a classic evaluation demand. Straight line gives smooth, comparable charges - sensible where the asset gives equal benefit each year (buildings, fixtures). Reducing balance matches heavier early charges to assets that lose most value early and whose repair costs rise later, keeping total running cost roughly even (vehicles). Changing method mid-life breaches consistency, so a change must be justified by a genuinely different pattern of benefit - and you should be able to state the effect: switching from straight line to reducing balance raises the early-year depreciation charge and lowers profit, while later years reverse the effect. If asked to compute both for comparison, remember they diverge most in the middle years; straight line is linear in time, reducing balance is a constant percentage of a shrinking base, so it never quite reaches zero. Irrecoverable debts and the allowance. A debt confirmed as uncollectable is written off: Dr Irrecoverable debts expense, Cr Trade receivables (both the personal account and the control account). At the year end, a further allowance for doubtful debts is estimated for debts that may fail: the allowance is netted against receivables in the statement of financial position, but only the movement touches the statement of profit or loss - an increase is an expense, a decrease is credited (income). If a written-off debt is later recovered: Dr Bank, Cr Irrecoverable debts recovered (income) - or, in the two-step version, Dr Bank/Cr Debts written off, then adjust. Test yourself on the sequence AQA favours: write off £1,500 during the year; existing allowance £1,200; required allowance now 2% of remaining receivables of £80,000 = £1,600. Statement of profit or loss charge: write-off £1,500 + increase in allowance £400 = £1,900; receivables shown as £78,400. The miscellany. Drawings of goods at cost: Dr Drawings, Cr Purchases. Rent receivable with an accrued balance: add to other income, show the accrued amount as a current asset. Wages and salaries: an operating expense; watch for the question that gives 'wages and salaries accrued by £2,000' and asks for the statement of financial position accrual. Commission receivable often arrives with an income received in advance element - same T-account logic as expenses, reversed. And remember the overdraft stays a current liability even when the business is otherwise profitable; classifying it as non-current is a common three-mark error. Exam craft: for explain the effect on profit of failing to record an adjustment , trace both statements. Omitted £1,000 rent accrual: profit overstated £1,000, current liabilities and accruals understated £1,000 - so equity is also overstated. Omitted £400 prepayment: profit understated £400, current assets understated £400. Depreciation omitted: profit overstated, and non-current assets overstated by the same amount. Saying 'profit would be wrong' earns nothing; saying by how much, in which statement, and the knock-on to equity, earns all of them. Assemble the full picture once, as a self-test, before you sit Paper 1: take any trial balance with six adjustments and produce both statements end to end in under 40 minutes. The typical 20-mark question follows this exact arc - a handful of unadjusted figures, an accrual, a prepayment, a depreciation calculation (often part-year), a write-off with an allowance movement, and a closing inventory valuation with a net-realisable-value twist. Every mark maps to a line you have just drilled; the evaluation marks sit in explaining which concept forced each treatment and what would be misstated without it. The limited company statement of profit or loss (3.16) has the same skeleton as the sole trader's but ends differently and adds three lines. After gross profit and operating expenses comes operating profit ; then finance costs (interest on debentures and loans) are deducted to give profit before tax ; then taxation is deducted to give profit for the year . Appropriations - dividends - come after the statement, not inside it: they are distributions of profit, not expenses, so they never reduce operating profit. Ordinary share dividends are proposed or paid; only paid (or declared) dividends reduce retained earnings in the year-end statement. Finance costs deserve their own discipline. Debentures are long-term borrowing: the holders are creditors, not owners, so debenture interest is an expense (finance costs) whether or not it has been paid - an unpaid half-year is an accrual. Dividends, by contrast, are returns to owners and are appropriations. This single classification split - creditor return = expense, owner return = appropriation - is worth marks in almost every company question, and it also explains gearing behaviour you will meet in ratio analysis: debenture interest must be paid in profit or loss, dividends need not be. Where a question gives a debenture issued mid-year at 8%, charge only the months outstanding, and remember the cash raised adds to the statement of financial position while the nominal value adds to non-current liabilities. The company statement of financial position separates capital and reserves. Ordinary share capital is the nominal value of shares issued (10,000 £1 shares = £10,000). Share premium records the excess over nominal value received on issue: issuing 100,000 £1 shares at £1.50 raises £150,000, split £100,000 share capital and £50,000 premium. Retained earnings accumulate profits less dividends. Revaluation reserve holds upward asset revaluations. Non-current liabilities include debentures (long-term loans, with interest as the finance cost above). Two share issues are examinable: a rights issue raises cash (shares offered to existing holders, usually at a premium) and increases both share capital and premium; a bonus issue issues free shares by capitalising reserves (usually share premium) - equity total is unchanged, only its composition moves, and no cash is raised. Equity section example £ Ordinary share capital (440,000 £1 shares) 440,000 Share premium 20,000 Retained earnings 375,000 Total equity 835,000 How that table was built: opening capital 400,000 + bonus issue of 40,000 £1 shares (1-for-10, funded from share premium) = 440,000; premium 60,000 − 40,000 transferred = 20,000; retained earnings 320,000 + profit for the year 95,000 − dividends paid 40,000 = 375,000. Notice the discipline: bonus issues move value between reserves but leave total equity at 835,000 determined by capital + premium + retained earnings, and dividends reduce retained earnings even when described as 'final' or 'interim'. Worked example: rights issue versus bonus issue A company with 400,000 £1 shares (premium £60,000) makes a 1-for-4 rights issue at £1.60: 100,000 new shares raise £160,000 cash - Dr Bank 160,000, Cr Share capital 100,000, Cr Share premium 60,000. Share capital rises to 500,000, premium to 120,000, total equity rises £160,000. A 1-for-10 bonus issue instead: 40,000 free shares - Dr Share premium 40,000, Cr Share capital 40,000. No cash moves; total equity is unchanged; premium falls to 20,000. Exam distinction in one line: rights issue = cash in, equity up; bonus issue = reserves reshuffled, equity unchanged. Partnerships (3.15) add one structural idea: how profit is divided . The Partnership Act default is equal shares, but the partnership agreement usually overrides with terms you must apply exactly: interest on capital (a reward for funds invested), partner salaries (paid before residual sharing), interest on drawings (a penalty for withdrawing early), and a residual profit-sharing ratio. None of these are expenses of the partnership - they are appropriations, re-cutting the same total profit between partners. The mechanics live in the appropriation account and the current accounts ; capital accounts are usually fixed (only changed by capital injections or withdrawals), so current accounts absorb everything else, including drawings. The double entries behind the appropriation are worth knowing because questions ask for them: interest on capital and salaries are credited to the partner's current account (Dr Appropriation, Cr Current account); interest on drawings is debited to the current account (Dr Current account, Cr Appropriation); drawings themselves are Dr Current account, Cr Bank/Purchases. The capital account stays untouched at £60,000 and £40,000 unless partners introduce or withdraw capital - that fixedness is the point of the two-account design, giving a stable measure of permanent investment and a fluctuating measure of entitlement less withdrawals. In the statement of financial position, list capital accounts first, then current account balances; a debit balance on a current account is shown as a deduction. Worked example: appropriation account and current accounts Partners Ash and Birch share residual profits 3:2. Capital: Ash £60,000, Birch £40,000. Interest on capital 5%. Birch's salary £12,000. Interest on drawings: Ash £600, Birch £400. Profit for the year before appropriations £98,000. Appropriation account £ Profit for the year before appropriations 98,000 Add: interest on drawings (600 + 400) 1,000 Less: interest on capital (5% × 60,000 + 5% × 40,000) = 3,000 + 2,000 (5,000) Less: Birch's salary (12,000) Residual profit 82,000 Share: Ash (3/5 × 82,000) 49,200 Share: Birch (2/5 × 82,000) 32,800 Current accounts Ash £ Birch £ Interest on capital 3,000 2,000 Salary - 12,000 Share of residual profit 49,200 32,800 Less: interest on drawings (600) (400) Less: drawings - - Balance c/d 51,600 46,400 Check: 51,600 + 46,400 = 98,000, the whole profit, as it must be. A debit (overdrawn) current account - drawings exceeding entitlement - is a deduction within equity, not a receivable. Ratio changes are the harder variant. If Ash and Birch move from 3:2 to 1:1 on a £90,000 profit: old shares 54,000/36,000, new shares 45,000/45,000 - Birch gains £9,000 at Ash's expense, and the examiner wants the transfer identified, not both calculations alone. Apply the new ratio from the agreed date only unless the deed says otherwise, and keep all other appropriations (interest, salaries) unaffected by the change. Conclude any such question by checking the total distributed still equals the profit available - the single best error check in partnership questions. When the profit-sharing ratio changes , AQA wants the effect quantified: compute each partner's share under the old ratio and the new ratio on the year's profit and show the transfer between them. Keep concepts in view: business entity (partners' private affairs stay out; interest on capital exists because funds belong to the firm), prudence (provide for doubtful debts before appropriating profit), and consistency (apply deed terms identically each year). In the statement of financial position, each partner's equity = fixed capital account + current account balance - mirror this format from the sole trader layout and the company equity section, and the three business types become one template with three variations. In the exam, company and partnership questions are usually worth 15-25 marks and follow a fixed recipe: adjust a trial balance, produce a statement (or an extract), then complete the equity section or the appropriation/current accounts. Budget your time by mark density: the mechanics earn steadily, but the final two marks of a 25-marker usually sit in an explain or evaluate part - the concept behind a treatment, or the effect of an omitted adjustment - so never spend all your minutes on the tables.
