topics.searchText: accounting Accounting Ratio Analysis Calculate the full AQA ratio set from financial statements: gross and operating margins, mark-up, ROCE, current and acid test, receivables, payables and inventory days, gearing and interest cover (AQA 7127, 3.8 with appendix) (AO2). Select valid comparatives - prior year, industry norm, plan - and interpret movements with plausible business causes (3.8) (AO2/AO3). Analyse profitability, liquidity and gearing together, recognising trade-offs such as liquidity versus profitability and risk versus return (3.8) (AO3). Evaluate the limitations of ratio analysis: historical cost, estimates, window dressing, single-year data, inflation and non-financial factors (3.17) (AO3). Communicate a justified recommendation for a named stakeholder, integrating calculations with qualitative evidence (3.17) (AO3). ROCE = operating profit ÷ (equity + non-current liabilities). Using profit for the year or total assets is the most common formula error. Current ratio benchmark ~1.5-2:1, acid test ~1:1 - but benchmarks are starting points for investigation, not verdicts. Working capital cycle = inventory days + receivables days − payables days: the gap the business must finance. Gearing above 50% is high by convention, but judge it with interest cover and cash flow stability, never alone. Every interpretation answer: calculate, compare (prior year/industry), identify cause, state consequence, then conclude with limitations. Gross profit margin Gross profit ÷ revenue × 100: the percentage of each £1 of sales left after cost of sales, to cover expenses and profit. Mark-up Gross profit ÷ cost of sales × 100: the percentage added to cost to set the selling price. Return on capital employed (ROCE) Operating profit ÷ capital employed × 100, where capital employed = equity + non-current liabilities; measures the return generated on all long-term funds. Working capital Current assets − current liabilities: the cushion of short-term resources available to meet short-term obligations. Acid test ratio (Current assets − inventory) ÷ current liabilities: liquidity without relying on selling inventory; below 1 needs investigation of receivables quality and the overdraft. Gearing Long-term debt ÷ capital employed × 100 (alternative: debt ÷ (debt + equity)); the proportion of long-term funds that is borrowed. Above 50% is conventionally high. Interest cover Operating profit ÷ finance costs: how many times profit could pay the interest bill; below about 2-3 signals danger. Window dressing Legally recording transactions near the year end to flatter the statements - e.g. delaying payments to raise the current ratio - improving appearance without improving substance. Profitability ratios answer one question in three ways: is the business generating adequate return from its sales and from the funds invested in it? The formulas are fixed in the AQA appendix, so formula recall earns nothing by itself - the marks are in calculation accuracy , comparison and causal interpretation . Ratio Formula What it measures Gross profit margin Gross profit ÷ revenue × 100 Trading profitability after cost of sales Mark-up Gross profit ÷ cost of sales × 100 Percentage added to cost in pricing Operating profit margin Operating profit ÷ revenue × 100 Overall cost control after overheads ROCE Operating profit ÷ capital employed × 100 Return on all long-term funds (equity + non-current liabilities) Formula discipline: use operating profit - not profit for the year - in both the operating margin and ROCE, and capital employed is equity plus non-current liabilities (equivalently, non-current assets plus current assets minus current liabilities). Using the wrong profit or the wrong denominator is the most common calculation error and zeroes the interpretation built on it. Worked example: two-year profitability calculation Data (year ended 31 March): 2025 - revenue £900,000, gross profit £315,000, operating profit £90,000, equity £600,000, non-current liabilities £300,000. 2024 - revenue £800,000, gross profit £280,000, operating profit £72,000, equity £550,000, non-current liabilities £300,000. Ratio 2025 2024 Gross profit margin 315,000/900,000 = 35.0% 280,000/800,000 = 35.0% Operating profit margin 90,000/900,000 = 10.0% 72,000/800,000 = 9.0% ROCE 90,000/900,000 = 10.0% 72,000/850,000 = 8.5% Interpretation: the gross margin held at 35%, so trading economics (pricing versus direct costs) were stable. The operating margin improved from 9% to 10% - overheads grew more slowly than sales, evidence of operating leverage. ROCE rose from 8.5% to 10.0%: a better return even though capital employed grew from £850,000 to £900,000. The A* move is the decomposition: ROCE = operating margin × capital turnover (revenue ÷ capital employed). Here 10.0% = 10.0% × 1.00 in 2025, versus 8.5% = 9.0% × 0.94 in 2024 - so the improvement came from both margin and asset productivity, a two-cause explanation that scores above a one-cause answer. Causes to attach to movements, ready-made for exams. A falling gross margin: price discounting in a competitive market; rising input costs not passed on; inventory losses (theft, obsolescence) inflating cost of sales; or a sales-mix shift towards lower-margin lines. A rising margin: price rises absorbed by customers; cheaper suppliers; better purchasing (bulk discounts); or - the sceptical check - a one-off reclassification. A falling operating margin with a stable gross margin: overhead creep (admin, distribution) outpacing sales; a falling margin with a rising gross margin suggests overheads were cut - a strategy with service-quality consequences worth mentioning. For mark-up, remember its exam use: with mark-up of 25% you can reconstruct cost of sales (100/125 of revenue) in incomplete-records questions - profitability ratios are computational tools, not just commentary. ROCE invites benchmarking against three yardsticks: the prior year (trend), the industry (is 10% good for this sector?), and the cost of debt (if ROCE exceeds the interest rate on borrowing, gearing magnifies returns to shareholders; if not, it destroys them). That third comparison is the bridge to gearing in section 2 - and a favourite examiner link. When asked to evaluate profitability, resist one-number conclusions: a high margin on tiny revenue is worse than a modest margin on huge revenue, so pair margins with turnover and ROCE with growth. And state the movement in plain words before quantifying: 'ROCE improved by 1.5 percentage points because operating profit grew 25% while capital employed grew only 6%' is an analytical sentence; 'ROCE went up' is not. Improvement strategies earn evaluation marks when tied to trade-offs. Raise the gross margin by raising prices (risk: volume loss), renegotiating supply (risk: quality), or pushing high-margin lines (risk: alienating existing customers). Improve ROCE by raising margin, increasing capital turnover (sweating the assets: sell idle equipment, outsource), or returning idle capital to investors. Every strategy has a second-order effect on another ratio - price rises may lengthen receivables days; asset disposals cut future capacity - and saying so explicitly is what separates the top band from mid band in AQA's 25-mark Section C questions. Worked example: mark-up as a computational tool A business prices at a mark-up of 25% on cost. If revenue is £150,000, cost of sales = 150,000 × 100/125 = £120,000 and gross profit = £30,000 (a margin of 20%). In incomplete-records questions this runs in reverse: a trial balance fragment showing revenue £150,000 and a known 25% mark-up implies cost of sales £120,000; any gap between that computed figure and the ledger's cost of sales points to unrecorded purchases, theft or stock losses. Mark-up is therefore not just commentary - it is the input that reconstructs missing figures, which is why the AQA appendix lists it alongside the margins. Two distortions deserve a reflex. Sales mix : a stable blended gross margin can hide two offsetting movements - higher prices on a shrinking line, lower prices on a booming one - so where mix data is given, comment on the components rather than the blend. One-off items : a disposal profit inside other income lifts the operating margin in the year of sale and vanishes the next; restructuring costs depress one year only. When the question supplies a note ('operating profit includes £25,000 profit on disposal of a warehouse'), strip it out before interpreting, and state that you have done so - examiners reward the explicit adjustment, because it shows you are reading the accounting policies behind the number, not just the number. Industry benchmarking needs the same care to earn marks. A 35% gross margin is excellent in grocery (high turnover, low margin) and poor in jewellery (low turnover, high margin) - what matters is the combination of margin and capital turnover that produces ROCE, so a low-margin, fast-turning business can out-return a high-margin, slow one. Always ask what a benchmark measures: national averages smear very different business models together; a named competitor of similar scale is better evidence; the business's own plan is the fairest test of management performance. Where the question supplies prior-year data only, use the trend and add that industry norms would sharpen the conclusion - that sentence is itself an analysis mark, and in evaluation questions it becomes the 'further information required' point. Common calculation errors to drill out: using revenue in the ROCE denominator (that gives asset turnover, not return); averaging capital employed when the question gives one figure (average is only required if both opening and closing are given - follow the data provided); computing payables days on revenue instead of purchases (use cost of sales or credit purchases as directed); and confusing a 35% margin with 35% growth. Set answers out in a small table - ratio, 2025, 2024, movement - because AQA markers credit clear working, and an error in one figure then costs one mark, not the thread of the interpretation built on it. Liquidity asks whether short-term obligations can be met; efficiency asks how fast working capital turns; gearing asks who financed the business and how risky the structure is. The three interlock - a business can be profitable yet illiquid, liquid yet inefficient, and efficient yet dangerously geared - so AQA rewards answers that connect them. Ratio Formula Benchmark/guide Current ratio Current assets ÷ current liabilities ~1.5-2:1 Acid test (Current assets − inventory) ÷ current liabilities ~1:1 Inventory turnover Cost of sales ÷ average inventory (or 365 ÷ inventory days) Sector-specific Trade receivables days Trade receivables ÷ credit sales (revenue) × 365 Compare with credit terms Trade payables days Trade payables ÷ credit purchases (cost of sales) × 365 Compare with suppliers' terms Gearing Non-current liabilities ÷ (equity + non-current liabilities) × 100 >50% high by convention Interest cover Operating profit ÷ finance costs >2-3× comfortable Worked example: liquidity and efficiency, two years 2025: inventory £75,000, receivables £110,000, cash £15,000, current liabilities £150,000 (of which payables £120,000), cost of sales £585,000. 2024: inventory £60,000, receivables £80,000, cash £60,000, current liabilities £160,000 (payables £115,000), cost of sales £520,000. Ratio 2025 2024 Current ratio 200,000/150,000 = 1.33:1 200,000/160,000 = 1.25:1 Acid test 125,000/150,000 = 0.83:1 140,000/160,000 = 0.88:1 Receivables days 110,000/900,000 × 365 = 45 days 80,000/800,000 × 365 = 37 days Payables days 120,000/585,000 × 365 = 75 days 115,000/520,000 × 365 = 81 days Inventory days 75,000/585,000 × 365 = 47 days 60,000/520,000 × 365 = 42 days Working capital cycle 47 + 45 − 75 = 17 days 42 + 37 − 81 = −2 days Read the story: the current ratio edged up but cash collapsed from £60,000 to £15,000, receivables days stretched by 8 days (looser credit control, or a customer problem), payables days shortened (paying earlier - possibly straining cash or earning early-payment discounts), and inventory moved slower. Net effect: the working capital cycle swung from −2 days (suppliers effectively financed the business) to +17 days the business must fund itself. Liquidity looked stable while its quality worsened - exactly the layered reading AQA's top band rewards. The acid test below 1 is acceptable here only if receivables are collectable; note receivables of £110,000 cover most of the £150,000 current liabilities, so the ratio depends on collection discipline. Efficiency commentary patterns: receivables days above stated credit terms signal weak credit control or disputed invoices - chasing them releases cash at zero cost; payables days below suppliers' terms may waste discounts, but very long payables days risk supply refusal and signal cash distress to the market; slow inventory ties up cash, incurs storage and risks obsolescence - and under the prudence concept may need writing down to net realisable value, hitting gross profit. Efficiency links to profitability directly: cash trapped in working capital cannot earn ROCE elsewhere; that is the overtrading diagnosis - rapid revenue growth funded by stretching payables and an overdraft, where margins look healthy but the cash cycle runs dry. Spot the symptoms: rising revenue with falling liquidity, payables days rising, ROCE fine but cash negative. Gearing is the structural risk ratio. In the example above, gearing = 300,000/900,000 = 33% (2025) versus 35% (2024) - falling as equity accumulates. High gearing cuts both ways: with interest cover of 3.0 (90,000/30,000), shareholders are geared for upside if returns on assets exceed the 12% cost of debt implied by 36,000 on 300,000... check the question's given rate - but if operating profit falls by half, cover drops to 1.5 and the business is near the edge. Evaluation points AQA expects: interest is a fixed obligation paid before any dividend; secured lenders take assets on default; high gearing removes flexibility to borrow for opportunities; but debt is often cheaper than equity and interest is tax-deductible, so modest gearing is rational. Never conclude 'gearing is high, therefore bad' without interest cover, cash stability and the purpose of the borrowing (growth funding versus survival refinancing) on the table. Connect the three families in your conclusions: improving profitability by stretching payables days damages supplier goodwill (qualitative), tightening receivables days improves liquidity but may cost sales, cutting inventory improves the cycle but risks stockouts. The exam's higher-order demand is a recommendation : 'extend the overdraft facility and tighten credit control rather than cut inventory, because...' with figures quoted as evidence. That sentence structure - recommendation, evidence, mechanism - is the template for full marks. Worked example: spotting overtrading from the numbers A retailer doubles revenue from £400,000 to £800,000. Gross margin holds at 40%. Inventory rises from £50,000 to £130,000; receivables from £35,000 to £95,000; payables from £45,000 to £130,000; the bank account moves from £10,000 credit to a £60,000 overdraft. Liquidity: current ratio 1.55:1 to 1.30:1; acid test 0.94:1 to 0.71:1. The margins tell a growth story; the working capital accounts tell a funding crisis - inventory and receivables grew faster than equity could finance, so the gap was bridged by stretching payables and the overdraft. Remedies in priority order: inject equity or long-term debt (match funding to the asset growth); slow the growth; tighten receivables and inventory control. An examiner's one-line diagnosis: profitable on the statement of profit or loss, starving on the statement of financial position . Company questions may also pull in the investment ratios from the AQA appendix, so keep the set in working memory: earnings per share = profit attributable to ordinary shareholders ÷ number of ordinary shares; dividend per share and dividend yield (dividend ÷ market price × 100 - income as a percentage of what the share costs today); dividend cover = earnings per share ÷ dividend per share (how safely the dividend is paid; cover below about 2 signals strain); and price/earnings = market price ÷ earnings per share (how many years of current earnings the market is paying for - a confidence and growth expectation measure). They belong in answers about shareholders and valuation, and they inherit every limitation listed in section 3 - a window-dressed profit inflates EPS exactly as it inflates the margins. Seasonality is a final reading caution that shows genuine understanding. A year-end snapshot can misrepresent a seasonal business: a retailer measured in January looks cash-rich and inventory-poor; the same business in November is the reverse. If the question flags a seasonal trade, recommend reading month-end figures through the cycle and comparing like month with like month. And remember the units: days should be sensible (a grocer with 60 inventory days and a car dealer with 60 are telling opposite stories), receivables days beyond credit terms means something is wrong operationally - disputed invoices, a distressed customer, or weak administration - and saying which, with the evidence available, is the analytical standard. Finally, connect liquidity back to the concepts. Inventory at cost in the current ratio assumes it is worth that - under prudence, write down to net realisable value anything damaged, obsolete or slow-moving before computing the ratio, or your liquidity picture is flattered by stock that will never convert at cost. Receivables in the acid test assume collection - deduct any allowance for doubtful debts, and treat a customer-specific problem as a write-off issue, not just a days ratio. This is the cross-topic reflex AQA likes: an adjustment question in Paper 1 and a ratio question may test the same underlying event from two directions, and students who see both directions answer twice as fast. Calculation is the cheap half of 3.17. The examinable skill is interpretation and communication : selecting the right ratios for the question, comparing them against the right benchmarks, reading causes behind the numbers, and delivering a conclusion a stakeholder could act on. Build answers on a five-step frame and the 25-mark extended question becomes structured rather than improvised. Calculate - the specified ratios, to one decimal place or a sensible number of days, with formulas shown. Compare - prior year (trend), industry norm (cross-section), plan or target, and named competitors where given. A ratio without a comparison is a fact without meaning. Explain - the plausible business cause of each movement: pricing, cost inflation, credit policy, purchasing terms, funding structure. Assess - the consequence for the stakeholder in question: will a supplier be paid? can the bank rely on cover? does the investor get yield or growth? Conclude with limitations - what the figures cannot tell you, and what further information you would want. Stakeholders need different lenses, and naming the lens shows application. A supplier deciding to sell on credit reads liquidity first (acid test, receivables days, working capital), then gearing. A bank reads interest cover, gearing and cash flow before any margin. A shareholder reads ROCE, the company investment ratios (earnings per share, dividend yield, dividend cover, price/earnings - specified for companies in the AQA appendix), and gearing for risk. Management reads the efficiency set and margins against budget. Two facts matter more than the rest when the question says evaluate for stakeholder X : most accounting data is historical, and stakeholders' decisions are about the future. Now the limitations - the marks that separate A* from A. Historical cost : statements record what was paid, so inflation distorts margins (revenue is at current prices, depreciation at historic cost, overstating profit in real terms) and non-current asset values may bear no relation to market value. Estimates everywhere : depreciation rates, useful lives, allowance percentages and inventory valuations are judgemental, so two identical businesses can report different profits by policy choice - always check whether the comparative years used consistent policies. Window dressing : legitimate transactions timed to flatter ratios. Worked example: window dressing the current ratio Current assets £200,000 (including cash £50,000), current liabilities £150,000: current ratio 1.33:1, acid test 125,000/150,000 = 0.83:1. Two days before the year end, the business pays £20,000 of payables, replenishing the balance after the year end. Current ratio after: 180,000/130,000 = 1.38:1 - improved. Acid test after: 105,000/130,000 = 0.81:1 - worsened, because cash (an acid asset) left while inventory stayed. The lesson doubles the marks: window dressing works on the ratio it targets but often damages another - and a reader comparing current ratio with acid test spots the manipulation. Combine with a statement that the underlying position is unchanged: the same obligations exist on 2 January. Single-year, single-company snapshots : one bad year may be investment spending (new stores depress margins now, raise them later); one good year may be luck. Non-financial factors : staff turnover, customer satisfaction, brand, technology and ESG performance shape future cash flows and appear nowhere in the ratios. Data comparability : different year ends, one-off items (restructuring costs, disposal profits), and IFRS-versus-UK terminology all cloud trend reading. The A* evaluation ends with further information required : cash flow statements (profit is an opinion, cash is a fact), segmental data, industry benchmarks, and the notes to the accounts. Command-word mapping for Paper 1 Section C. Analyse the performance: calculate, compare, explain causes - two linked chains of reasoning minimum. Evaluate the financial position: weigh two-sided evidence (liquidity improved but quality worsened), reach a supported judgement, and state what would change your mind. Discuss the usefulness of ratio analysis: balance the framework's power (comparability, early warning, communication) against the limitations above, and conclude on usefulness for a stated purpose - usefulness is always relative to the decision at hand, which is the sentence examiners underline. Two additions complete the toolkit. First, the statement of cash flows : profit is built on accruals and estimates, cash is a fact - a company reporting rising profits while cash flow from operations falls is a classic warning combination (profits booked ahead of cash, or working capital absorbing the profit). When a question offers cash flow data, use it as your truth-test in the conclusion. Second, comparability hygiene : check year ends match, watch for one-off items in either year, confirm depreciation policies and allowance rates are consistent across the comparison, and translate any IFRS terminology (revenue/turnover, inventory/stock, receivables/debtors) before computing - mixed terminology is a common source of 'error' in student answers and a gift of an easy fix. Push the limitations beyond the standard list when the question allows, because the top band rewards developed rather than listed points. Estimates : depreciation rates, useful lives, allowance percentages and inventory valuations are judgemental, so two identical businesses can report different profits by policy choice alone - check whether the comparative years use consistent policies before trusting a trend. Window dressing takes several forms beyond delaying payables: offering unusually generous year-end credit terms to pull sales forward, deferring routine maintenance (cash preserved, expense avoided, risk accumulated), and classifying a short-term loan as long-term to polish liquidity ratios. Non-financial factors - staff turnover, customer satisfaction, brand strength, technology, environmental performance - shape future cash flows and appear nowhere in the ratios; an answer that names one or two relevant to the scenario (a restaurant with high staff turnover, a manufacturer with an ageing machine fleet) turns a generic limitation into applied analysis. A skeleton for the 25-mark answer, worth committing to memory: paragraph 1 - profitability (two ratios calculated, compared, causes, one limitation); paragraph 2 - liquidity and efficiency (same structure); paragraph 3 - gearing and risk (including interest cover); paragraph 4 - judgement for the named stakeholder with the two strongest pieces of evidence both ways; closing sentence - the further information that would refine the decision. Under exam timing, write the topic sentence of each paragraph first, then fill with figures: if you run out of time, the skeleton alone often secures the structure marks. One closing discipline: keep your conclusions conditional and evidence-bound . 'The company is illiquid' is a claim; 'on these figures the company's liquidity is weakening - the acid test fell to 0.83:1 and cash covers only a tenth of current liabilities - so, pending sight of the cash flow statement and an aged receivables schedule, credit terms beyond 30 days would be imprudent' is an A* conclusion. The difference is the mechanism (which figure, which direction, what follows) and the stated boundary of the evidence. Ratio analysis never proves anything on its own; your job is to show the reader exactly how far the numbers carry the argument, and where judgement takes over.

topics.searchText: accounting Accounting Costing and Budgeting Classify costs as fixed, variable, semi-variable or stepped, and direct or indirect, and split semi-variable costs using the high-low method (AQA 7127, 3.10/3.12) (AO2). Calculate contribution, break-even output and revenue, margin of safety and target-profit output, and evaluate the uses and limitations of break-even analysis (3.10) (AO2/AO3). Calculate overhead absorption rates, absorbed overhead and under/over absorption, and reconcile marginal and absorption costing profits when inventory levels change (3.12) (AO2/AO3). Prepare cash budgets with receipts and payments timed correctly, and evaluate the purposes of budgeting including behavioural effects such as budgetary slack (3.9) (AO2/AO3). Calculate materials, labour and overhead variances against a flexed budget, and explain plausible causes and interdependence (3.11) (AO2/AO3). Break-even units = fixed costs ÷ contribution per unit; margin of safety = actual − break-even; target-profit units = (fixed costs + target profit) ÷ contribution per unit. Marginal costing values inventory at variable production cost and writes off fixed overheads as period costs; absorption costing carries fixed overhead in inventory - profits differ when inventory levels change. OAR always uses BUDGETED overhead ÷ BUDGETED activity. Under-absorption = actual overhead > absorbed overhead. Cash budgets forecast cash, not profit: sales on credit become receipts next month; purchases are paid a month after buying; depreciation never appears. Variances compare ACTUAL with FLEXED budget. Materials: price (paid vs standard price) and usage (used vs standard for actual output). Labour: rate and efficiency. Contribution Selling price per unit minus variable cost per unit: the amount each unit contributes towards fixed costs and then profit. Total contribution = units × contribution per unit. Break-even output The output at which total revenue equals total cost and profit is nil: fixed costs ÷ contribution per unit (or fixed costs ÷ C/S ratio for revenue). Margin of safety Actual or budgeted output minus break-even output: how far sales can fall before the business makes a loss; express in units or as a percentage of sales. Semi-variable cost A cost with a fixed element and a variable element (e.g. telephone line rental plus call charges); split using the high-low method: variable cost per unit = change in cost ÷ change in output. Overhead absorption rate (OAR) Budgeted overhead ÷ budgeted activity (units, machine hours or labour hours): the rate used to charge fixed production overheads to units under absorption costing. Under/over absorption The difference between overheads absorbed (OAR × actual activity) and overheads actually incurred; under-absorption is an expense adjustment, over-absorption a credit. Flexed budget The original budget adjusted to the actual level of output, so that variances compare like with like: comparing actual results with the unflexed budget measures nothing useful. Budgetary slack Deliberately understating budgeted revenue or overstating budgeted costs to make targets easier to achieve - a behavioural flaw of imposed or loosely reviewed budgets. Cost behaviour - not cost type - drives every management accounting decision in Paper 2. Fixed costs (rent, salaries, insurance) do not move with output within a relevant range; variable costs (materials, piece-rate labour, sales commission) move in direct proportion; semi-variable costs (electricity with a standing charge) contain both; stepped costs (a second supervisor hired once output passes a threshold) jump at activity points. Separately, direct costs trace to a unit (materials, direct labour); indirect costs (overheads) do not. A cost can be direct and fixed (a dedicated supervisor for one production line) - the two classifications answer different questions, and confusing them is a classic error. The high-low method splits a semi-variable cost: take the highest and lowest activity levels (not the highest and lowest costs), compute variable cost per unit = change in cost ÷ change in units, then fixed cost = total cost at either point − variable element. With output of 4,000 units costing £38,000 and 9,000 units costing £78,000: variable = 40,000/5,000 = £8 per unit; fixed = 38,000 − (4,000 × 8) = £6,000; predicted cost at 7,000 units = 6,000 + (7,000 × 8) = £62,000. Two cautions for evaluation marks: the method uses only two observations, so outliers distort it; and it assumes linearity and a stable fixed element, so it is an estimate, not a law. Worked example: make-or-buy and limiting factors Make-or-buy. A component costs £18 per unit to make: materials £7, direct labour £6, variable overhead £3, plus £2 of absorbed fixed overhead. A supplier quotes £16. Compare the RIGHT figures: the variable cost of making is £16 (7 + 6 + 3) - the £2 absorbed fixed overhead continues whatever you choose. Making and buying are cost-identical on variable cost, so decide on capacity and quality; had the quote been £17, buying saves £1 per unit of contribution while capacity is freed for other work. The exam rule: exclude fixed costs that do not change, include any that do. Limiting factor. Products A and B: contribution per unit A £12, B £9 - A looks better. But machine hours are scarce: A needs 4 hours, B needs 2. Contribution per machine hour: A £3.00, B £4.50 - B ranks first . Rank by contribution per unit of the scarce factor, allocate capacity accordingly, then calculate the optimal production plan and total contribution. The mistake AQA watches for is ranking by contribution per unit; the evaluation point is that the 'correct' plan maximises total contribution, not unit contribution. Multi-product questions use the C/S ratio differently: with a constant sales mix, weighted-average contribution per unit (or weighted C/S ratio) feeds the same formulas - break-even revenue = fixed costs ÷ weighted C/S ratio. If the mix shifts towards lower-contribution products, break-even rises even when total sales hold - a subtlety worth one sentence in any mixed-mix answer. Sensitivity language to reuse: 'each £1 fall in selling price raises break-even by fixed costs ÷ new contribution' - concrete and computable rather than vague. Where does management accounting data come from, and how reliable is it? Estimates of variable and fixed splits come from past records (hence high-low), engineering studies, or supplier quotes; they carry sampling error and may reflect a cost structure that has changed (a new energy contract, automation replacing labour). Strong answers acknowledge the evidence base behind the numbers before recommending action - 'the £8 variable cost per unit is an estimate from two observations; before committing to the 12,000-unit plan, management should re-estimate using regression or supplier quotations' - and that habit converts a calculation answer into an evaluation answer. Contribution = selling price − variable cost per unit, and it is the engine of short-run decisions. Break-even output = fixed costs ÷ contribution per unit; break-even revenue = fixed costs ÷ C/S ratio, where the C/S (contribution/sales) ratio = contribution per unit ÷ selling price; margin of safety = budgeted output − break-even output (in units, or ÷ budgeted output × 100 as a percentage); target-profit output = (fixed costs + target profit) ÷ contribution per unit. On a break-even chart, total revenue and total cost lines cross at break-even; the contribution chart plots contribution against fixed costs and shows profit building only after the fixed line is covered. Learn to describe the chart as well as compute it - AQA asks for both. Worked example: full break-even analysis Fixed costs £84,000; selling price £24; variable cost £14; budgeted output 11,000 units; target profit £36,000. Contribution per unit = 24 − 14 = £10. Break-even output = 84,000 ÷ 10 = 8,400 units . Break-even revenue = 8,400 × 24 = £201,600 (check: C/S ratio = 10/24 = 41.67%; 84,000 ÷ 0.4167 = £201,600). Margin of safety = 11,000 − 8,400 = 2,600 units , or 2,600/11,000 × 100 = 23.6% of budgeted sales. Target profit £36,000: units = (84,000 + 36,000) ÷ 10 = 12,000 units . Interpretation: each unit sold beyond 8,400 adds £10 of profit; 12,000 units × £10 − 84,000 = £36,000. If variable cost rose to £16, contribution falls to £8 and break-even jumps to 10,500 units - the sensitivity examiners ask you to comment on. Decisions using marginal costing: make-or-buy - compare the buying price with the marginal cost of making (only relevant variable costs; fixed costs usually continue, so include them only if they change); special orders below normal price - accept if contribution is positive and spare capacity exists, but consider the reaction of regular customers; limiting factors - when a scarce resource (machine hours, materials) caps output, rank products by contribution per unit of the scarce factor, not contribution per unit. All are short-run tools: in the long run fixed costs must be covered and prices must deliver a normal profit, which is the standard evaluation point. The limitations of break-even analysis, ready to deploy in a 12-marker: it assumes linear costs and revenue (no bulk discounts, no economies of scale, one price for all units); it assumes all output is sold at the same price (ignores stock-building and price discrimination); fixed costs are constant over all output ranges (in truth they step); it handles one product or a constant mix only; and it is a static model - demand uncertainty, competitor response and cost inflation sit outside it. Its strengths are equal: transparent, cheap, communicates risk through the margin of safety, and gives a first-pass target for pricing and capacity. The A* judgement: break-even analysis is a planning aid to be stress-tested (what if price falls 5%? variable cost rises 10%?), not a decision machine. Draw and label the chart if the question asks: horizontal axis output, vertical axis £; fixed costs as a horizontal line starting on the vertical axis; total cost rising with the gradient of variable cost per unit; total revenue rising from the origin with the gradient of the selling price; the intersection labelled break-even; margin of safety as the horizontal gap between budgeted output and break-even. A contribution chart replaces the total-cost line's separation by plotting a contribution line rising at contribution per unit against a horizontal fixed-cost line - profit exists only where contribution exceeds fixed costs, and the crossing point is break-even. Describing these features precisely (gradients, starting points, the meaning of the gap) earns method marks in many structured questions, so practise sketching both once under time pressure. Absorption costing exists because financial statements need inventory values that include production overhead. The mechanism runs in stages. Allocation assigns whole overhead items to the departments that caused them (a production supervisor's salary to that production department). Apportionment splits shared items on a sensible basis (rent by floor area, power by machine hours). Reapportionment then charges service departments (maintenance, canteen) to production departments - by repeated distribution or the step method, questions will state the basis. Finally an overhead absorption rate charges overheads to units: OAR = budgeted overhead ÷ budgeted activity, with activity usually machine hours (machine-intensive), labour hours (labour-intensive) or units. Worked example: OAR and under/over absorption Budgeted overhead £180,000; budgeted machine hours 24,000; actual overhead £176,000; actual machine hours 22,000. OAR = 180,000 ÷ 24,000 = £7.50 per machine hour . Overhead absorbed = 7.50 × 22,000 = £165,000 . Under-absorption = 176,000 − 165,000 = £11,000 - added to production cost in the statement of profit or loss. Diagnose the cause: hours fell 2,000 below budget (activity effect: 2,000 × 7.50 = £15,000 under), while spending came in £4,000 under budget (spending effect: −4,000). Net −£11,000. Two causes, two directions - the decomposition examiners reward. Over-absorption (absorbed exceeds actual) is credited; under-absorption is charged. Both arise from two sources: actual activity differing from budget, or actual spending differing from budget. The conceptual criticism AQA expects: arbitrary rates distort unit costs when products consume overheads unevenly - which is the gap ABC was invented to close. Worked example: reapportionment of a service department Production departments: Machining (overhead £60,000, 20,000 machine hours) and Assembly (£40,000, 10,000 labour hours); service department Maintenance (£20,000), which works 60% for Machining and 40% for Assembly. Reapportion Maintenance: Machining +£12,000 → £72,000; Assembly +£8,000 → £48,000. Machining OAR = 72,000 ÷ 20,000 machine hours = £3.60 per machine hour . Assembly OAR = 48,000 ÷ 10,000 labour hours = £4.80 per labour hour . Choosing the base follows the cause: machine hours where machines dominate the work, labour hours where people do. Where a question offers both bases and asks which is more appropriate, it wants the causal justification, not a coin flip - and where a service department serves other service departments too, use repeated distribution until the residuals become immaterial, as the question directs. Activity-based costing pools overheads by activity (set-ups, inspections, ordering, machine running) and charges products through cost drivers (number of set-ups, number of inspections). The logic: products cause activities, activities cause costs. ABC improves accuracy where overheads are high and product diversity is real (a complex product that needs many set-ups absorbs its true cost instead of being subsidised by simple high-volume lines). Its costs: data collection is expensive, drivers are not always measurable, and the choice of driver is still a judgement. For 12-mark evaluation: ABC gives better product-level decisions (pricing, dropping products) in modern overhead-heavy environments; traditional absorption is cheaper to run and adequate where overheads are low or products are homogeneous - the classic 'set-ups' versus 'machine hours' contrast. Marginal versus absorption costing is a guaranteed comparison question. Both treat selling and administration overheads as period costs; they differ only on fixed production overhead: marginal costing expenses it as incurred; absorption costing defers it inside inventory values. So when inventory increases , absorption shows higher profit (some fixed overhead rides in closing inventory into next period); when inventory falls , absorption shows lower profit; when inventory is unchanged, profits are identical. The reconciliation: difference in profit = change in inventory units × fixed overhead per unit. Example: fixed overhead per unit £6; inventory rises from 1,000 to 2,500 units; absorption profit = marginal profit + 1,500 × 6 = marginal profit + £9,000. State also the arguments: marginal costing aids short-run decisions (contribution logic) but understates inventory value against IAS 2, which absorption satisfies; absorption smooths reported profit and matches total production cost to units sold, but can let managers hide cost overruns in inventory build-ups - a link to creative accounting in topic 5. When the comparison is asked as a 12-marker, the frame that scores: define both methods' treatment of fixed production overhead (AO1); compute or reconcile the profit difference via the inventory change (AO2); then evaluate on three axes - decision relevance (marginal/contribution logic wins for short-run choices), external reporting compliance (absorption satisfies inventory valuation rules), and behavioural risk (inventory build-ups can defer overhead into stock and flatter profit - absorption invites it, marginal exposes it). Close with the purpose judgement: a business should manage by marginal costing and report by absorption costing; the 'difference' is a reporting convention, not a dispute about facts. Structure your comparison answers as a table in your head - inventory value, fixed overhead treatment, decision usefulness, external reporting - then a judgement on purpose : management decision-making favours marginal costing; statutory statements require absorption. Questions often set a small profit calculation under both methods for the same data; practising the reconciliation by the change-in-inventory shortcut saves five minutes and removes the arithmetic risk of building both statements in full. Two refinements complete 3.12. First, non-production overheads (selling, distribution, administration) are period costs under both methods - never absorbed into units - so a unit cost that includes advertising has misclassified. Second, norms for the exam : fixed overhead per unit for reconciliations uses only fixed PRODUCTION overhead divided by normal (budgeted) output; variable costs per unit are identical under both methods; and if asked for 'the profit under marginal costing', build it as sales − variable cost of sales − all fixed costs, in that order, rather than adapting an absorption statement - fewer steps, fewer errors. Under time pressure, the inventory-change shortcut (difference = change in units × fixed overhead per unit) converts one full statement into one line of arithmetic. Worked example: ABC versus traditional absorption Set-up costs £60,000. Product X: 2,000 units, 10 set-ups; Product Y: 8,000 units, 90 set-ups. Traditional (machine hours, 50,000 total): rate £1.20; X absorbs 2,000 × 2 hours × 1.20 = £4,800 (per unit £2.40); Y absorbs 8,000 × 5 hours × 1.20 = £48,000 (per unit £6.00). ABC (driver = set-ups, 100 total): rate £600 per set-up; X = 10 × 600 = £6,000 (£3.00 per unit); Y = 90 × 600 = £54,000 (£6.75 per unit). Y, the complex product, was under-costed by traditional absorption - simple X subsidised it. Decisions that follow: Y's pricing and any 'drop Y' analysis were built on wrong costs. That single contrast is the standard way to earn the ABC evaluation marks. A budget is a quantified plan for a period, and budgeting earns its place in the specification through purposes you must be able to evaluate: planning (forcing management to look forward), coordination (aligning production, purchasing, sales and finance), communication and motivation (targets that stretch but are attainable), control (variances flag where reality departs from plan), resource allocation, and authorisation of spending. The master budget gathers the functional budgets (sales, production, purchases, labour, overheads) into budgeted financial statements plus a cash budget . Evaluation angle: budgets only deliver these benefits if targets are realistic and accepted - unattainable targets demotivate; too-easy targets (budgetary slack) invite complacency; participative budgeting (managers set their own targets) improves commitment but invites slack, a tension worth stating in any 25-marker. The cash budget is where marks are won or lost on timing. Rules: credit sales become receipts one or more months later (per the stated terms); purchases are paid the month after buying (or per terms); wages, rent and overheads follow their stated patterns; depreciation is never in a cash budget (no cash moves); capital purchases hit cash when paid; VAT and discounts only if specified. Work from receipts − payments = net cash flow, add opening balance, get closing balance - which becomes next month's opening balance. Worked example: two-month cash budget Opening cash January: £5,000. Sales: December £40,000, January £50,000, February £60,000 - half for cash, half collected one month later. Purchases: December £24,000, January £30,000, February £32,000 - paid one month after purchase. Wages £10,000 and overheads £6,000 per month, paid in the month. Equipment £15,000 paid in February. January £ February £ Receipts: cash sales (50% current month) + prior month credit collections 25,000 + 20,000 = 45,000 30,000 + 25,000 = 55,000 Payments: purchases (prior month) (24,000) (30,000) Payments: wages + overheads (16,000) (16,000) Payments: equipment - (15,000) Net cash flow 5,000 (6,000) Opening balance 5,000 10,000 Closing balance 10,000 4,000 Read it as management would: February closes at £4,000 after the equipment purchase - tight but positive; a 10% sales shortfall would tip February negative, so a modest overdraft facility is prudent. That interpretive sentence is the difference between a calculation answer and a management answer. Preparation sequence matters for full-question marks: the sales budget comes first (it drives everything), then production budget = budgeted sales + budgeted closing inventory − opening inventory, then purchases, labour and overhead budgets, and finally the cash budget and budgeted statements. A question asking 'state the order of preparation and why' is testing that dependency chain - sales is the principal budget factor in most businesses, though a scarce resource (limited machine capacity, scarce skilled labour) can cap sales instead, in which case the limiting factor leads. Link this back to the limiting-factor ranking in section 1: the same scarce resource logic governs both the operating plan and the budget structure. Standard costing and variance analysis (3.11) compares actual results with a flexed budget - the original budget restated at the actual output level. Variance sign convention: favourable (F) raises profit against the flexed budget; adverse (A) reduces it. The core calculations: Variance Formula Materials price (Standard price − actual price) × actual quantity purchased/used Materials usage (Standard quantity for actual output − actual quantity) × standard price Labour rate (Standard rate − actual rate) × actual hours Labour efficiency (Standard hours for actual output − actual hours) × standard rate Fixed overhead expenditure Budgeted fixed overhead − actual fixed overhead Fixed overhead volume (Actual output − budgeted output) × fixed overhead per unit (absorption costing) Sales price (Actual price − standard price) × actual units sold Sales volume (profit) (Actual units − budgeted units) × standard profit/contribution per unit Worked example: a full variance set Standard: 3 kg of material at £5 per kg (£15 per unit); 1.5 hours of labour at £12 per hour (£18 per unit). Budgeted output 4,000 units. Actual output 4,000 units; materials used 12,400 kg costing £59,520; labour 6,200 hours costing £74,400. Materials price: actual price = 59,520 ÷ 12,400 = £4.80; (5.00 − 4.80) × 12,400 = £2,480 Favourable . Materials usage: standard for actual output = 4,000 × 3 = 12,000 kg; (12,000 − 12,400) × 5 = £2,000 Adverse . Labour rate: actual rate = 74,400 ÷ 6,200 = £12.00; variance nil . Labour efficiency: standard hours = 4,000 × 1.5 = 6,000; (6,000 − 6,200) × 12 = £2,400 Adverse . Causes that fit the pattern: cheap material (£4.80 vs £5) of lower quality - explaining BOTH the price saving and the excess usage and slow work; a possible training or machine-calibration problem behind the efficiency loss. The interdependence sentence - 'the favourable price variance was purchased at the cost of adverse usage and efficiency' - is precisely what analysis marks are for. Note also: with output at budget, the flexed budget equals the original; with output at 4,500 units, every usage/efficiency standard would first be restated at 4,500 units. Evaluation of standard costing: it quantifies control, supports responsibility accounting and highlights exceptions worth managing attention - but standards age (price lists, wage awards change), over-precise targets can drive dysfunctional behaviour (buying cheap material to 'win' the price variance), and some variances are interdependent so must be read together. In the exam: calculate precisely, then explain each variance with a cause that is consistent with the others, and close with the interdependence point. If asked to 'evaluate the variance analysis for management', add that only controllable variances warrant action, and that uncontrollable adverse variances (a market-wide price rise) need re-forecasting, not blame. Worked example: flexing before analysing Budget: 4,000 units, sales revenue £96,000, variable costs £56,000, fixed costs £30,000, profit £10,000. Actual: 4,500 units, revenue £105,000, variable costs £63,500, fixed costs £30,400. Flexed budget at 4,500 units: revenue 4,500 × 24 = £108,000; variable costs 4,500 × 14 = £63,000; fixed £30,000; profit £15,000. Sales price variance: (24.00 − 105,000/4,500) × 4,500 = (24 − 23.333) × 4,500 = £3,000 Adverse . Sales volume (contribution) variance: (4,500 − 4,000) × standard contribution 10 = £5,000 Favourable . Variable cost variance: 63,000 − 63,500 = £500 Adverse ; fixed overhead expenditure: 30,000 − 30,400 = £400 Adverse . Against the UNFLEXED budget, revenue is £9,000 favourable - but that mixes selling more units with selling them cheaper. Flexing isolates the two effects: more units (good) at a discounted price (bad). That is the entire point of the technique and a one-sentence explanation AQA repeatedly rewards. Close the topic with the exam pattern: a 20-mark question typically gives a budget and actuals, asks for three or four variances (6-8 marks), the flexed budget (3-4 marks), then causes and interdependence (5-6 marks); a 25-marker may add 'evaluate the usefulness of the standard costing system'. Whatever the wrapper, the sequence is fixed: flex, calculate with F/A labels, explain consistently, evaluate with behaviour and controllability. Practise writing the explanation sentence in the same breath as each calculation - 'the adverse usage variance of £2,000 reflects the cheaper material buckling on the press, which also explains the £2,400 adverse efficiency variance' - because that habit is what turns variance analysis from arithmetic into management accounting.

topics.name: Ethics, Technology and Society
topics.subject: accounting
topics.searchText: accounting Accounting Ethics, Technology and Society Explain the five fundamental ethical principles - integrity, objectivity, professional competence and due care, confidentiality, professional behaviour - and apply them to scenarios (AQA 7127, 3.18) (AO1/AO2). Identify ethical threats (self-interest, self-review, familiarity, intimidation, advocacy) and evaluate appropriate safeguards (3.18) (AO2/AO3). Analyse techniques of creative accounting and window dressing and evaluate their impact on the business, the accounting function and stakeholders (3.18) (AO2/AO3). Evaluate the benefits and costs of computerised accounting systems and the strengths and risks of spreadsheet modelling (3.1) (AO2/AO3). Assess data security threats and safeguards, including UK GDPR duties, and communicate justified recommendations (3.1/3.18) (AO3). The five principles come as a package: a technically perfect but dishonest computation breaches integrity and objectivity even if it is arithmetically correct. Threats: self-interest (financial stake), self-review (checking your own work), familiarity (long relationships), intimidation (pressure from client or employer), advocacy (promoting the client's position). Creative accounting distorts every ratio built on profit or assets - margins, ROCE, gearing - so users inherit the distortion; auditors and governance exist to detect it. Accounting software automates double entry and reporting but concentrates risk: one database error or breach multiplies; backups, access controls and audit trails are not optional. Spreadsheets are powerful modelling tools but weak controls: no audit trail, formula rot, version chaos - validate inputs, protect cells, document versions. Integrity Being straightforward and honest in all professional and business relationships; not being associated with information the accountant believes is materially false or misleading. Objectivity Not allowing bias, conflict of interest or undue influence of others to override professional judgement. Professional competence and due care Maintaining knowledge and skill at the level required and acting diligently in accordance with applicable standards. Confidentiality Not disclosing professional information without proper authority or using it for personal advantage, subject to legal duties to disclose. Professional behaviour Complying with laws and regulations and avoiding conduct that discredits the profession. Creative accounting Manipulating the presentation of financial information within (or beyond) the rules to present a misleading picture of performance or position - e.g. overstating revenue or hiding liabilities. Window dressing Legal timing of transactions just before the year end to improve reported figures or ratios (e.g. delaying payments to raise the current ratio), improving appearance without substance. Data protection (UK GDPR) The regime governing personal data: lawful, fair and transparent processing; purpose limitation; data minimisation; accuracy; storage limitation; security; and accountability. The accountant's role (3.1) is to provide information for decision-making and control - and that role only works if the information is trustworthy. Ethics is therefore not an appendix to accounting; it is the condition on which the entire specification depends. The profession's code (ICAEW and equivalent international codes, which AQA's 3.18 draws on) rests on five fundamental principles , and exam questions either ask you to state and explain them or - far more often - drop you into a scenario and ask which principle is threatened and what should happen. Principle Meaning Scenario trigger Integrity Straightforward and honest; no association with false or misleading information Being asked to leave a figure out of the accounts Objectivity No bias, conflict of interest or undue influence over judgement Valuing the asset owned by a relative's firm Professional competence and due care Up-to-date skills; diligent work to standards Using out-of-date tax rules; rushing a job Confidentiality No disclosure without authority; no use of information for personal gain Telling a friend a client is for sale Professional behaviour Comply with laws; no conduct discrediting the profession Overstating qualifications; regulatory breaches The code then names five threats to those principles, and scenario questions are built directly from them. Self-interest : your own stake distorts judgement - a performance bonus tied to reported profit, shares in the client, or a close personal relationship with a supplier you are evaluating. Self-review : you check your own work - the preparer of a forecast then audits it, or an audit firm sells consulting on the system it audits. Familiarity : long or close relationships breed sympathy - auditing the same client for fifteen years, or your brother runs the business. Intimidation : pressure replaces judgement - 'agree with this valuation or lose the engagement'; threats of dismissal for raising a query. Advocacy : promoting the client's position compromises independence - acting as the client's spokesman in a dispute while also reporting on its statements. Safeguards are the counter-moves, and answers score by matching threat to safeguard specifically: professional safeguards - independent regulation and inspection of audit firms, codes of ethics with disciplinary consequences, mandatory second-partner review of significant judgements, rotation of audit partners after a set period; firm safeguards - quality control procedures, consultation on difficult matters, independence declarations each year; personal safeguards - declining the engagement or the instruction, escalating to senior management or the audit committee, and whistleblowing to a regulator where internal routes fail and the public interest is engaged. The judgement step AQA rewards: identify the threat, name the principle breached, propose the proportionate safeguard, and say what should happen if it fails (resign, disclose). Doing nothing is never an acceptable answer in this specification. Confidentiality deserves its boundary drawn precisely because it is the principle students most often overstate. It is NOT a licence to conceal wrongdoing: the law can compel disclosure (court orders, money laundering regulations), the public interest can justify it (reporting fraud to a regulator), and the client can consent. Equally, confidentiality binds after the engagement ends. In exam answers, treat a request to 'keep quiet about a £500,000 overstatement' as a threat to integrity FIRST (false information) with confidentiality used as the cover story - that ordering shows genuine understanding rather than memorisation. Ethics questions also test the impact chain (3.18's core demand): how does an unethical act flow through the business, the accounting function and stakeholders? Build the chain in every answer: the act (overstated profit) → internal consequences (bonuses paid from fictitious profit, dividends from capital, decisions taken on false margins) → external consequences (investors misprice shares, lenders extend credit on false gearing, employees' pensions hold worthless equity, HMRC collects wrong tax) → discovery (restatements, resignations, fines, audit collapse) → long-run damage (the market discounts all of the company's numbers; the profession's credibility falls). Enron (2001) and WorldCom (2002) are the canonical illustrations: Enron used off-balance-sheet vehicles to hide debt; WorldCom capitalised operating expenses to inflate profit; both collapsed, their auditor (Arthur Andersen) failed with them, and the regulatory response (Sarbanes-Oxley, stricter audit independence) reshaped the profession. Name them, one line each, and always bring the analysis back to the scenario in the question. Threat-to-safeguard matching drill Scenario Threat Principle at risk Proportionate safeguard Bonus depends on hitting a profit target Self-interest Objectivity, integrity Independent review of reported figures; disclosure of incentive scheme Audit firm sells IT consulting to its audit client Self-interest / self-review Objectivity, independence Limit non-audit services; audit committee pre-approves work Preparing then checking your own cash flow forecast Self-review Professional competence Independent reviewer signs off the model Auditing a client owned by a close friend Familiarity Objectivity Declare and withdraw; reassign the engagement 'Remove the query or lose the contract' Intimidation Integrity, objectivity Escalate; document; resign the engagement if unresolved Speaking for a client in a tax dispute you also audit Advocacy Objectivity Separate the roles; another team acts as advocate Two boundary topics complete the picture. Conflicts of interest : acting for two parties whose interests clash (auditing two competing clients, or advising both sides of a sale) is managed by disclosure and consent where genuine independence is possible, and by declining where it is not - the test is whether a reasonable, informed observer would doubt the accountant's objectivity. Whistleblowing : internal escalation (line manager, senior management, audit committee) comes first; external disclosure to a regulator (or prescribed person) is protected when it is reasonably believed to be in the public interest; the last resort is resigning with a written record of the concern. Answers that show this staged reasoning - not a single jump to 'tell the press' - score the evaluation marks. Culture is the mechanism that makes all of this stick, and it is worth one developed paragraph in any 25-marker. Tone at the top - whether directors genuinely expect honest numbers or merely compliant ones - flows through the accounting function: where the chief executive 'adjusts' quarters, staff learn that estimates are negotiable; where the audit committee asks difficult questions, staff learn that evidence matters. That is why governance safeguards (independent non-executive directors, audit committees, internal audit reporting lines outside the finance department) are ethical devices, not just administrative ones: they change the incentives under which the accountant exercises judgement. Weave the point into stakeholder answers: the accountant in business (3.1) is often the first line of defence, because manipulation passes through the ledger before it reaches the market. Creative accounting manipulates reported numbers to mislead; window dressing is its mildest, usually legal, cousin - timing transactions around the year end. Both matter to the accountant-in-business (3.1) because the accounting function is where the manipulation happens, and to stakeholders (3.18) because they rely on the numbers the manipulation corrupts. Distinguish the two precisely in definitions and the distinction itself earns marks. Technique Mechanism Effect on statements/ratios Ethical status Early revenue recognition Booking orders not yet delivered (realisation breached) Revenue and profit overstated now; reversed later Breach of concepts; often fraudulent Capitalising expenses Operating costs recorded as non-current assets (WorldCom's line costs) Profit overstated; assets overstated; future depreciation spreads the lie Fraud Off-balance-sheet financing Debt hidden in unconsolidated vehicles (Enron) Gearing understated; ROCE flattered Breach of substance over form Cookie-jar provisions Over-providing in good years, releasing in bad years Smooths profit; misleads trend analysis Breach of prudence in reverse Inventory overstatement Inflating closing inventory Gross profit overstated this period; detectable next Fraud Window dressing Delaying payables; year-end bulk sales on easy terms Current ratio and revenue flattered briefly Legal but misleading The arithmetic behind the manipulation is worth internalising because questions increasingly ask you to quantify. Overstate closing inventory by £40,000: cost of sales understated £40,000, gross and net profit overstated £40,000, current assets and equity overstated £40,000 - and next year's opening inventory inflates cost of sales, reversing the effect, which is why a one-year 'miracle' followed by an unexplained margin fall is a red flag sequence. Understate the allowance for receivables by £25,000: profit and net receivables overstated by £25,000. Every manipulated figure then contaminates the ratios: the gross margin, ROCE and current ratio read from those statements are fiction with clean arithmetic. The stakeholder impact analysis is the exam's evaluation core, and it must be specific to each group. Shareholders and potential investors : buy or hold at a price built on false profits; on discovery the share price collapses - wealth transferred to those who sold first. Lenders : advance credit on understated gearing; covenants measured on fake numbers; recoveries fall short in the collapse. Employees : pensions often hold the employer's shares; jobs go in the aftermath; the bonus pool paid out of fictional profit was never real. Suppliers and customers : extended credit to a hollow business; unfulfilled orders. Government : understated profits mean understated tax (or in some manipulations, tax paid on phantom profit); regulatory resources consumed. The accounting profession : every scandal degrades public trust in all accounts, which is why regulation tightened after Enron - and why integrity, not just compliance, is a principle rather than a rulebook. Detection and prevention occupy the positive half of any evaluation. Auditors provide independent verification - but Enron showed independence can be compromised by consulting fees (a self-interest threat) and long tenure (familiarity), so safeguards followed: audit committee oversight, partner rotation, limits on non-audit services. Corporate governance structures - a board with independent non-executives, an audit committee, internal audit - separate the people who run the business from the people who check it. Accounting standards (IAS 2 inventory, IAS 16 property, plant and equipment; the substance-over-form principle) narrow the space for manipulation. Ratio cross-checks - comparing the current ratio with the acid test, profit growth with operating cash flow - expose techniques that improve one number and degrade another. And the honest counterweight: most businesses do not manipulate, standards and audit make manipulation harder than ever, and window dressing is often management behaving legally within rules - the evaluation is about the incentive and the consequence , not a claim that all reporting is rotten. Why does it recur? Because the incentives are real, and naming them is analysis. Remuneration : bonuses and share options priced on reported profit pay today for numbers that may be fiction tomorrow. Debt covenants : gearing or interest-cover tests measured on the accounts create a motive to move the measurement. Market expectations : missing analyst forecasts by a penny moves share prices, so the temptation is to 'manage' earnings into line - the practice called earnings management, creative accounting's respectable-sounding sibling. Survival : loss-making businesses fear that honest numbers trigger lender withdrawal. Every one of these incentives is visible in the case studies: Enron's executives were compensated on the inflated profits; WorldCom's controllers were pressured from above. The counter-incentives - audit, regulation, imprisonment for fraud, director disqualification - exist to make honesty cheaper than dishonesty, and the exam answer evaluates whether they currently do. UK context sharpens the evaluation. Audit and reporting are overseen by the Financial Reporting Council (FRC), which sets accounting and auditing standards and inspects audit quality; auditors of public interest companies face independent review; and successive scandals (Carillion among them) have driven debate about audit-market competition and the splitting of audit from consulting. You do not need the reform details - you need the direction of travel: regulators respond to manipulation by tightening independence, expanding audit scope and lengthening accountability chains. For an evaluation conclusion, that regulatory response is evidence that the problem is real, costly and permanent - which is why the ethical principles in section 1 are written as duties rather than aspirations. Worked example: reading the red flags in two years of figures Year 1: revenue £500,000; gross profit £150,000 (30%); receivables £60,000 (43 days); allowance for receivables £9,000 (15% of receivables); operating cash flow £120,000. Year 2: revenue £700,000; gross profit £252,000 (36%); receivables £126,000 (66 days); allowance £5,000 (4% of receivables); operating cash flow £115,000. Signal Reading Gross margin up 6 points on 40% revenue growth Either genuine pricing power - or sales pulled forward / revenue recognised early Receivables days 43 → 66 Sales booked but cash not collected - the classic early-recognition fingerprint Allowance percentage 15% → 4% Provision cut exactly when receivables age - profit managed through the estimate Profit up ~£87,000 but operating cash flow flat Earnings quality failing: profit not converting to cash No single flag is proof - growth businesses legitimately show all four for honest reasons - but the combination demands investigation: cut-off testing at the year end, confirmation of the largest receivables, and re-computation of the allowance. This is the auditable version of the scepticism the ethical principles require, and it links 3.18 back to the ratio toolkit of topic 3. Technology changed what the accounting function does (3.1): much of the mechanical double entry is now automated, and the accountant's value moved to design, control, interpretation and assurance. For the exam you need a balanced benefits-and-costs evaluation, the specific strengths and risks of spreadsheets, and data security duties under UK GDPR - three things AQA asks about directly. Computerised accounting system Benefits Costs / risks Entry and processing Speed; double entry automated from one input (invoice posted to sales, customer and VAT records at once); validation checks (unbalanced entries rejected) Software and training costs; implementation time; a wrong masterfile rule multiplies errors silently Reporting Instant trial balance, aged receivables, budgets-versus-actuals; dashboards for non-financial managers Over-reliance: users trust output without understanding the model behind it Control Audit trails (who entered what, when); access levels by role; automatic control account totals Concentration risk: one database is one point of failure; needs backups and security investment Integration E-commerce, banking feeds, payroll connect directly; less re-keying, fewer transcription errors Dependency on suppliers; upgrade and compatibility costs; cyber attack surface widens with connectivity The evaluation line to remember: computerisation removes clerical error and speeds processing, but it concentrates risk rather than removing it - one corrupted file, one breach, one misconfigured automation affects everything, so control shifts from checking arithmetic to controlling access, backup and change. A strong answer names both sides of that shift. Connect software to the rest of the specification and the benefits become concrete rather than generic. The control accounts you drilled in topic 1 are produced automatically - aged debtor reports, control account totals and lists of balances reconcile in seconds, so error detection shifts from manual comparison to exception review. Recurring entries (depreciation, accrual reversals, standing orders) post on schedule, removing the classic sources of year-end error. Validation prevents the trial balance ever disagreeing: most packages refuse unbalanced entries outright, which is why suspense-account questions are rarer in the software age - but understanding them remains essential, because someone must know what the software is doing. Integration with incomplete records (3.14): where a business adopts proper software mid-year, the earlier records remain incomplete, so the accountant still needs mark-up and margin techniques to bridge the gap - technology changes the mix of skills, it does not abolish the syllabus. Spreadsheets are the accountant's most-used tool and a favourite exam topic. Strengths: flexible modelling of any scenario; instant what-if analysis - change a cell and every dependent figure recalculates; cheap and universally available; ideal for break-even models, cash budgets, sensitivity tables and quick consolidations. Worked what-if: a model holds selling price £20, variable cost £12, fixed costs £60,000, so break-even = 60,000 ÷ 8 = 7,500 units. Raise price by £2: contribution 10, break-even 6,000 units - one keystroke, and the margin of safety, target profit and chart all update. For management, that interactivity is the entire value: pricing decisions, cost-cutting options and volume scenarios can be compared in minutes. The risks are just as examinable. Formula errors propagate silently - a range missed by one row corrupts every downstream total, and famous public spreadsheet failures (mis-sorted ranges, hardcoded overrides) show they happen to experts; no audit trail - unlike accounting software, spreadsheets rarely record who changed what, so errors hide; version control - 'budget_v7_final_FINAL.xlsx' is the industry joke because it is real: multiple copies diverge and decisions get taken on stale files; input errors - no validation unless deliberately added. Safeguards: separate inputs from calculations (an assumptions sheet feeding locked formula cells); data validation on input cells; cell protection; version control with a single master; documentation of formulas; and independent review of any model that feeds significant decisions. For 12-mark questions the shape is always the same: capability, then risk, then controls, then judgement on fitness for purpose - a quick what-if model is low risk; a statutory consolidation built by one person in a spreadsheet is high risk. Data security completes the section, and it now has statutory teeth. UK GDPR requires that personal data (employee records, customer names, payment details) be processed lawfully and transparently, collected for specified purposes, minimised, kept accurate, retained only as long as necessary, processed securely , and handled accountably - the business must be able to demonstrate compliance. Security safeguards to recommend in answers, mapped to threats: access controls and role-based permissions (threat: insider misuse); encryption of data at rest and in transit (threat: stolen laptops, intercepted files); frequent automated backups held offline or in a separate location (threat: ransomware, which encrypts live data and demands payment - backups are the recovery route); multi-factor authentication and staff training against phishing (threat: credential theft - the most common breach route); patching and firewalls (threat: exploitation of known weaknesses); an incident response plan (threat: everything - GDPR requires reporting qualifying breaches to the Information Commissioner's Office within 72 hours, and affected individuals where risk is high). Penalties scale with turnover, and the reputational damage of a breached customer database outlasts any fine - the evaluation point that security spending is cheap relative to the downside. Worked scenario: prioritising a security budget A 20-person wholesaler holds customer names, addresses, cardholder data and staff payroll. Budget allows four of six measures: (1) offline daily backups, (2) multi-factor authentication, (3) staff phishing training, (4) encryption of laptops, (5) a marketing analytics platform, (6) a new website theme. Take (1): ransomware without backups means either payment or data loss - existential. Take (2): stolen credentials are the most common breach route; MFA blocks the cheapest attack. Take (3): phishing defeats technical controls by tricking people; training addresses the human layer. Take (4): a lost laptop holding customer data is a notifiable breach - encryption makes the data unreadable and the breach largely containable. Reject (5) and (6): neither reduces risk. The reasoning pattern - threat, control, consequence - is exactly the structure AQA rewards in recommendation questions. The wider-society angle (3.18, and the 'society' in this topic's title) deserves two sentences in any extended answer: automation of bookkeeping shifts employment from clerical processing towards analysis and assurance - a structural change the accountant-in-business must manage through training; and stakeholders increasingly expect reporting to cover environmental and social impacts alongside financial results, so the accounting function's duty - honest, complete, decision-useful information - now extends beyond the traditional statements. That extension is exactly why the ethical principles of section 1 apply to dashboards, spreadsheets and databases as much as to ledger accounts: the medium changed, the duty did not. Two closing evaluation habits for this topic. First, quantify where the question permits: 'the current ratio improves from 1.33:1 to 1.38:1' or 'backup costs of a few hundred pounds against a ransom demand of thousands' - numbers anchor ethical and technological judgements just as they anchor financial ones. Second, finish with the decision-usefulness test that runs through the whole specification: information - in a ledger, a spreadsheet or a dashboard - exists to help someone make a better decision, and every ethical principle, software feature and security control in this topic is ultimately a way of keeping that information true. If your conclusion sentence states what the decision-maker can now rely on, and what they still cannot, you have met the highest standard the 3.18 extended questions set.

topics.name: Persia and the Greek World
topics.subject: ancient-history
topics.searchText: ancient-history Ancient History Persia and the Greek World Ionian Revolt The rebellion of the Greek city-states of Ionia (499-494 BC) against Persian rule, led initially by Aristagoras of Miletus; its suppression triggered Darius' invasion of Greece. Herodotus The 'father of history' (c. 484-425 BC); his Histories are the principal narrative source for the Persian Wars, written in the generation after the events. Hoplite A Greek citizen-soldier equipped with shield (aspis), spear and bronze panoply, fighting in the phalanx formation. Trireme The Greek warship with three banks of oars and a bronze ram; decisive in the naval battle of Salamis. Hellenotamiai The treasurers of the Delian League, which later became the Athenian empire. Spartiate A full citizen of Sparta, entitled to membership of the phalanx and the syssition (mess). Ephor One of five annually elected Spartan magistrates who overseen the kings and exercised extensive power. Satrapy One of the provinces of the Persian Empire, governed by a satrap responsible to the Great King. Background. The Persian Empire under Darius I (522-486 BC) controlled Ionia — the Greek city-states of the Asia Minor coast — through local tyrants and satraps. In 499 BC Aristagoras of Miletus, having failed in an attack on Naxos, launched the Ionian Revolt , appealing for help to mainland Greece. Athens and Eretria sent ships; the Greeks burned Sardis (498 BC) before the revolt was crushed by 494 (the naval defeat at Lade). The revolt matters for three reasons: it gave Persia a pretext to punish Athens and Eretria; it taught Persia the difficulty of coastal campaigning; and Herodotus frames it as the origin (aitiai) of the wars. Darius' expedition (492-490 BC). Mardonius' campaign (492) re-subdued Thrace and Macedonia before the fleet was wrecked at Athos. In 490 a seaborne force under Datis and Artaphernes destroyed Eretria and landed at Marathon .
