Herodotus' cause-analysis is partial: he omits Persia's wider strategic interest in the Aegean and presents the wars as personal revenge narratives — a standard AO2 evaluation point. Marathon (490 BC). c. 9,000-10,000 Athenians and 1,000 Plataeans under Miltiades defeated a larger Persian force. Herodotus gives the Greek dead as 192 against 6,400 Persian — numbers most historians doubt. The Athenian phalanx charged the Persians (running the mile of arrow-range), thinned its centre and enveloped the wings. The battle's significance: it ended the first invasion, made Athens the saviour of Greece, and — with Themistocles' silver-mines windfall (483 BC, Laurion) — funded the fleet that won Salamis. The lone Spartan march (arrived after the battle, Pheidippides' Spartans celebrating the Carneia) illustrates Greek disunity. Xerxes' invasion (480-479 BC). Xerxes crossed the Hellespont on pontoon bridges with a massive land force (Herodotus' 1,700,000 is impossible; modern estimates 150,000-300,000) and a large fleet, fed by a supply chain along the Thracian coast. Thermopylae (480 BC). Leonidas held the pass with c. 300 Spartiates, 700 Thespians and allied contingents; the pass fell after the local betrayal (Ephialtes' path), and the rearguard died to cover the retreat. Strategically the delay achieved little, but the moral exemplum (Simonides' epitaph: 'go tell the Spartans') shaped Greek memory. The simultaneous naval action at Artemisium damaged the Persian fleet and prepared Salamis. Salamis (480 BC). Themistocles evacuated Athens and trapped the Persian fleet in the narrow strait — either by genuine strategy or by secret message to Xerxes (Herodotus records the alleged trick; the standard essay debate). The Persian fleet, outflanked in confined waters where the heavier Greek triremes and disciplined rams excelled, was destroyed. Salamis' significance: it secured the Greek mainland's sea communications and forced Xerxes to withdraw with Mardonius. Plataea (479 BC). The largest hoplite army yet assembled (Herodotus: 38,700 Spartans and helots among c. 110,000 Greeks) under Pausanias destroyed Mardonius' army and ended the invasion. The parallel victory at Mycale freed Ionia. The wars' aftermath: the Delian League (478 BC) turned Athens' leadership into empire (thesaurus at Delos, phoros tribute), setting up the Peloponnesian War; Sparta's prestige declined. Method. Herodotus (writing c. 440-425 BC) claims autopsy, enquiry (historia) and reportage of what he heard — he names his sources and distinguishes versions. Problems. (1) Chronology : he wrote a generation after the events; oral tradition distorted detail. (2) Numbers : Persian army sizes (1,700,000+) and casualty figures are rhetorical exaggerations. (3) Bias : pro-Athenian framing (Athens as saviour of Greece); anti-Persian moralising (barbarian decadence, e.g. Xerxes' flogging of the Hellespont); the speeches are composed, not recorded. (4) Narrative patterning : divine causation, dreams and omens structure the story — Herodotus balances human and divine causation but the patterns may be literary. Value. Despite this, Herodotus is indispensable: he preserves the only connected narrative, names his informants, and his critical method (testing versions, noting disagreements) is genuine historiography. OCR essays reward the pairing: 'Herodotus says X — but consider the source's problems — the judgement must weigh both'. Arguments: Greek advantages. (1) Hoplite and naval excellence : the phalanx's discipline (Marathon) and the trireme's ram in confined waters (Salamis). (2) Strategy : Themistocles' fleet, the evacuation of Athens, the choice of Salamis' narrows. (3) Motivation : defence of homeland vs conscripted multi-national levies. (4) Unity at crisis points : the Hellenic League's combined command at Plataea. Arguments: Persian weaknesses. (1) Logistics : Xerxes' supply chain along the coast was vulnerable; the fleet needed the army. (2) Command : Xerxes' departure after Salamis; Mardonius' fall at Plataea. (3) Diversity of the levies : reluctant conscripts, language barriers (Herodotus' catalogue). (4) Naval limits : Persian ships crewed by levied Phoenicians, Egyptians, Ionians — quality uneven. Counter-considerations. Greek disunity (the Spartans' Carneia delay, Themistocles' threats to the allies); Persian successes (Eretria's destruction, the Acropolis burn); the wars were close-run (Herodotus' own theme: fortunes reverse). OCR technique : a 30-mark essay needs a thesis, four developed points with named battles/sources, counter-considerations, and a judgement (e.g. Greek tactical brilliance — Salamis' narrows and the phalanx — mattered more than Persian logistical weakness, though both were necessary; the decisive factor was leadership: Themistocles' strategy and Pausanias' command). For source questions, use Herodotus' specifics (numbers, speeches) against the reliability analysis above.

topics.name: Athens in the Age of Pericles
topics.subject: ancient-history
topics.searchText: ancient-history Ancient History Athens in the Age of Pericles Ekklesia The Athenian citizen assembly, meeting on the Pnyx; the sovereign body — all male citizens over 18 could attend, speak and vote. Boule The council of 500 (50 from each of the ten tribes), prepared the assembly's agenda and administered the state; membership by lot for a year. Heliaia The people's jury-courts (dikasteria); large juries (up to 501) of citizen volunteers paid from c. 451 BC (2 obols, later 3). Ostracism Annual vote to exile for ten years any citizen deemed dangerous to the democracy (needed 6,000 quorum); used against Themistocles (471) and Cimon (461). Phoros The tribute paid by Delian League members, assessed by Aristides as 460 talents; the financial base of Athens' navy and building programme. Misthophoria Payment for public service (jury service, later office-holding) — Pericles' reform that opened democracy to the poor (thetes). Kleroterion The stone allotment machine that randomised selection to office and juries — democracy by lot. Pericles Athenian statesman (c. 495-429 BC), dominant from c. 461-429; strategos re-elected annually; Plutarch's subject. The institutions. Athenian democracy rested on three bodies: the ekklesia (assembly — the sovereign decision-making body, ~40 meetings a year, quorum 6,000 for sensitive votes); the boule (council of 500 — agenda-setting and administration, by lot, 50 per tribe, rotated through the pyrtaneis); and the heliaia (jury-courts — up to 501 jurors, paid 2 obols from c. 451, 3 later). Magistracies were filled by lot (the kleroterion) except the strategoi (generals), elected annually and re-electable — Pericles held the generalship continuously. Pericles' reforms : jury pay (misthophoria) opened the courts to thetes (the poorest class), radicalising participation. Radical nature and limits. Direct democracy: citizens voted laws personally, no representatives. Limits: citizenship restricted by Pericles' citizenship law (451/450 BC — both parents Athenian, excluding ~half the population from the democracy: women, metics, slaves had no role); the assembly's susceptibility to demagogues; ostracism's misuse for faction. Thucydides' Pericles (funeral oration) calls Athens 'the school of Hellas' — the standard pro-democracy quotation; the Old Oligarch (Pseudo-Xenophon) supplies the hostile case (the demos rules in its own interest). League to empire. Founded 478 BC (naval defence against Persia), the Delian League's members paid phoros tribute or supplied ships. Athens' leadership hardened: Naxos' secession crushed (c. 470); the treasury moved to Athens (454 BC); tribute became compulsory. The Peace of Callias (c. 449 BC, disputed) ended hostilities with Persia, but Athens kept the tribute — the empire's money now bought Pericles' building programme. The empire's instruments. Cleruchies (Athenian settlements on allies' land), garrisons, the tribute assessment (460 talents by Aristides), the federal courts pulled to Athens, and the Athens Coinage Decree (c. 450 — allies used Athenian weights, measures and silver). Kallias' peace and the empire's economics: Plutarch records the allies' resentment (the 'enslaved' League, per the rhetors); the standard essay debate: protective hegemony vs exploitation — use the tribute lists, the Coinage Decree, and the revolts (Naxos, Thasos 465) as evidence both ways. Leadership (461-429 BC). Pericles dominated Athens for three decades — elected strategos annually, never a tyrant but 'first citizen' (Thucydides). His ascendancy: the Ephialtic reforms (461 — stripped the Areopagus of powers, radicalised democracy); ostracising rivals (Cimon 461, Thucydides son of Melesias 443); his marriage-alliance politics (Aspasia's salon, per Plutarch). Thucydides' assessment: Athens under Pericles 'in name a democracy, in fact rule by the first man' — the standard evaluative quotation. The building programme (447-429 BC). Funded by the phoros: the Parthenon (447-432, Iktinos and Kallikrates, Pheidias' sculptures), the Propylaia, the Temple of Athena Nike, the Hephaisteion. Plutarch's Life defends the programme (the money was for war — spending it on beauty and the gods was legitimate; the allies' resentment is the counter-case). The programme's significance: Periclean Athens' self-image (the imperial capital of Hellas); employment (the poor benefited); the arts' golden age (tragedy: Sophocles, Euripides). Plutarch and Thucydides as sources. Plutarch (c. AD 46-120, writing 500 years later): biographical, moralising, drawn from earlier writers (Stesimbrotus, Ion of Chios); his Life of Pericles preserves anecdotes (Aspasia, the ostracisms, the building programme's defence) but is not a political history — reliability limited by date and moral purpose. Thucydides (c. 460-400): contemporary, exiled general, analytical; his Pericles (Books 1-2) is admiring but written with hindsight and against the post-Periclean demagogues — his praise of Pericles serves his thesis (Athens failed when it lost him). OCR essays weigh both: 'Plutarch preserves the anecdotes, Thucydides the political analysis — neither is neutral'. 'How democratic was Athenian democracy?' FOR: direct participation (ekklesia, heliaia), sortition, pay (misthophoria), the power of the courts (ostracism, euthynai audits). AGAINST: restricted citizenship (451/450 law), women/metics/slaves excluded, demagogue influence, the elite's informal power (Pericles' ascendancy). Judgement: radically democratic for its citizens, unrepresentative of its population — the standard balanced answer. 'Was the Athenian empire tyrannical?' FOR: tribute without consent (post-Callias), crushed revolts (Naxos, Thasos), cleruchies, the Coinage Decree, federal courts in Athens. AGAINST: Persia's continued threat (the Peace of Callias disputed), protection and stability, the League's original purpose, Athens' naval supremacy as the allies' interest. Judgement: the empire began as protection and became extraction — the 454 treasury move is the turning point; say why. OCR method. A 30-mark essay: thesis, four developed points (institutions, empire, individuals, sources), counter-considerations, judgement with the question's wording. For source questions (Plutarch extracts), test the anecdote against Thucydides and the institutional record.

topics.name: Sparta
topics.subject: ancient-history
topics.searchText: ancient-history Ancient History Sparta Agoge The Spartan state education: boys taken at 7 into packs, trained for obedience, endurance and war; the institution that made the Spartiate. Helot The enslaved population of Laconia and Messenia, bound to the land; outnumbered Spartiates several times over and controlled by annual war declarations and the krypteia. Perioikoi Free inhabitants of Spartan towns ('dwellers-around'); craftsmen and traders, no political rights, obliged to military service. Dual kingship Two hereditary kings (Agids and Eurypontids), religious, military and judicial leaders, checked by the ephors and gerousia. Gerousia The council of 28 elders (over 60, elected for life) plus the two kings; prepared business for the assembly and tried capital cases. Ephors Five annually elected magistrates; overseen the kings (oath of monthly swap), could prosecute kings, controlled the krypteia. Krypteia The secret service of young Spartiates who policed the helots — annual war declaration (Plutarch) institutionalised control. Syssition The common mess — Spartiates ate together, contributing food monthly; membership was the mark of full citizenship. Structure. Spartan society had three tiers: the Spartiates (full citizens, ~8,000 adult males at the peak, declining to ~1,000 by Aristotle's day), the perioikoi (free 'dwellers-around' — craftsmen and traders with no political rights, military service obligatory) and the helots (the enslaved majority of Laconia and, after the Messenian Wars, Messenia — outnumbering Spartiates perhaps 7:1). The helots farmed the kleroi (allotments) that fed each Spartiate's syssition contribution — the economic base of the Spartan citizen's freedom for war. Control of the helots. The helots' numbers dictated the constitution's character: Sparta was a garrison state. Controls: the annual war declaration on the helots (Plutarch — institutionalised murder without pollution), the krypteia (young Spartiates' secret police), the obligatory hoplite readiness, and the systemic terror (Xenophon records the helots' willingness to die — their fear of the Spartans). The Messenian revolt (464-460) — the Third Messenian War — showed the system's fragility and Sparta's dependence on allies. The agoge. Boys taken at 7 into age-packs (agelai); trained in endurance (one cloak, barefoot, short rations), obedience (the eirens' discipline), theft tolerated (resourcefulness) but being CAUGHT punished — the standard paradox; the ritual theft of cheese (Plutarch); at 20 into the syssition; at 30 full citizenship (homologoi). Girls too: gymnastics (the running races, per Xenophon and Plutarch) — Sparta's women were famously different (Plutarch on their freedom, the 'thigh-flashers' joke of the comic poets). Military culture. The syssition's messes built the phalanx's cohesion; the agoge's obedience built the discipline that won Plataea's day. Xenophon's Constitution of the Lacedaemonians idealises the system (Lycurgus' design) while admitting decline in his own day (c. 360s). The standard essay debate: Sparta's military excellence (the finest hoplites of Greece) vs its demographic fragility (declining Spartiate numbers, helot control) — the system that made Sparta strong made it rigid. Institutions. The dual kingship : two hereditary kings (Agids and Eurypontids) — religious leaders, military commanders (one on campaign), judges in some cases; checked by the ephors' oath (monthly swap of the mutual oath: king rules by the laws, Sparta keeps the king). The gerousia : 28 elders (over 60, elected for life by acclamation) plus the kings — prepared business, tried capital cases. The ephors : five annually elected — extensive power (prosecuting kings, the krypteia, foreign policy), the real check. The assembly (apella): Spartiates over 30 — voted (by acclamation, no debate) on the gerousia's proposals. Nature. The Spartan constitution (the 'Great Rhetra', per Plutarch/tyrtaios? — Tyrtaios' poems) was a mixed constitution (kingly, aristocratic, democratic elements) — admired by Aristotle and the philosophers as stable. The reality: oligarchic dominance (gerousia + ephors) with a passive assembly. Xenophon idealises Lycurgus' design; the standard essay: how 'Lycurgan' was Sparta really — the reforms attributed to a legendary lawgiver, the institutions evolving over time. Xenophon (c. 430-354 BC). An Athenian aristocrat who admired Sparta (exiled, lived in Scillus near Olympia); his Constitution of the Lacedaemonians is the fullest ancient account of the agoge and syssition — idealising (Lycurgus' divine design) but contemporary-adjacent and detailed; his Hellenica covers Spartan hegemony (404-362). Reliability: idealisation (Sparta as the model constitution), but his detail is unmatched — the standard pairing with Plutarch. Plutarch (c. AD 46-120). Wrote 500+ years later; his Lycurgus and Agis/Cleomenes preserve the traditions (the war declaration, the krypteia, the cheese theft) from earlier writers (Aristotle, Sosibius) — biographical and moralising; reliability limited by date. Tyrtaios (7th century BC, elegies) — the earliest poetic evidence (the messes, the phalanx's ethos, the Messenian Wars). Essay technique. A 30-mark essay: thesis, four developed points (society, agoge, constitution, sources), counter-considerations, judgement. Standard questions: 'How far was Sparta's strength military?' (FOR: the phalanx, the agoge, Plataea; AGAINST: the helot fragility, the declining Spartiate numbers, the rigidity — Leuctra 371 broke the myth); 'How reliable are Xenophon and Plutarch for Spartan society?' (weigh idealisation against detail); 'Was the Spartan constitution democratic?' (the apella's acclamation vs the ephors' power — oligarchic reality, mixed theory).

topics.name: Alexander the Great
topics.subject: ancient-history
topics.searchText: ancient-history Ancient History Alexander the Great Granicus (334 BC) Alexander's first major victory over the Persians in Asia Minor, against a satrapal army under Memnon and Arsames. Issus (333 BC) Alexander's victory over Darius III in person, in a narrow coastal plain; Darius fled, his family captured. Gaugamela (331 BC) The decisive victory over Darius III near Arbela; Alexander's oblique attack broke the Persian line. Companion cavalry The hetairoi — Alexander's elite cavalry, the hammer of his battles; the somatophylakes were his bodyguards. Phalanx The Macedonian infantry formation with the sarissa (5-6m pike); the anvil to the Companion cavalry's hammer. Proskynesis The Persian ritual prostration before the Great King; Alexander's attempt to impose it (327 BC) — Callisthenes' resistance and death. Callisthenes Aristotle's grand-nephew, Alexander's official historian; resisted proskynesis (327 BC), executed in the Pages' Conspiracy. Hephaestion Alexander's closest friend and second-in-command; died 324 BC — Alexander's grief extreme (Plutarch). Granicus (334 BC). Alexander crossed the Hellespont (c. 35,000 Macedonians and allies) and defeated the satrapal army under Memnon and Arsames at the Granicus river — the Companion cavalry's frontal charge across the river broke the Persian line; Alexander fought in the front line (his helmet split, per Plutarch). The victory opened Asia Minor; the Greek cities' liberation (the panhellenic claim). Issus (333 BC). Darius III met Alexander in person in the narrow coastal plain near Issus — the terrain neutralised Persian numbers; Alexander's oblique attack (the Companion wedge at the weakened centre) broke the line; Darius fled (his mother, wife and children captured — treated honourably, the standard propaganda point). The victory opened the Levant and Egypt (the oracle of Siwah, 331 — Alexander declared son of Ammon). Gaugamela (331 BC). The decisive battle: Darius' massive army on open ground (chosen by the Persians); Alexander's oblique advance (the 'Hammer and Anvil' — the phalanx held, the Companion cavalry's wedge found the gap); Darius fled again; Babylon and the Persian capitals (Susa, Persepolis — burned 330, revenge for Athens or accident?) fell. The wars' end: Darius murdered by Bessus (330) — Alexander's pursuit and avenging of Darius (the legitimate successor claim). Military leadership. Alexander fought in the front line (Granicus' split helmet, the siege of Malli's arrow — 325 BC, near-fatal wound); his tactics: the oblique advance, the Companion wedge, the phalanx's discipline; the sieges (Halicarnassus, Tyre's mole — 332, the seven-month siege). His leadership: sharing hardship (the march through Gedrosia's desert — though the cost was extreme), promoting Persians (the epigonoi — 30,000 Persian youths trained in Macedonian style), the mass wedding at Susa (324 — Macedonians married Persians). The mutinies. Alexander's relationship with his Macedonians soured: the Hyphasis mutiny (326 BC — the army refused to cross the Ganges; Alexander sulked in his tent, then turned back); the Opis mutiny (324 BC — the army mutinied at the Persian promotions; Alexander's speech (Arrian), the reconciliation banquet); the purges (Philotas and Parmenion, 330 — the conspiracy; Cleitus, 328 — killed by Alexander in a drunken quarrel). The standard essay debate: Alexander the great commander vs Alexander the autocrat — the mutinies and purges as evidence. Divine sonship. Siwah's oracle (331 — son of Ammon); the panhellenic claim (Zeus-Ammon); the deification push: proskynesis (327 — the Persian prostration imposed on Macedonians; Callisthenes' resistance and execution); the divine honours (the cities' cults); the Gedrosian march's costs. Self-presentation: Homer's model (Achilles — Alexander slept with the Iliad, per Plutarch); the Homeric kingship (the leader in front); Herakles' lineage (the Argead claim). The standard essay: Alexander's deification — genuine belief or propaganda? The sources disagree (Arrian admiring, Curtius hostile). The sources. Plutarch (c. AD 100): biographical, moralising — his Life preserves the anecdotes (Bucephalus, the Gordian knot, Cleitus' murder, the grief for Hephaestion); reliability limited by date (400 years) and moral purpose. Arrian (c. AD 130-150): wrote from Ptolemy and Aristobulus (eyewitnesses) — the most military-detailed; admiring (Alexander 'philitatos' — the divine call), but the admiration colours the account. Curtius Rufus (1st century AD): hostile — the corruption theme (the king corrupted by success); his sources unknown. Reliability: all three wrote centuries later; the eyewitness tradition (Ptolemy, Aristobulus, Callisthenes) survives only in fragments; the standard OCR pairing: 'Arrian for the battles, Curtius for the corruption, Plutarch for the anecdotes — none is neutral'. 'Alexander was a great military commander.' FOR: Granicus, Issus, Gaugamela's tactics (the oblique advance, the wedge); the sieges (Tyre); the front-line leadership (Malli); the march to the Indus. AGAINST: the mutinies (Hyphasis, Opis) and purges (Philotas, Cleitus) — the command's human cost; the Gedrosian march's losses; the empire's fragility after his death. Judgement: the campaigns were brilliant — the oblique tactics and personal leadership unmatched; but 'great' must weigh the cost (the army's suffering, the purges) — the standard balanced answer. 'Alexander's deification was political propaganda.' FOR: Siwah's convenient timing, proskynesis' imposition (Macedonian resistance), the divine honours' political use. AGAINST: Alexander's genuine belief (his mother's cults, the Iliad's model); the Macedonian acceptance of divine kingship. Judgement: both — genuine belief deployed politically; say why the distinction matters. OCR method. A 30-mark essay: thesis, four developed points with named battles/sources, counter-considerations, judgement. For source questions: use the extract's specifics (Arrian's numbers, Curtius' moralising) against the reliability analysis.

topics.name: The Late Republic
topics.subject: ancient-history
topics.searchText: ancient-history Ancient History The Late Republic Consul One of two annually elected chief magistrates of the Republic; commanded armies, presided over the senate — the Republic's executive. Senate The council of ~300 ex-magistrates (seniores); advised the magistrates, controlled finance and foreign policy — the Republic's real power. Tribune One of ten tribunes of the plebs; protected plebeians (veto, auxilium), proposed laws to the plebeian assembly — the Gracchi's office. Dictator The six-month emergency magistracy; Sulla's and Caesar's violations (dictator perpetuus) broke the Republic's rules. Gracchi Tiberius (tribune 133 BC) and Gaius (123-122 BC) Gracchus — land reformers whose deaths began the Republic's crisis. Optimates The senatorial 'best men' faction — defended the senate's traditional power. Populares Politicians who appealed to the people (tribunes, assemblies) against the senate — Caesar's method. Proscription Sulla's purge (82 BC) — lists of enemies executed, property confiscated; the civil war's terror. Magistracies. The consuls (two annually elected, the Republic's executive — armies, the senate's presidency); the praetors (judges); the censors (the census, morality); the tribunes of the plebs (ten — the plebeians' protectors, veto power, proposed laws); the dictator (six months, emergency only). The senate (~300 ex-magistrates): advised (senatus consulta — 'decrees of the senate' = the magistrates' advice), controlled finance, foreign policy and the provinces; the Republic's real power. The assemblies : the comitia centuriata (military — elected consuls, declared war), the comitia tributa and the concilium plebis (tribal — elected tribunes, passed laws — the plebiscites). The cursus honorum. The ladder of offices: quaestor (finance), aedile (games, streets), praetor, consul — with age minima and the two-year gap; competition for office drove faction (the optimates vs populares). Patronage : the clientela (patrons and clients) — the social glue; the nobiles' (nobles') dominance (consulships in families). The Gracchi (133-121 BC). Tiberius Gracchus (tribune 133): land reform (the lex Sempronia agraria — the public land's limit, 500 iugera), funded by Attalus' bequest; bypassed the senate (took the bill to the plebeian assembly, deposed his fellow tribune Octavius — unconstitutional), sought re-election; killed in the senate-house riot (133 — the first political murder in Rome since the kings). Gaius Gracchus (tribune 123-122): grain law (subsidised grain), courts to the equites, citizenship proposals; died in the senatus consultum ultimum's crackdown (121 — the 'final decree', the emergency powers). Significance: the Gracchi normalised political violence, faction and the tribunate's use against the senate — the Republic's crisis begins here (Cicero's and Sallust's claim). Marius and Sulla. Marius (consul 107, 104-100, 86): the military reform (recruited the propertyless — the capite censi; the professional army, loyal to its general, not the state — the Marian reforms' consequence: civil war); the Jugurthine and Cimbrian wars. Sulla (consul 88, dictator 82-79): the march on Rome (88 — the first, against Marius; the civil war 83-82); the proscriptions (82 — ~2,000 senators/equites listed and killed); the dictatorship (unconstitutional duration); the reforms (the senate's powers restored, the tribunate's castration). Significance: Sulla showed that armies could take Rome — Caesar learned from him. The First Triumvirate (60 BC). Caesar, Pompey and Crassus — an unofficial alliance (Caesar's consulship 59, the land bills, the Gallic command). Cicero's opposition : the consul of 63 (the Catiline conspiracy), the optimates' voice; his letters (Ad Atticum, Ad Familiares) preserve the Republic's fall from the inside — the standard source. The fall (49-44 BC). Crassus' death (Carrhae, 53) broke the triumvirate; Julia's death (54) broke the Caesar-Pompey bond; the senate (Pompey's party) ordered Caesar to disband (49); Caesar crossed the Rubicon (49 — civil war); Pompey defeated at Pharsalus (48) and murdered in Egypt; Caesar's dictatorship (dictator perpetuus, 44 — the unconstitutional title); the Ides of March (44 — the assassination by Brutus and Cassius, the Republic's last hope). Caesar's significance: the populares' method (the tribunician laws, the people's support), the army's loyalty (the Marian legacy), the dictatorship's normalisation — the Republic's institutions could not contain him. Cicero's letters (Ad Atticum, Ad Familiares, Ad Quintum): the Republic's fall from the inside — contemporary, candid, but partisan (Cicero's self-image) and fragmentary (the letters survive unevenly). Cicero's speeches (the Catilinarians, Pro Milone): published and edited — not verbatim. Plutarch (c. AD 100): the Lives (Caesar, Pompey, Cicero, Marius, Sulla) — biographical, moralising, from earlier writers (Sallust, Pollio); 500 years' distance. Suetonius (c. AD 120): the Twelve Caesars — anecdotal, gossipy. Appian (2nd century AD): the Civil Wars — the fullest narrative of the period, from earlier sources. Sallust (c. 40 BC): the Catiline conspiracy — contemporary, moralising (the Republic's decadence theme). Reliability: the standard pairing — 'Cicero for the inside view, Sallust for the moralising, Plutarch/Suetonius for the anecdotes, Appian for the narrative — none neutral'. Essay technique. A 30-mark essay: thesis, four developed points, counter-considerations, judgement. Standard questions: 'Was the Republic doomed before Caesar?' (FOR: the Gracchi's violence, the Marian army, Sulla's example; AGAINST: the Republic survived crises, the institutions held until 49); 'Was Caesar a tyrant?' (the dictatorship's normalisation vs the reforms' popularity); 'How reliable are Cicero's letters?' (candid but partisan). Use the sources against each other and the events.

topics.name: Julio-Claudian Rome
topics.subject: ancient-history
topics.searchText: ancient-history Ancient History Julio-Claudian Rome Principate Augustus' settlement (27 BC): rule disguised as the restoration of the Republic — the princeps ('first citizen') with tribunician and proconsular powers. Princeps The 'first citizen' — Augustus' title; the constitutional disguise over monarchical power. Tribunicia potestas The tribune's powers (veto, sacrosanctity) held by the emperor — the legal base of the principate. Imperium maius Greater military command than any governor — Augustus' and Claudius' authority over the provinces. Res Gestae Augustus' own account of his achievements ('the things done'); the principal inscriptional source for his image. Praetorian Guard The emperor's bodyguard (~9 cohorts, Sejanus' command under Tiberius); kingmakers after Caligula's murder (41). Aerarium The public treasury; Augustus' division of finance (the fiscus — the emperor's private treasury) split public and imperial money. Pater patriae 'Father of the fatherland' — Augustus' title (2 BC); the paternal image of imperial rule. The settlement (27 BC). After Actium (31 BC), Augustus 'restored the Republic' (27 — the constitutional settlement: the provinces returned to the senate, the title 'Augustus' granted); the reality: the principate — the princeps' powers: tribunicia potestas (the tribune's veto and sacrosanctity), imperium maius (greater command), the censorial power, the pontifex maximus (12 BC). The Res Gestae (Augustus' own account): 'I transferred the Republic from my power to the dominion of the senate and people of Rome' — the image over the reality (the standard essay point). The working. The principate worked through the disguise: the senate's consent (the constitutional forms), the army's loyalty (the donatives), the aerarium's finance (the fiscus split), the succession problem (no constitutional heir — Tiberius, then the dynastic accidents). Augustus' image: pater patriae (2 BC), the moral legislation (the Julian laws — marriage, adultery), the building programme ('I found Rome brick and left it marble', per Suetonius), the pax Romana. Tiberius (14-37 AD). The reluctant princeps (the senate's consent scene, per Tacitus); the Sejanus affair (the praetorian prefect's conspiracy, 31 — Tiberius' withdrawal to Capri); the treason trials (the maiestas cases — Tacitus' theme); characterised as gloomy and suspicious (Tacitus' hostile portrait). Gaius (Caligula, 37-41). The beginning popular (the donatives, the exiles' return); the later madness (Suetonius' anecdotes — the horse consul, the bridge over Baiae; the standard reliability problem); the German bodyguard, the divine honours; assassinated by the praetorians (41). Claudius (41-54). Found hiding behind a curtain after Caligula's murder — the praetorians' kingmaking (the donative); the conquest of Britain (43); the freedmen's administration (Narcissus, Pallas); the Agrippina affair (the marriage, Nero's adoption); characterised as weak (Suetonius) but effective (the administration, the conquest). Nero (54-68). The beginning (the quinquennium — Seneca and Burrus' guidance, the golden age claim); the later descent (Agrippina's murder, 59; the Great Fire, 64 — the Christians blamed; the Golden House; the Senate's hostility); the rebellions (the Pisonian conspiracy, 65; Vindex and Galba, 68); suicide (68 — the Julio-Claudian line ended). Imperial image. The emperors' self-presentation: Augustus' Res Gestae (the achievements' account — the image over reality); the coinage (the emperor's portrait, the victory types); the buildings (the Forum of Augustus, the Golden House's excess); the moral legislation (the Julian laws); the divine honours (the imperial cult). The standard essay: the image vs the reality — 'the princeps disguised the monarch'; the emperors' varying images (Tiberius' gloom, Gaius' divinity, Claudius' weakness, Nero's artistry). The sources. Tacitus (c. AD 100-110): the Annals — the Julio-Claudians' history; hostile to the principate (the liberty theme, the treason trials); stylised (the character sketches, the innuendo); contemporary-adjacent but under Trajan's freed speech — the standard evaluation: Tacitus' hostility colours everything. Suetonius (c. AD 120): the Twelve Caesars — biographical, anecdotal, gossipy (the horse consul, the curtain-hiding); organised by topic not chronology; the archive-based but uncritical. Cassius Dio (c. AD 220): the Roman History — senatorial, later (200 years), from earlier sources (the annals' tradition); balanced but distant. Reliability: all three wrote after the events (Tacitus 40-50 years, Suetonius 60, Dio 150); the senate's perspective (all senators); the standard OCR pairing: 'Tacitus for the political analysis, Suetonius for the anecdotes, Dio for the overview — all senatorial, all hostile to the principate's excesses'. 'Augustus restored the Republic.' FOR: the settlement's forms (27 BC — the provinces returned, the title granted), the senate's consent, the Res Gestae's claim. AGAINST: the powers (tribunicia potestas, imperium maius), the army's loyalty, the dynastic reality (the succession). Judgement: the principate's disguise — the image restored the Republic, the reality founded the monarchy; say why the disguise mattered. 'The Julio-Claudian emperors were increasingly autocratic.' FOR: Tiberius' treason trials, Gaius' divinity, Claudius' freedmen, Nero's Golden House and murders; the praetorians' kingmaking; the senate's decline. AGAINST: the constitutional forms persisted (the senate's consent, the magistracies); the administration's effectiveness (Claudius); the quinquennium's golden age. Judgement: autocratic drift — but the principate's forms constrained it; the standard balanced answer. OCR method. A 30-mark essay: thesis, four developed points with named emperors/sources, counter-considerations, judgement. For source questions: use the extract's specifics (Tacitus' characterisations, Suetonius' anecdotes) against the reliability analysis.

topics.name: The World of the Hero
topics.subject: classical-civilisation
topics.searchText: classical-civilisation Classical Civilisation The World of the Hero kleos Glory or fame won through great deeds, especially in song; kleos aphthiton ('imperishable glory') is the epic's promise that heroic deeds live on in poetry after death. timē Honour — material and social standing expressed through prizes (gera), booty, seats of precedence and public recognition; its loss triggers the plot of the Iliad. mēnis Wrath — the first word of the Iliad; the divine-scale anger of Achilles, distinguished from ordinary anger by its cosmic consequences. nostos Homecoming; the governing theme of the Odyssey, which follows Odysseus' long-delayed return to Ithaca and the restoration of his oikos. mētis Cunning intelligence; Odysseus' defining quality (epithet polutropos, 'of many turns'), deployed through disguise, lies and stratagem rather than force. xenia Guest-friendship: a reciprocal pact protected by Zeus Xenios obliging hosts to shelter, feed and gift guests before questioning them, and guests to behave with restraint. aristeia A hero's peak of battle-excellence; Achilles' aristeia spans Iliad 20–22, culminating in the killing of Hector. formula A repeated phrase fixed to a character or action (e.g. 'swift-footed Achilles', 'rosy-fingered Dawn') that fits the dactylic hexameter and enabled oral composition. type-scene A recurring narrative template (arming, sacrifice, supplication, arrival) varied for each occasion — an oral-compositional building block. moira Fate or allotted portion; it bounds even the gods, as when Zeus weighs the fates of Sarpedon (Iliad 16) and Hector (Iliad 22) on his golden scales. H408/11 The World of the Hero is the compulsory component: 2 hours 30 minutes, 100 marks, 40% of the A Level. You study one of Homer's Iliad or Odyssey in depth, and Virgil's Aeneid, which all candidates study. The paper has three sections: Section A focuses solely on Homer and contains two sets of questions — one on the Iliad, one on the Odyssey — and you answer on the text you studied; Section B contains questions on the Aeneid, all compulsory; Section C offers a stimulus (a passage from Homer and one from Virgil) plus a choice of essays, in which you are expected to make use of secondary sources and academic views. There are three question types: a 10-mark stimulus question , a 20-mark essay and a 30-mark essay . The 30-mark essays are marked against Levels of Response grids that explicitly credit the use of secondary sources, scholars and academic works — so A* answers must weave in scholarship (e.g. Parry and Lord on oral tradition; Griffin; Nicholson's The Mighty Dead ; Weil's The Iliad, or the Poem of Force ) rather than bolt it on. Prescribed books: Iliad 1, 3, 4, 6, 9, 10, 16, 17, 18, 19, 22, 23, 24; Odyssey 1, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 16, 17, 18, 19, 21, 22, 23; Aeneid 1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12. Any translation is permitted; printed passages are taken from Rieu (Penguin) and Kline (poetryintranslation.com) for Homer, and West (Penguin) and Kline for Virgil. Plan the paper by weight: the 30-mark essays are marked on Levels of Response grids (knowledge, analysis, evaluation and scholars), the 20-mark essays on knowledge and analysis, the 10-mark stimulus on direct response to the printed passage. On this component AO1 is worth 18% and AO2 22% of the A Level — analysis and evaluation dominate, so A* preparation means practising arguments, not recapping plots. Section C's stimulus questions require you to read the printed Homer and Virgil passages cold and to write with secondary views in support; its essays expect comparison across the epics. The epics were composed orally in dactylic hexameter long before writing was used for literature. Milman Parry and Albert Lord demonstrated that the poems are built from formulae (fixed phrases that fill metrical slots), type-scenes and recurring themes — the toolkit of bards who compose-in-performance, as Lord observed among Yugoslav guslars. Rhapsodes performed Homer at festivals such as the Panathenaia; tradition credits the Athenian tyrant Peisistratus with a 6th-century BC 'recension' that standardised the text. The great unresolved question — one poet or many? — divides Analysts (who detected seams and inconsistencies), Unitarians (who stressed artistic unity) and the oral-formulaic middle ground: consistent characterisation and design (Griffin, Edwards) coexist with formulaic diction, which most scholars now treat as compatible with a single monumental poet working within an oral tradition (Nicholson stresses how the poems preserve Bronze Age memory within an 8th-century BC composition). For analysis, always ask what the technique does : Epithets ('swift-footed Achilles', 'Odysseus of many wiles', 'rosy-fingered Dawn') serve metre first, but also fix characterisation — Hector is still 'glorious' even in defeat, reinforcing the code he dies by. Some formulae are deliberately context-stretching: dead warriors speak words 'fitting the moment'. Type-scenes (arming, sacrifice, supplication, arrival) create expectation and then variation: Achilles' arming in Iliad 19 dwells on the new armour made by Hephaestus; Priam's supplication in 24 inverts the heroic refusal of the embassy in 9. Similes create a second world: lions, storms and fires transfer emotion from battlefield to nature, while domestic similes (the weeping woman of Iliad 22; Odysseus crying like a widow captured at the fall of her city, Odyssey 8) reverse the comparison to expose what war costs. Extended similes can foreshadow and mark significance. Speeches stage debate — the embassy in Iliad 9 is a structured agon of offer and refusal; divine speeches (Athena's restraint of Achilles' sword, Iliad 1) drive dual motivation. Odyssey technique adds flashback : the poem opens in medias res, and Books 9–12 (the Apologoi) retrospectively recount the wanderings. The structure is itself thematic: nostos delayed by divine hostility, achieved by mētis. Ring composition frames both epics: the Iliad opens with Chryses' supplication (a priest dishonoured) and closes with Priam's (a father dishonoured) — the frame is the theme of timē and its limits; Achilles' two speeches in Books 1 and 24 mirror each other. Type-scenes build the structure: the supplication chain runs through the poem (Chryses 1; Lycaon 21; Priam 24), and the arming scenes (Achilles in 19 with divine armour) mark the turning points. The dactylic hexameter itself (six feet, long-short-short) is the engine of formulae — names and phrases chosen for their metrical shape — and the Peisistratean recension tradition is the transmission's evidence that the text was fixed for Panathenaic performance by the 6th century BC. Iliad. The heroic code demands timē — material honour and public standing. Achilles' mēnis begins when Agamemnon strips Briseis, a geras that embodies his timē (Iliad 1); his withdrawal is a protest against dishonour, and Athena's intervention makes his anger simultaneously divine and human (dual motivation). In the embassy of Book 9, Odysseus, Phoenix and Ajax offer restitution, and Achilles articulates the two fates: a long, obscure life at home, or a short life with imperishable kleos (kleos aphthiton). Crucially, he questions the code itself — 'one and the same lot for the man who hangs back and the man who battles hard' — the first crack in the heroic worldview. Patroclus' death converts withdrawal into revenge; the aristeia of Books 20–22 (including the killing of the suppliant Lycaon in 21) shows heroism at its most brutal, before Book 24 transfigures it: Priam's supplication, the kiss of the hands that killed his son, Zeus' two urns of good and evil, and the shared weeping of two men bound by mortality produce pity beyond the code. Weil reads the Iliad as 'the poem of force' — force turns people into things — while Griffin stresses the poem's pathos and humanity. Odyssey. The poem revalues heroism around nostos and mētis . Odysseus' polutropos intelligence — disguise, false tales, the stratagems of Ithaca — replaces brute valour; he refuses Calypso's offer of immortality ( Odyssey 5), choosing wife and home over kleos among the dead, an explicit reversal of Achilles' choice in Iliad 9. Heroism is also endurance (the tortures of Books 5–12; the restraint of the Beggar in his own hall) and justice: the slaughter of the suitors in Book 22 punishes their systemic abuse of xenia. Recognition is progressive — Telemachus (16), Eurycleia's scar (19), the bed test (23), Laertes in the orchard (24) — each testing identity against memory and knowledge. Penelope is the moral centre: her weaving trick (2) and her test of the bed (23) show mētis equal to her husband's, and her fidelity wins 'a fame that reaches the heavens' (24) — kleos for a woman won through virtue, not arms. A* judgement should ask whether the two ideals conflict: the Iliad's hero wins glory by dying young; the Odyssey's by surviving home — Homer seems to expose the cost of the first by dramatising the value of the second. The prescribed books supply the evidence: Patroclus' aristeia and death (16) drive Achilles back to war; the shield of Achilles (18) — Hephaestus' two cities at peace and at war — is the poem's image of the world the war is destroying; Hector's farewell (6) and the ransom (24) frame the family theme. The embassy (9) stages the code's three voices: Odysseus (offer and timē), Phoenix (the story of Meleager — the parable of the hero who waits too long) and Ajax (the appeal to friendship); Achilles' reply questions the code — and Book 24 answers him with pity rather than honour. The immortals are anthropomorphic — they wound (Aphrodite, Iliad 5; Ares), grieve, quarrel and even lose their horses — yet their scope of power exceeds mortals', and they keep the plot in motion. Their relationship with mortals is reciprocal: honour flows upward through sacrifice, prayer and libation; aid flows downward. Motivation is often dual: Athena rouses and restrains Achilles (Iliad 1, 22), but his rage is his own; Zeus weighs the fates of Sarpedon (16) and Hector (22) on the golden scales — fate (moira) binds even Zeus. In the Odyssey , Zeus opens with a theodicy: humans blame the gods for woes they bring on themselves through their own recklessness (1). Athena is Odysseus' advocate and mask-maker; Poseidon the avenging antagonist; Calypso and Circe test the pull of home against divine beds; the slaughtered cattle of Helios (12) prove that divine justice cannot be evaded. Xenia is the Odyssey's moral architecture, protected by Zeus Xenios. The code obliges the host to shelter, feed, bathe and gift a guest before even asking his name, and the guest to respond with gratitude and restraint: Positive: Telemachus received by Nestor (Odyssey 3 — not a prescribed book; cite Menelaus, Odyssey 4) and the Phaeacians (7–8), where the palace sequence stages ideal hospitality; Eumaeus the swineherd offers perfect xenia to a beggar he does not recognise (14–16); Odysseus repays it with life and reward. Negative: Polyphemus eats his guests and has no assemblies or laws (9) — civilisation defined by its absence; the suitors devour Odysseus' oikos and plot his son's murder (1–2, 13–22); Paris' breach of Menelaus' hospitality begins the Trojan War itself. Family is the oikos — the household as social, economic and emotional unit. Hector, Andromache and Astyanax (Iliad 6) give the war its human price: Hector prays his son may outshine him, while the baby fears his horsehair crest — the helmet of timē terrifies the family it protects. Priam and Achilles in Book 24 exchange grief across enemy lines through the shared facts of fatherhood and mortality. In the Odyssey , four generations of one oikos reunite — Penelope, Telemachus, Laertes — through tests of memory and knowledge. Women hold real authority within the oikos but no public role: Penelope's weaving trick and bed test win kleos; Helen is 'dog-faced', beauty and blame inseparable; Clytemnestra is the ever-present foil for female fidelity; Arete's judgement carries weight among the Phaeacians. Slaves are differentiated: the loyal swineherd Eumaeus and cowherd Philoetius are named, trusted and rewarded; the disloyal Melanthius and the twelve maids are executed (22); Briseis' lament for Patroclus (Iliad 19) gives a captive woman interiority. Homer humanises all of these groups while depicting a patriarchal world — the tension A* answers should exploit. The suitors' compound is the anti-oikos: they consume, they court Penelope by force, they plot Telemachus' murder — the poem defines the household by its violation. Helen's self-blame at Hector's funeral (24 — 'shameful me, that Zeus planted a doomed destiny') gives the war's other side a woman's voice; Arete's authority among the Phaeacians (7) shows a queen whose judgement the king obeys; Nausicaa (6 — not a prescribed book) stages guest-friendship from the girl's side. Slaves' loyalty is tested to the end: Eumaeus and Philoetius are rewarded (wives, property and a place in the restored oikos, 24); Melanthius and the twelve maids are executed (22) — the oikos restored by violence as well as reunion.

topics.subject: classical-civilisation
topics.searchText: classical-civilisation Classical Civilisation Greek Theatre City Dionysia The great Athenian festival of Dionysus Eleuthereus (late March/April) at which tragedies, satyr-plays and comedies competed; the dramatic context of the set plays. choregos A wealthy citizen who funded and trained a chorus as a public duty (liturgy/litourgia) — the financial backbone of Athenian drama. skene The stage building providing the scene's backdrop, doors for entrances/exits and (from the 5th century) a roof usable as a playing area. ekkylema The wheel platform rolled out through the skene doors to reveal interior scenes, usually tableaux of violence (e.g. Agave with Pentheus' head). mechane The crane by which gods appeared above the stage — hence deus ex machina; used for Euripides' divine endings (Bacchae). parabasis The choral interlude in old comedy where the chorus, speaking for the poet, addresses the audience directly and drops the fiction. agon A formal, structured debate in drama (e.g. Aeschylus vs Euripides in Frogs; Dionysus and Pentheus in Bacchae). hamartia Aristotle's term for the protagonist's tragic mistake or error — best read as a miscalculation rather than a moral flaw; central to interpretations of Oedipus. catharsis Aristotle's claim that tragedy purges the emotions of pity and fear in the audience; the standard ancient defence of tragedy's value. peripeteia The reversal of fortune in a tragedy; in Oedipus Tyrannus it coincides with the anagnorisis (recognition) at the shepherd's revelation. Drama at Athens was a civic and religious institution , not secular entertainment. The City Dionysia honoured Dionysus Eleuthereus with a procession (pompe), sacrifice and the display of tribute and orphans before competition began: three tragedians each presented a tetralogy of three tragedies plus a satyr-play, then five comedians a single play each. The archon selected the poets and allotted each a choregos , a rich citizen funding and training the chorus as a liturgy — theatre ran on private wealth spent for public honour. The audience, filling the Theatre of Dionysus (traditionally c.14,000–17,000), comprised male citizens alongside metics, foreigners and (debated) women; ten judges drawn by lot ranked the plays — democracy in the seating, adjudication by lottery. The theatre space evolved through the 5th and 4th centuries BC. The koilon (auditorium, initially wooden banks, later stone) curved round the orchestra (dancing floor for chorus and dithyramb); the skene gave doors and backdrop; the proskenion and its roof extended playing space. Machinery shaped staging: the ekkylema (wheel platform) revealed interior violence, and the mechane (crane) lowered gods — Euripides' Bacchae ends with Dionysus ex machina. The Theatre of Thorikos, a coastal deme theatre with an irregular, elongated auditorium, shows drama rooted below the polis level. The prescribed vases picture the performance itself: the Pronomos Vase shows a victorious team — actors, costumes, masks, aulos-player, playwright, Dionysus; the Choregos Vase (Comic Angels) a comic chorus with choregoi; the Basel Dancers krater a chorus in costume; the British Museum chous (B509, c.480 BC) two chorus-men dressed as birds; the Douris kylix the death of Pentheus; the Phiale Painter pelike tragic actors dressing. These are the evidence base for Section A commentary questions — know appearance, style, content and original location. Competition ran over several days: dithyrambic choruses of 50 men and boys (one for each tribe) opened the festival; tragedy filled the following days in tetralogies; comedy closed it. Before performance the poets held a proagon — presenting their casts without costume — and after it the judges awarded crowns and prizes, with the didaskalika records preserving results. The audience composition is debated: the war orphans paraded in armour, and women, metics and foreigners attended alongside citizens — but the precise proportion of women is genuinely open, since the evidence (Aristophanes' jokes about women in the audience; the vases' seating scenes) is comic or ambiguous. Theatre was also political space: announcements were made to the assembled city — the tribute display, and in Frogs' earlier version the debate on restoring citizen rights to the disenfranchised. Origins and development. Aristotle (Poetics) traced tragedy to improvisation by dithyramb leaders — a hymn to Dionysus — and defined it as the imitation (mimesis) of a serious, complete action in elevated language, effecting catharsis of pity and fear. From satyr-play roots it developed through the 5th century BC: Aeschylus introduced the second actor, reduced the chorus and built connected trilogies (his Agamemnon shows the form at its most ceremonial); Sophocles added the third actor, developed scene-painting and built plays on character in crisis; Euripides brought psychological realism, rhetoric and gods onstage by crane. All three expanded actors' roles against the chorus: tragedy's history is the progressive victory of dialogue over song. Aristotle's theories — peripeteia (reversal), hamartia (tragic mistake), catharsis (purgation) — are tools, not verdicts. Applied to Oedipus Tyrannus : the peripeteia (the shepherd's revelation) coincides exactly with the recognition, which Aristotle thought the plot's ideal shape; but hamartia is contested — is Oedipus rash (killing at the crossroads, cursing the murderer publicly), or simply ignorant of facts no enquiry could spare him? Note also the plot's religious frame: Apollo's oracles drive every character, and the plague in the prologue punishes the unavenged murderer's pollution (miasma). Bacchae : Dionysus' revenge on Thebes for denying his divinity. The prologue epiphany, the palace miracle (Dionysus' escape from bonds), Pentheus' agon with the disguised god, the messenger speeches from Cithaeron, the sparagmos (Agave with her son's head) and the deus ex machina ending structure a plot in which resistance to a god, not ignorance, destroys the house. The two plays give Section B essays their material: fate and free will, prophecy, the polis and its kings, tragic heroism, and the role of women (Jocasta; Agave) and foreigners (the Lydian god and his Asian maenads). Satyr-play is the fourth member of each tragic tetralogy: burlesque with a chorus dressed as satyrs under Silenus, on the same myths treated absurdly — the only complete survivor is Euripides' Cyclops. The development can be tracked through the tragedians' innovations: Aeschylus' second actor (Aristotle credits him), his connected trilogies (the Oresteia's legal and religious resolution), his choral writing; Sophocles' third actor, scene-painting and skene development, and plays built on a single character in crisis; Euripides' rhetorical debates, realistic characters, and prologues that state the myth in advance. Aristotle also transmits the tradition that tragedy's subject matter moved from the satyric and Dionysiac to the heroic — 'it was not long before serious subjects ousted the trivial' (Poetics) — which the exam expects you to weigh against the plays themselves: the Bacchae is nothing if not Dionysiac. Oedipus Tyrannus is the exam's set-text anchor. Plot devices to cite: the plague prologue; Teiresias' accusations; Jocasta's dismissal of prophecy (which triggers the fatal enquiry); the Corinthian messenger's 'relief' that becomes the catastrophe; the old Theban shepherd's refusal to speak, then confession — the recognition; the blinded Oedipus revealed by the ekkylemma. Dramatic irony governs the play: every speech about the murderer is spoken by the murderer to an audience that knows the myth. For religion: Apollo's oracle at Delphi (and to Laius before him) structures fate against free will — Oedipus acts to escape prophecy and so fulfils it; for the polis: the king is saviour (the Sphinx) then pollution; Thebes' health and the king's oikos are one. For tragic heroism: Oedipus the detective — his relentless pursuit of truth is both his greatness and his destruction; punishment falls on eyes that saw too late. Bacchae answers themes of divine justice and the polis: Pentheus, king of Thebes, denies Dionysus' divinity, imprisons him, mocks his rites, and is led — dressed as a maenad — to death on Cithaeron by the god himself; his mother Agave carries back his head. Cite: the prologue (Dionysus states the plot in advance — fate, not suspense); the bonds-miracle of the palace scene; the herdsman's two messenger speeches (the miracle on the mountain, then the sparagmos); the chorus' piety against Pentheus' rationalism; the god's cruelty in the ex machina ending (exile for the survivors — divinity beyond human ethics). The prescribed Douris kylix shows Pentheus' death in red-figure c.480 BC — before either surviving play — proving myth preceded drama and giving AO3-style comparison of visual and literary treatment; the Capodarso krater fragment pictures Jocasta and Oedipus. For both plays, weigh ancient vs modern reception : Aristotle admired Oedipus as the tragic plot; modern readers stress its detective structure and moral ambiguity, or read Bacchae as psychodrama of repression and ecstasy. A* answers hold ancient theory and modern interpretation together. For Oedipus Tyrannus, also cite: the Sphinx backstory — Oedipus' salvation of Thebes is the reason he is king, so his rise and fall are one arc; the self-blinding with Jocasta's brooches, revealed by the ekkylemma; Creon's regency and the exile question; the chorus' closing wisdom — 'count no man happy until he has died free of pain'. For Bacchae, cite: the Teiresias-and-Cadmus scene (old men dressing as worshippers — religion as choice against ridicule); the two herdsman speeches (the mountain miracle, then the sparagmos report); Agave's recognition scene, where the god corrects her illusion with cruelty; and the chorus' hymns — piety in lyric against the palace's rationalism. Nature of old comedy. Aristophanes' own parabases claim comedy began in komos revelry and phallic song; its 5th-century BC development produced a form whose tools are personal invective, obscenity, parody and topical satire, aimed at politicians (Cleon), intellectuals (Socrates in Clouds), poets and the audience itself. Structure: prologue (fantastic premise), parodos, agon (formal debate), parabasis (chorus speaks for the poet), episodes, exodos; plot devices include parody of tragedy, choral interludes and breaking the illusion. Frogs (405 BC) is the set text. Premise: Dionysus, starved of good tragedy since Euripides' death, descends to Hades with slave Xanthias (whose loaded-jokes opening parodies tragedy's solemnity) to bring back a poet — Heracles' street-map of the underworld, the frog-chorus, the Mysteries procession, then the contest: Aeschylus vs Euripides weighed in the scales — style, prologues, lyrics, and finally political utility: which poet can save the city? Aeschylus wins; Pluto sends him home with instructions to advise Athens. Cite for comedy's themes: the satire of tragedy (parody of Euripides' prologues; the weighing of verses); religion (the katabasis, the Eleusinian-flavoured mystic chorus, death and the afterlife as comic geography); the polis (the play was performed in a city losing the Peloponnesian War — its civic advice and reported effect were famous, and later tradition credited it with Athens' decision to recall the exiles). Humour types to name: personal abuse, knockabout slave comedy (Xanthias), literary parody, obscenity, and topical political jokes whose modern loss you should note as an interpretive limit. Styles compared : Aeschylus' grandeur vs Euripides' wit inside the play mirrors the tragedians' real contrast; Aristophanes' Frogs stages the debate the whole component is about — what drama is for. A* answers use the play as evidence for how a 5th-century audience understood tragedy, and weigh it against Aristotle's later theory. For Frogs, also cite: the disguise contest (Dionysus and Xanthias both dressed as Heracles, the lion skin swapped back and forth — a running gag that parodies epic heroism); the underworld geography (Charon's ferry, Aeacus' gatekeeping, the frog-chorus on the lake); the Mysteries chorus whose initiation language frames the descent; the judging scenes — Euripides' prologues tripped up by Aeschylus' oil-flask interruptions, the scales in which verses are physically weighed, and the final test of political utility: Aeschylus wins because his poetry makes men fighting-fit ('Seven Against Thebes filled them with courage') and returns to advise the city. The play's civic advice was topical in a city losing the war, and the reported effect was famous enough for later tradition to credit it with Athens' recall of the exiles.

topics.searchText: classical-civilisation Classical Civilisation Imperial Image divi filius 'Son of the Divine (Julius Caesar)' — Octavian's core claim from 42 BC, when the Senate deified Caesar; legitimacy and god-close charisma inherited from his adoptive father. princeps 'Leading citizen' — the republican-sounding title behind the principate: first man of the state, not (nominally) king or dictator. imperator The acclamation of a victorious commander by his troops; Augustus' use (and monopolisation) of it fused military glory with one-man rule. triumph The crowning Roman military-religious ceremony — procession of spoils, captives and the commander in triumphal dress to Jupiter's temple; Augustus celebrated a triple triumph in 29 BC. Res Gestae Divi Augusti Augustus' first-person record of his deeds, inscribed at his Mausoleum and copied across the empire (the Ankara Monument survives); the set text for H408/22. clipeus virtutis The golden shield (27 BC) the Senate hung in the Curia honouring Augustus' virtus, clementia, iustitia and pietas — the virtues as an official image. Ara Pacis Augustae The Altar of Augustan Peace (13–9 BC): procession friezes of the imperial family, myth panels (Aeneas, Roma? — Romulus/Remus, Tellus) and pax-plenty iconography. genius The guardian spirit of a man (or the state/household); after 12 BC? (the Lares reform) Augustus' genius was worshipped alongside the Lares at the crossroads shrines. pater patriae 'Father of the fatherland' — conferred on Augustus by Senate and people in 2 BC, the culminating title of his self-presentation. Carmen Saeculare Horace's hymn commissioned for the Secular Games (17 BC), sung by choirs of boys and girls — the state commissioning poetry for Augustus' new age. Caesar's assassination in 44 BC left an 18-year-old heir: Gaius Octavius, Caesar's adoptive son. The association was essential and dangerous . Benefits: the dead Caesar's popularity with the plebs and the army; the settlement of veterans; the glamour of descent from Venus and Aeneas (the Julian clan's illustrious men and gods); and legitimacy — the will made him heir, the deification (Temple of Divus Iulius, 42 BC) made him divi filius . Dangers: Caesar had been murdered for tyranny; 'king' (rex) was poison in a fundamentally anti-monarchical society. Octavian managed both: the comet at the funeral games (Sidus Iulium) backed the apotheosis — the prescribed denarius with the eight-rayed comet beside Augustus' head; while the aureus pairing his bare head with Caesar's laureate one claims inheritance. The triumvirate (43 BC) was openly unconstitutional — hence the justification of civil war in the Res Gestae: those who murdered his father were punished, and those who waged war on the state ('a faction') were conquered in two battles (Philippi). Antony was never named: the war of 32–31 BC was presented as Rome against a woman and her oriental court — Horace's Odes 1.37 makes Cleopatra a fatale monstrum whose death is no ordinary woman's; Epodes 9 celebrates Actium. The settlement of 27 BC renamed him Augustus, 'the revered one', returning (nominally) the res publica to Senate and people — Res Gestae 34 is the set-text core: 'after I had extinguished civil wars... I transferred the state from my own power to the control of the senate and people of Rome'. The triumvirate itself was openly unconstitutional — a three-man commission of proscription modelled on Sulla's, whose death lists killed Cicero among thousands; the Res Gestae never mentions it. Sextus Pompey's naval blockade starved Italy until Agrippa won Naulochus (36 BC), after which Octavian broke with Lepidus and had only Antony left. The coins are the mass media of the transition: the aureus pairing bare-headed Octavian with the laureate Caesar claims inheritance at the moment of apotheosis; the aureus of Octavian seated on a bench holding a scroll projects clementia and legality; the denarius with Pax holding the olive branch and cornucopia sells peace while civil war still ran. Note how the image meets each audience: the plebs read grain and games, the army read land and pay, the elite read titles, offices and restoration — the same image, different dialects. The image: a capable commander whose wars were glorious, defensive and beneficial. The triple triumph of 29 BC (Dalmatia, Actium, Egypt) staged victory in the Republic's supreme ceremony — its religious pompe, its spoils, its captives; the Res Gestae counts the triumphs, the salutations as imperator, the settlements of veterans and the wars 'won by land and sea'. Reality : Agrippa won Naulochus (36 BC) and commanded at Actium; the Alpine and Balkan campaigns were grinding; the Parthian recovery of the standards (20 BC) was a negotiated settlement, not a war — presented as a triumph (the Prima Porta breastplate's central scene shows a Parthian returning a standard beneath the sky-god, with Apollo and Artemis of Delos below). The prescribed coins package the claims: Pax with olive branch and cornucopia (peace and plenty); sacrificial implements above a tripod and patera (piety as military); the Gaius and Lucius aureus (the heirs as princes of the youth). Justification of civil wars runs through the sources: Philippi avenged the father; the Perusine War is omitted; Sextus Pompey is dismissed as 'a pirate' (Res Gestae 25); Antony's campaign is a war against Cleopatra, not citizens. The Kalabsha Gate relief shows Octavian making offering to Egyptian deities — conqueror as pharaoh, domination dressed as accommodation. For Section B: weigh image against reality — the salutations, triumphs and standard-recovery as image; Agrippa's commands and the body-count as reality; and the Res Gestae's silences as evidence of deliberate shaping. The triumph's regalia made its message visible: the commander in toga picta and laurel crown on the quadriga, spoils and placards displaying the conquests, captives walking before the chariot, the procession climbing to Jupiter Capitolinus — military glory ending in religion. Augustus' triple triumph spread over three days (Dalmatia, Actium, Egypt), and the Res Gestae counts the salutations as imperator (21 in all), the colonies settled and the sums distributed — each a claim to have converted war into public benefit. The Parthian settlement was dressed as victory twice: the standards' return (20 BC) was celebrated with an arch in the Forum, and the Prima Porta breastplate makes the diplomacy the statue's central image — a negotiated return staged as a conquest won under the sky-god's favour. Religious leader. Augustus rebuilt 82 temples (Res Gestae 20), restored lapsed priesthoods, became pontifex maximus (12 BC) and reformed the crossroads cult: the Lares were paired as Lares Praestites and worshipped with the genius Augusti — the state worshipping the ruler's guardian spirit, divinity by association without divinity by claim. His closeness to Apollo was architectural and personal: the Temple of Apollo Palatinus joined his modest house on the Palatine (Suetonius describes the house's plainness as image). The Ara Pacis Augustae (13–9 BC) is the set-text monument: the altar of Augustan peace, its friezes process the imperial family with senators and priests (the real religious elite), its panels flank myth with allegory — Aeneas' sacrifice (pietas), the wolf-and-twins panel and Tellus with babies and plenty (peace's fruits). The Secular Games (17 BC) staged a new age: Horace's Carmen Saeculare, commissioned by the state and sung by choirs of boys and girls, calls on Apollo and Diana for the new saeculum. Culture hero. The myth of Saturn's Golden Age — Augustus as a new Saturn, peace and plenty returning (Horace Odes 4.15; the iconography of Pax, Ceres? — the Ara Pacis' Tellus) — reframed the strongman as restorer. Pater Patriae and the family. The title (2 BC) completes the Res Gestae's arc — 'father of the fatherland', quoted with the Senate's and people's words (ch. 35). The clipeus virtutis (27 BC) fixed the four virtues: virtus, clementia, iustitia, pietas — clementia after civil war is a pointed image. The moral legislation (lex Iulia de maritandis ordinibus and de adulteriis, 18 BC) incentivised marriage and childbearing, criminalised adultery — and was enforced against his own daughter Julia (Suetonius, Life of Augustus, the extracts on his family discipline). The imperial family as role models : the Gaius and Lucius aureus presents the heirs veiled with shields and priestly symbols; the Head of Livia carries the pudicitia iconography of the Roman matron; Augustus himself modelled modest living — the Prima Porta statue's barefoot pose and Cupid (divine descent via Venus) beside a general's breastplate. The Secular Games' machinery made the new age official: heralds summoned everyone to a spectacle no one alive had seen; 27 boys and 27 girls of citizen parents sang the Carmen Saeculare by day and by night; sacrifices to Apollo and Diana (and to Juno, the Fates and Ilithyia) closed each sequence. The genius-worship had its own mechanics: the crossroads shrines (compita) rebuilt, with images of the two Lares and the genius Augusti, served by the neighbourhood magistri — the state's religion reaching every street. The moral legislation's penalties were practical as well as symbolic: adultery became a public crime tried by standing courts, with fathers (and in some cases husbands) bound to prosecute, and the childbearing incentives (ius trium liberorum) gave legal privileges to parents of three. The building programme was image made physical. Suetonius' famous claim — he 'found Rome brick and left it marble' (ch. 28–29) — sums the programme: the Forum of Augustus (built from spoils, its Temple of Mars Ultor avenging both Philippi and the standards, its porticoes lined with statues of summi viri and the Julian family — history as image), the Mausoleum (28 BC, a dynastic tomb on the Campus Martius — the Res Gestae's intended home), the Theatre of Marcellus, aqueducts and the Forum's triumphal arches. The Res Gestae closes with the empire's edges: embassies from India, and the closure of the gates of Janus three times (ch. 13) — peace as military achievement. Evaluating the Res Gestae is the Section B staple. For propaganda: it is first-person, selective and silent where damaging (Antony unnamed; the Perusine War absent; civil wars as 'a faction'); it presents negotiated settlements as victories; its claim to have restored the res publica (ch. 34) coexists with permanent tribunician power and command of army and provinces. For history: its facts check out — the building lists, the dates, the populations enrolled — Mommsen called it 'the queen of inscriptions'; Zanker reads the visual programme (coins, statues, buildings) as a coherent imperial ideology; Wallace-Hadrill stresses its address to every social class; Galinsky treats it as self-conscious self-presentation rather than lying. Its audiences differed: the bronze copies across the empire, bilingual in Greek and Latin, addressed the Greek east as well as Rome; the plebs read grain, games and buildings; the elite read titles and virtue. Later representations test long-term success. The Sebasteion at Aphrodisias (Claudian era) built three-storey porticoes of reliefs: divinities, emperors, and the ethne — conquered peoples of land and sea — an imperial cult complex that takes Augustus' image for granted a generation after his death. Suetonius' Life of Augustus (2nd century AD) balances the image: clementia, modesty, generosity against adultery, cruelty and luxury in the private extracts — evidence that the self-presentation fixed the terms of debate even when contradicted. A* judgement: the image outlasted its contradictions — that is its success; the final topic is assessing how far it lasted beyond his lifetime, and Suetonius is the proof that it did. The Forum of Augustus deserves the detail: its porticoes displayed statues of the summi viri — great Romans of the Republic — each with an elogium (career summary), the Julian family at the centre with Aeneas and Romulus flanking; history as a curated image with Augustus' line as its spine. The Mausoleum was begun in 28 BC — the dynastic tomb intended to house the Res Gestae, and the proof that the image was planned for posterity. The Sebasteion at Aphrodisias, built a generation later under Claudius, is the best test of long-term success: three storeys of reliefs — divinities above, emperors below, with panels of the conquered ethne (peoples of land and sea, Britannia among them) — an imperial cult complex in a Greek city that takes Augustus' entire image for granted. Suetonius' extracts make the terms of debate explicit: clementia and modesty in the public chapters against adultery, cruelty and luxury in the private ones — the image survived its contradictions.

topics.name: Greek Religion
topics.subject: classical-civilisation
topics.searchText: classical-civilisation Classical Civilisation Greek Religion reciprocity (do ut des) 'I give so that you give' — the contractual logic of Greek cult: honour (sacrifice, libation, votives) flows upward; aid, protection and fertility flow downward. anthropomorphism The gods' human-like form and psychology — body, family, jealousy, deceit — as established for the Greeks by Homer and Hesiod (cf. Herodotus 2.53). hero cult Worship of an exceptional dead mortal at or near their tomb, with chthonic-style offerings; heroes protected communities and were prayed to for aid (e.g. Theseus, Brasidas at Amphipolis). mystery cult A cult of initiation (e.g. the Eleusinian Mysteries) promising benefits through secret rites known only to initiates; participation was a matter of personal choice. incubation Ritual sleep in a god's sanctuary — especially that of Asclepius at Epidaurus — during which the god healed the sleeper or prescribed a cure in a dream. asebeia Impiety — a prosecutable offence at Athens (e.g. Socrates, 399 BC); religious authority lay with the polis, its laws and its customs rather than a scripture or church. hecatomb A sacrifice of (originally) a hundred cattle; the great public burnt offerings of state festivals, e.g. on the ash altar of Zeus at Olympia. libation The pouring of wine, water or oil to the gods — at symposia, oaths and sacrifices, in both state and private contexts; the regular renewing of reciprocity. votive offering A dedication (statue, relief, armour, anatomical model) made to a god in thanks or hope — from private anatomical votives at the Asclepieion to state treasures at Delphi and Olympia. Panathenaia Athena's state festival: annual (Lesser) and four-yearly Greater (with games from 566 BC), culminating in the procession to the Acropolis and the hecatomb; the peplos for Athena was woven and presented. The Olympians are anthropomorphic : they have bodies, genealogies (Hesiod's Theogony), moods, jealousies and limitations — but not omnipotence or omniscience. Their scope of power is bounded: Zeus weighs fates on his scales (Iliad 16, 22) rather than simply commanding outcomes; gods cannot reverse what is fated. The relationship with mortals is reciprocal : mortals give honour — sacrifice, libation, votives, festivals — and gods give protection, fertility, victory and healing. Greek cult is contractual (do ut des), not creedal: there is no revealed truth to believe, only powers to honour correctly. Homer and Hesiod were foundational: Herodotus (2.53) credits them with teaching the Greeks the gods' genealogies, epithets and forms barely four centuries before his own writing — the literary sources of the gods' characters. Common epithets map the gods' different roles and contexts: Zeus Agoraios (of the agora), Zeus Phratrios (of the brotherhoods), Zeus Philios (of friendship), Zeus Herkeios (of the courtyard) — one god with many functions; the exam asks how far these were thought of as separate, distinct entities (they were not: one Zeus, many cult titles — but each with its own cult, icon and priest). Hero cults are the other half of Greek worship: exceptional dead mortals — founders, leaders, the glorious dead — received offerings at their tombs and were prayed to for aid, in a chthonic (underworld) register contrasting with Olympian sacrifice. Examples: Theseus' bones translated to Athens by Cimon (c.470s BC); Brasidas buried and honoured as founder-hero at Amphipolis. Worship ranged across Panhellenic (Zeus at Olympia, Apollo at Delphi), localised (Athena Polias at Athens, city-specific cults) and personal (household gods, private vows) — the spectrum the whole component measures. The Olympian roster is fixed by tradition: Zeus, Hera, Poseidon, Demeter, Athena, Apollo, Artemis, Ares, Aphrodite, Hephaestus, Hermes and (in the Athenian list) Hestia or Dionysus — twelve names worshipped Panhellenically, but each with local cults, iconographies and festivals. Hesiod's Theogony supplies the genealogy that orders them; his Works and Days supplies their justice — Zeus who watches all and punishes wrongdoing. Hero cult fills the space between gods and the dead: exceptional mortals received tombs, offerings and prayers for aid — Herakles was worshipped as both hero and god across Greece; city founders (Theseus at Athens) and war dead (Brasidas at Amphipolis) drew cult; and the chthonic register (offerings poured into the earth, at dusk, to the dead below) contrasts with Olympian sacrifice (burnt on the altar, by day, to the gods above). Mystery cults inverted the communal norm: participation was a matter of personal choice and initiation, open across the usual barriers. The Eleusinian Mysteries of Demeter and Persephone (whose Homeric Hymn explains the myth) promised initiates better prospects — for the harvest and for death; the ritual was secret, with two grades (mystes, then epoptes at a later Great Eleusinia). The prescribed red-figure plaque of the cult of Eleusis (c.400–300 BC) shows Demeter and Persephone with initiates — the evidence base. Mystery cults offered what the polis could not: individual religious experience, hope and a personal relationship with the divine. The healing cult of Asclepius blurs the god/hero boundary: a mortal healer deified, worshipped as both god and hero, with incubation (ritual sleep) and miracle cures recorded in the iamata inscriptions at Epidaurus.
